title: Benefits of Sensing Color
one_liner: Sensing color allows for checking fruit ripeness, identifying illness through skin color changes, and finding objects in cluttered environments.
content: There are many benefits to sensing color. Color differences let us check whether fruit is ripe, tell whether a child is sick by looking at small changes in the color of the skin, and find objects in clutter.
motivation_md: Color sensing is a vital biological and computational tool that provides critical information about the state and identity of objects in the environment.
recap_md: [ "Color helps determine the ripeness of food.", "Small color changes in skin can indicate health status.", "Color facilitates object detection and segmentation in complex scenes." ]

title: Newton's Prism Experiment
one_liner: Isaac Newton used prisms to demonstrate that white light is composed of elemental colors that cannot be further subdivided.
content: Isaac Newton revealed several intrinsic properties of light in experiments summarized by his drawing. A pinhole of sunlight enters through a window shade, and a lens focuses the light onto a prism. The prism then divides the white light into many different colors. These colors are elemental: if one of the component colors is passed through a second prism, it doesn't split into further components.
motivation_md: Newton's experiments were fundamental in proving that white light is not a single entity but a mixture of distinct spectral components.
recap_md: [ "A prism divides white light into a spectrum of different colors.", "Spectral colors are elemental and do not split further when passed through additional prisms.", "The experiment demonstrates that color is an intrinsic property of light components." ]

title: Spectrum
one_liner: The spectrum is the collection of different colors into which white light can be decomposed.
content: Newton understood that white light could be decomposed into different colors and invented the term spectrum.
motivation_md: The term provides a formal name for the range of colors produced when light is separated into its constituent wavelengths.
recap_md: [ "The spectrum represents the decomposition of white light.", "The term was coined by Isaac Newton." ]

title: Diffraction
one_liner: Diffraction is the process where constructive interference of scattered light separates light into different wavelengths based on their angle.
content: One way to separate light into components is through diffraction, where constructive interference of scattered light occurs in different directions for different wavelengths of light. A simple spectrograph, an apparatus to reveal the spectrum of light, can be based on diffraction from a compact disk (CD). Light passes through a slit and strikes the CD tracks. Constructive interference from the light waves striking the tracks will occur at a different angle for each wavelength of the light, yielding a separation of the different wavelengths of light according to their angle of diffraction. The spectrograph gives an immediate visual representation of the spectral components of colors in the world.
motivation_md: Diffraction provides a physical mechanism to analyze the spectral composition of light from everyday objects.
recap_md: [ "Diffraction uses constructive interference to separate light by wavelength.", "The angle of diffraction depends on the wavelength of the light.", "Spectrographs use diffraction to visualize the spectral components of light." ]

title: Power Spectrum
one_liner: The power spectrum is the light intensity measured at each wavelength, which largely determines the color appearance of light.
content:
(see figure: The light spectra from some everyday objects, analyzed by the spectrograph of @fig-colorWavelengths. (a) A leaf, with some yellowish highlights, shows primarily green, with a little red (red and...)

The light intensity at each wavelength is called the power spectrum of the light. The color appearance of light is determined by many factors, including the image context in which the light is viewed; but a very important factor in determining color appearance is the power spectrum. In this initial discussion of color, we will assume that the power spectrum of light determines its appearance, although you should remember that this is true only within a fixed visual context.

Why does the sky look blue? And why does it look orange during a sunset? 
[FIGURE:58872bcf02e66cbd | A photograph of a bright sun setting over a dark ocean horizon, casting a vibrant orange and red glow across the sky. A small sailboat is visible in the distance on the right side of the horizon.]

@fig-examples1 shows a spectrograph visualization of some light power spectra (the right image of each row) along with the image that the spectrograph was pointed toward (left images). @fig-sources shows the spectrum of a blue sky, plotted as intensity as a function of wavelength.

[FIGURE:f2b579d46ac7c835]

[FIGURE:1bad511a36366936 | A vertical photograph of a green tree against a vast, clear blue sky. In the background, rolling green mountains are visible under a few scattered white clouds, illustrating the natural blue color of...]

Power spectrum of blue skylight @blueskyWiki.
motivation_md: Quantifying light intensity across wavelengths is essential for understanding why we perceive specific colors, such as the blue of the sky or the orange of a sunset.
recap_md: [ "The power spectrum measures light intensity as a function of wavelength.", "It is a primary factor in determining the perceived color of light.", "Visual context also influences color appearance alongside the power spectrum." ]

title: Reflectance Spectrum
one_liner: The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ describes how a surface scales the incident light's power spectrum at each wavelength during diffuse reflection.
content:
When light reflects off a surface, the power spectrum alters in ways that depend on the surface's characteristics and geometry. These changes in light allow us to perceive objects and surfaces by observing their influence on the reflected light. The interaction between light and a surface can be quite complex. Reflections can be specular or diffuse, and the reflected power spectrum may depend on the relative orientations of the incident light, surface, and the observed reflected ray. In its full generality, the reflection of light from a surface is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF). For this discussion, we will focus on diffuse surface reflections, where the power spectrum of the reflected light, $r(\lambda)$, is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the power spectrum of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface:
$$r(\lambda) = k \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) s(\lambda),$$
where the proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry. This diffuse reflection model characterizes most matte reflections. Such wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter. The incident power spectrum is then multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the attenuating filter. Some reflectance spectra of real-world surfaces are plotted in @fig-sourcerefl. The flower *Hepatica Nobilis* (solid line) is blue, while *Pyrostegia venusta* (dotted line) is orange.

(see figure: Reflectance spectra from two flowers @Arnold2010. The blue *Hepatica nobilis* flower @nobilis and the orange flower, *Pyrostegia venusta* @venusta}.)
motivation_md: To understand why objects have color, we must model how surfaces selectively reflect different wavelengths of the light that hits them.
recap_md: [ "The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ represents a surface's wavelength-specific scaling factor.", "Reflected light $r(\lambda)$ is the product of incident light and the reflectance spectrum.", "This model effectively describes matte or diffuse reflections." ]

title: Diffuse Reflection Model
one_liner: The diffuse reflection model calculates reflected light as a wavelength-by-wavelength product of incident light and the surface's reflectance spectrum.
content:
For diffuse surface reflections, the power spectrum of the reflected light, $r(\lambda)$, is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the power spectrum of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface:
$$r(\lambda) = k \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) s(\lambda),$$
where the proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry. This diffuse reflection model characterizes most matte reflections. Such wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter. The incident power spectrum is then multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the attenuating filter.
motivation_md: This model simplifies complex light-surface interactions into a manageable mathematical form suitable for describing matte surfaces.
recap_md: [ "Reflected light is proportional to the product of incident light and surface reflectance.", "The constant $k$ accounts for the specific geometry of the reflection.", "This model is applicable to most matte surfaces and attenuating filters." ]

title: Transmittance Spectrum
one_liner: A transmittance spectrum describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of light as it passes through an attenuating filter.
content: Wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter. The incident power spectrum is multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the attenuating filter. This follows the same mathematical logic as the diffuse reflection model, where the output light is the product of the input light and the spectral properties of the medium.
motivation_md: Understanding transmittance is necessary for modeling how filters, lenses, and other semi-transparent materials alter the color of light passing through them.
recap_md: [ "The transmittance spectrum scales the incident power spectrum at each wavelength.", "It models the effect of attenuating filters on light.", "It uses the same multiplicative logic as the diffuse reflection model." ]

title: Representation Level
one_liner: The representation level defines the system used to make explicit certain types of information present in a signal for both input and output.
content: The representation level defines which representation will be used for the input and output. A representation is a system of making explicit certain types of information present on a signal. For instance, an image could be represented by the sequence of values that encode the color of each pixel, or it could be represented using a Fourier decomposition. The choice of representation will make explicit certain types of information while hiding other information, which will become harder to access. The algorithm used to implement the mapping between input and output is strongly dependent on the representation used. Examples such as using position encoding to represent location illustrate the dramatic effect that the choice of representation and algorithm can have in the final system performance.
motivation_md: The choice of representation determines what information is easily accessible to an algorithm. Selecting the right representation is critical because it dictates the complexity and performance of the mapping between input and output.
recap_md: - A representation is a system that makes specific information in a signal explicit while hiding other details.

title: Hardware Level
one_liner: The hardware level describes the physical implementation of the representation and algorithm in a device.
content: The hardware level is where the representation and algorithm are implemented in a physical device. Marr noted that when trying to explain visual phenomena, one needs to find the right level to use to describe it. For instance, the trichromatic color theory of human perception is explained by the hardware level (i.e., by the three color receptors in our retina). In contrast, the bistable nature of the Necker cube is likely related to the 3D representation, and illusions shown in @fig-measuringScene are likely due to the representation and algorithm used, being rather independent of the particular hardware implementation.
motivation_md: Understanding the physical substrate of a system helps distinguish between phenomena caused by the underlying machinery (like retinal receptors) versus those caused by the abstract processing logic.
recap_md: - The hardware level refers to the physical device or biological structure that executes an algorithm.

title: Independence of Marr's Levels
one_liner: Marr's three levels of understanding—computational, representational, and hardware—can be studied relatively independently.
content: Marr postulated that the three levels of understanding (computational, representation, and hardware) can be studied relatively independently, despite their loose coupling. Each problem needs description at the appropriate level. This principle is often ignored in modern computer vision, where tasks are sometimes tightly connected to an architecture, such as a neural net, without a clear understanding of what is being computed or what the representations mean.
motivation_md: Decoupling the 'what' (computation) from the 'how' (algorithm/representation) and the 'where' (hardware) allows researchers to solve vision problems systematically without being distracted by implementation details.
recap_md: - Computational, representational, and hardware levels are loosely coupled and can be analyzed separately.

title: Primal Sketch
one_liner: The primal sketch represents changes in an image, such as edges and junctions, and their spatial organization.
content: The primal sketch represents changes in the image, including edges, junctions, and zero-crossings, as well as their spatial organization.
motivation_md: The primal sketch serves as the first stage of visual processing, extracting basic geometric features from raw pixel intensities to simplify subsequent analysis.
recap_md: - Captures image changes like edges, junctions, and zero-crossings.

title: 2.5D Sketch
one_liner: The 2.5D sketch estimates the distance to visible surfaces at each pixel and includes depth discontinuities and surface orientations.
content: The 2.5D sketch contains an estimation of the distance between the observer and the visible surfaces in the world at each pixel, also called a depth map. It also contains information about depth discontinuities and surface orientations.
motivation_md: It bridges the gap between 2D image features and 3D object recognition by providing a viewer-centered map of the scene's geometry.
recap_md: - Estimates distance (depth) from the observer at each pixel.

title: Depth Map
one_liner: A depth map is an estimation of the distance between the observer and visible surfaces at each pixel.
content: A depth map, also referred to as a 2.5D sketch, contains an estimation of the distance between the observer and the visible surfaces in the world at each pixel. It also contains information about depth discontinuities and surface orientations.
motivation_md: Depth maps provide a way to represent the 3D structure of a scene from a specific viewpoint, which is essential for navigation and object interaction.
recap_md: - Represents the distance to surfaces for every pixel in an image.

title: 3D Model Representation
one_liner: The 3D model representation describes objects as 3D shapes along with their spatial organization.
content: In the 3D model representation, objects are represented as 3D shapes together with their spatial organization.
motivation_md: This level of representation allows for viewpoint-independent object recognition and reasoning about the physical world in three dimensions.
recap_md: - Represents objects as 3D shapes in a spatially organized manner.

title: Gauge-Figures
one_liner: Gauge-figures are arrows used in a 2.5D sketch to represent the orientation of surfaces.
content: In a 2.5D sketch, gauge-figures are arrows that represent surface orientation. In such a sketch, dashed lines represent surface orientation discontinuities, while black lines represent occlusion boundaries. Pixel intensities represent the distance between the observer and the visible surfaces, where intensity typically increases with depth (represented by gray levels).
motivation_md: Gauge-figures provide a visual tool for researchers to represent and verify the local surface geometry estimated by a vision system.
recap_md: - Arrows that indicate the orientation of a surface in a 2.5D sketch.

title: Object Boundaries

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Object boundaries indicate pixels that delineate the boundaries of any object, typically corresponding to changes in surface color, texture, and orientation.
content: Object boundaries indicate pixels that delineate the boundaries of any object. Boundaries between objects generally correspond to changes in surface color, texture, and orientation.
motivation_md: Identifying object boundaries is fundamental for segmenting an image into distinct entities based on visual cues like color and texture.
recap_md:
- Object boundaries delineate the edges of objects in an image.
- They are often marked by changes in surface color, texture, or orientation.

title: Surface Orientation Changes

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Changes in surface orientation produce image intensity variations because intensity is a function of the angle between the surface and incident light.
content: Changes in surface orientation indicate locations where there are strong image variations due to changes in the surface orientations. A change in surface orientation produces changes in the image intensity because intensity is a function of the angle between the surface and the incident light.
motivation_md: Understanding how surface geometry affects light reflection allows computer vision systems to infer 3D shapes from 2D intensity variations.
recap_md:
- Surface orientation changes cause variations in image intensity.
- Intensity depends on the angle between the surface and the incident light source.

title: Shadow Edges

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Shadow edges represent transitions between dark and light areas, which can be soft and slow.
content: Shadow edges represent the transition between dark and light areas. In many contexts, shadows are soft, creating slow transitions between dark and light, which can make them difficult to detect.
motivation_md: Distinguishing shadow edges from physical object boundaries is crucial for accurate object recognition and scene understanding.
recap_md:
- Shadow edges mark the transition between illuminated and shaded regions.
- These transitions are often soft and gradual rather than sharp.

title: Contact Edges

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: A contact edge is a boundary between two objects in physical contact where no depth discontinuity exists.
content: Contact edges are boundaries between two objects that are in physical contact. Because the objects are touching, there is no depth discontinuity at these edges.
motivation_md: Identifying contact edges helps in understanding the spatial relationships and physical interactions between objects in a scene.
recap_md:
- Contact edges occur where two objects physically touch.
- Unlike occlusion boundaries, contact edges do not have a depth discontinuity.

title: Occlusion Boundaries

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Occlusion boundaries occur when one object is partially in front of another, generally producing depth discontinuities.
content: Occlusion boundaries happen when an object is partially in front of another. These boundaries generally produce depth discontinuities. In specific simplified models, objects may be positioned so they do not occlude each other but still occlude the background.
motivation_md: Occlusion boundaries are key indicators of depth and the relative ordering of objects within a 3D environment.
recap_md:
- Occlusion boundaries occur when one object blocks the view of another.
- They are typically characterized by a sharp discontinuity in depth.

title: Image Gradient

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: The image gradient measures the degree and direction of intensity variation within an image.
content:
If we think of the image $\ell (x,y)$ as a function of two continuous variables, we can measure the degree of variation using the gradient: $$\nabla \ell = \left( \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \right)$$ The direction of the gradient indicates the direction in which the variation of intensities is larger. If we are on top of an edge, the direction of larger variation will be in the direction perpendicular to the edge.

Gradient of an image at one location.
[FIGURE:7b4ca0a1aca130ce | A red vector labeled $\nabla \ell$ is drawn over a blurred grayscale background that transitions from dark to light. The vector points in the direction of the steepest increase in brightness, making...]
motivation_md: The gradient provides a mathematical way to locate edges by identifying where image intensity changes most rapidly.
recap_md:
- The gradient $\nabla \ell$ consists of partial derivatives in the $x$ and $y$ directions.
- The gradient vector points in the direction of maximum intensity increase, perpendicular to the edge.

title: Discrete Partial Derivatives

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Discrete partial derivatives approximate the variation of image intensity at specific pixel locations.
content:
Because an image is not a continuous function and we only know the values of $\ell (x,y)$ at discrete pixel locations, we approximate the partial derivatives by: 
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} &\simeq \ell(x,y) - \ell(x-1,y) \\
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} &\simeq \ell(x,y) - \ell(x,y-1) 
\end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: Since digital images are composed of discrete pixels, standard continuous calculus must be adapted into discrete approximations to calculate gradients.
recap_md:
- Partial derivatives are approximated using the difference between adjacent pixel values.
- $\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x}$ is approximated as $\ell(x,y) - \ell(x-1,y)$.

title: Edge Strength and Orientation

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Edge strength is the gradient magnitude, while edge orientation is the direction perpendicular to the gradient.
motivation_md: Quantifying the magnitude and direction of intensity changes allows for the filtering and classification of edges in computer vision tasks.
recap_md:
- Edge strength $e(x,y)$ is defined as the magnitude of the gradient vector.
- Edge orientation $\theta(x,y)$ is calculated using the arctan of the ratio of partial derivatives.

title: Cotermination
one_liner: If two or more 3D lines terminate at the same point, their corresponding projections will also terminate at a common point.
content: Cotermination is a property of projection where if two or more 3D lines terminate at the same point, the corresponding projections in the 2D image will also terminate at a common point.
motivation_md: This property allows a vision system to infer that lines meeting at a junction in a 2D image likely meet at a single vertex in the 3D world, helping reconstruct object topology.
recap_md: - Lines that meet in 3D space will also meet at a common point in their 2D projection.

title: Smoothness
one_liner: A smooth 3D curve will project into a smooth 2D curve.
content: Smoothness is a projection property stating that a smooth 3D curve will project into a smooth 2D curve in the image plane.
motivation_md: This principle ensures that continuity in the physical world is preserved in visual data, allowing for the reliable tracking of curved edges and surfaces.
recap_md: - Continuity and smoothness in 3D curves are preserved during the projection into 2D curves.

title: Generic View
one_liner: Under a generic view, nonaccidental properties are shared by the image and the 3D world.
content:
Under a generic view, nonaccidental properties will be shared by the image and the 3D world. In a world where all 3D edges are vertical or horizontal, and under parallel projection with the camera's horizontal axis parallel to the ground, vertical 3D lines project into vertical 2D lines. Conversely, horizontal lines generally project into oblique lines. Therefore, we can assume any vertical line in the image is also a vertical line in the world.

However, the assumption that vertical 2D lines are also 3D vertical lines will not always work. As shown in (Figure 1.1.6), there are particular viewpoints that make a horizontal line project into a vertical line, but this requires an accidental alignment between the object and the line of sight. While accidental alignments can occur, a generic view assumption considers only those views where properties in the image reliably reflect properties in the 3D world.
motivation_md: The generic view assumption allows us to treat visual features as representative of the 3D world rather than as coincidental alignments, simplifying the process of 3D reconstruction.
recap_md: - Nonaccidental properties in an image are assumed to correspond to actual 3D structures.

title: 3D Vertical Edge Constraint
one_liner: In a 3D vertical edge, the derivative of $Y$ along the edge is $1/ \cos(\theta)$.
motivation_md: This constraint provides a mathematical relationship to recover the depth or orientation of vertical structures from their 2D image coordinates.
recap_md: - The derivative of the 3D coordinate $Y$ with respect to the image coordinate $y$ is determined by $1/ \cos(\theta)$ for vertical edges.

title: 3D Horizontal Edge Constraint
one_liner: In a 3D horizontal edge, the coordinate $Y$ does not change, meaning its derivative along the edge is zero.
content:
In a 3D horizontal edge, the coordinate $Y$ will not change. Therefore, the derivative along the edge should be zero: 

$$\begin{aligned}
\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$ 

where the vector $\bf t$ denotes direction tangent to the edge, ${\bf t}=(-n_y, n_x)$. 

[FIGURE:5f500182448f5285 | A diagram showing a curved boundary of a green region. At a point on the boundary, two orthogonal vectors are drawn: a normal vector $\mathbf{n} = (n_x, n_y)$ pointing outward and a tangent vector...]

We can write this derivative as a function of derivatives along the $x$ and $y$ image coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned}
\partial Y / \partial {\bf t} =  \nabla Y \cdot {\bf t} = -n_y \partial Y / \partial x + n_x \partial Y / \partial y
\end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: By identifying horizontal edges where depth change is zero, we can establish constraints that help solve for the 3D structure of an object from its 2D boundaries.
recap_md: - The derivative of $Y$ along a horizontal edge's tangent vector $\bf t$ is zero.

title: Constraint Propagation
one_liner: Constraint propagation moves 3D information from boundaries into the interior of flat image regions.
content:
Most of the image consists of flat regions where we do not have edge constraints and thus lack enough local information to infer surface orientation. Therefore, we need criteria to propagate information from the boundaries, where we do have information about the 3D structure, into the interior of flat image regions. This problem is common in many visual domains.

[FIGURE:d1fedd32a0ecbb96 | A single solid green circle is positioned in the lower right quadrant of a white square frame. It represents an image patch without context, illustrating the difficulty of inferring 3D shape from...]

[FIGURE:922a25e5bebb5f69 | A green cube is shown in a three-quarter perspective view. On its right-facing side, a small circular region is highlighted with a dashed outline, and four arrows point inward toward this circle from...]

Information about its 3D orientation is propagated from the surrounding edges.
motivation_md: Since local information is often missing in the middle of surfaces, propagation allows us to use known boundary data to fill in the 3D structure of the entire object.
recap_md: - Information about 3D structure is often only available at edges and must be spread to the interior.

title: Planarity Constraint
one_liner: The planarity constraint assumes object faces are planar, meaning the second-order derivatives of the 3D coordinates are zero.
content:
If we assume that the object faces are planar, then flat image regions impose constraints on the local 3D structure where the second-order derivatives of $Y$ should be zero:
$$\begin{aligned}
\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 &= 0  \\
\partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 &= 0 \\  
\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x &= 0 
\end{aligned}$$
To approximate these continuous partial derivatives, we can apply the first-order derivative approximation twice. The result is $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y)$, and similarly for $\partial^2 X / \partial x^2$.
motivation_md: Assuming surfaces are flat (planar) provides the necessary mathematical constraints to solve for the 3D shape of an object's faces when only the edges are known.
recap_md: - Planar faces require that the second-order partial derivatives of the 3D coordinate $Y$ equal zero.

title: Simple Inference Scheme
one_liner: Constraints can be written as an overdetermined system of linear equations and solved using the pseudoinverse.
content:
All the different constraints described previously can be written as an overdetermined system of linear equations. Each equation will have the form:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} = b_i
\end{aligned}$$
where $\mathbf{Y}$ is a vectorized version of the image $Y$. There might be many more equations than there are image pixels. For instance, if a pixel is inside a planar face, there will be three equations corresponding to the planarity constraint, such as $\mathbf{a}_i = [0, \dots, 0, -1, 2, -1, 0, \dots, 0]$ and $b_i=0$.

We can solve the system of equations by minimizing the cost function:
$$\begin{aligned}
J = \sum_i w_i (\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} - b_i)^2
\end{aligned}$$
where $w_i$ is an optional weight for each constraint. In matrix form, the system is $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$. Since the system is overdetermined, we can use the pseudoinverse to compute the solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\bf Y = (\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{b}
\end{aligned}$$
This can be solved efficiently because the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is very sparse.
motivation_md: This scheme provides a unified way to combine various geometric constraints into a single optimization problem that can be solved computationally to reconstruct 3D scenes.
recap_md: - Geometric constraints are formulated as a linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$.

title: Maximum A Posteriori Learning
one_liner: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) learning infers the most probable hypothesis by combining a prior distribution with a likelihood function using Bayes' rule.
motivation_md: While maximum likelihood estimation only considers the data, MAP learning allows us to incorporate prior knowledge or beliefs about which hypotheses are more likely before seeing any data, leading to more robust inference.
recap_md: - MAP learning finds the hypothesis that maximizes the posterior probability $p(f | \text{data})$.

title: Linear Least-Squares Regression
one_liner: Linear least-squares regression aims to model the relationship between two variables using a line fitted to observed data pairs.
content:
One of the simplest learning problems is known as linear least-squares regression. In this setting, we aim to model the relationship between two variables, $x$ and $y$, with a line.

As a concrete example, imagine $x$ represents the temperature outside, and $y$ represents the number of people at the beach. We train (i.e., fit) our model on many observed examples of {`temperature outside`, `number of people at the beach`} pairs, denoted as $\{x^{(i)},y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. At test time, this model can be applied to predict the $y$ value of a new query $x'$, as shown in @fig-intro_to_learning-ols_train_test.

(see figure: The goal of learning is to use the training data to predict the $y$ value of the test query. In our example we find that for every 1 degree increase in temperature, we can expect $\sim 10$ more...)
motivation_md: It provides a simple, interpretable way to predict a continuous numerical value based on the linear relationship observed in historical data.
recap_md: - Models the relationship between variables $x$ and $y$ as a straight line.

title: L2 Loss
one_liner: L2 loss measures the sum of squared differences between predicted values and ground truth targets.
motivation_md: The L2 loss penalizes larger errors more heavily than smaller ones due to the squaring operation, making it a standard choice for regression problems where we want to minimize the distance to the target.
recap_md: - Defined as the squared difference between the prediction and the target: $(\hat{y} - y)^2$.

title: Program Induction
one_liner: Program induction is a broad class of learning algorithms where the hypothesis space consists of computer programs, such as Python code.
content:
Program induction is one of the broadest classes of learning algorithm. In this setting, our hypothesis space may be all Python programs. 

(see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)

In linear least-squares, the learned function is an algebraic expression that maps $x$ to $y$, and learning consists of searching over two scalar parameters, $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$. In contrast, @fig-intro_to_learning-program_induction_system_diagram shows Python program induction solving the same problem. In this case, the learned function is a Python program that maps $x$ to $y$. Learning consists of searching over the space of all possible Python programs (within some max length). This is a much harder search problem than finding two scalars. Using too powerful a hypothesis space when a simpler one will do can lead to pitfalls in generalization.

(see figure: Python program induction finds a Python program that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)
motivation_md: Program induction allows for learning extremely complex, algorithmic relationships that cannot be easily captured by simple algebraic formulas or fixed-parameter models.
recap_md: - Searches over a hypothesis space of computer programs rather than just numerical parameters.

title: One-Hot Code
one_liner: A one-hot code represents class labels as a vector where exactly one element is 1 and all others are 0.
content:
A convenient representation for class labels is to let $\mathbf{y}$ be a $K$-dimensional vector, for $K$ possible classes, with $y_k = 1$ if $\mathbf{y}$ represents class $k$, and $y_k = 0$ otherwise. This representation is called a one-hot code, since just one element of the vector is on ("hot"). Each class has a unique one-hot code. These codes are the targets for the function we are learning. Our goal is to learn a function $f_{\theta}$ that outputs vectors $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ that match the one-hot codes, thereby correctly classifying the input images.

An example of one-hot codes for representing $K$=5 different classes:

[FIGURE:b8af1eed48fae94a | A diagram illustrating one-hot encoding for $K$ classes. Three vertical vectors of length 5 are shown, labeled 'class: 1', '2', and 'K'. In the vector for class 1, the first cell is black...]
motivation_md: Categorical labels like 'cat' or 'dog' cannot be used directly in mathematical optimization; one-hot encoding converts these categories into a numerical format suitable for distance metrics and loss functions.
recap_md: - Represents $K$ classes as $K$-dimensional vectors.

title: 0-1 Loss
one_liner: The 0-1 loss function evaluates to 1 for a misclassification and 0 for a correct classification.
content:
To minimize misclassifications, we might use the so-called 0-1 loss:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbb{1}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\neq\mathbf{y}),
\end{aligned}
$$ 

where $\mathbb{1}$ is the indicator function that evaluates to 1 if and only if its argument is true, and 0 otherwise.
motivation_md: The 0-1 loss directly counts the number of errors, which is the most intuitive metric for classification accuracy.
recap_md: - Uses an indicator function to penalize any incorrect prediction with a value of 1.

title: Cross-Entropy Loss
one_liner: Cross-entropy loss is a continuous and differentiable function used to maximize the log likelihood of ground truth observations.
motivation_md: Unlike 0-1 loss, cross-entropy is differentiable, allowing for the use of gradient-based optimization methods like backpropagation in neural networks.
recap_md: - Defined as $-\sum y_k \log \hat{y}_k$ for $K$ classes.

title: Probability Mass Function (pmf)
one_liner: A probability mass function (pmf) is a vector of probabilities for discrete classes that sums to one.
content: For the interpretation of model outputs as probabilities to be valid, we require that $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ represent a probability mass function (pmf). A pmf $\mathbf{p}$, over $K$ classes, is defined as a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sums to 1. In other words, $\mathbf{p}$ is a point on the $(K-1)$-simplex, which we denote as $\mathbf{p} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$.
motivation_md: Defining model outputs as a pmf ensures that predictions behave like true probabilities, allowing for consistent statistical reasoning and the use of information-theoretic loss functions.
recap_md: - A vector where each element is between 0 and 1 and the total sum is 1.

title: Image Segmentation
one_liner: Image segmentation is a domain of modern computer vision research heavily influenced by the principles of perceptual organization discovered by gestalt theory.
content: Perceptual organization remains an intriguing and rich area of research with many visual mechanisms still poorly understood. The list of principles of perceptual organization discovered by the gestalt theory have impacted a lot of modern research in computer vision, in particular in the domain of image segmentation.
motivation_md: Image segmentation exists to partition visual data into meaningful regions, a task that relies on understanding how the human visual system organizes sensory input into coherent objects.
recap_md:
- It is a key domain in computer vision research.
- It is deeply influenced by gestalt principles of perceptual organization.

title: Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
one_liner: The ecological approach to visual perception studies the eye in the context of the body and the real-world environment it inhabits.
content:
While previous theories of perception considered that the simplest scenario to study vision was assuming a static camera taking a snapshot in a controlled lab setting, James J. Gibson postulated that, to understand vision, one should take an ecological approach to visual perception. The study of the eye should be done in the context of the body that supports it and the world it lives in.

Experimental science based in simple visual stimuli allowed for measuring quantities, reporting results, and reproducing findings, but the simple stimuli were very limiting. Dealing with real-world stimuli is messy, and no one had good theories on how to use them experimentally. Gibson argued that, to understand perception, the experimental lab should be like real life. Many of the displays used by gestalt psychologists were too simple and unlikely to occur in the real world. They provide useful knowledge, but fall short of unraveling the true nature of the visual system.
motivation_md: Traditional lab-based vision studies used static, artificial stimuli that failed to capture how biological visual systems actually function in complex, dynamic, real-world environments.
recap_md:
- Vision should be studied in the context of the body and the environment.
- Real-world stimuli are necessary to understand the true nature of the visual system.
- It critiques the use of overly simplified lab displays as insufficient for explaining perception.

title: Ground Plane
one_liner: The ground plane is the primary surface for terrestrial animals, serving as the center of their perception and behavior.
content:
The ground plane is the most important surface for terrestrial animals, it is the center of their perception and behavior. The ground provides the support for action and a reference for perception. Other notions of ecological importance are the concepts of layout, place, and enclosure.

Drawing by Gibson showing how few lines induce a strong 3D percept of a ground plane.

[FIGURE:ec27a980e52fb1da | A series of converging lines representing an optic flow pattern. The lines originate from the top and right edges and fan out towards the bottom and left, creating a sense of perspective and forward...]
motivation_md: For terrestrial beings, the ground is the constant physical reference point that enables navigation and spatial orientation.
recap_md:
- It is the most important surface for terrestrial perception.
- It provides a reference for perception and support for action.
- Simple line patterns can induce a strong 3D perception of this plane.

title: Ecological Optics
one_liner: Ecological optics is the study of light that converges into an observer as a result of interactions with surfaces in a complex environment.
content: Gibson made a distinction between the light studied by optical physics and the one that is relevant for perception, which he called ecological optics. According to Gibson, physicists are interested in studying light in simplified settings such as the light emitted by point sources that send rays into an infinite space, or that interact with surfaces or lenses once. Ecological optics instead studies the light that converges into the observer, which is the result of countless interactions with all the surfaces in a messy environment.
motivation_md: Standard physics often simplifies light to point sources and single reflections, which does not accurately reflect the complex, multi-reflected light environment that biological eyes must interpret.
recap_md:
- It focuses on light relevant to perception rather than theoretical physics.
- It considers light resulting from interactions with many surfaces in a "messy" environment.
- It emphasizes light converging at the point of observation.

title: Ambient Optic Array
one_liner: The ambient optic array is the set of light rays converging at a point of observation that contains information about the environment and the observer.
content: The ambient optic array is the set of light rays that converge into a point of observation. And this point of observation can be occupied by an observer who will move around the world. This moving ambient optic array will contain information about the environment and also about the observer themself.
motivation_md: To understand how an observer perceives their surroundings while moving, we need a concept that describes the structured light available at their specific location in space.
recap_md:
- It consists of light rays converging at a specific point of observation.
- It provides information about both the environment and the observer's own movement.
- It is a dynamic structure that changes as the observer moves.

title: Affordance
one_liner: Affordance refers to the action possibilities that an environment or object offers to an observer.
content: Another key concept in Gibson's theory is the notion of affordance introduced by Gibson in 1966. A path affords locomotion from one point to another, an obstacle affords collision, and a stairway affords both descent and ascent. An object is a substance enclosed by a surface. The affordance of an object is generally a direct consequence of its properties: a hollow object can contain substances, a detached object affords carrying, an object with a sharp edge affords cutting, and so on. Animate objects are controlled by internal forces, and they afford social interaction.
motivation_md: Perception is not just about identifying objects, but about understanding what those objects allow an organism to do in its environment.
recap_md:
- It describes the functional possibilities provided by the environment (e.g., a path affords locomotion).
- It is often a direct consequence of an object's physical properties.
- It extends to social interactions provided by animate objects.

title: Direct Perception
one_liner: Direct perception is the process of picking up information directly from the rich ambient optic array without the need for additional mental processing.
content: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from the ambient array. This is in contrast with other theories of visual perception that assume that the input stimuli is very impoverished and that perception is indirect as it has to be complemented by additional processes. The indirect theory of perception is the most common one. However, the important message to learn here is that, when building a perceptual system, the richer the input is, one might hope that the solution to the perception problem will be simpler.
motivation_md: If the environment provides sufficiently rich information, complex internal mental reconstructions may be unnecessary, simplifying the theoretical model of how vision works.
recap_md:
- It involves picking up information directly from the ambient optic array.
- It assumes the environment provides sufficient information for perception without complex internal processing.
- It contrasts with the "indirect perception" theory which views sensory input as impoverished.

title: Information Pickup
one_liner: Information pickup is the process by which an observer extracts environmental information directly from the ambient optic array.
content: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from the ambient array. This is in contrast with other theories of visual perception that assume that the input stimuli is very impoverished and that perception is indirect as it has to be complemented by additional processes. The indirect theory of perception is the most common one. However, the important message to learn here is that, when building a perceptual system, the richer the input is, one might hope that the solution to the perception problem will be simpler.
motivation_md: This concept explains the mechanism of direct perception, focusing on the extraction of existing environmental invariants rather than the construction of mental representations.
recap_md:
- It is the central mechanism of direct perception.
- It involves gathering information directly from the rich ambient optic array.
- It suggests that a richer input simplifies the problem of perception.

title: Rods and Cones
one_liner: The retina contains two types of photoreceptors: rods for low-light vision and cones for color vision.
content: The retina contains photoreceptors called the rods and cones. Rods are used in low-light levels, and the cones are used in color vision. In low-light, only the rods operate and our vision becomes black and white.
motivation_md: To understand how the human eye processes different lighting conditions and perceives color versus grayscale.
recap_md:
- Rods are photoreceptors specialized for low-light levels.
- Cones are photoreceptors responsible for color vision.
- In low-light environments, only rods operate, resulting in black and white vision.

title: L, M, and S Cones
one_liner: The human visual system uses L, M, and S cones to sample light at long, medium, and short wavelengths, creating a 3D description of color.
content:
The human visual system analyzes the incident light power spectrum with only three different classes of photoreceptors, called the L, M, and S cones because they sample at the long, medium, and short wavelengths. This gives the human visual system a three-dimensional (3D) description of light, with each photoreceptor class taking a different weighted average of the incident light power spectrum.

(see figure: A diagram showing a mosaic of red, green, and blue circles representing the spatial distribution of L, M, and S cones in a human retina. The red and green circles are most numerous and are arranged...)

(see figure: A graph showing the normalized spectral sensitivity curves for the three types of human cone cells: S (short-wavelength, blue curve), M (medium-wavelength, green curve), and L (long-wavelength, red...)

Figure (a) shows the spatial sampling pattern for each of the three cone classes. The L cones are colored red, the M cones green, and the S cones are colored blue. Note the hexagonal packing of the cones in the retina and the stochastic assignment of L, M, and S cones over space. Note also the much sparser spatial sampling of the S cones than of either the L or M cones. Figure (b) shows the spectral sensitivity curves for the L, M, and S cones. This sampling pattern was measured from near the fovea, where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
motivation_md: Explains how the biological structure of the eye reduces complex light spectra into a manageable three-dimensional signal for the brain.
recap_md:
- L, M, and S cones correspond to long, medium, and short wavelength sensitivities.
- The spatial distribution of cones is stochastic and hexagonal, with S cones being the sparsest.
- Cone responses provide a 3D weighted average of the incident light power spectrum.

title: Fovea
one_liner: The fovea is a region of the retina where cones are close-packed and rods are absent.
content: The fovea is a specific area of the retina where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed. Measurements of cone sampling patterns and spectral sensitivity curves are often taken from near this region.
motivation_md: Identifies the area of the eye responsible for the highest visual acuity and most concentrated color perception.
recap_md:
- The fovea contains no rods.
- Cones are close-packed in this region for high-resolution sampling.

title: Cone Response Model
one_liner: Photoreceptor responses are modeled as the product of a spectral sensitivity matrix and an incident light spectrum vector.
motivation_md: Provides a mathematical framework to calculate how a specific light spectrum will be perceived by the human eye.
recap_md:
- The model uses a $3 \times N$ matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ to represent cone sensitivities.
- The resulting vector represents the 3D response of the L, M, and S cones to an input spectrum $\mathbf{t}$.

title: Color Metamerism
one_liner: Color metamerism occurs when two different light spectra appear identical to the eye because they produce the same cone responses.
content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same to our eyes. There's a high-dimensional space of light spectra, and we're only viewing projections onto a 3D subspace in the colors we see.
motivation_md: Explains why different physical light sources (like a LED vs. a natural sunset) can be perceived as the same color.
recap_md:
- Metamers are physically different light spectra that are perceived as identical.
- Metamerism results from projecting high-dimensional light spectra onto a 3D visual subspace.

title: Color Reproduction System
one_liner: A color reproduction system is defined by spectral sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's sensitivity curves.
content:
We can define a color reproduction system by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range. The three curves, $\mathbf{C}$, should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or
$$
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}},
$$
where $\mathbf{R}$ is any full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix. We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors. Note, the basis vectors do not need to be orthogonal, and most color system basis vectors are not.

(see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...)
motivation_md: Establishes the mathematical requirements for cameras and displays to accurately represent colors perceived by humans.
recap_md:
- A color system is defined by a $3 \times N$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$ of spectral sensitivity curves.
- System curves must be a linear combination of the eye's sensitivity curves via a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{R}$.

title: Primary Lights
one_liner: Primary lights are a set of three lights whose combination produces the colors in a reproduction system.
content: Primary lights are a sum of three lights used to produce colors in a reproduction system. For the example of a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel are the primary lights. The spectra of the three primary lights are written as column vectors of the matrix $\mathbf{P}$, which serves as the amplitude controls for the system.
motivation_md: Defines the fundamental building blocks (like Red, Green, and Blue) used by displays to synthesize a range of colors.
recap_md:
- Primary lights are the basic spectral components used to synthesize colors.
- In a display, the pixel sub-elements act as the primary lights.
- The spectra of these lights are represented as column vectors in a matrix $\mathbf{P}$.

title: Gamut
one_liner: The gamut is the range of colors that can be produced by a positive combination of a specific set of primary lights.
content: The gamut is the range of colors that can be produced by the positive combination of a given set of primary lights. Because primary light amplitudes must be positive values, some input colors may fall outside this range.
motivation_md: Explains the physical limitations of color displays and why some real-world colors cannot be perfectly reproduced.
recap_md:
- The gamut represents the total range of reproducible colors for a system.
- It is limited by the requirement that primary light combinations must use positive values.

title: Indirect Perception
one_liner: Indirect perception is the theory that visual input is impoverished and must be complemented by additional mental processes to form a complete representation of the environment.
content: In contrast to Gibson's theory of direct perception, which suggests the ambient optic array contains all necessary information for information pickup, other theories of visual perception assume that input stimuli are impoverished. These theories posit that perception is indirect because it must be complemented by additional processes to interpret the environment. The indirect theory of perception is the most common framework. A key insight from this debate is that when building a perceptual system, a richer input might allow for a simpler solution to the perception problem.
motivation_md: This concept highlights the fundamental debate in psychology and computer vision regarding whether sensory data is sufficient for understanding the world (direct) or requires complex internal modeling to fill in gaps (indirect).
recap_md:
- Indirect perception assumes sensory input is too impoverished to be understood without additional processing.
 - It contrasts with Gibson's theory of direct perception and information pickup.
 - The theory suggests that internal mechanisms must complement external stimuli to form a coherent perception.

title: Gibson's View on Stimuli
one_liner: Gibson rejected the term 'stimuli' because it implied the environment stimulates the observer, whereas he believed the observer actively picks up information.
content: Gibson did not like the term stimuli because it implied that the environment stimulates the observer. For Gibson, it is important to stress that the observer is only picking up information.
motivation_md: Gibson sought to shift the focus of perception from a passive process where the environment acts on the subject to an active process where the observer extracts information.
recap_md:
- Gibson avoided the term 'stimuli' to emphasize active observation.
 - He viewed perception as the process of 'picking up' information rather than being stimulated.

title: Networks of Interconnected Cells
one_liner: Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved that the brain is composed of networks of individual, interconnected neurons rather than a continuous mass.
content: For a long time, researchers believed the brain was not composed of individualized cells like the rest of the body. In 1890, Santiago Ramón y Cajal used Golgi's stain to isolate individual neurons, proving that the brain is composed of networks of interconnected cells. This was the first time such networks were observed, as demonstrated in his work on the anatomy of the retina. Ramón y Cajal subsequently mapped most of the brain, and his drawings remain a reference in the field. Both Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in 1906 for this work.
motivation_md: Understanding that the brain is made of discrete, interconnected units (neurons) is the foundation of modern neuroscience and the inspiration for artificial neural networks.
recap_md:
- Santiago Ramón y Cajal proved the brain consists of individual neurons.
 - These neurons form networks of interconnected cells.
 - This discovery moved neuroscience away from the idea of the brain as a continuous, non-cellular mass.

title: Retina
one_liner: The retina is a neural structure that transforms light into electrical impulses through layers of specialized neurons.
content: The retina is a remarkable part of the brain that transforms light into impulses. Light is first transformed into an electric signal by photoreceptors (rods and cones). It is then processed by several layers formed by various types of neurons, including amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells. Finally, ganglion cells transmit the output of the retina through the optic nerve to the rest of the brain. While the studies of Ramón y Cajal revealed the circuitry of these layers, they provided limited information regarding their functional behavior or how these circuits process information.
motivation_md: The retina is the first stage of visual processing, performing significant computation before visual information even reaches the main body of the brain.
recap_md:
- Photoreceptors (rods and cones) convert light into electrical signals.
 - Processing occurs across layers of amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells.
 - Ganglion cells send the final processed signal to the brain via the optic nerve.

title: Receptive Field
one_liner: A receptive field is the specific region of the input stimulus space that must be stimulated to produce a response in a neuron.
content:
The retina was one of the first visual structures studied from a functional perspective. In 1938, Haldan Keffer Hartline popularized the concept of the receptive field, which had been introduced by Charles Scott Sherrington in 1906 within the tactile domain. The receptive field of a neuron corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space—the retina, in the case of a visual neuron—that must be stimulated in order to produce a response in the neuron. Most neurons in the visual processing stream are activated only when light shines on a precise portion of the retina. Only stimulation within the receptive field (RF) of a neuron produces a response.

[FIGURE:542154188035b8df | A schematic diagram of a large rectangular area labeled 'Image/visual field'. Inside this field, a smaller circular region with a dashed border and light gray fill is labeled 'RF', representing the...]
motivation_md: The concept of a receptive field allows scientists to map how specific sensory inputs relate to the activity of individual neurons, forming the basis of spatial sensory processing.
recap_md:
- The receptive field (RF) is the area in the stimulus space that triggers a neuron.
 - Visual neurons typically respond only to light in a specific, precise portion of the retina.
 - Stimulation outside the RF does not produce a response in that specific neuron.

title: Center-Surround Organization
one_liner: Center-surround organization describes receptive fields consisting of a circular central region and a surrounding ring with antagonistic responses to light.
content: Steven Kuffler (1953) studied the organization of the retina and showed that ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization. By recording the response of ganglion cells to small spots of light, Kuffler and Hartline identified two types of cells. On-center cells activate when light hits the middle of the receptive field and deactivate when light hits the surrounding ring. Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior. These findings suggest the retina performs contrast enhancement, a discovery that has motivated extensive research in computational neuroscience and neuromorphic engineering. Haldan Keffer Hartline received the Nobel Prize in 1967 for these discoveries on visual information processing.
motivation_md: Center-surround organization is a fundamental mechanism for edge detection and contrast enhancement, allowing the visual system to emphasize boundaries rather than uniform illumination.
recap_md:
- Ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with antagonistic center and surround regions.
 - This organization enables the retina to perform contrast enhancement.
 - It distinguishes between on-center and off-center cell types.

title: On-Center and Off-Center Cells
one_liner: On-center and off-center cells are neurons with concentric receptive fields that respond oppositely to light stimulation in their central versus surrounding regions.
content: Research by Hartline and Kuffler revealed two types of ganglion cells based on their center-surround organization. On-center cells are activated when a spot of light is inside a small central region of the receptive field and are deactivated (firing below their average rate) when light is projected onto the surrounding ring. Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior. When a cell with an ON-center Receptive Field (RF) is illuminated in its inner part, the firing rate increases. Conversely, stimulating the outer part of an ON-center RF causes inhibition. An OFF-center RF responds with inhibition to central light and excitation to light in the surround. These mechanisms allow the retina to perform contrast enhancing operations.
motivation_md: These cell types are the building blocks of spatial vision, allowing the brain to detect local changes in brightness and identify shapes and edges.
recap_md:
- ON-center cells fire more when the center is lit and less when the surround is lit.
 - OFF-center cells fire less when the center is lit and more when the surround is lit.
 - This antagonistic relationship is essential for detecting visual contrast.

title: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
one_liner: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) is a six-layered structure that receives retinal input and transmits it to the visual cortex.
content: The axons of ganglion cells from both eyes project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). The LGN is composed of six layers of neurons, and its output is directed to the visual cortex and other visual areas. Although it receives inputs from both eyes, the signals are not mixed, and the neurons in this area remain monocular. LGN neurons possess concentric (center-surround) receptive fields. While its full role is not completely understood, the LGN may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation, and saccadic suppression. Notably, only 5 percent of its input connections come from the retina, while 95 percent are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
motivation_md: The LGN acts as a sophisticated relay station, likely filtering or modulating visual information based on feedback from the brain before it reaches the cortex.
recap_md:
- The LGN is a six-layered structure that maintains monocular separation of eye inputs.
 - It features center-surround receptive fields similar to retinal ganglion cells.
 - The vast majority of its inputs are feedback connections from the cortex, not direct retinal signals.

title: Color Matching Functions
one_liner: Color matching functions are the spectral sensitivities of the three photosensors in a color measurement system, represented as row vectors in a matrix.
content: The color matching functions are the spectral sensitivities as a function of wavelength for each of the three photosensors in a color measurement system. These spectral curves are written as the row vectors of a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$.
motivation_md: To mathematically model how a sensor or eye responds to light, we need to quantify its sensitivity at every wavelength. These functions allow us to transform a continuous light spectrum into a discrete set of three response values.
recap_md: [ "- Color matching functions represent the spectral sensitivity of photosensors across different wavelengths.", "- They are mathematically organized as the rows of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$." ]

title: Color Matching Derivation
one_liner: This derivation establishes the matrix conditions required for a color reproduction system to perfectly match the human eye's response to light.
content:
For a given set of primary lights $\mathbf{P}$, we seek to find a matrix of color sensitivity curves $\mathbf{C}$ and a $3 \times 3$ mixing matrix $\mathbf{M}$ that allow perfect reproduction of colors as viewed by a human observer. Let the spectrum of light reflecting from a surface be $\mathbf{t}$. The eye's response is modeled as $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \mathbf{t}$. The color matching system senses the light as $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$, applies controls $\mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$, and outputs light $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. For perfect reproduction, the eye's response to this output must match its response to the original light: $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \mathbf{t}$.

Since this must hold for any $\mathbf{t}$, we require $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$. This implies that the subspace of the eye responses must be the same as that measured by the sensing system, meaning $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$ for some full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{R}$. Substituting this into the matching equation leads to the condition $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_3$. Thus, the required conditions are:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{C} &= \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \\ \mathbf{M} &= (\mathbf{C P})^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$ are the human photoreceptor sensitivities. For a system to be physically realizable, the elements of the primary spectra $\mathbf{P}$ must be non-negative.

[FIGURE:77907696848a7f82 | A graph showing three color matching functions, \bar{r}(\lambda), \bar{g}(\lambda), and \bar{b}(\lambda), plotted against wavelength \lambda in nanometers from 400 to 700. The blue curve...]

[FIGURE:fec594ff8e0f61e8 | A plot showing three narrow vertical spikes representing primary light spectra on a wavelength axis from 400 to 750 nm. A blue spike is located near 440 nm, a green spike near 540 nm, and a red spike...]
motivation_md: To ensure that a display (like a monitor) reproduces colors that look identical to the original scene to a human, we must derive the mathematical relationship between the display's primaries, the sensors, and the eye's biology.
recap_md: [ "- Perfect color reproduction requires the sensor subspace $\mathbf{C}$ to be a linear transformation of the eye's sensitivity $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$.", "- The mixing matrix $\mathbf{M}$ must satisfy $\mathbf{M} = (\mathbf{C P})^{-1}$ to ensure the system output matches the input response.", "- Physical realizability requires non-negative primary spectra $\mathbf{P}$." ]

title: Color Matching Conditions
one_liner: The Color Matching Conditions define the matrix relationships between sensors, primaries, and the human eye required for accurate color reproduction.
content:
The conditions required for color matching in a color reproduction system are given by:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{C} &= \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{M} &= (\mathbf{C P})^{-1}, \end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$ are the human photoreceptor sensitivities, $\mathbf{C}$ is the color measurement matrix, $\mathbf{P}$ represents the primary light spectra, $\mathbf{M}$ is the mixing matrix, and $\mathbf{R}$ is a full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix.
motivation_md: These conditions provide the fundamental linear algebra framework for designing cameras and displays that accurately mimic human color perception.
recap_md: [ "- The sensor sensitivities $\mathbf{C}$ must be a full-rank linear combination of human eye sensitivities $\mathbf{C}_{\text{eye}}$.", "- The mixing matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is the inverse of the product of the sensor matrix and the primary matrix $\mathbf{C P}$." ]

title: Tristimulus Values
one_liner: Tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are coordinates obtained by projecting an input light spectrum onto three color-matching functions.
content: To find the CIE color coordinates, one projects the input spectrum onto the three color-matching functions to find coordinates called tristimulus values, labeled $X$, $Y$, and $Z$.
motivation_md: Tristimulus values provide a standardized way to represent any visible color as a set of three numbers, facilitating consistent color communication across different devices.
recap_md: [ "- Tristimulus values are denoted as $X$, $Y$, and $Z$.", "- They are calculated by projecting an input light spectrum onto specific color-matching functions." ]

title: CIE Chromaticity Coordinates
one_liner: CIE chromaticity coordinates $x$ and $y$ are normalized tristimulus values that represent color independently of intensity.
content: CIE chromaticity coordinates are calculated by normalizing tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ to remove overall intensity variations. The coordinates are defined as $x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}$ and $y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}$.
motivation_md: By normalizing for intensity, chromaticity coordinates allow us to describe the 'quality' of a color (its hue and saturation) regardless of how bright or dim the light is.
recap_md: [ "- Chromaticity coordinates $x$ and $y$ are derived from normalized $X, Y, Z$ tristimulus values.", "- $x = X / (X+Y+Z)$ and $y = Y / (X+Y+Z)$.", "- Normalization removes variations caused by overall light intensity." ]

title: Spatial Resolution and Color Interaction
one_liner: Human perception of spatial resolution varies significantly across different directions in color space.
content: Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution. For some directions in color space, the eye is very sensitive to fine spatial modulations, while for other color space directions, the eye is relatively insensitive. Some color coordinate systems take advantage of this disparity to enable efficient representation of images by sampling image data sparsely along color axes where human perception is insensitive to blurring.
motivation_md: Understanding that the eye is less sensitive to detail in certain color dimensions allows for more efficient image compression and transmission by prioritizing data where the eye is most sensitive.
recap_md: [ "- Human spatial sensitivity depends on the direction in color space.", "- This disparity allows for efficient image representation by sampling insensitive axes more sparsely." ]

title: Lab Color Space Blur Insensitivity
one_liner: The Lab color space separates luminance from color components, exploiting the eye's relative insensitivity to blurring in the 'a' and 'b' channels.
content:
In a red-green-blue (RGB) representation, the eye is sensitive to high spatial frequency changes in both red and green. However, a rotation and nonlinear stretching of color coordinates can transform an image into the L, a, b color space. In this space, the eye is very sensitive to blurring of the L component (luminance) but is relatively insensitive to blurring of the a or b components. This effect is commonly exploited in image compression, allowing some image components to be sampled more coarsely than others.

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) RGB components. (c) RGB components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls2)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls1 (b) and @fig-girls1 (c). (a) R component blurred, G and B components sharp. (b) G component blurred, R and B components...)

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) Lab components. (c) Lab components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls4)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls3 (b) and @fig-girls3 (c). Fig (a) L component blurred, a and b components sharp. (b) a component blurred, L and b...)
motivation_md: The RGB space is not optimized for human perception because the eye's sensitivity to detail is spread across all channels. Lab space isolates detail into the luminance channel, making it easier to compress color data without noticeable loss in quality.
recap_md: [ "- The eye is sensitive to high-frequency changes in all RGB channels.", "- In Lab space, the eye is sensitive to blurring in the L (luminance) channel but insensitive to blurring in the a and b (chrominance) channels.", "- This property is used in image compression to sample color components more coarsely." ]

title: Learning as a Meta-Algorithm
one_liner: Learning is a meta-algorithm that extracts lessons from past experience to output algorithms for solving future problems.
content:
The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past experience in order to solve future problems. Typically, this involves searching for an algorithm that solves past instances of the problem, which can then be applied to future instances. In this context, "past" and "future" refer to what the learner has previously seen versus what they will see next. Because learning is itself an algorithm that outputs other algorithms, it can be understood as a meta-algorithm.

(see figure: Learning is an algorithm that outputs algorithms.)
motivation_md: By viewing learning as a meta-algorithm, we can apply algorithmic analysis to the process of learning itself, helping us design better systems that adapt to new data.
recap_md: [ "- Learning extracts lessons from past experience to solve future problems.", "- It functions as a meta-algorithm: an algorithm that outputs other algorithms.", "- 'Past' and 'future' are defined by the learner's sequence of observations." ]

title: Zeroth-Order Optimization
one_liner: Zeroth-order optimization finds a function's minimum by sampling parameter values and observing the resulting loss without access to gradient information.
content: In the simplest setting, called zeroth-order optimization, the update function only gets to observe the value $J(\theta)$. The only way, then, to find $\theta$'s that minimize the loss is to sample different values for $\theta$ and move toward the values that are lower.
motivation_md: This technique is used when the analytical gradient of a function is unavailable or impossible to compute, allowing for optimization based solely on function evaluations.
recap_md:
- Relies only on observing the loss value $J(\theta)$ rather than derivatives.
 - Minimizes loss by sampling different parameter values and moving toward those with lower costs.

title: First-Order Optimization
one_liner: First-order optimization uses the gradient of the cost function to determine the direction of steepest descent for parameter updates.
content: For gradient-based optimization, also called first-order optimization, the update function takes as input the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters at the current operating point, $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$. This reveals hugely useful information about the loss that directly tells us how to minimize it: just move in the direction of steepest descent, that is, the gradient direction.
motivation_md: By using the gradient, the optimizer knows exactly which direction reduces the loss most efficiently, making it much faster than random sampling.
recap_md:
- Uses the gradient $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)$ to guide parameter updates.
 - Follows the direction of steepest descent to minimize the cost function.

title: Learning Rate
one_liner: The learning rate $\eta$ is a hyperparameter that controls the step size of parameter updates during optimization.
content: This algorithm has two hyperparameters, the learning rate $\eta$, which controls the step size (learning rate times gradient magnitude), and the number of steps $K$. If the learning rate is sufficiently small and the initial parameter vector $\theta^0$ is random, then this algorithm will almost surely converge to a local minimum of $J$ as $K \rightarrow \infty$. However, to descend more quickly, it can be useful to set the learning rate to a higher value.
motivation_md: It determines the balance between convergence speed and stability; a small rate ensures convergence but is slow, while a large rate speeds up descent but may overshoot.
recap_md:
- Controls the step size as the product of $\eta$ and the gradient magnitude.
 - Small values guarantee convergence to a local minimum over many steps.

title: Learning Rate Schedule
one_liner: A learning rate schedule decays the learning rate over time to allow for large initial steps followed by fine-tuning near the minimizer.
content:
A generally useful strategy is to start with a high value for $\eta$ and then decay it until convergence according to a learning rate schedule. Researchers have come up with innumerable schedules, and they generally work by calling some function $\texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)$ to get the learning rate on each iteration of descent:
$$
\eta^{k} = \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k)
$$
