Generally, we want an update rule where $\eta^{k+1} < \eta^k$, so that we take smaller steps as we approach the minimizer. A few simple and popular approaches are given below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-k} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \beta^{-\lfloor k/M \rfloor} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{stepwise exponential decay}\\
    \texttt{lr}(\eta^0,k) &= \frac{(K - k)}{K} \eta^0 &\quad\quad \triangleleft\quad \text{linear decay}
\end{aligned}
$$
motivation_md: Starting with a high learning rate helps escape local minima and speed up early training, while decaying it ensures the model settles precisely into a minimum without oscillating.
recap_md:
- Adjusts the learning rate $\eta$ dynamically during training iterations.
 - Common strategies include exponential, stepwise exponential, and linear decay.

title: Momentum
one_liner: Momentum accelerates optimization by incorporating a weighted combination of the previous update direction and the current gradient.
content:
Could we do a smarter update than just taking a step in the direction of the gradient? Of the countless ideas that have been proposed, one of the few that has stuck is momentum. Momentum makes the analogy to skiing even more precise: momentum is like the inertia of the skier, carrying them over the little bumps and imperfections in the ski slope and increasing their speed as they descend along a straight path. In math, momentum just means that we set the parameter update to be a direction $\mathbf{v}^{k+1}$, given by a weighted combination of the previous update direction, $\mathbf{v}^{k}$, plus the current negative gradient:
$$
\mathbf{v}^{k+1} = \mu \mathbf{v}^{k} - \eta\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta^k)
$$
The weight $\mu$ in this combination is a new hyperparameter, sometimes simply called the momentum. The full algorithm is given in @alg-gradient_descent_gradient_descent_with_momentum.

(see figure: Gradient descent with momentum algorithm.)
motivation_md: It helps the optimizer navigate noisy gradients and small local optima by maintaining a sense of direction and velocity from previous steps.
recap_md:
- Uses a weighted sum of the previous update and the current negative gradient.
 - Introduces a hyperparameter $\mu$ to control the influence of past updates.

title: One-Sided Derivative

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

one_liner: A one-sided derivative allows gradient descent to function at points of discontinuity by using the gradient value from an infinitesimal step away.
content: In cases where a function is discontinuous and the analytical derivative is undefined at the discontinuity, gradient descent can still function by using a one-sided derivative. This means we set the gradient at the discontinuity to be equal to the gradient value an infinitesimal step away from the discontinuity in a fixed arbitrary direction. Under the hood, for each atomic discontinuous operation, frameworks like Pytorch require that we define its gradients at the discontinuities, and the one-sided gradient is a standard choice. This is why it can be fine in deep learning to use functions like rectified nonlinear units (ReLU), which have discontinuous gradients.
motivation_md: Many common neural network components, like ReLU, are not differentiable at specific points; one-sided derivatives provide a practical way to compute updates regardless.
recap_md:
- Defines the gradient at a discontinuity using the value from a nearby point.
 - Enables optimization of functions with discontinuous gradients like ReLU.

title: Vanished Gradient

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

one_liner: A vanished gradient occurs when the gradient is near zero everywhere, causing gradient descent to progress extremely slowly.
content: In some cases where a function is continuous, the gradients may not be well-behaved. We have a gradient that has nearly vanished when it is near zero everywhere. Consequently, gradient descent with a fixed learning rate will be slow in these regions.
motivation_md: Identifying vanished gradients is crucial because they prevent the model from learning effectively, as the updates become too small to reach the minimum in a reasonable time.
recap_md:
- Characterized by gradient values that are near zero across the parameter space.
 - Results in extremely slow convergence for standard gradient descent.

title: Exploding Gradient

position.section_title: What Kinds of Functions Can Be Minimized with Gradient Descent?

one_liner: An exploding gradient occurs when the gradient at the minimizer goes to infinity, leading to failures in convergence.
content: In scenarios where the function is continuous but the gradients are not well-behaved, the gradient at the minimizer may go to infinity. We call this an exploding gradient, and this leads to failures of convergence during the optimization process.
motivation_md: Exploding gradients cause massive updates that can make the model parameters diverge, making it impossible to find a stable solution.
recap_md:
- Occurs when gradients reach extremely high or infinite values.
 - Causes optimization to fail by preventing convergence to a stable minimum.

title: Refraction
one_liner: Refraction is the phenomenon where light changes direction when passing from one medium to another, such as from air to water.
content: Refraction describes how light changes direction when changing medium, for example, moving from air to water. This phenomenon was described by Ptolemy in his studies of vision and optics.
motivation_md: Understanding how light bends when transitioning between materials is fundamental to optics and the study of how images are formed by the eye and lenses.
recap_md: - Refraction is the change in direction of light when it enters a different medium.

title: Pinhole Camera
one_liner: The pinhole camera is a simple optical device that projects an image through a small aperture.
content: The pinhole camera is an optical device that projects an image through a small hole. It was described and invented as a means to understand how light travels and forms images.
motivation_md: The pinhole camera provides the simplest model for image formation, serving as the foundation for understanding more complex camera systems and the human eye.
recap_md: - A pinhole camera projects an image through a small aperture without a lens.

title: Lenses
one_liner: Lenses are optical elements that focus light to project images, such as the crystalline lens in the human eye.
content: Kepler understood lenses and how the eye projected a reverse picture into the retina. He identified the role of the crystalline lens as the focusing element of images in the eye. This contrasted with previous theories which suggested the crystalline lens was a sensitive element that only selected perpendicular rays reaching the eye.
motivation_md: Lenses are the primary components used to focus light in both biological eyes and artificial cameras, allowing for the creation of sharp images.
recap_md: - Lenses act as focusing elements to project images onto a surface like the retina.

title: Perception as Inference
one_liner: Perception is the process by which the mind forms ideas of vision by finding representations of objects most likely to explain sensory input.
content:
Hermann von Helmholtz proposed that perception is a process of inference. The general rule of vision is that objects are imagined as being present in the field of vision if they would produce the same impression on the nervous mechanism under ordinary conditions. Thus, the mind makes perceptions out of sensations, finding representations of the object most likely to explain the sensory input. This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.

[FIGURE:4c0eccf5247e3f61 | A Venn diagram showing the additive color model with three overlapping circles of red, green, and blue light. The overlap of red and green creates yellow, green and blue creates cyan, red and blue...]

Helmholtz also emphasized the active role of the viewer. By changing our position and noticing how images change (such as a table in front of us), we find out that the stationary form of the object in space is the cause of the changing image in our eyes. This concept of using movement to resolve ambiguity foreshadows unsupervised learning methods in computer vision.

(see figure: Hermann von Helmholtz invented the ophthalmoscope at age 29. Images from @Helmholtz1925)
motivation_md: This idea shifts the view of vision from a passive recording of light to an active computational process of reconstructing the world from ambiguous data.
recap_md: - Perception is the mind's attempt to find the most likely explanation for sensory input. - Visual ideas are formed based on what objects would normally produce a given nervous impression.

title: Trichromacy
one_liner: Trichromacy is the theory that the eye has three classes of receptors, each sensitive to different wavelengths of light.
content:
The theory of trichromacy, codeveloped by Hermann von Helmholtz and Thomas Young, posits that the eye has three classes of receptors. Each class is sensitive to different wavelengths of light.

[FIGURE:4c0eccf5247e3f61 | A Venn diagram showing the additive color model with three overlapping circles of red, green, and blue light. The overlap of red and green creates yellow, green and blue creates cyan, red and blue...]
motivation_md: Trichromacy explains how humans perceive a wide spectrum of colors using only three types of color-sensitive cells, forming the basis for color reproduction in screens and cameras.
recap_md: - The eye uses three distinct types of receptors to perceive color. - Each receptor type responds to different wavelengths of light.

title: Ophthalmascope
one_liner: The ophthalmascope is an instrument developed to observe the retina of the human eye using colinear viewing and illumination.
content:
The ophthalmascope is an instrument developed by Hermann von Helmholtz to observe the retina of the human eye. The key to its design is the use of colinear viewing and illumination directions. Glass plates along a diagonal allow an ophthalmologist to view the eye while reflecting illumination from a light source into it. This allows for the observation of blood vessels and branches of the retinal artery and vein over the optic nerve.

(see figure: Hermann von Helmholtz invented the ophthalmoscope at age 29. Images from @Helmholtz1925)
motivation_md: Before this invention, it was difficult to see the interior of a living eye; it provided a vital tool for both medical diagnosis and the study of visual anatomy.
recap_md: - An instrument used to view the internal structures of the eye, such as the retina. - It utilizes colinear viewing and illumination to make the retina visible.

title: Bayesian Methods for Vision Inference
one_liner: Bayesian methods in computer vision relate to finding the most likely representation of an object given sensory input.
content: Bayesian methods for computer vision inference relate to the viewpoint that the mind finds representations of objects most likely to explain sensory input. It treats perception as a statistical inference problem where the goal is to determine the most probable cause of the observed data.
motivation_md: Bayesian methods provide a mathematical framework for dealing with the inherent uncertainty and ambiguity in visual data.
recap_md: - Perception is modeled as finding the most likely explanation for sensory data. - It provides a statistical basis for computer vision inference.

title: Unconscious Inference
one_liner: Unconscious inference refers to the psychic acts of ordinary perception where the mind reaches 'unconscious conclusions' about the world based on sensory responses.
content: Unconscious inference describes the psychic acts of ordinary perception as unconscious conclusions, distinguishing them from conscious logical conclusions. For example, while an astronomer consciously computes star positions, a person's eye responding to pressure by seeing light is an unconscious conclusion about the world. This process of making inferences about the environment based on sensory responses is a central topic in computer vision.
motivation_md: This concept explains why we perceive a stable world automatically and why certain optical illusions occur when the mind's 'unconscious logic' is misled.
recap_md: - Perception involves automatic, 'unconscious conclusions' about the environment. - It distinguishes between deliberate reasoning and the automatic processing of sensory data.

title: Training Phase
one_liner: The training phase is the stage of learning where we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of a problem.
content: Learning usually consists of two phases: the training phase, where we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of the problem (training data).
motivation_md: To create a functional algorithm, we first need to analyze historical data to find patterns and rules that solve the problem effectively.
recap_md: - The training phase involves searching for an algorithm that performs well on past instances. - It utilizes training data to establish the mapping between inputs and outputs.

title: Testing Phase
one_liner: The testing phase is the stage where a learned algorithm is deployed to solve new instances of a problem.
content: The testing phase is the stage where we deploy our learned algorithm to solve new instances of the problem.
motivation_md: After an algorithm is trained, we must evaluate its performance on unseen data to ensure it can generalize beyond the examples it has already seen.
recap_md: - The testing phase involves deploying a learned algorithm on new problem instances. - It occurs after the training phase to verify the algorithm's effectiveness.

title: Supervised Learning
one_liner: Supervised learning is the process of learning a functional mapping from examples consisting of input-output pairs.
content:
Learning from examples is also called supervised learning. In this context, an algorithm is a computable mapping from inputs to outputs, and an example is defined as an {`input`, `output`} pair. For instance, a set of examples might look like:

$$\begin{aligned}
    &{\texttt{input:} [2,3], \texttt{output:} 36\}\nonumber \\
    &{\texttt{input:} [7,1], \texttt{output:} 49\}\nonumber \\
    &{\texttt{input:} [5,2], \texttt{output:} 100\}\nonumber \\
    &{\texttt{input:} [2,2], \texttt{output:}16\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$

This kind of learning, where you observe example input-output behavior and infer a functional mapping that explains this behavior, is called supervised learning.
motivation_md: When we have historical data with known correct answers, supervised learning allows us to automate the discovery of the underlying rules that produce those answers.
recap_md: - Supervised learning involves learning from examples consisting of input-output pairs. - The goal is to infer a functional mapping that explains the observed behavior.

title: Learning Noncomputable Functions
one_liner: Noncomputable functions are functions for which no algorithm exists that can solve the task in finite time.
content: Some things are not learnable from examples, such as noncomputable functions. An example of a noncomputable function is a function that takes as input a program and outputs a 1 if the program will eventually finish running, and a 0 if it will run forever. It is noncomputable because there is no algorithm that can solve this task in finite time. However, it might be possible to learn a good approximation to it.
motivation_md: Understanding the limits of computation helps define what can and cannot be perfectly learned by an algorithm, though approximations may still be useful.
recap_md: - Noncomputable functions cannot be solved by any algorithm in finite time. - While they are not perfectly learnable, they can sometimes be approximated.

title: Fitting a Model
one_liner: Fitting a model to data is another name for learning from examples or supervised learning.
content: Another name for this kind of learning is fitting a model to data.
motivation_md: This terminology emphasizes the statistical and mathematical nature of finding a function that best represents the underlying structure of a dataset.
recap_md: - Fitting a model is a synonym for learning from data. - It describes the process of adjusting a model's parameters to match observed examples.

title: Unsupervised Learning
one_liner: Unsupervised learning involves creating a model or representation of input data without being provided target outputs.
content: Even without examples, we can still learn. Instead of matching input-output examples, we can try to come up with an algorithm that optimizes for desirable properties of the input-output mapping. In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.
motivation_md: When labeled data is unavailable or expensive to obtain, unsupervised learning allows us to discover hidden patterns, structures, or efficient representations within the raw data itself.
recap_md: - Unsupervised learning uses input data without corresponding target outputs. - The learner optimizes an objective function to find useful representations or properties of the data.

title: Objective Function
one_liner: An objective function is a mathematical expression that a learner optimizes to score model outputs or compare them to target answers.
content: The learner has to come up with a model or representation of input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs. Commonly, $f$ is referred to as the learned function. The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to minimize, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
motivation_md: To automate learning, we need a quantitative way to measure how well an algorithm is performing so that we can systematically improve it.
recap_md: - An objective function scores model outputs to guide the optimization process. - It is often called a loss function when the goal is minimization.

title: Reinforcement Learning
one_liner: Reinforcement learning is a type of learning where an algorithm tries to maximize a reward function that measures the quality of its outputs.
content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards. This kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.
motivation_md: Reinforcement learning is used when an agent must learn to make a sequence of decisions by receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties.
recap_md: - Reinforcement learning aims to maximize a reward function. - The reward function maps outputs to numerical scores representing quality.

title: Reward Function
one_liner: A reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores that explicitly measures the quality of a learned function's output.
content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes these scores.
motivation_md: In reinforcement learning, the learner needs a quantitative way to evaluate its performance. The reward function provides a numerical signal that the learner seeks to maximize, defining what 'success' looks like for a given task.
recap_md:
- A reward function $r: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ maps model outputs to scalar scores. 
- It serves as the explicit measure of quality in reinforcement learning systems.

title: Key Ingredients of Learning
one_liner: A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients: an objective, a hypothesis space, and an optimizer.
content:
A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients:

1. Objective: What does it mean for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well?

2. Hypothesis Space: What is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will we search over?

3. Optimizer: *How*, exactly, do we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective?

These three ingredients, when applied to large amounts of data, and run on sufficient hardware (referred to as compute) can do amazing things. While learning algorithms are central, the data and compute often turn out to be more important.

[FIGURE:606f041122e8e0fc | A block diagram representing a machine learning system. 'Data' flows into a central 'Learner' box from the left, and 'Compute' flows in from the bottom. The 'Learner' box contains three components...]
motivation_md: To build or understand any machine learning system, one must identify its core components: what it is trying to achieve, the range of possible solutions it considers, and the method it uses to find the best one.
recap_md:
- The three pillars of a learning algorithm are the objective, the hypothesis space, and the optimizer.
- Success depends on these ingredients combined with sufficient data and computational power.

title: Learned Function
one_liner: A learned function is an algorithm $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps inputs to outputs.
content: A learner outputs an algorithm, $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, which maps inputs, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, to outputs, $\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}$. Commonly, $f$ is referred to as the learned function.
motivation_md: The ultimate goal of a learning process is to produce a reusable mapping that can take new, unseen inputs and predict their corresponding outputs.
recap_md:
- The learned function $f$ maps the input space $\mathcal{X}$ to the output space $\mathcal{Y}$.
- It represents the final predictive model produced by the learning algorithm.

title: Loss Function
one_liner: A loss function scores model outputs or compares them to targets to define an objective the learner seeks to minimize.
content: The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\mathcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to *minimize*, whereas an objective function can be used to describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
motivation_md: Learning requires a mathematical way to penalize errors. A loss function quantifies the 'cost' of a model's prediction, allowing the optimizer to navigate toward better parameters.
recap_md:
- A loss function $\mathcal{L}$ measures the discrepancy between model outputs and target values.
- While 'objective function' is a general term, 'loss' specifically refers to a value we aim to minimize.

title: Hypothesis Space Parameterization
one_liner: Specifying how a hypothesis space is parameterized is crucial because optimizers and objectives treat different parameterizations differently.
content:
The hypothesis space can be described by a set $\mathcal{F}$ of all the possible functions under consideration by the learner. For example, one hypothesis space might be "all mappings from $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$" and another could be "all functions $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that satisfy the conditions of being a distance metric." 

Commonly, however, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our *parameterized* hypothesis space is $y = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ are the parameters. This example corresponds to the space of affine functions from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, but this is not the only way to parameterize that space. Another choice could be $y = \theta_2\theta_1 x + \theta_0$, with parameters $\theta_0$, $\theta_1$, and $\theta_2$. These two choices parameterize *exactly the same space*; that is, any affine functions can be represented by either parameterization and both parameterizations can only represent affine functions. However, these two parameterizations are not equivalent, because optimizers and objectives may treat different parameterizations differently. Because of this, to fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.
motivation_md: Even if two models can represent the same set of functions, the way we describe them (parameterization) affects how easily an optimizer can find the best solution.
recap_md:
- The hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all functions the learner considers.
- Parameterization defines how numerical parameters map to specific functions in that space.
- Different parameterizations of the same space can lead to different optimization behaviors.

title: Overparameterized Models
one_liner: Overparameterized models use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data.
content: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks are overparameterized.
motivation_md: Modern deep learning often relies on models with massive capacity to find better solutions and generalize well, even if they have far more parameters than data points.
recap_md:
- Overparameterization involves using more parameters than required to fit the training data.
- This property is a hallmark of modern neural networks and computer vision models.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization

position.section_title: Empirical Risk Minimization: A Formalization of Learning from Examples

one_liner: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is a framework for learning from examples by minimizing the average loss over the training data.
motivation_md: Since we cannot know the true error on all possible future data, we use the average error on the data we *do* have (the training set) as a proxy for performance.
recap_md:
- ERM seeks the function $f$ in the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ that minimizes the average training loss.
- It formalizes supervised learning as an optimization problem over a finite dataset.

title: Maximum Likelihood Learning
one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning seeks the hypothesis that assigns the highest probability to the observed data.
motivation_md: This approach provides a statistical foundation for learning, treating the model as a probability distribution and finding the parameters that make the observed data most plausible.
recap_md:
- Maximum likelihood learning maximizes the probability of the observed targets given the inputs and the model.
- Many common loss functions in ERM have a direct interpretation as maximizing likelihood.

title: Similar Triangles Derivation

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Similar triangles relate the distance from the sensing plane to the pinhole with the object's spatial coordinates to determine image coordinates.
motivation_md: This derivation provides the geometric foundation for mapping 3D world coordinates to 2D image coordinates in a pinhole camera model.
recap_md:
- Similar triangles establish that the ratio of image position to focal length equals the ratio of object position to depth.
- The resulting equations are $x = f \frac{X}{Z}$ and $y = f \frac{Y}{Z}$.

title: Perspective Projection Equations

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: The perspective projection equations describe how 3D points are mapped to a 2D plane, where distant objects appear smaller due to inverse scaling by depth.
content: The equations $x = f \frac{X}{Z}$ and $y = f \frac{Y}{Z}$ are called the perspective projection equations. Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller through the inverse scaling by $Z$. These equations apply not just to pinhole cameras but to most lens-based cameras and human vision as well.
motivation_md: These equations mathematically model how the physical world is projected onto a sensor or retina, accounting for the natural phenomenon where distance affects apparent size.
recap_md:
- Perspective projection uses the equations $x = f \frac{X}{Z}$ and $y = f \frac{Y}{Z}$.
- Objects undergo inverse scaling by their distance $Z$ from the camera.
- This model is applicable to pinhole cameras, lens-based cameras, and biological vision.

title: Depth-Dependent Size Scaling

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller through inverse scaling by their distance $Z$.
content: Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller through the inverse scaling by $Z$.
motivation_md: This concept explains the visual effect of perspective where an object's image size is inversely proportional to its distance from the observer.
recap_md:
- Image size is inversely proportional to the depth $Z$.
- As $Z$ increases, the projected size of the object decreases.

title: Telephoto Approximation

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Orthographic projection models telephoto lenses where object size in the image is roughly independent of distance.
content: Orthographic projection is a good model for telephoto lenses, where the apparent size of objects in the image is roughly independent of their distance to the camera.
motivation_md: When objects are very far away or the field of view is very narrow, the depth-dependent scaling of perspective projection becomes negligible, allowing for a simpler mathematical model.
recap_md:
- Telephoto lenses can be modeled using orthographic projection.
- In this model, image size does not significantly change with object distance.

title: Aperture Blur-Brightness Tradeoff
one_liner: Increasing aperture size brightens an image but introduces blur, a tradeoff resolved by using a lens to focus light.
content:
While pinhole cameras can form good images, they suffer from a serious drawback: the images are very dim because not much light passes through the small pinhole to the sensing plane. One can try to let in more light by making the pinhole aperture bigger. However, that allows light from many different positions to land on a given position at the sensor plane, resulting in a bright but blurry image. Putting a lens in the larger aperture can give the best of both worlds, capturing more light while redirecting the light rays entering the camera so that each sensor plane position maps to just one surface point, creating a focused image on the sensor plane.

(see figure: Brightness/sharpness trade-offs in image formation. From left to right a small pinhole will create a sharp image, but lets in little light, so the image may appear dark for a given exposure time. A larger pinhole lets in more light and generates a brighter image, but each sensor element records light from many different image positions, creating a blurry image. A lens can collect light reflected over many different angles from a single point, allowing a bright, sharp image.)

(see figure: Physical demonstration of the trade-offs illustrated in . (a) Gumby subject, illumination light, barrier with the three apertures, and white projection screen. Also, a light source is added to illuminate the subject. (b) Picture of Gumby. (c) Images formed by light through the three apertures. (d) Detail of the three apertures (small pinhole, large pinhole, and lens).)
motivation_md: Pinhole cameras face a fundamental conflict between image brightness and sharpness; understanding this tradeoff explains why lenses are necessary for high-quality imaging.
recap_md:
- Small apertures produce sharp but dim images.
- Large apertures produce bright but blurry images.
- Lenses allow for both high brightness and sharp focus by redirecting light rays.

title: Geometric Optics
one_liner: Geometric optics is an approximation that analyzes light as rays, ignoring wave effects like diffraction.
content: Geometric optics is an approximation used to analyze how light passes through lenses while ignoring effects like diffraction, which are due to the wave nature of light.
motivation_md: By treating light as rays rather than waves, we can simplify the analysis of lenses and mirrors using basic geometry.
recap_md:
- Light is treated as rays traveling in straight lines.
- Wave-like properties such as diffraction are ignored for simplicity.

title: Snell's Law
one_liner: Snell's Law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the indices of refraction of two media.
content:
Snell's Law relates the bending angles of refraction, $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, to the indices of refraction, $n_1$ and $n_2$, at a material interface. At a material boundary, the relationship is given by the equation:

$$n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$$

where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are the angles with respect to the surface normal of the incident and outgoing light rays, and $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the indices of refraction of the materials. Snell's law can be derived by matching the wavelength of light projected along the material interface boundary across each side of the boundary.

(see figure: A diagram illustrating Snell's Law of refraction at a horizontal interface between two media with refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$. A light ray travels from the top medium ($n_1$) into the bottom...)

(see figure: A photograph of a straight black rod partially submerged in water, demonstrating the effect of refraction. The rod appears to bend sharply at the water's surface, making the submerged portion look...)
motivation_md: Snell's Law is fundamental for understanding how light bends when entering different media, which is the physical basis for how lenses focus light.
recap_md:
- The formula is $n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$.
- Angles are measured relative to the surface normal.
- It describes the bending of light at the interface of two different materials.

title: Index of Refraction
one_liner: The index of refraction $n$ is a material property where both the wavelength and speed of light are inversely proportional to $n$.
content: Both the wavelength and the speed of light in a medium are inversely proportional to the index of refraction of that medium, denoted as $n$. The value of $n$ for a vacuum is 1.
motivation_md: This value quantifies how much a medium slows down light, which determines how much light will bend when entering or leaving that medium.
recap_md:
- Denoted by $n$, with $n=1$ for a vacuum.
- Higher $n$ corresponds to slower light speed and shorter wavelengths within the medium.

title: Ray Tracing Rules for Lenses
one_liner: Rules for tracing light through a lens include rays passing through conjugate points, parallel rays focusing at the focal distance, and rays through the center proceeding in a straight line.
content:
The rules for tracing light travel through a lens include the following:

1. Every ray passing through one conjugate point and passing through the lens then passes through the other conjugate point. This is the fundamental focusing property of a lens.

2. Parallel rays entering the lens all focus to a point at distance $f$ behind the lens. In this case, one of the focal points is at infinity.

3. Any ray passing through the center of the thin lens proceeds in a straight line, as if through a pinhole at the center of the lens. Thus, lenses, like pinholes, render the world in perspective projection.
motivation_md: Ray tracing rules provide a geometric framework for understanding how lenses redirect light to form images, allowing for the prediction of image position and properties.
recap_md: [ "- Rays from one conjugate point converge at the corresponding conjugate point after passing through the lens.", "- Parallel rays entering the lens focus at a distance $f$ behind the lens.", "- Rays passing through the center of a thin lens continue in a straight line, creating a perspective projection." ]

title: Lens Magnification
one_liner: The magnification of a lens is the ratio $a/b$, where $a$ is the distance of an in-focus object and $b$ is the distance to the sensor plane.
content: Because focused rays render positions onto a plane as does a line passing through the center of the lens, the magnification of a lens is simply $a/b$, where $a$ is the distance of an in-focus object to the lens, and $b$ is the distance from the lens to a sensor plane.
motivation_md: Magnification quantifies the relationship between the size of an object in the physical world and its corresponding image size on a camera sensor.
recap_md: [ "- Magnification is calculated as the ratio of object distance $a$ to sensor distance $b$.", "- It describes how positions in the world are scaled when rendered onto an imaging plane." ]

title: Focal Plane
one_liner: The focal plane is a plane outside the camera that is conjugate to the sensor plane, ensuring objects within it are focused sharply.
content: Assume that the lens is part of a camera, focusing light from the world onto the camera's sensor. If a plane outside of the camera, called the focal plane, and the camera's sensor plane are at conjugate positions, then an object in the focal plane is focused sharply onto the sensor plane. All rays from a point on the object's surface will come into focus at a point in the sensor plane.
motivation_md: Identifying the focal plane is essential for determining which parts of a 3D scene will appear sharp in a 2D image.
recap_md: [ "- The focal plane and the sensor plane are at conjugate positions.", "- Objects in the focal plane are imaged with maximum sharpness on the sensor." ]

title: Circle of Confusion
one_liner: A circle of confusion is the blurred spot on a sensor plane formed by light from a point not located on the focal plane.
content: If a plane outside of the camera, called the focal plane, and the camera's sensor plane are at conjugate positions, then an object in the focal plane is focused sharply onto the sensor plane. However, objects in front of the plane of focus by $\delta_a$ will, in general, come to focus some distance $\delta_b$ behind the sensor plane. This will image a point in the focal plane to a circle of confusion at the sensor plane.
motivation_md: The circle of confusion defines the limit of acceptable focus, helping to determine the depth of field in an imaging system.
recap_md: [ "- Points outside the focal plane appear as blurred circles rather than sharp points on the sensor.", "- The size of this circle depends on the distance of the object from the plane of focus." ]

title: Depth of Field Derivation
one_liner: The depth of field $D$ is derived using similar triangles and the f-number, resulting in the approximation $D \approx 2 N C U^2 / f^2$.
content: A camera's f-number, written $N$, is the ratio of the focal length of the lens divided by the diameter of the lens aperture $A$: $N = f/A$. Let the diameter of the circle of confusion be $C$. If the distance $U$ of the focal plane to the camera is much larger than the focal length of the lens ($U >> f$), then the diameter of the focal plane that is imaged onto the circle of confusion is approximately $C U/f$. By similar triangles, we have $$\frac{D_1 f}{C U} = \frac{U - D_1}{\frac{f}{N}}$$ and $$\frac{D_2 f}{C U} = \frac{D_2+U}{\frac{f}{N}}$$ Defining the depth of field $D$ to be $D = D_1 + D_2$, we have $$D = \frac{2 N C U^2 f^2}{f^4 - N^2 C^2 U^2}$$ When the circle of confusion $C$ is much smaller than the lens aperture $f/N$, then the term $N^2 C^2 D^2$ can be ignored relative to $f^4$, and we have $$D \approx \frac{2 N C U^2}{f^2}$$ [FIGURE:93a4280ea2d7838f | A close-up photograph of a yellow tape measure lying on a wooden surface, demonstrating shallow depth of field. The numbers 10, 11, and 12 (marked with a 1F arrow for one foot) are in sharp focus...] [FIGURE:e8cb2dc85de1bd8d | A close-up photograph of a yellow measuring tape lying on a wooden surface with a shallow depth of field. The tape measure is in sharp focus around the 11-inch and 12-inch (1F) marks, while the...] [FIGURE:c19f28e4f61b0f02 | A close-up photograph of a yellow tape measure placed vertically next to a gap between two wooden floorboards. The focus is sharpest around the 12-inch mark, while the markings further away (like 7...] Note the region of sharp focus doubles as the f-number increases from f/2.0 to f/4.0 and f/8.0.
motivation_md: Deriving the depth of field formula allows photographers and engineers to calculate the range of distances that will appear sharp based on lens parameters.
recap_md: [ "- The depth of field is derived from the geometry of similar triangles and lens aperture.", "- For large distances, the depth of field is approximately proportional to the f-number $N$.", "- Increasing the aperture size (decreasing $N$) results in a shallower depth of field." ]

title: Depth of Field
one_liner: Depth of field is the region around the focal plane where the resulting blur on the sensor is smaller than a specified tolerance.
content: The region around the plane of focus that results in a blur at the sensor plane that is smaller than some tolerance is called the depth of field. We can calculate the depth of field from geometric optics.
motivation_md: Understanding depth of field is crucial for controlling which parts of a scene are in focus, a key creative and technical aspect of photography.
recap_md: [ "- It defines the range of distances where objects appear acceptably sharp.", "- It is determined by the tolerance for the size of the circle of confusion." ]

title: f-number
one_liner: The f-number $N$ is the ratio of a lens's focal length to its aperture diameter.
content: A camera's f-number, written $N$, is the ratio of the focal length of the lens divided by the diameter of the lens that light passes through, called the aperture, $A$: $N = f/A$.
motivation_md: The f-number provides a standardized way to describe the light-gathering ability and depth of field characteristics of a lens, independent of its absolute size.
recap_md: [ "- The f-number $N$ is calculated as the ratio $f/A$.", "- It relates the focal length to the physical size of the aperture opening." ]

title: Aperture
one_liner: The aperture is the diameter of the lens opening through which light passes.
content: The aperture, $A$, is the diameter of the lens through which light passes. It is used to define the camera's f-number $N$, which is the ratio of the focal length $f$ divided by the aperture: $N = f/A$.
motivation_md: Controlling the aperture allows for the regulation of the amount of light reaching the sensor and the manipulation of the depth of field.
recap_md: [ "- Aperture is the physical diameter of the opening that admits light into the camera.", "- It is inversely proportional to the f-number for a given focal length." ]

title: Image Output Layer
one_liner: A sigmoid transformation scaled by 255 is a common output layer for image synthesis problems to map values to the standard RGB range.
content:
In image synthesis problems, the desired output is typically a 3D array with dimensions $N \times M \times 3$, and values in the range $[0,255]$. A sigmoid multiplied by 255 is a typical output transformation for this setting. The equation for this layer is:

$$\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{out}}}[i] = 255*\texttt{sigmoid}(\textcolor[rgb]{1.0, 0.4, 0.38}{x_{\texttt{in}}}[i])$$

This is a common layer for image output problems.
motivation_md: Standard image formats represent color values in the range [0, 255]. Since raw neural network outputs can be any real number, a specific transformation is needed to squash and scale these values into the valid range for image visualization.
recap_md:
- Use a sigmoid function to squash raw inputs into a [0, 1] range.
- Multiply by 255 to map the output to the standard 8-bit color intensity range.

title: Softmax Temperature Parameter
one_liner: The temperature parameter $\textcolor[rgb]{0.2, 0.6, 1.0}{\tau}$ is used to scale how peaky or confident the softmax predictions are.
content: In the softmax definition, a temperature parameter $\textcolor[rgb]{0.2, 0.6, 1.0}{\tau}$ is added. This parameter is used to scale how peaky, or confident, the predictions are.
motivation_md: By adjusting the temperature, we can control the entropy of the output distribution, making it either more uniform or more concentrated on the highest-scoring class.
recap_md:
- The parameter $\tau$ scales the confidence of the softmax output.
- Higher temperatures lead to smoother distributions, while lower temperatures make predictions more 'peaky'.

title: Translating Neural Network Outputs
one_liner: Using neural network outputs in practice requires translating them into actual pictures, actions, or decisions.
content: The output layer is the input to the loss function, completing the specification of the deep learning problem. However, using the outputs in practice requires translating them into actual pictures, actions, or decisions. For a classification problem, this might mean taking the argmax of the softmax distribution to report a single class. For image prediction problems, it might mean rounding each output to an integral value since common image formats represent RGB values as integers.
motivation_md: Neural networks output continuous numerical values, but real-world applications often require discrete categories or specific data formats like integers for pixels.
recap_md:
- Classification outputs are often converted to a single class using the argmax function.
- Image outputs may require rounding to integers to match standard RGB formats.

title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

one_liner: Neural networks are effective because they are high capacity, differentiable, possess good inductive biases, run efficiently on parallel hardware, and build abstractions.
content:
Almost all modern computer vision algorithms involve deep nets because they are a good architecture for five primary reasons:

1. They are high capacity (big enough nets are universal approximators).
2. They are differentiable (the parameters can be optimized via gradient descent).
3. They have good inductive biases (neural architectures reflect real structure in the world).
4. They run efficiently on parallel hardware.
5. They build abstractions.
motivation_md: Understanding why neural networks dominate modern AI helps in choosing the right tools and architectures for complex problems like computer vision.
recap_md:
- Neural networks are universal approximators that can be optimized using gradients.
- Their design reflects real-world structures and allows for efficient parallel computation.

title: Neural Network Capacity

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

one_liner: Neural networks have high capacity, meaning large networks can span a massive hypothesis space to find true solutions.
content: Neural networks are high capacity. This relates to the size of the hypothesis space, which can be made very big if we use a large neural network with many parameters. Because of this, we can usually be sure that our true solution (or a close approximation to it) does indeed lie in the space spanned by the neural net architecture.
motivation_md: To solve complex problems, a model must be flexible enough to represent the underlying function; high capacity ensures the model isn't too simple to find the truth.
recap_md:
- High capacity allows for a very large hypothesis space.
- Large networks are likely to contain the true solution or a close approximation within their span.

title: Universal Approximators

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

one_liner: Sufficiently large neural networks are universal approximators, capable of representing a wide range of functions.
content: Neural networks are high capacity; big enough nets are universal approximators.
motivation_md: This theoretical property guarantees that, given enough parameters, a neural network can represent any continuous function, justifying their use for complex tasks.
recap_md:
- Large neural networks have the capacity to approximate any function.
- This property is a core reason for the versatility of deep learning architectures.

title: Differentiability of Neural Networks

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

one_liner: Neural networks are differentiable, allowing their parameters to be optimized via gradient descent.
content: Neural networks are differentiable, meaning the parameters can be optimized via gradient descent. Searching for the solution within the hypothesis space is relatively easy since we can use gradients to direct us toward ever better fits to the data.
motivation_md: Without differentiability, searching for the optimal parameters in a high-dimensional space would be computationally infeasible.
recap_md:
- Differentiability enables the use of gradient-based optimization.
- Gradients provide a direction to improve the model's fit to the data efficiently.

title: Inductive Biases in Neural Networks

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

one_liner: Neural networks have good inductive biases, meaning their architectures reflect real-world structures to improve generalization.
content: Neural networks have good inductive biases; their architectures reflect real structure in the world. These architectures impose constraints and regularizers that bias the search toward solutions that capture true structure about the visual world, leading to learned solutions that generalize well.
motivation_md: Purely data-driven search is difficult; inductive biases help the model focus on patterns that are likely to be true in reality, such as spatial locality in images.
recap_md:
- Inductive biases reflect real-world structures within the network architecture.
- These biases act as constraints that help the model generalize to new data.

title: Dataset Bias
one_liner: Dataset bias occurs when training data represents only a specific slice of the world, often influenced by the background of researchers.
content: One cause of algorithmic bias can be a bias in the contents of the training dataset. Any dataset represents only one slice of the possible images and labels that one could capture from the world, and the samples taken may be influenced by the background of the researchers gathering the dataset. For example, common objects from households across the globe show that image recognition performance is often significantly better for first-world households, likely due to better representation of such imagery in training datasets. (see figure: Images of household items, and their recognized classes by five object recognition systems @DeVries2019. The systems tend to perform worse for non-Western countries and for lower-income households...) As shown in the household item examples, systems tend to perform worse for non-Western countries and for lower-income households.
motivation_md: Machine learning models inherit the limitations of their training data. Understanding dataset bias is essential for identifying why models fail for certain demographics and for developing more equitable AI systems.
recap_md: - Dataset bias arises when training data represents only a limited slice of real-world diversity.

title: Fairness GAN
one_liner: Fairness GAN is an algorithm that includes a classifier trained to perform poorly on predicting protected attributes to improve dataset fairness.
content: Fairness GAN is an algorithm that includes a classifier trained to perform as poorly as possible on predicting the classification result based on a protected attribute. For example, the algorithm can be designed to predict an attractiveness label while gaining no benefit from knowing the gender or skin tone of the subject. This approach produces a debiased dataset that shows improvement in various fairness metrics.
motivation_md: This technique was developed to remove correlations between target labels and protected attributes like gender or race, ensuring that models trained on the data do not rely on sensitive characteristics.
recap_md: - Fairness GAN uses a classifier designed to fail at identifying protected attributes.

title: GAN-based Data Augmentation
one_liner: GAN-based data augmentation removes correlations between protected attributes and target labels by generating balanced pairs of realistic images.
content: This approach addresses the problem of removing correlations between a protected attribute and a target label by using GANs to generate pairs of realistic-looking images that are balanced with respect to each protected attribute. For instance, if "wearing hat" is a protected attribute correlated with "wearing glasses," a GAN can augment the dataset with paired examples of people wearing hats both with and without glasses. When this augmented dataset is combined with the original dataset, performance in a variety of fairness measures is improved. ![In this example “wears hat” is deemed to be a protected attribute, but it is correlated with another attribute, which in this example is “wears glasses” @Ramaswamy2021. The GAN-based method generates sets of images where wearing hats is not correlated with wearing glasses.](figures/fairness/augmentation.jpg){#fig-augmentation}
motivation_md: Standard datasets often contain accidental correlations between attributes. GAN-based augmentation allows researchers to synthesize missing data combinations, creating a more balanced training set that prevents models from learning biased associations.
recap_md: - GANs generate synthetic image pairs to balance the representation of protected attributes.

title: Counterfactual Analysis
one_liner: Counterfactual analysis disentangles algorithmic and dataset bias by modifying specific variables in probe images and observing the resulting changes in decisions.
content: Counterfactual analysis is a method used to distinguish whether a biased result is caused by algorithmic bias or by biases in the testing dataset. This is achieved through experimentation, specifically by modifying variables of a probe image and examining the algorithm's decision. GAN models, when coupled with human labeling to learn directions in the latent space corresponding to changes in desired attributes, allow for such experimental intervention. These studies provide a clean assessment of bias related to a modified variable by observing variations in classification results along a transect. (see figure: A GAN creates sequences of faces, called **transects**, where only one attribute changes @Balakrishnan2020)
motivation_md: It is often unclear if a model's failure is due to its internal logic or a skewed test set. Counterfactual analysis allows researchers to isolate specific variables to see exactly how they influence a model's output.
recap_md: - Counterfactual analysis uses GANs to modify single attributes while keeping others constant.

title: Transects
one_liner: Transects are paths through a GAN's latent space where only one specific variable is modified while others remain constant.
content: In the context of GANs and counterfactual reasoning, transects are paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable or attribute is modified. The variation in an algorithm's classification results along the images of the transect provides a clean assessment of any bias related to the variable being modified. (see figure: A GAN creates sequences of faces, called **transects**, where only one attribute changes @Balakrishnan2020)
motivation_md: Transects provide a controlled way to visualize and test how a machine learning model responds to incremental changes in a single feature, which is essential for identifying specific biases.
recap_md: - A transect is a sequence of images generated by moving along a single dimension in a GAN's latent space.

title: Differential Privacy
one_liner: Differential privacy allows extracting aggregated information about a population from a database without revealing information about any single individual.
content: **Differential privacy** allows extracting aggregated information about a population from a database without revealing information about any single individual.
motivation_md: As data collection becomes more pervasive, protecting individual privacy while still allowing for meaningful statistical analysis is a critical challenge in data science and ethics.
recap_md: - Differential privacy focuses on population-level insights rather than individual data.

title: Differential Privacy Framework
one_liner: The differential privacy framework guarantees that study participants are not affected by their data usage, regardless of other available information sources.
content: Differential privacy is a theoretical framework that guarantees participants in a study will not be affected by allowing their data to be used, regardless of what other studies, datasets, or information sources are available. One approach to meeting this guarantee is to inject enough randomness into each recorded observation to ensure no individual's data can be reconstructed, while still allowing scientific conclusions to be formed by averaging over many samples. For example, a survey on sensitive topics might instruct participants to flip a coin: if heads, they answer truthfully; if tails, they answer randomly. While this protects individuals even if data is leaked or hacked, it requires collecting more data to maintain the same accuracy guarantees for population averages.
motivation_md: This framework solves the problem of linkage attacks where anonymized data is deanonymized by combining it with other datasets, providing a mathematical guarantee of privacy.
recap_md: - Randomness is injected into data to prevent the reconstruction of individual records.

title: Light Ray
one_liner: A light ray is an abstraction describing electromagnetic radiation heading in a particular direction from a specific location in space.
content: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation that exhibits wave effects like diffraction. However, for many imaging models, it is helpful to introduce the abstraction of a **light ray**, which describes light radiation heading in a particular direction from a particular location in space (@fig-lightSpray). A light ray is specified by its position, direction, and intensity as a function of wavelength and polarization. In this geometric treatment, diffraction effects are ignored. ![A light ray from the sun strikes a surface and generates outgoing rays of intensity and color depending on the angles of the incoming and outgoing rays relative to the surface orientation.](figures/imaging/brdf.png){#fig-lightSpray width="75%"}
motivation_md: Modeling light as waves is computationally complex. The light ray abstraction simplifies optics by treating light as straight lines, making it easier to calculate reflections and image formation.
recap_md: - A light ray is defined by its position, direction, and intensity.

title: Infomax Representations

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: Infomax representations capture as much information as possible about the input signal within neural activations.
content: Infomax representations are designed to capture, in the neural activations, as much information as possible about the input signal.
motivation_md: The goal is to ensure that the internal representations of a neural network retain the maximum amount of relevant information from the original input signal for downstream processing.
recap_md: - Aim to maximize the information captured in neural activations.

title: Tensor

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: A tensor is a multidimensional array and serves as the primary data structure in deep learning.
content: The main data structure in deep learning is the tensor, which is a multidimensional array. In general, everything in deep learning is represented as tensors: the input, activations, weights, and outputs. If data is not natively represented as a tensor, the first step before feeding it to a deep net is to convert it into a tensor format. Most often, these tensors consist of real numbers, where the elements are in $\mathbb{R}$.
motivation_md: Deep learning requires a unified mathematical framework to handle high-dimensional data, parameters, and signals. Tensors provide a consistent structure for these operations.
recap_md: - Tensors are multidimensional arrays used to represent all data in deep learning.

title: Channels

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: Channels refer to the number of neurons in a layer, analogous to color channels in an input image.
content: The activations in a network are represented as tensors. For Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks, the activation tensors have shape $N \times C_{\ell}$, where $C_{\ell}$ is the number of neurons on layer $\ell$. These are sometimes called channels in analogy to the color channels of an input image. In other architectures, such as convolutional networks, activation layers may have additional dimensions, resulting in shapes like $N \times C_{\ell} \times H_{\ell} \times W_{\ell}$.
motivation_md: The term 'channels' helps generalize the concept of feature dimensions across different types of neural network architectures, from simple vectors to complex image volumes.
recap_md: - Channels represent the number of neurons or feature dimensions in a specific layer.

title: Batch

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: A batch is a collection of training samples processed in parallel through a neural network.
content: Normally, neural networks do not process one image at a time; instead, they run a batch of images all at once, processed in parallel. A batch sampled from the training data can be denoted as $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\texttt{batch}}}$. When represented as a tensor, the batch has shape $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C_0 \times H \times W}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times K}$.
motivation_md: Processing data in batches improves computational efficiency through parallelization and provides a more stable estimate of the gradient during training compared to single-sample updates.
recap_md: - Batches allow for parallel processing of multiple data samples.

title: Linear Layers
one_liner: Linear layers are the primary components of deep nets, containing almost all parameters in the form of weights and biases.
motivation_md: Linear layers provide the fundamental transformation that allows a network to learn relationships between inputs and outputs by adjusting weights and biases.
recap_md: - Linear layers contain the learnable weights and biases of a network.

title: Activation Layers
one_liner: Activation layers add nonlinearity to a network by applying pointwise scalar-to-scalar mappings.
content:
(see figure: Common pointwise nonlinearities.)

If a net only contained linear layers, it could only compute linear functions because the composition of $N$ linear functions is a linear function. Activation layers add nonlinearity. These layers are typically pointwise functions, applying a scalar-to-scalar mapping on each dimension of the input vector. Typically, parameters of these layers, if any, are not learned, though they can be.
motivation_md: Without nonlinearity, a multi-layer network would be mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer, severely limiting its ability to model complex data.
recap_md: - Activation layers introduce nonlinearity to the model.

title: Threshold Activation
one_liner: The threshold activation is a pointwise function that outputs 1 if the input is positive and 0 otherwise.
motivation_md: This function acts as a hard switch, mimicking the 'all-or-nothing' firing behavior of biological neurons.
recap_md: - Outputs 1 for positive inputs and 0 for non-positive inputs.

title: Sigmoid Activation
one_liner: The sigmoid activation is a pointwise function that maps input values to a range between 0 and 1.
motivation_md: The sigmoid function provides a smooth, differentiable alternative to the threshold function, mapping any real-valued input into the $(0, 1)$ interval, which can be interpreted as a probability.
recap_md: - Maps inputs to a smooth curve between 0 and 1.

title: Accidents Happen
one_liner: Accidental alignments occur when unrelated object contours line up from a specific viewpoint, violating the Gestalt principle of continuity.
content: In computer vision, the generic view principle suggests we assume observations are not due to coincidental viewpoints. However, in photographs containing thousands of tiny images, accidents are common. These coincidences often involve the principle of continuity: generically, if you see smooth, continuous line segments, you assume they lie on a single object because it is a significant coincidence for two separate objects to line up their contours exactly. (see figure: Source: Migrant Mother (1936), by Dorothea Lange. On the right are four examples of coincidences that violate the Gestalt principle of continuity. From top-left clockwise: finger boundary aligns with lip contour, cloth aligns with eye, creases align on two different shirts, sleeve boundary is tangent to line on a different shirt.) For example, in Dorothea Lange's "Migrant Mother," a finger boundary may align with a lip contour, or creases may align across two different shirts. Vision algorithms must be developed carefully to handle these exceptions, as older rule-based methods often failed by assuming such accidents would never occur.
motivation_md: In computer vision, we often rely on the 'generic viewpoint' assumption—that what we see isn't a fluke of our specific position. However, real-world images are so complex that accidental alignments happen frequently. Understanding these 'accidents' is crucial for building robust algorithms that don't get fooled by coincidental visual overlaps.
recap_md: - Accidental alignments occur when separate objects appear continuous due to a specific camera viewpoint.

title: Cues for Support
one_liner: Visual cues such as drop shadows and string tension help determine whether an object is supported by or in contact with a surface.
content: We can often tell by looking whether one object supports another based on specific visual evidence. The relative location between an object and its shadow on the ground is a powerful cue for contact. (see figure: Cues for support. The relative location between an object, and its shadow on the ground is a powerful cue for contact.) For instance, a drop shadow provides a strong cue that an object is above a surface, while a slack string can provide evidence that an object is resting on the surface.
motivation_md: Determining physical contact and support between objects is a fundamental task for spatial reasoning. By identifying cues like shadows and mechanical tension, vision systems can infer the 3D relationships and physical stability of a scene from 2D images.
recap_md: - Drop shadows indicate the distance between an object and the surface below it.

title: Light Field Cameras
one_liner: Light field cameras use an array of tiny lenses to capture a scene from hundreds of different viewing angles simultaneously.
content: Specially designed cameras called light field cameras capture what a scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles. While a raindrop can naturally refract a panorama of its surroundings, these cameras use an array of tiny lenses to achieve a similar effect. (see figure: A naturally occurring light field camera. This picture of raindrops on a window contains hundreds of tiny images of the scene, one in each raindrop. The images to the right are individual zoomed in raindrops from the photo on the left.) From this high density of information, light field cameras can perform advanced tasks such as triangulating the depth of objects and synthetically refocusing an image after it has been captured.
motivation_md: Standard cameras collapse all light hitting a pixel into a single value, losing directional information. Light field cameras preserve the direction of incoming light rays, allowing for post-capture adjustments like refocusing and depth estimation that are impossible with traditional photography.
recap_md: - Light field cameras capture a scene from multiple viewpoints using micro-lens arrays.

title: Plato's Cave Allegory
one_liner: Plato's Allegory of the Cave serves as a metaphor for how images are crude 2D projections of a much richer 3D reality.
content: In the Allegory of the Cave, Plato imagined prisoners whose only experience of reality is through shadows cast on a wall. Looking at images is similar: an image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state, collapsing 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded, and materials are only depicted by how photons bounce off their surfaces, omitting what lies beneath. One job of a vision system is to infer the unseen reality from the limited information provided by the projection. The allegory involves layers of indirection, where shadows are cast by puppets controlled by puppeteers acting out interpretations of a broader reality.
motivation_md: This philosophical metaphor highlights the 'inverse problem' of computer vision: we must reconstruct a complex, three-dimensional world from limited, two-dimensional, and often occluded visual data.
recap_md: - Images are 2D projections that collapse 3D geometry and occlude most of the scene.

title: Material Recognition: Wetness

position.section_title: How Do You Know Something Is Wet?

one_liner: The visual system can recognize materials and states like wetness by interpreting changes in appearance, such as darkening.
content: Our visual system allows us to recognize materials and their properties, such as whether something is hot, cold, soft, hard, or wet, without physical contact. (see figure: Why does wet sand look dark? The answer to this question is interesting, but not as much as the question itself.) For example, we can distinguish wet sand from dry sand because wet sand typically looks darker. A key challenge for vision is determining whether a surface is dark because it is wet or because it is under a shadow.
motivation_md: Recognizing material properties is essential for interacting with the world safely and effectively. Understanding why wetness changes an object's appearance helps in developing algorithms that can distinguish between material changes and lighting changes.
recap_md: - Visual systems identify material states like wetness through appearance cues like darkening.

title: Algorithmic Fairness
one_liner: Algorithmic Fairness is the study of ensuring algorithms perform equitably across different people, groups, and cultures without reflecting or creating biases.
content: The field of Algorithmic Fairness studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures. It seeks to address algorithmic biases and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms do not reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures.
motivation_md: As computer vision systems are deployed in society, it is critical to ensure they do not discriminate. This field provides the tools and frameworks to measure, understand, and mitigate disparate impacts on different demographic groups.
recap_md: - Algorithmic Fairness aims to identify and mitigate biases in computational models.

title: Facial Detection
one_liner: Facial detection is the process of determining whether a face exists within a specific region of an image.
content: Facial detection asks whether there is a face in some image region.
motivation_md: Facial detection is the foundational first step for any face-related task, such as recognition, emotion analysis, or filtering, by locating the relevant pixels for further processing.
recap_md: - Facial detection identifies the presence and location of faces in an image.

title: Facial Analysis
one_liner: Facial analysis involves measuring attributes of a face, such as pose and identity, and evaluating system performance across demographic groups.
content: Facial analysis refers to measuring additional attributes of the face, including pose and identity. It is important to characterize the performance of facial analysis systems across demographic groups. Studies, such as the Face Recognition Vendor Test by NIST, have examined the accuracy of face recognition algorithms across sex, age, and race. These studies found that false positive rates can vary significantly—sometimes by a factor of 100—between different demographic groups. It is essential to report both false negative and false positive rates for each group to understand the biases of any facial analysis system in use.
motivation_md: Beyond simply finding a face, we often need to know who the person is or what they are doing. However, these systems can have vastly different accuracy rates for different populations, making rigorous bias analysis a requirement for ethical deployment.
recap_md: - Facial analysis extracts specific traits like identity and pose from a detected face.

title: Feedback Connections
one_liner: Feedback connections are neural inputs to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) originating from the primary visual cortex and other higher-order brain areas.
content: While the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) receives input from the retina, 95 percent of the LGN inputs are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
motivation_md: Feedback connections allow higher-level cortical processing to modulate or filter sensory information at earlier stages, such as the LGN, before it reaches the cortex.
recap_md:
- Feedback connections originate in the primary visual cortex and other areas.
- They constitute 95 percent of the inputs to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).

title: Visual Cortex
one_liner: The visual cortex is a region of the brain where cells exhibit complex responses and specialized processing beyond the concentric receptive fields found in early visual stages.
content: Concentric receptive fields are very common in the early layers of visual processing, but things become more interesting when studying cells in the visual cortex. One challenge was that the techniques used to record the responses of cells in the optic nerve could not be applied to record the activity of cells in the cortex.
motivation_md: The visual cortex exists to transform basic retinal signals into complex representations of the visual world, such as edges, shapes, and motion.
recap_md:
- The visual cortex processes information beyond the early stages of the optic nerve.
- Cells in the cortex exhibit more complex response properties than concentric receptive fields.

title: Oriented Simple Cell
one_liner: An oriented simple cell is a visual cortex neuron that increases its firing rate when stimulated by a bar of light at a specific preferred orientation.
content:
An oriented simple cell shows increased firing rate when stimulated with an oriented bar in the positive region of the receptive field (RF) with the preferred orientation. These cells are found in the visual cortex and come in different types, as illustrated in the following figure:

(see figure: Receptive fields (RF) for retinal ganglion cells and oriented receptive fields from the primary visual system. (a) ON-center RF. (b) OFF-center RF. (c-d) Two types of oriented simple cell. (e) Sketch of the response of the cell from (c) to an oriented bar with different orientations in the center of its RF. The gray bar corresponds to the moment the bar is visible.)
motivation_md: Oriented simple cells are the building blocks of edge detection, allowing the visual system to identify the orientation of boundaries in an image.
recap_md:
- Oriented simple cells are found in the visual cortex.
- They respond most strongly to bars of light at a specific preferred orientation.

title: V1
one_liner: V1, or the primary visual cortex, is the first cortical area for visual processing, organized into layers and functional columns.
content:
The first visual area in the visual cortex is called V1. It is a sheet of neurons arranged along several layers. Neurons in V1 are organized along columns. When probing with an electrode from the surface to the bottom of V1, all the cells found are selective to the same orientation. Moving the electrode along one horizontal direction reveals that the preferred orientation changes smoothly (orientation columns). Moving the electrode along the perpendicular horizontal direction shows that cells change eye preference, alternating between the two eyes with some binocular cells between them (ocular dominance columns). A section of around 1 $\times$ 3 mm (called a hypercolumn) covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field.

(see figure: Visual pathways. The retina projects the axons of the ganglion cells into the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). In each hemisphere, the LGN gets inputs from both eyes (the LGN on the right gets the right side of each retina, which corresponds to the left side of the visual field). The output of the LGN is divided into three channels; the parvocellular, magnocellural, and koniocellular (not shown). Those channels project into the primary visual cortex following a very regular architecture organized along hypercolumns. The koniocellular pathway projects into the color blobs in the upper layer of the visual cortex. Figure modified from @kandel-neural.)
motivation_md: V1 serves as the primary entry point for visual information into the cortex, where it is organized systematically to facilitate the extraction of basic features like orientation and binocular depth.
recap_md:
