one_liner: Data, priors, and hypothesis spaces are interchangeable tools that all serve to constrain the search for a solution.
content: Data, priors, and hypotheses all constrain the search for a mapping by ruling out parts of the full space. A general principle is that what can be achieved with any one of these tools can also be achieved with any other. However, they differ in the nature of the constraint: the hypothesis space places hard constraints that cannot be violated, while data and priors apply soft constraints that can be violated at the cost of a penalty. If data is scarce, one can use strong priors or structural constraints; if domain knowledge is lacking, one can collect more data. As Ilya Sutskever noted, 'methods ... are extra training data in disguise.'
motivation_md: This principle highlights the flexibility in machine learning design. It suggests that there are multiple ways to solve a problem—either through better architecture, more data, or smarter regularization.
recap_md: [RECAP_MD]

title: Dimensionality Reduction

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

one_liner: Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data and activations to a lower dimensionality, such as 2D, to enable visualization of deep representations.
content:
Deep representations are typically much higher-dimensional than 1D or 2D data distributions. To visualize them, we apply tools from dimensionality reduction. These tools project high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. For example, techniques like t-SNE can map 38,400-dimensional embeddings down to 2D to provide a rough view of how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
motivation_md: Deep neural networks operate in extremely high-dimensional spaces (often tens of thousands of dimensions), making it impossible for humans to visualize the internal representations directly. Dimensionality reduction solves this by compressing these representations into 2D or 3D while attempting to preserve the relative distances and structure of the data, allowing researchers to see how the network clusters or separates different semantic classes.
recap_md: - Projects high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional spaces (like 2D) for visualization.

title: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

one_liner: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize high-dimensional embeddings by mapping them to 2D.
content:
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset. It projects high-dimensional data (such as 38,400-dimensional embeddings) to a lower dimensionality, like 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective of such tools is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. In visualizations using t-SNE, different colors often represent different semantic classes, showing how the network remaps input images into disentangled representations.

(see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...)
motivation_md: t-SNE is specifically designed to handle the visualization of complex, high-dimensional datasets where local structure is important. It helps researchers understand how deep learning models, like Transformers, organize data internally by creating 2D maps where similar inputs are grouped together.
recap_md: - Maps high-dimensional embeddings to 2D for visual analysis.

title: Computation Graph
one_liner: A computation graph is a visualization of a neural network as a sequence of modular blocks or layers chained together.
content:
A key idea of neural nets is to decompose computation into a series of layers. In this context, we think of layers as modular blocks that can be chained together into a computation graph. For example, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be visualized as a sequence of these layers.

(see figure: In this chapter we will visualize neural nets as a sequence of layers, which we call a computation graph.)
motivation_md: Decomposing complex mathematical functions into a graph of simpler operations makes it easier to implement automatic differentiation and organize the architecture of deep learning models.
recap_md: - Represents neural networks as a sequence of modular layers.

title: Forward Pass
one_liner: The forward pass is the process where a layer takes inputs and transforms them into outputs, potentially using parameters.
content:
Each layer takes in some inputs and transforms them into some outputs. We call this the $\texttt{forward}$ pass through the layer. If the layer has parameters, we consider the parameters to be an input to a parameter-free transformation:

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}},\theta)
\end{aligned}$$

Graphically, the forward operation of a layer depicts the flow from input and parameters to the output.

(see figure: Forward operation of a neural net layer.)
motivation_md: The forward pass is the fundamental execution step of a neural network, where data flows from the input through various transformations to produce a prediction or result.
recap_md: - Transforms inputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and parameters $\theta$ into outputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$.

title: Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

position.section_title: The Trick of Backpropagation: Reuse of Computation

one_liner: Backpropagation is a dynamic programming strategy that reuses shared terms in the chain rule to efficiently compute gradients for all parameters.
motivation_md: Calculating gradients independently for every parameter in a deep network would be computationally prohibitive. By recognizing that the chain rule involves redundant multiplications, backpropagation allows us to compute all necessary gradients in a single backward sweep, drastically reducing the computational cost.
recap_md: - Identifies shared terms in the chain rule across different parameter gradients.

title: Backward for a Generic Layer
one_liner: The backward function for a generic layer computes local gradients and propagates error signals using a recurrence relation.
content:
To implement backpropagation, we look at a generic layer in isolation to determine how to update its parameters. We define two key arrays of partial derivatives: $\mathbf{g}_l \triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l}$ (the gradient of the cost with respect to the layer output) and $\mathbf{L}$, the gradient of the layer with respect to its inputs ($\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}$) and parameters ($\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$).

(see figure: A generic layer in the computation graph. The braces represent the part of the computation graph we need to consider in order to evaluate $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{g}in$.)

The gradient needed to update $\theta$ is computed as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\theta}
\end{aligned}$$

Computing $\mathbf{L}$ is a local process requiring the functional form of the derivative $f^{\prime}$ evaluated at the operating point. Computing $\mathbf{g}$ is done iteratively via a recurrence relation:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} \end{aligned}$$

This recurrence is the essence of backprop, sending error signals backward through the network. The full `backward` function takes $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ as inputs and produces $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$ as outputs.
motivation_md: By defining a standard interface for a 'backward' pass at the layer level, deep learning frameworks can automatically compute gradients for any complex architecture by simply composing these modular blocks.
recap_md: - Computes parameter gradients $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}$ using local layer gradients $\mathbf{L}^{\theta}$.

title: The Full Backpropagation Algorithm

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm consists of a forward pass to compute activations followed by a backward pass to compute gradients.
content:
The full backpropagation algorithm requires ordering operations so that the necessary arrays for updates are ready. First, we compute a forward pass through the entire network, starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.

(see figure: Forward pass.)

Next, we compute a backward pass, iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ and obtaining the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer.

(see figure: A schematic diagram of the backpropagation process in a neural network. Red arrows flow from right to left, starting with a value of 1 entering a loss derivative block $\mathcal{L}'$, then passing...)
motivation_md: To update a network's weights, we need the values of the internal activations (from the forward pass) and the error signals (from the backward pass). This two-step process ensures all required information is available for the gradient calculations.
recap_md: - Performs a forward pass to generate activations $\mathbf{x}_l$.

title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
one_liner: Backpropagation in batch mode computes the average gradient over a set of datapoints to update model parameters.
motivation_md: Training on single examples is noisy and inefficient. Batch mode allows for more stable gradient estimates and takes advantage of parallel hardware (like GPUs) to speed up the training process.
recap_md: - Computes gradients for multiple datapoints simultaneously.

title: Merge Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

one_liner: The merge operator mathematically concatenates two input variables into a single multidimensional output variable.
content: The merge operator is defined mathematically as variable concatenation: $$\texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$$ This results in a new multidimensional variable. The backward pass equation is straightforward. To compute the gradient of the cost with respect to $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}$, denoted as $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$, we have: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^{a} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}^a} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\\ &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\Big[\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\Big]^\mathsf{T}\\ &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[1, 0]^\mathsf{T} \end{aligned}$$ and likewise for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$. In practice, this means we pick out the first half of the $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ gradient vector for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ and the second half for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$. The merge operator provides an explicit way of constructing multidimensional variables within the framework of backpropagation.
motivation_md: In complex neural architectures, it is often necessary to combine information from different paths. The merge operator formalizes how multiple inputs are concatenated into a single vector and how gradients are correctly routed back to their respective sources during training.
recap_md: - The merge operator concatenates two or more input vectors into a single multidimensional output vector.

title: Branch Operator

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

one_liner: The branch operator sends copies of a single input to multiple downstream nodes, resulting in the summation of their gradients during the backward pass.
content: The branch operator is defined mathematically as variable copying: $$\texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$$ In branching, copies of the same output are sent to multiple downstream nodes. Consequently, multiple gradients come back to the branch module from different downstream paths. The inputs to this module on the backward pass are $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}$, which can be written as the gradient vector $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$. The backward pass output is computed as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}&= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}\\ &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\ &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\ &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b][1, 1]^\mathsf{T}\\ &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b \end{aligned}$$ Thus, branching simply sums both the gradients passed backward to it.
motivation_md: When a single variable or parameter is used in multiple parts of a model, we need a way to aggregate the influence it has on the final loss. The branch operator explains why gradients from different paths should be added together.
recap_md: - Branching involves sending identical copies of an input to multiple downstream paths.

title: Parameter Sharing
one_liner: Parameter sharing involves sending a single parameter as input to multiple different layers, causing gradients to summate during backpropagation.
content: Parameter sharing consists of a single parameter being sent as input to multiple different layers. This can be considered a branching operation. (see figure: Parameter sharing is equivalent to branching a parameter in the computation graph.) Because it functions as a branch, gradients summate for shared parameters. If $\{\theta^i\}^N_{i=1}$ is a set of variables that are all copies of one free parameter $\theta$, then: $$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i \frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta^i}$$
motivation_md: Parameter sharing reduces the number of unique parameters a model must learn, which can improve efficiency and act as a form of regularization. It is a fundamental concept in architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks.
recap_md: - Parameter sharing is mathematically equivalent to a branching operation in a computation graph.

title: Backpropagation to the Data
one_liner: Backpropagation treats parameters and data symmetrically, allowing the optimization of input data to minimize a loss function just like model parameters.
content: Backpropagation does not distinguish between parameters and data; it treats both as generic inputs to parameterless modules. Consequently, backprop can be used to optimize data inputs to the graph just like it is used to optimize parameter inputs. In the forward direction of the full computation graph, the inputs are the data and parameter settings, and the output is the loss. In the backward direction, the input is the number 1 and the outputs are the gradients of the loss with respect to both the data and parameters. For a learning problem using a neural net $F = f_L \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ and loss function $\mathcal{L}$, the full graph is $J(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{y}, \theta) \triangleq \mathcal{L}(F(\mathbf{x}_0), \mathbf{y}, \theta)$. This function can be viewed as a single computation block. (see figure: Full forward and backward passes for a learning problem $\min J(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y},\theta)$, collapsed into a single computation block.) Data inputs and parameter inputs play symmetric roles: just as we optimize parameters to minimize loss by descending the parameter gradient, we can optimize input data by descending the data gradient.
motivation_md: While backpropagation is usually associated with updating weights, the same mathematical machinery can be applied to the input itself. This allows for techniques like generating adversarial examples or visualizing what a network has learned.
recap_md: - Backpropagation treats data and parameters as symmetric inputs to the computation graph.

title: Visualizing Neuron Activation
one_liner: Input visualization uses backpropagation to find the input image that most activates a specific neuron, revealing the visual features the neuron is sensitive to.
content: Backpropagation to the data can be used to visualize the input image that most activates a specific neuron in a neural net. To do this, we define the cost $J$ to be the negative of the value of the probed neuron: $J(\mathbf{x}_0,\theta) = -x_{l}[i]$ for the $i$-th neuron on layer $l$. (see figure: Visualizing the optimal image of a cat according to a particular neural net. The net we used is called Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) @radford2021learning and here we found the image...) Such visualizations are a useful way to determine what visual features a given neuron is sensitive to. Researchers often combine this method with a natural image prior to find images that strongly activate the neuron while still looking like natural photographs.
motivation_md: Neural networks are often seen as 'black boxes.' Visualizing the inputs that maximize specific activations helps researchers interpret what features (like edges, textures, or objects) different parts of the network are actually looking for.
recap_md: - To visualize a neuron's preference, we minimize the negative of its activation value using backpropagation to the input.

title: Low-level Features
one_liner: Low-level features are mathematically simple tokens extracted from an image that serve as the building blocks for higher-level visual interpretations.
content: In building vision systems, we aim to parse an image into useful tokens or low-level features. These features are mathematically simple processing results that serve as the initial stages of visual processing, similar to how the human visual system operates. These tokens are essential for later constructing complex visual interpretations of the real world.
motivation_md: Raw pixel data is too complex to interpret directly. By extracting low-level features like edges or simple textures, we simplify the data into a format that higher-level algorithms can use to recognize objects and scenes.
recap_md: - Low-level features are simple mathematical tokens extracted during the initial stages of image processing.

title: Signal Processing
one_liner: Signal processing provides the essential mathematical tools for computer vision and image processing tasks.
content: Signal processing provides essential tools for computer vision scientists. It involves the study and application of mathematical techniques to analyze and modify signals, presented here specifically from a computer vision and image processing perspective.
motivation_md: Images are essentially two-dimensional signals. Understanding signal processing allows us to perform fundamental operations like noise reduction, sharpening, and feature extraction in a mathematically rigorous way.
recap_md: - Signal processing is a foundational field providing tools for analyzing and manipulating data in computer vision.

title: Signal
one_liner: A signal is a measurement of a physical quantity as a function of another independent quantity, such as time or space.
content: A signal is a measurement of some physical quantity (such as light, sound, height, or temperature) as a function of another independent quantity (such as time, space, wavelength, etc.).
motivation_md: Defining a 'signal' allows us to treat diverse types of data—like audio recordings or digital images—under a unified mathematical framework.
recap_md: - A signal maps an independent variable (like space or time) to a physical measurement (like light intensity).

title: Edge Normal Vector

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: The unit norm vector perpendicular to an edge is defined as the gradient of the edge function divided by its magnitude.
motivation_md: In image processing, knowing the direction perpendicular to an edge is essential for understanding the orientation of boundaries and shapes within a scene.
recap_md: - The edge normal vector ${\bf n}$ is a unit vector perpendicular to a detected edge.

title: Edge Thresholding

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Edge thresholding is the process of deciding which pixels correspond to sharp intensity variations versus uniform regions based on edge strength.
content:
The first decision that we will perform is to decide which pixels correspond to edges (regions of the image with sharp intensity variations) and which ones belong to uniform regions (flat surfaces). We will do this by simply thresholding the edge strength $e(x,y)$. In the pixels with edges, we can also measure the edge orientation $\theta(x,y)$. @fig-gradient and @fig-edge visualize the edges and the normal vector on each edge.

(see figure: Gradient and edge types.)

(see figure: Three panels showing different edge classifications for a scene with 3D blocks. The first panel, '3D orientation', highlights edges in red and green based on their spatial direction. The second...)
motivation_md: To analyze an image, we must first distinguish between structural boundaries (edges) and the flat surfaces they bound by filtering out low-intensity noise.
recap_md: - Pixels are classified as edges if their edge strength $e(x,y)$ exceeds a certain threshold.

title: Recovering World Coordinates
one_liner: Recovering world coordinates involves determining the 3D locations of visible points from their 2D image positions.
content: We want to recover world coordinates $X(x,y)$, $Y(x,y)$, and $Z(x,y)$ for each image location $(x,y)$. Given the simple image formation model described before, recovering the $X$ world coordinates is trivial as they are directly observed: for each pixel with image coordinates $(x,y)$, the corresponding world coordinate is $X(x,y) = x$. Recovering $Y$ and $Z$ will be harder as we only observe a mixture of the two world coordinates (one dimension is lost due to the projection from the 3D world into the image plane). Here we have written the world coordinates as functions of image location $(x,y)$ to make explicit that we want to recover the 3D locations of the visible points.
motivation_md: The goal of vision is often to reconstruct the 3D structure of a scene from 2D data, though the loss of one dimension during projection makes this mathematically challenging.
recap_md: - $X$ coordinates are often directly observable from the image plane coordinates.

title: Figure-Ground Segmentation
one_liner: Figure-ground segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into foreground objects and the background.
content:
The classical visual illusion "two faces or a vase" is an example of figure-ground segmentation problem.

[FIGURE:a46fdb251057dbbb | A classic Rubin's vase optical illusion consisting of a black silhouette against a white background. The central black shape can be perceived as a vase or goblet, while the white negative space on...]

Segmentation of an image into figure and ground is a classical problem in human perception and computer vision that was introduced by Gestalt psychology. In this simple world, deciding when a pixel belongs to one of the foreground objects or to the background can be decided by simply looking at the color values of each pixel. Bright pixels that have low saturation (similar values of the red-blue-green [RBG] components) correspond to the white ground plane, and the rest of the pixels are likely to belong to the colored blocks that compose our simple world. In general, the problem of image segmentation into distinct objects is a very challenging task.
motivation_md: To interact with or recognize objects, a system must first distinguish which parts of an image constitute a single entity (the figure) versus the surrounding environment (the ground).
recap_md: - Figure-ground segmentation distinguishes foreground objects from the background.

title: Gestalt Psychology
one_liner: Gestalt psychology introduced the classical problem of segmenting an image into figure and ground.
content: Segmentation of an image into figure and ground is a classical problem in human perception and computer vision that was introduced by Gestalt psychology.
motivation_md: Gestalt psychology provides the theoretical framework for understanding how humans organize visual stimuli into coherent groups and objects.
recap_md: - Gestalt psychology is the origin of the figure-ground segmentation problem in perception studies.

title: Border Ownership
one_liner: Border ownership refers to the principle that the foreground object owns the common edge shared with the background.
content:
Border ownership: The foreground object is the one that owns the common edge.

[FIGURE:11d0f8a4b8cad0cb | A diagram illustrating border ownership and occlusion. An orange, elongated blob lies on top of a green, irregular blob. The dashed black lines indicate the shared boundary where the orange shape...]
motivation_md: Determining which object "owns" a boundary is crucial for resolving depth and understanding which object is occluding another.
recap_md: - The shared edge between two regions is attributed to the foreground object.

title: Nonaccidental Properties
one_liner: Nonaccidental properties are image features that likely reflect actual 3D world structures rather than accidental viewpoints.
content:
Despite that in the projection of world coordinates to image coordinates we have lost a great deal of information, there are a number of properties that will remain invariant and can help us in interpreting the image. 

[FIGURE:b2cd80b67cc832bd | A diagram illustrating two nonaccidental properties in computer vision. The top half, labeled 'Collinearity', shows two separate line segments that lie on the same straight path. The bottom half...]

Note that those invariances refer to the process of going from world coordinates to image coordinates. The opposite might not be true. For instance, a straight line in the image could correspond to a curved line in the 3D world but that happens to be precisely aligned with respect to the viewers point of view to appear as a straight line. Also, two lines that intersect in the image plane could be disjointed in the 3D space.

However, some of these properties (not all), while not always true, can nonetheless be used to reliably infer something about the 3D world using a single 2D image as input. For instance, if two lines coterminate in the image, then, one can conclude that it is very likely that they also touch each other in 3D. If the 3D lines do not touch each other, then it will require a very specific alignment between the observer and the lines for them to appear to coterminate in the image. Therefore, one can safely conclude that the lines might also touch in 3D.

These properties are called nonaccidental properties because they will only be observed in the image if they also exist in the world or by accidental alignments between the observer and scene structures. Under a generic view, nonaccidental properties will be shared by the image and the 3D world.
motivation_md: Because 2D images are ambiguous, vision systems rely on properties that are statistically unlikely to be accidental to make reliable inferences about 3D geometry.
recap_md: - Nonaccidental properties are features in a 2D image that likely correspond to real 3D structures.

title: Collinearity
one_liner: Collinearity is the property where a straight line in the 3D world projects as a straight line in a 2D image.
content: Collinearity: a straight 3D line will project into a straight line in the image.
motivation_md: This property allows us to infer the existence of straight edges and surfaces in the physical world by observing straight lines in an image.
recap_md: - Straight lines in 3D space remain straight when projected onto a 2D image plane.

title: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
one_liner: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a pointwise nonlinearity that acts as a graded threshold function, providing non-zero gradients over half its domain for gradient-based learning.
content: The Rectified linear unit (relu) is a pointwise nonlinearity which is like a graded version of a threshold function. It has the advantage that it yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, thus being amenable to gradient-based learning.
motivation_md: Standard threshold functions have zero gradients almost everywhere, making them difficult to optimize using gradient descent. ReLU provides a non-zero gradient for positive inputs, allowing neural networks to learn effectively while still introducing necessary nonlinearity.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Universal Approximation Theorem
one_liner: The universal approximation theorem states that a network with a single hidden layer can, in principle, perform any continuous input-output mapping.
content:
Deep nets can perform nonlinear classification and, in principle, any continuous input-output mapping. The universal approximation theorem states that this is true even for a network with just a single hidden layer. The caveat is that the number of neurons in the hidden layers will have to be very large in order to fit complicated functions.

Technically, this theorem only holds for continuous functions on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^N$. For example, a neural net cannot fit noncomputable functions.
motivation_md: This theorem provides the theoretical foundation for neural networks, proving that they are expressive enough to represent any continuous function given sufficient width, justifying their use as general-purpose function approximators.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Network Width
one_liner: Network width refers to the number of neurons in a single hidden layer.
content: A hidden layer with $N$ neurons can fit a scalar function with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ bumps. The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width. If different layers have different numbers of neurons, then we may specify the width per layer. Here we will assume all layers have the same width and simply speak of the width of the network.
motivation_md: Width determines the capacity of a single layer to represent features; increasing width allows a network to capture more simultaneous patterns or 'bumps' in a function.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Network Depth
one_liner: Network depth is the number of layers in a neural network.
content: As we increase the width of a network, we can fit ever more complicated functions. Increasing the depth of a network, that is, its number of layers, can also be an effective way to increase the capacity of the net, but its effect is a bit different than increasing width.
motivation_md: Depth allows networks to learn hierarchical representations, where deeper layers compose features from earlier layers to represent increasingly complex concepts.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Depth Separations
one_liner: Depth separations describe cases where deep networks require exponentially fewer parameters than shallow networks to represent certain functions.
content: Interestingly, it is sometimes the case that deep nets require far fewer parameters to fit data than wide nets. Evidence for this statement comes mostly from empiricism, where deeper nets just work better in practice on many popular problems. However, there is also the beginning of a mathematical theory of when and why this can happen. The basic idea of this theory is to establish that there are certain classes of function that can be represented with a polynomial number of neurons in a depth $d$ network but require an exponential number of neurons in a depth $d^\prime$ network, for certain $d^\prime < d$. Arguments along these lines are called depth separations.
motivation_md: Understanding depth separations helps explain why deep architectures are often more efficient and powerful than shallow ones, providing a mathematical basis for the success of deep learning over simple wide networks.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Backpropagation

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: Backpropagation is an algorithm for gradient-based learning that searches the hypothesis space for the best fit to data.
content: Deep learning typically involves using gradient-based optimization to search the hypothesis space for the best fit to the data. The backpropagation algorithm is used for gradient-based learning with neural nets. However, it is certainly possible to optimize neural nets with other methods, including zeroth-order optimizers like evolution strategies.
motivation_md: Backpropagation provides a computationally efficient way to calculate the gradients of a loss function with respect to every weight in a deep network, enabling the use of gradient descent for training.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Hebbian Learning

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up approach where neurons wire up based on feedforward patterns of activity rather than error feedback.
content: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up approach where neurons wire up based on the feedforward pattern of activity in the net. Unlike backpropagation, which is a top-down algorithm where errors at the output are propagated backward (feedback), Hebbian learning relies on the principle that neurons that "fire together, wire together." This means the weight of the connection between two neurons increases whenever they are active at the same time. While it does not explicitly minimize a loss function, it can lead to effective neural representations, such as infomax representations or memory banks. It is considered more biologically plausible than backpropagation because it can be computed locally.
motivation_md: Hebbian learning offers a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation, allowing for local weight updates without the need for global error signals or complex coordination across the entire network.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Hebb's Rule

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

one_liner: Hebb's rule states that the connection weight between two neurons increases when they are active at the same time.
content: The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." This means that we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time.
motivation_md: Hebb's rule provides a simple, local mechanism for learning associations and patterns in data based on temporal correlation of neural activity.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Linearity of Reflection
one_liner: Surface reflection behaves linearly, meaning the reflection from a sum of light sources is the sum of their individual reflections.
content: In general, surface reflection behaves linearly: the reflection from the sum of two light sources is the sum of the reflections from the individual sources.
motivation_md: This principle simplifies the analysis of complex lighting environments by allowing us to treat multiple light sources independently and sum their effects.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Building a Pinhole Camera

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: A simple pinhole camera can be constructed using two pieces of paper to project an image through a small opening.
content: Making pinhole cameras is a good exercise to gain an intuition of the image projection process. A very simple setup is formed by two pieces of paper, one with a hole on it. With the right illumination conditions, you can see an image projected on the white piece of paper in front of the opening. You can use this setup to see the effect of changing the distance between the projection plane and the pinhole. By making the hole large, you will get a brighter, but blurrier image.
motivation_md: Building a physical camera helps develop an intuitive understanding of how light rays are restricted to form images and how geometry affects image quality.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Paper Bag Pinhole Camera

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: A paper bag can be transformed into a light-tight pinhole camera where the viewer stands inside to see an inverted image.
content:
A pinhole camera can be made using a paper bag with a hole in it. One sticks their head inside the bag, which has been padded to be opaque. The needed elements are an aperture to let light through, mechanisms to block stray light, a projection screen, and some method to view or record the image on the projection screen.

[FIGURE:18330c2f1d066976 | A three-step hand-drawn diagram illustrating how to construct a pinhole camera using grocery bags. Step 1 shows a single grocery bag. Step 2 shows newspaper placed inside the bag to block light. Step...]

[FIGURE:ac2f6d5425374e84 | A hand-drawn diagram and a photograph illustrating how to use a grocery bag as a pinhole camera. The diagram shows a person with a bag over their head, with labels pointing to a 'side with hole' and...]

Following steps 1–4, you can turn a paper bag into a light-tight pinhole camera, with the viewer inside. Newspapers can be added between two layers of paper bags to make a light-tight enclosure. Walking with this camera is challenging because you only get to see an upside-down version of what is behind you.
motivation_md: This technique demonstrates that a camera is essentially a light-tight box with an aperture, and provides a first-person experience of image inversion.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Accidental Camera

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Accidental cameras are formed when environmental surfaces like windows and walls naturally restrict light rays to create faint, often unnoticed images.
content:
For an image to appear, we need some way of restricting the rays that hit a wall so that each location only gets rays from different directions. While a pinhole camera is one way of forming a picture, in most settings, light rays are restricted by accidental surfaces present in the space, such as other walls, ceilings, floors, or obstacles. For instance, in a room, light rays entering via a window are partially blocked. Generally, the lower part of a wall will see the top of the world outside, while the top part of the wall will see the bottom part of the world outside. As a consequence, most walls will appear as having a faint blue tone on the bottom because they reflect the sky.

(see figure: A photograph of a corner in a room with light beige walls and a wooden parquet floor. A small three-drawer wooden nightstand sits in the corner, and a window with orange floral curtains is on the...)

(see figure: A photograph of a room where light entering through a window with horizontal blinds casts a faint, inverted, and blurry image of the outside world onto the opposite wall. A person stands by the...)

Turning the room into a pinhole camera by closing most of the window helps to focus the picture that appears on the wall. The world is full of accidental cameras that create faint images often ignored by the naive observer.
motivation_md: Understanding accidental cameras reveals that image formation is a natural geometric consequence of light restriction, not just a property of manufactured devices.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: World Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: World coordinates define a 3D position $(X, Y, Z)$ relative to the camera's pinhole, with the Z-axis perpendicular to the sensing plane.
content: In the world coordinate system, the origin is defined as the camera's pinhole. The coordinates of a 3D position of a point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world are given by $\mathbf{P} = (X, Y, Z)$. In this system, the $Z$ axis is perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane (projection plane).
motivation_md: Establishing a standard 3D coordinate system relative to the camera is the first step in mathematically modeling how the 3D world is projected onto a 2D surface.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Camera Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Camera coordinates describe the position of points on the projection plane or virtual camera plane relative to the pinhole.
content: The camera projection plane is located behind the pinhole at a distance $f$ from the origin. Let the coordinates in the camera projection plane, $x$ and $y$, be parallel to the world coordinate axes $X$ and $Y$ but in opposite directions. For simplicity, it is useful to create a virtual camera plane that is radially symmetrical to the projection plane with respect to the origin and placed in front of the camera. The coordinates in the virtual camera plane will have the same sign as the world coordinates (i.e., both images are identical apart from a flip).
motivation_md: Defining coordinates on the projection plane allows us to calculate exactly where a 3D point will appear in the resulting 2D image.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Virtual Camera Plane

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: The virtual camera plane is a radially symmetrical plane placed in front of the pinhole to avoid image inversion in mathematical models.
content: The camera projection plane is behind the pinhole at a distance $f$ from the origin. For simplicity, it is useful to create a virtual camera plane that is radially symmetrical to the projection plane with respect to the origin and is placed in front of the camera. This virtual camera plane creates a projected image without the inversion of the image. The coordinates in the virtual camera plane have the same sign as the world coordinates $x$ and $y$.
motivation_md: Using a virtual plane in front of the pinhole simplifies the math of perspective projection by removing the negative signs associated with image inversion.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: Image Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

one_liner: Image coordinates $(n, m)$ are typically measured in pixels and are related to camera coordinates via an affine transform.
content: Image coordinates are typically measured in pixels. Both the camera coordinate system $(x,y)$ and the image coordinate system $(n,m)$ are related by an affine transform.
motivation_md: Image coordinates bridge the gap between the continuous geometry of light rays and the discrete grid of pixels in a digital sensor.
recap_md: [object Object]

title: 2D Convolution
one_liner: 2D convolution involves flipping a filter vertically and horizontally and sliding it over an image to compute inner products.
content:
In two dimensions, the processing is analogous to the 1D case: the input filter is flipped vertically and horizontally, then slid over the image to record the inner product with the image everywhere. Mathematically, this is expressed as:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n,m\right] = h \left[n,m\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n,m\right] =  \sum_{k,l}h \left[n-k,m-l \right] \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[k,l \right]$$
motivation_md: 2D convolution is the fundamental operation for image processing and computer vision, allowing for the application of spatial filters that can detect edges, blur images, or extract features by considering local neighborhoods of pixels.
recap_md: - 2D convolution slides a flipped filter across an image to calculate local inner products.

title: 2D Convolution Procedure
one_liner: To compute a 2D convolution, flip the kernel both ways and sum the products of kernel values with the corresponding image patch pixels.
content:
To compute one of the pixels in the output image, we start with an input image patch (for example, $3 \times 3$ pixels), we flip the convolutional kernel upside-down and left-right, and then we multiply all the pixels in the image patch with the corresponding flipped kernel values and sum the results. The output image reflects the specific processing of the kernel; for instance, a kernel that averages vertically and takes differences horizontally will accentuate horizontal differences and diminish vertical changes.

(see figure: Illustration of a 2D convolution of an input image with a kernel of size $3 \times 3$.For the pixels in the boundary we assumed that input image has zero values outside its boundary. The red and...)
motivation_md: Understanding the step-by-step procedure of 2D convolution is essential for implementing image filters and understanding how local pixel interactions produce global image transformations.
recap_md: - Flip the convolutional kernel both vertically and horizontally before multiplying.

title: Translation Invariance: Convolution vs Rotation
one_liner: Convolution can implement translation-invariant operations like defocusing, but it cannot implement rotation because rotation is not translation-invariant.
content:
Not all image transformations can be implemented as convolutions. For a transformation to be a convolution, it must be translation invariant, meaning the operation is the same regardless of which output pixel is being computed. For example, defocusing is a convolution because each output pixel is a local average of its neighborhood, applied uniformly across the image. In contrast, rotation is a linear operation but is not translation invariant. Different output pixels require looking at input pixels in a location-specific way (e.g., grabbing pixels from different relative directions depending on the corner), so rotation cannot be written as a spatially invariant operation.

(see figure: Fig (a) Defocusing an image can be written as a convolution. (b) Rotation can't be written as a convolution.)
motivation_md: Distinguishing between translation-invariant and location-dependent operations helps determine when convolution is an appropriate mathematical tool for a given image transformation task.
recap_md: - Convolution requires translation invariance, where the same operation applies to every pixel.

title: Associative Property of Convolution
one_liner: The associative property allows convolutions to be applied in any order.
content:
Convolutions are associative, meaning they can be applied in any order:
$$\ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_2 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right] = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]) = (\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right]) \circ \ell_3\left[n\right]$$
In practice, for finite length signals, the associative property might be affected by how boundary conditions are implemented.
motivation_md: The associative property allows for the pre-computation of multiple filters into a single kernel, significantly improving computational efficiency in multi-stage signal processing pipelines.
recap_md: - Convolution is associative: $(\ell_1 \circ \ell_2) \circ \ell_3 = \ell_1 \circ (\ell_2 \circ \ell_3)$.

title: Distributive Property of Convolution
one_liner: Convolution is distributive with respect to addition.
content:
Convolution is distributive with respect to the sum:
$$\ell_1\left[n\right] \circ (\ell_2\left[n\right] + \ell_3\left[n\right] ) = \ell_1\left[n\right] \circ \ell_2\left[n\right] +  \ell_1 \left[n\right] \circ \ell_3 \left[n\right]$$
motivation_md: The distributive property allows complex signals or filters that are sums of simpler components to be processed individually and then combined, simplifying mathematical analysis.
recap_md: - Convolution distributes over addition: $f \circ (g + h) = (f \circ g) + (f \circ h)$.

title: Shift Property of Convolution
one_liner: Translating either the input signal or the kernel by a constant results in an output translated by that same constant.
content:
If the input signal $\ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$ is translated by a constant $n_0$, the result of the convolution with the same kernel $h\left[n\right]$ is the same output as before but translated by the same constant $n_0$:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]$$
Translating the kernel is equivalent:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}}\left[n-n_0\right] =  h\left[n\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n-n_0\right]  = h\left[n-n_0\right] \circ \ell_{\texttt{in}}\left[n\right]$$
motivation_md: The shift property demonstrates the translation invariance of convolution, ensuring that the relative position of features in a signal is preserved in the output.
recap_md: - Shifting the input or the kernel by $n_0$ shifts the output by $n_0$.

title: Support Property of Convolution
one_liner: The convolution of signals with lengths N and M results in a signal with a length at most N + M - 1.
content: The convolution of a discrete signal of length $N$ with another discrete signal of length $M$ results in a discrete signal with length $L \leq M+N-1$.
motivation_md: Knowing the support (length) of the output signal is necessary for memory allocation and for managing boundary effects in digital signal processing.
recap_md: - The output length $L$ of convolving signals of length $N$ and $M$ is $L \leq M+N-1$.

title: Discrete Impulse Function
one_liner: The discrete impulse function is the identity for convolution, taking the value 1 at zero and 0 elsewhere.
content:
The impulse $\delta \left[n\right]$ is the identity function for convolution. It takes the value 1 for $n=0$ and is zero everywhere else:
$$\delta \left[n\right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } n=0\\ 0 & \quad \text{if } n \neq 0 \end{cases}$$
The convolution of the impulse with any other signal $\ell\left[n\right]$ returns the same signal:
$$\delta \left[n\right] \circ \ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n\right]$$
motivation_md: The impulse function serves as a fundamental building block in signal processing, allowing any signal to be represented as a sum of shifted impulses and defining the impulse response of a system.
recap_md: - The impulse $\delta[n]$ is 1 at $n=0$ and 0 otherwise.

title: Simplex
one_liner: The $(K-1)$-simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$, is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1.
content: The $(K-1)$-simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$, is the set of all $K$-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1. $K$-dimensional one-hot codes live on the vertices of $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
motivation_md: The simplex provides a geometric framework for probability distributions, ensuring that categorical outputs are properly normalized and non-negative.
recap_md: - The $(K-1)$-simplex consists of $K$-dimensional vectors that sum to 1. - One-hot codes represent the vertices of this geometric structure.

title: Softmax Function
one_liner: The softmax function squashes a vector into the range $[0,1]$ and normalizes it to sum to 1, creating a valid probability mass function.
content: To ensure that the output of our learned function $f_{\theta}$ has the property $f_{\theta} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$, we can compose two steps: (1) first apply a function $z_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$, (2) then squash the output into the range $[0,1]$ and normalize it to sum to 1. A popular way to squash is via the softmax function. Using softmax is a modeling choice; we could have used any function that squashes into a valid pmf, that is, a nonnegative vector that sums to 1. $$\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{z} = z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\ &\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\\ &\quad \quad \hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}. \end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: In classification, we need model outputs to represent probabilities. The softmax function transforms arbitrary real-valued scores into a normalized distribution where all values are between 0 and 1 and sum to 1.
recap_md: - Softmax squashes $K$-dimensional vectors into a valid probability mass function. - It is a modeling choice used to ensure model outputs live on the simplex.

title: Logits
one_liner: Logits are the values in $\mathbf{z}$ and can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
content: The values in $\mathbf{z}$ are called the logits and can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
motivation_md: Logits represent the raw scores produced by a model before normalization, allowing for a linear representation of class evidence before it is squashed into probabilities.
recap_md: - Logits are the input values to the softmax function. - They represent unnormalized log probabilities for different classes.

title: Softmax Regression
one_liner: Softmax regression is a family of learning methods that maps input data to class labels using the softmax function.
content: Softmax regression models classification by defining the output as $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \texttt{softmax}(z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))$. (see figure: Softmax regression for image classification. The $\odot$ symbol represents an elementwise product. The cross-entropy loss is the negative of the sum over elementwise agreements between the prediction...) For example, if a prediction places 40 percent probability on the true class, the loss is $-\log 0.4$. This learning problem refers to the whole family of learning methods that have this general form. (see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.) The hypothesis space is only partially specified and the optimizer is left unspecified, allowing the key ingredients of the learning problem to be developed in isolation and then mixed and matched.
motivation_md: Softmax regression provides a standard framework for multi-class classification, allowing researchers to treat the model architecture, loss function, and optimization strategy as modular components.
recap_md: - It models classification by mapping inputs to a probability distribution over classes. - The approach is modular, allowing different hypothesis spaces and optimizers to be used within the same general form.

title: Metalearning
one_liner: Metalearning, or learning to learn, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space consists of learning algorithms.
content: Learning to learn, also called metalearning, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space is learning algorithms. Recall that learners train on past instances of a problem to produce an algorithm that can solve future instances. The goal of metalearning is to handle cases where the future problem is itself a learning problem, such as finding a least-squares line fit. Since least-squares regression is itself a learning algorithm, the learner has learned to learn. Because learning is a meta-algorithm (an algorithm that outputs an algorithm), metalearning is a meta-meta-algorithm. This can be visualized by adding another outer loop on top of a learner. (see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.) This idea can be applied recursively to construct meta-meta-...-metalearners. Humans perform multiple levels of this process, having evolved to be taught how to learn quickly.
motivation_md: Metalearning aims to improve the efficiency of the learning process itself, allowing systems to adapt to new tasks more quickly by leveraging experience from previous learning problems.
recap_md: - Metalearning is the process of learning how to learn by treating learning algorithms as the hypothesis space. - It functions as a meta-meta-algorithm that can be applied recursively.

title: Evolution as a Learning Algorithm
one_liner: Evolution is a learning algorithm according to the definition of meta-algorithms.
content: Evolution is a learning algorithm according to our present definition.
motivation_md: By framing evolution as a learning algorithm, we can understand biological adaptation through the same mathematical lens used for machine learning and optimization.
recap_md: - Evolution fits the definition of a learning algorithm. - It represents a high-level process of adaptation and optimization over time.

title: Gradient Descent
one_liner: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that finds parameters to minimize loss by calculating the direction of steepest descent.
content: Once you have specified a learning problem (loss function, hypothesis space, parameterization), the next step is to find the parameters that minimize the loss. This is an optimization problem, and the most common optimization algorithm used is gradient descent. Gradient descent is like a skier making their way down a snowy mountain, where the shape of the mountain is the loss function. There are many varieties of gradient descent, forming a family called gradient-based learning algorithms. All share the same basic idea: at some operating point, calculate the direction of steepest descent, then use this direction to find a new operating point with lower loss.
motivation_md: Optimization is central to machine learning; gradient descent provides a computationally efficient way to iteratively improve model parameters by following the local geometry of the loss surface.
recap_md: - Gradient descent minimizes loss by iteratively moving in the direction of steepest descent. - It is the foundation for a wide family of gradient-based learning algorithms.

title: Operating Point
one_liner: An operating point refers to a particular setting of parameters where the loss is currently being evaluated.
content: We use the term operating point to refer to a particular point (setting of the parameters) where we are currently evaluating the loss.
motivation_md: Defining an operating point allows us to discuss the state of an optimization process at a specific moment, providing a reference for calculating gradients and updates.
recap_md: - An operating point is a specific set of parameter values. - It is the location on the loss surface where evaluation and gradient calculation occur.

title: Neural Net Enthusiasm Cycles
one_liner: Interest in neural networks has historically fluctuated through cycles of ebbs and flows, often aligning with broader trends in learning algorithms.
content: Interest in neural nets has gone through a series of ebbs and flows. These cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms more generally, but there have also been phases where interest in neural nets was low while interest in other learning algorithms was high.
motivation_md: Understanding the historical context of neural networks helps researchers recognize that progress in the field is not always linear and is often influenced by broader trends in machine learning.
recap_md: - Interest in neural networks has historically fluctuated through cycles of high and low enthusiasm. - These cycles often, but not always, correlate with interest in learning algorithms more broadly.

title: Deep Learning
one_liner: Deep learning systems emerged from stacking perceptrons to perform complex operations, a development that gained significant momentum in the 1980s.
content:
In the 1980s, interest in learning algorithms and neural nets began to surge again because researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic. These systems were the precursors to the **deep learning** systems that dominate today. During this decade, several vision-specific architectures were introduced, including Kunihiko Fukushima's Neocognitron, a precursor to modern convolutional neural networks. In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. demonstrated how these networks can be efficiently trained, and their system was used for recognizing handwritten digits by the US Postal Service. A peak of this research was the publication of *Parallel Distributed Processing* by David Rumelhart and Jay McClelland, which mixed neuroscience with computational models of distributed processing.

[FIGURE:a3cfb172cb1c2c7f | The book cover of 'Parallel Distributed Processing' features a blue background with a complex white wireframe grid of interconnected cubes. In the center, a bright yellow, ribbon-like helical...]
motivation_md: Deep learning was developed to overcome the limitations of simple perceptrons, allowing for the processing of complex logic and high-dimensional data like images.
recap_md: - Deep learning systems are built by stacking perceptrons to perform complex operations and logic. - Early breakthroughs in the 1980s led to the development of convolutional neural networks and efficient training methods. - The field was influenced by both neuroscience and computational models of distributed processing.

title: Boosting
one_liner: Boosting is a learning algorithm used to improve performance, notably applied by Viola and Jones in 2001 for efficient face detection.
content:
Major advances occurred in the relative quiet of the 1990s and early 2000s. For example, in 2001, Paul Viola and Michael Jones published a method that used a simple learning algorithm called **boosting** to detect faces in photos.

[FIGURE:596845fd313f7059 | A grainy, black and white photograph of a man sitting at a desk with a CRT monitor. A double-lined square bounding box is drawn around his face, demonstrating the output of a face detection algorithm.]
motivation_md: Boosting was utilized to create efficient and accurate classifiers, such as those needed for real-time face detection in images.
recap_md: - Boosting is a learning algorithm used to enhance the performance of simple models. - It was famously applied by Viola and Jones to achieve effective face detection in photographs.

title: End-to-End Learning
one_liner: End-to-end learning uses a single system to process every stage from raw input pixels to final output predictions.
content: The traditional vision pipeline was replaced with learned modules. In 2012, a deep neural net called AlexNet dramatically outperformed all existing methods for image classification by using learning **end-to-end** for each processing stage, from the input pixels to the output predictions.
motivation_md: End-to-end learning simplifies the vision pipeline by replacing manually engineered stages with a single learned system, leading to significant performance gains.
recap_md: - End-to-end learning processes every stage from input to output within a single learned system. - This approach replaced traditional multi-stage pipelines with integrated neural network modules.

title: ImageNet Moment
one_liner: The "ImageNet Moment" refers to the 2012 breakthrough where AlexNet's superior performance demonstrated the power of deep learning for image classification.
content:
The dramatic performance of AlexNet was first demonstrated at the 2012 ImageNet competition, an event that has come to be called the "ImageNet Moment." WordNet is an electronic dictionary used to define word hierarchies, which relates to the taxonomy used in such competitions.

[FIGURE:9133e16e89bc417c | A hierarchical tree diagram representing a taxonomy of entities. The root node is 'entity', which branches into 'object', then into 'artifact' and 'living'. The 'artifact' branch further divides into...]
motivation_md: This moment marked a paradigm shift in computer vision, proving that deep learning could vastly outperform traditional hand-engineered algorithms on large-scale datasets.
recap_md: - The ImageNet Moment occurred in 2012 when AlexNet won the ImageNet competition. - It demonstrated the superiority of deep neural networks over previous image classification methods.

title: Learning-Based Vision as a Mapping Finder
one_liner: Learning-based vision acts as a mapping finder, using algorithms to discover the relationship between input and output that human scientists previously designed by hand.
content: Learning-based vision is similar to other approaches in that it studies the structure of the input, the structure of the output, and the mapping between the two. The big difference is how you find the mapping. In this sense, learners are like a new kind of vision scientist, playing the same role as humans who previously determined how vision works through deep thought. Machine learners often come up with similar vision algorithms as those designed by humans, but they are more powerful and have far exceeded human-designed algorithms in raw performance.
motivation_md: This perspective frames machine learning not as a departure from traditional vision science, but as an automated way to discover the complex mappings required for visual perception.
recap_md: - Learning-based vision focuses on finding the mapping between input and target output automatically. - Machine learners serve a role similar to human vision scientists but with greater computational power. - Learned algorithms often outperform those manually designed by humans.

title: The Summer Vision Project
one_liner: The 1966 Summer Vision Project was an optimistic early attempt at MIT to construct a significant part of a visual system over a single summer.
content: In 1966, Seymour Papert wrote a proposal for building a vision system as a summer project. The goal was to use summer workers effectively in the construction of a significant part of a visual system, dividing tasks among a group of MIT students. This project reflected the optimism of the early days of computer vision, though the task proved to be harder than expected.
motivation_md: The project illustrates the early belief that computer vision was a relatively simple problem that could be solved quickly, highlighting the unforeseen complexity of the field.
recap_md: - Proposed by Seymour Papert in 1966, the project aimed to build a visual system in one summer. - It distributed vision tasks among MIT students, reflecting early field optimism. - The project's failure revealed that computer vision is significantly more difficult than initially anticipated.

title: Blocks World

position.section_title: A Simple World: The Blocks World

one_liner: Blocks World is a simplified visual environment composed of basic 3D geometric figures, used by early scene interpretation systems to manage visual complexity.
content:
Because the visual world is too complex, early scene interpretation systems simplified it to build functional systems. Larry G. Roberts introduced the **Block world**, a world composed of simple 3D geometrical figures.

[FIGURE:0cd8ad064f44ea7a | A line drawing of two 3D geometric shapes from the 'Blocks World'. In the foreground is a wedge-like block with a rectangular base, a vertical back face, and a sloped front face. In the background is...]
motivation_md: Blocks World was created to reduce the complexity of the natural world into manageable geometric primitives, allowing early researchers to develop foundational vision algorithms.
recap_md: - Blocks World is a simplified environment consisting of basic 3D geometric shapes. - It was introduced by Larry Roberts to make the problem of scene interpretation more tractable.

title: Lanczos Interpolation
one_liner: Lanczos interpolation is a popular method used for image resampling and interpolation.
content: Other popular interpolation methods are the bicubic interpolation and the Lanczos interpolation.
motivation_md: Lanczos interpolation is used to provide a high-quality alternative to simpler methods like bilinear interpolation when resizing or resampling images.
recap_md: - Lanczos interpolation is a common technique for image resampling.

title: Upsampling Procedure
one_liner: Upsampling consists of a sequence of expansion followed by interpolation to increase the resolution of a signal.
motivation_md: Upsampling is necessary when an image needs to be displayed at a higher resolution than its original capture, requiring the estimation of missing pixel values between existing samples.
recap_md: - Upsampling involves expanding a signal by inserting zeros and then applying a convolutional interpolation filter.

title: Upsampling Matrix
one_liner: The upsampling operator can be expressed as a linear matrix operation that maps a signal to a higher-dimensional space.
content:
The upsampling operator is also a linear operation, therefore we can also write it in matrix form. For instance, for a 1D signal of length $N=4$ samples, if we upsample it by a factor $k=2$, then, using repeat padding for handling the boundary and the bilinear interpolation, we can write the upsampling operator as a matrix: $$\mathbf{U}_2 = \left[ 
\begin{array}{cccc}
1    & 0    & 0  & 0\\
0.5  & 0.5  & 0  & 0\\
0    & 1    & 0  & 0\\
0    & 0.5 & 0.5 & 0\\
0    & 0    & 1  & 0\\
0    & 0    & 0.5& 0.5\\
0    & 0    & 0  & 1\\
0    & 0    & 0  & 1
\end{array}
\right]$$

Multiplying this matrix by a signal of length 4, gives an output signal of length 8. The output samples at locations 1, 3, 5, 7, and 8 are copies of the input samples 1, 2, 3, and 4, while samples 2, 4, and 6 are computed as the average of two consecutive input samples. The last output sample is a copy of the last input sample because it corresponds to extending the input using repeat padding.
motivation_md: Representing upsampling as a matrix allows it to be integrated into linear algebra frameworks and optimization problems common in computer vision and deep learning.
recap_md: - Upsampling is a linear operation that can be represented by a matrix $\mathbf{U}_k$.

title: Aliasing Effects in Computer Vision
one_liner: Aliasing in computer vision can introduce noise, spurious features, and a lack of translation invariance in image processing pipelines.
content: Aliasing is a constant source of problems in many image processing pipelines. In computer vision, aliasing can introduce noise, spurious features and textures, and lack of translation invariance. In @sec-convolutional_neural_nets, we will discuss how aliasing affects the quality of some of the convolutional layers used in neural networks.
motivation_md: Understanding aliasing is critical because it explains why certain image processing steps produce visual artifacts or cause neural networks to fail on shifted images.
recap_md: - Aliasing causes noise, spurious textures, and breaks translation invariance.

title: Aliasing in Generative Image Models
one_liner: Aliasing is a common source of artifacts in generative models, such as GANs, when upsampling operations are performed incorrectly.
content: Aliasing is often a source of image artifacts in generative image models. One example is generative adversarial networks (@sec-generative_models) where images are produced as a sequence of learned convolutions and upsampling stages. When the upsampling operations are done without paying attention to aliasing, the output images show a number of artifacts, as has been shown in @Karras2021. Those artifacts can be removed by carefully implementing each stage to avoid aliasing.
motivation_md: Identifying aliasing as the cause of artifacts in GANs allows researchers to design better upsampling layers that produce cleaner, more realistic images.
recap_md: - Generative models like GANs often suffer from aliasing artifacts during upsampling.

title: Nonlinear Operators and Filter Banks
one_liner: Image understanding requires nonlinear operators, often built by applying simple nonlinearities to the outputs of linear filter banks.
content: Although linear filters can perform a wide range of operations, image understanding requires nonlinear operators. Sets of filters can be used to extract information about images, focusing on traditional families of filters that help explain the representational power of modern deep neural networks. Simple nonlinearities applied to the output of linear filters, such as the squaring nonlinearity, can be used to build useful image representations.
motivation_md: Linear filters alone cannot capture complex image structures; nonlinearities are essential for building representations that can distinguish between different textures and patterns.
recap_md: - Nonlinear operators are necessary for advanced image understanding beyond what linear filters provide.

title: Gabor Filter
one_liner: A Gabor filter is a localized image analysis operator formed by the product of a Gaussian function and a sinusoidal wave.
content:
In @sec-fourier_analysis we discussed several useful image representations: representing an image in the frequency domain and decomposing it into amplitude and phase, and also the analysis of image content across different scales and orientations. The Fourier transform is a tool that allows us to extract that information, but only globally. For this information to be useful it needs to be localized. For instance, the analysis of orientations of local image structures can be done using image gradients (@sec-image_derivatives), which are localized in space. In fact, we made use of image derivatives in @sec-simplesystem to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of a scene. Here we will discuss another family of filters that has a long history of being used for image analysis: Gabor filters.

@fig-1D_gabor_function (a) shows a one-dimensional (1D) sine function. This function has infinite support. When used as a representation, the Fourier coefficients are obtained as the scalar product between the sine wave and the input image. Each Fourier coefficient involves a point-wise multiplication between the wave and the input image and then the sum of the result. As a consequence of the infinite support of the wave, one single Fourier coefficient does not tell us anything about what happens locally inside the analyzed image.

A good start for a localized image analysis is to restrict the spatial support of a sinusoidal basis function. One function that has a local support (a lot of nice properties as we discussed in @sec-blur_filters) is the Gaussian function (@fig-1D_gabor_function [b]). The product of the Gaussian and the sine wave (or a cosine wave) gives the function with the profile shown in @fig-1D_gabor_function (c) called a Gabor filter. Gabor functions were introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946 @Gabor1946TheoryOC.

(see figure: Construction of a Gabor function. (a) Sine function. (b) Gaussian function. (c) Gabor function obtained as the product of (a) and (b).)

Gabor functions, originally proposed in 1D, were made popular as an operator for image analysis by Goesta Granlund in his paper *In Search of a General Picture Processing Operator* @GRANLUND1978155.

The sine phase Gabor function is zero mean. However, the cosine phase Gabor function is not zero mean. The Gaussian width $\sigma$ has to be sufficiently large so that the Gabor function behaves like a zero mean filter. All the previous definitions are given in the continuous domain. The discrete version of the Gabor function is obtained by sampling the continuous functions.

One important characteristic of Gabor filters is that they are very similar to the shape of some cortical receptive fields found in the mammalian visual system. This provides a hint that we're on the right track with these filters to build image representations.

Remember the description of simple and complex cells in the visual system from @sec-challenge_of_vision.
motivation_md: Standard Fourier analysis provides global frequency information but lacks spatial localization; Gabor filters solve this by windowing sinusoids with Gaussians to analyze frequency content within local regions.
recap_md: - A Gabor filter is the product of a Gaussian function and a sine or cosine wave.

title: Gabor Function Localization Optimality
one_liner: Gabor functions are the optimal functions for achieving the best simultaneous localization in both the spatial and frequency domains.
content: Gabor functions are localized in both the spatial and frequency domain. One remarkable property of the Gabor function is that it is the optimal function that achieves the best simultaneous localization in space and frequency.
motivation_md: The Uncertainty Principle dictates a trade-off between spatial and frequency resolution; Gabor functions are theoretically significant because they reach the lower bound of this trade-off.
recap_md: - Gabor functions provide optimal simultaneous localization in space and frequency.

title: High-Order Gaussian Derivatives
one_liner: High-order Gaussian derivatives are computed as the product of a Gaussian function and a Hermite polynomial of the same order as the derivative.
content:
The $n$-th order derivative of a Gaussian can be written as the product between a polynomial on $x$, with the same order as the derivative, times a Gaussian. The family of polynomials that result in computing Gaussian derivatives is called Hermite polynomials. The general expression for the $n$ derivative of a Gaussian is:
$$
g_{x^n}(x;  rac{\partial^{n} g(x)}{\partial x^n} = \left( \frac{-1}{\sigma \sqrt{2}} \right)^n H_n\left( \frac{x}{\sigma \sqrt {2}} \right) g(x; \sigma)
$$
The first Hermite polynomial is $H_0(x)=1$, the second is $H_1(x) = 2x$, the third is $H_2(x)=4x^2-2$, and they can be computed recursively as:
$$
H_n(x) = 2x H_{n-1}(x) - 2(n-1)H_{n-2}(x)
$$
For $n=0$ we have the original Gaussian. (see figure: Fig (a) 1D Gaussian with $\sigma=1$. (b–d) Gaussian derivatives up to order 3.)

In two dimensions, as the Gaussian is separable, the partial derivatives result on the product of two Hermite polynomial, one for each spatial dimension:
$$
\begin{split}
g_{x^n,y^m}(x,y; \sigma) & =  
\frac{\partial^{n+m} g(x,y)}{\partial x^n \partial y^m} \\
& = \left( \frac{-1}{\sigma \sqrt{2}} \right)^{n+m}
H_n\left( \frac{x}{\sigma \sqrt {2}} \right)
H_m\left( \frac{y}{\sigma \sqrt {2}} \right)
g(x,y; \sigma)
\end{split}
$$
[FIGURE:b941695d7813c9aa | A triangular arrangement of 2D images representing Gaussian derivatives up to order 6. The top row shows the base Gaussian $g$, and subsequent rows show partial derivatives $g_{x^n y^m}$ where the...]
[FIGURE:282ff8c4501cbc4e | A triangular arrangement of images showing 2D Gaussian partial derivatives $g_{x^n y^m}$ up to order 6. The top row shows the Gaussian $g$, and subsequent rows show increasing orders of derivatives...]
