A probabilistic graphical model is a graph that describes a class of probability distributions sharing a common structure. The graph has nodes, drawn as circles, indicating the variables of the joint probability. It has edges, drawn as lines connecting nodes to other nodes. In undirected graphical models, the edges are line segments without arrowheads.
motivation_md: Modeling complex systems with many variables is computationally difficult; graphical models provide a structured way to exploit modularity and independence, making inference and learning tractable.
recap_md: - Uses nodes to represent variables and edges to represent relationships between them.

title: Undirected Graphical Models
one_liner: In undirected graphical models, edges represent the conditional independence structure between variables.
content: In undirected graphical models, the edges indicate the conditional independence structure of the nodes of the graph. If there is no edge between two nodes, then the variables described by those nodes are independent, conditioned on the values of intervening nodes in any path between them in the graph. If two nodes do have a line between them, then we cannot assume they are independent.
motivation_md: Undirected models allow us to represent symmetric relationships between variables, which is particularly useful in spatial domains like image processing where pixels influence their neighbors in all directions.
recap_md: - Absence of an edge implies conditional independence between variables.

title: Belief Propagation
one_liner: Belief propagation is an efficient algorithm for estimating the states of unobserved variables in a graphical model by passing messages between nodes.
content:
Belief propagation (BP) is an algorithm used to perform inference efficiently by exploiting the structure of the joint probability. Given a probabilistic graphical model and observations, we use BP to estimate the states of unobserved variables, such as estimating a person's pose from image observations.

The algorithm reorganizes summations into partial sums called **messages**, which pass information from one node to another. For example, a message $m_{ij}(x_j)$ from node $i$ to node $j$ is a function of the states $x_j$ of the receiving node. To find the marginal probability at a node, the algorithm stores and reuses these messages in an optimal way, avoiding redundant computations that would occur if marginals were calculated independently for every node.
motivation_md: Calculating marginal probabilities in a large joint distribution is usually exponentially difficult. Belief propagation turns this into a local message-passing task, making inference efficient for many types of graphs.
recap_md: - Efficiently estimates unobserved variables by passing messages between nodes.

title: Hammersley-Clifford Theorem
one_liner: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem states that a positive probability distribution matches a graphical model's independence structure if and only if it factors over the graph's maximal cliques.
content:
The **Hammersley-Clifford theorem** defines the form a joint probability must have for any given graphical model. It states that a positive probability distribution has the independence structure described by a graphical model if and only if it can be written as a product of functions over the variables of each maximal clique:

$$p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \prod_{x_c \in x_i} \Psi_{c} (x_c),$$

where the product is over all maximal cliques $x_c$ in the graph $x_i$.
motivation_md: This theorem provides the fundamental link between the topology of a graph and the algebraic factorization of its probability distribution, allowing us to build complex models by defining local potential functions.
recap_md: - Relates the independence structure of a graph to the factorization of its joint probability.

title: Clique
one_liner: A clique is a set of nodes in a graph where every node is connected to every other node in the set.
content:
A **clique** is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique. These graphs illustrate the clique property:

![A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the same clique.](figures/graphical_models/cliques1.png){width="50%" #fig-chain}
motivation_md: Cliques are the building blocks of undirected graphical models; they represent the sets of variables that can be directly dependent on one another.
recap_md: - A subset of nodes where every pair of distinct nodes is adjacent.

title: Belief Propagation Message
one_liner: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$ is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
content: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is defined as the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
motivation_md: In probabilistic graphical models, we often need to calculate marginal probabilities. The belief propagation message serves as a summary of information from one part of a tree-structured graph, allowing for efficient local computation of these marginals without re-summing the entire joint distribution.
recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}$ represents the aggregated probability from the subtree rooted at $i$ excluding $j$.

title: Belief Propagation Message Update Rule
aliases: recursive belief propagation message update rule
one_liner: The belief propagation update rule computes messages by multiplying incoming messages with pairwise compatibility functions and marginalizing over the intermediate node's states.
content:
The recursive belief propagation message update rule is derived by marginalizing over the state probabilities at a node. As illustrated in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.), messages $m_{j+1,j}$ and $m_{kj}$ correspond to partial sums over nodes indicated in the graph. Marginalization over the states of all nodes leaving node $j$, not including node $i$, leads to the belief propagation message passing rule.

To compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:
1. Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node $j$, except for the message from node $i$ back to node $j$.
2. Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function $\psi_{ij}(x_i, x_j)$.
3. Marginalize over the variable $x_j$.

These steps are summarized in the following equation:

$$m_{j i}\left(x_i\right)=\sum_{x_j} \psi_{i j}\left(x_i, x_j\right) \prod_{k \in \eta(j) \backslash i} m_{k j}\left(x_jight)$$

where $\eta(j) \backslash i$ denotes the neighbors of node $j$ except for node $i$. Any local potential functions $\phi_{j}(x_j)$ are treated as an additional message into node $j$, such that $m_{0j}(x_j) = \phi_{j}(x_j)$. For continuous variables, the sum over the states of $x_j$ is replaced by an integral over the domain of $x_j$.

(see figure: Pictorial depiction of belief propagation message passing rules of equation (@eq-bpupdate), where $\odot$ indicates elementwise multiplication (i.e., the Hadamard product).)
motivation_md: To efficiently compute marginals in a tree, we need a way to pass information between nodes. This rule provides a recursive mechanism to update beliefs locally, ensuring that each message correctly summarizes the evidence from its respective branch of the graph.
recap_md: - Multiply all incoming messages to node $j$ (except from $i$) and the pairwise potential $\psi_{ij}$.

title: Nosey Neighbor Rule
one_liner: The nosey neighbor rule describes a node's message as a summary of what it has seen and heard from its neighbors about the state of the recipient node.
content: Belief Propagation follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (attributed to Brendan Frey): Every node is treated as a house in a neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."
motivation_md: This rule provides an intuitive metaphor for understanding how information flows in belief propagation, emphasizing that a message to a node is based on all information available to the sender except for information from the recipient itself.
recap_md: - A node's message to a neighbor summarizes its own evidence and information from all other neighbors.

title: Marginal Probability in Belief Propagation
one_liner: The marginal probability at a node in belief propagation is the product of all incoming messages to that node.
content:
(see figure: To compute the marginal probability at node $i$, we multiply together all the incoming messages at that node: $p_{i}$ as another message.)

The marginal probability at a node $i$ is the sum over the joint probabilities of all states except those of $x_i$. In a network with no loops, the conditional independence structure ensures that the marginal probability at a node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$. Because probabilities within each subtree are independent when conditioned on node $i$, the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of all the incoming messages:

$$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)}  m_{ji}(x_i)$$

The local clique potential at node $i$, $\psi_i(x_i)$, is included as one of the messages in the product of all messages into node $i$.
motivation_md: The ultimate goal of belief propagation is to find the marginal distribution of individual variables. This rule shows that once all messages have been passed, the marginal at any node can be computed simply by multiplying the incoming information.
recap_md: - Marginal probability $p_i(x_i)$ is the product of all incoming messages $m_{ji}(x_i)$.

title: Depth-First Update
one_liner: Depth-first update is a message passing protocol where messages travel from leaves to an arbitrary root and then back to the leaves.
content:
In a depth-first update, one node is arbitrarily picked as the root. Messages are then passed from the leaves of the tree (relative to that root node) up to the root, and then back down to the leaves.

[FIGURE:25f610399a220f05 | A tree graph with five nodes and four edges. The top-center node is labeled 'root'. Blue arrows indicate message passing from the four leaf nodes toward the root node, representing the first phase of...]

[FIGURE:9560b6515cfb38e6 | A tree-structured graph with five nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes, and the bottom node is...]

[FIGURE:455ef9a295437c12 | A diagram of a tree-structured graph with six circular nodes. Three blue arrows originate from the top-center node, pointing towards its three neighbors: the top-left node, the top-right node, and...]

[FIGURE:a33008ecd7f522ba | A tree graph with six nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes. The bottom node is connected...]

**Depth-first BP message passing schedule**: Select a root node. (a) Start at leaves; (b) proceed to root; (c) perform an outgoing sweep; and (d) compute remaining messages, ending at leaf nodes.
motivation_md: This schedule ensures that every node receives all necessary incoming information before it sends an outgoing message, providing a structured and efficient way to complete all message computations in exactly two passes.
recap_md: - Pick a root node and pass messages from leaves up to the root.

title: Parallel Update
one_liner: Parallel update is a message passing protocol where every node sends outgoing messages as soon as it has received the required incoming messages.
content:
In parallel update, at each turn, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received all the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:05fcd402b5e6435d | A diagram of a tree-structured graph with five nodes. Blue arrows indicate message passing from the four leaf nodes toward the two central internal nodes, representing the first step of a...]

[FIGURE:642603864966b118 | A tree graph with two internal nodes and four leaf nodes. Two blue arrows indicate bidirectional message passing along the central vertical edge connecting the two internal nodes.]

[FIGURE:8a28a6db9b463c3e | A tree-structured graph with five nodes. A central vertical edge connects a top-center node to a bottom-center node. The top node is connected horizontally to two leaf nodes, and the bottom node is...]

**Synchronous parallel update schedule** for BP message passing: Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages. This process typically proceeds in iterations.
motivation_md: Parallel updates are useful for distributed implementations of belief propagation, allowing nodes to work simultaneously rather than waiting for a sequential sweep to reach them.
recap_md: - Nodes send outgoing messages immediately upon receiving necessary incoming messages.

title: Belief Propagation Efficiency
one_liner: Belief propagation efficiently calculates marginals at all nodes using only twice the computation required for a single node.
content: When computing marginals at many nodes, the BP algorithm reuses messages. A single message-passing sweep through all nodes allows for the calculation of the marginal at any node (using depth-first update rules to calculate the marginal at the root). A second sweep from the root back to all leaf nodes calculates all remaining messages needed for every node's marginal probability. Consequently, calculating the marginal probabilities everywhere takes only twice the number of computations required to calculate the marginal probability at a single node.
motivation_md: Naive marginalization is computationally expensive. Belief propagation's efficiency makes it feasible to perform inference on large-scale graphical models by reusing intermediate results.
recap_md: - Messages are reused to calculate marginals at multiple nodes efficiently.

title: Disparity
one_liner: Disparity is the difference in position of a pixel between left and right camera images, often used to represent depth.
content: In graphical models for stereo vision, the unknown depth of each pixel in a scan line is often represented as an unobserved variable. This depth is frequently expressed as the **disparity** between the left and right camera images.
motivation_md: In stereo vision, depth cannot be measured directly from a single image. Disparity provides a measurable proxy for depth by comparing the relative shift of objects between two viewpoints.
recap_md: - Disparity represents the depth of a pixel by comparing left and right camera images.

title: Self-Attention Maps
one_liner: Self-attention maps visualize how each token in an image attends to others, often reshaped to the original image dimensions for interpretability.
content:
@fig-transformers-transformers_attn_ex gives an example of what self-attention maps can look like on the safari image. In this example, we are simply using patch color as the query and key features. Each attention map shows one row of $\mathbf{A}$ reshaped into the size of the input image.

(see figure: Example of self-attention maps where each token is an image patch and the query and key vectors are both set to the mean color of the patch, normalized to be a unit vector.)
motivation_md: Self-attention maps provide a way to interpret and visualize the internal relationships a Transformer model establishes between different parts of an input, such as image patches.
recap_md:
- Attention maps represent rows of the attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ reshaped to match the input spatial dimensions.
- They visualize which parts of the input the model focuses on for a given query token.

title: Multihead Self-Attention
one_liner: Multihead self-attention (MSA) runs multiple attention layers in parallel to capture different types of token similarities simultaneously.
content:
Despite their power, self-attention layers are still limited in that they only have one set of query/key/value projection matrices (namely, $\mathbf{W}_q$, $\mathbf{W}_k$, $\mathbf{W}_v$). These matrices define the notion of similarity that is used to match queries to keys. In particular, the similarity between two tokens $i$ and $j$ is measured as:
$$\begin{aligned}
     s_{ij} &= \mathbf{q}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_j\\
     &= (\mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{t}_i)^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t}_j\\
     &= \mathbf{t}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t}_j\\
     &= \mathbf{t}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{t}_j
\end{aligned}$$
What this shows is that $\mathbf{W}_q$ and $\mathbf{W}_k$ define some matrix $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_k$ that modulates how we measure similarity (dot product) between $\mathbf{t}_i$ and $\mathbf{t}_j$. A single self-attention layer therefore measures similarity in just one way.

What if we want to measure similarity in more than one way? For example, maybe we want our net to perform some set of computations based on color similarity, another based on texture similarity, and yet another based on shape similarity? The way transformers can do this is with multihead self-attention (MSA). This method simply consists of running $k$ attention layers in parallel. All these layers are applied to the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. This results in $k$ output sets of tokens, $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k$. To merge these outputs, we concatenate all of them and project back to the original dimensionality of $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^i &= \texttt{attn}^i(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}\\
    \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} &= \begin{bmatrix}
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[0,:] & \dots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[0,:]\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[N-1,:] & \dots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[N-1,:]\\
    \end{bmatrix} &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times kv}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}} &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}} \in \mathbb{R}^{kv \times d}
\end{aligned}$$
where $v$ is the dimensionality of the value vectors and $d$ is the dimensionality of the code vectors of the output. The matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$ merges all the heads; its values are learnable parameters. The other learnable parameters of MSA are the query, key, and value projections for each of the $k$ attention heads. Unlike in single-headed layers, the value vectors need not have the same dimensionality as the token code vectors, since we apply the projection matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$.
motivation_md: A single self-attention head can only measure similarity in one way (e.g., color). MSA allows the model to attend to different features—like shape, texture, and color—simultaneously by using multiple parallel heads.
recap_md:
- MSA runs $k$ independent attention heads in parallel on the same input tokens.
- Outputs from all heads are concatenated and projected back to the original dimensionality using a learnable matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\text{MSA}}$.
- This allows the model to learn multiple distinct similarity metrics for the same input data.

title: Transformer Architecture
one_liner: A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities.
content:
A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities. These two steps are analogous to linear layers interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities in an MLP, as shown below (@fig-transformers-transformer_vs_MLP):

(see figure: The basic transformer architecture versus an MLP.)
motivation_md: The transformer architecture provides a flexible framework for processing sequences by alternating between global information sharing (attention) and local feature transformation (MLP).
recap_md:
- Transformers stack self-attention layers with tokenwise nonlinearities.
- The structure is analogous to the alternating linear and nonlinear layers found in Multi-Layer Perceptrons.

title: ViT Architecture
one_liner: The ViT architecture extends the basic transformer template with layer normalization and residual connections.
content:
Beyond the basic transformer template, there are many variations that can be added, resulting in different particular architectures within the transformer family. Some common additions are normalization layers and residual connections. In @fig-transformers-ViT_arch we plot the ViT architecture from @dosovitskiy2020vit, showing where these additional pieces enter the picture.

(see figure: The ViT transformer architecture~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}. This set of layers forms a computational block, shaded in gray, that can be repeated $L$ times for a depth $L$ ViT. To clarify where the...)

This architecture uses layer normalization before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is done within each token (the token code vector is treated akin to a layer; each dimension of this vector is standardized by the mean and variance over all dimensions of this vector), so we refer to this layer as `token norm`. Notice that `token norm` is a tokenwise operation, just like our tokenwise MLP, but it performs a different kind of transformation and does not have learnable parameters. Residual connections are added around each group of layers.
motivation_md: Standard transformer blocks can be difficult to train at depth; the ViT architecture incorporates normalization and residual connections to improve gradient flow and training stability.
recap_md:
- ViT uses `token norm` (layer normalization) before attention and MLP blocks.
- Residual connections are applied around each major component to facilitate training.
- The architecture consists of a computational block that is repeated $L$ times.

title: Task-Specific Output Layers
one_liner: Task-specific output layers transform the final set of transformer tokens into the desired format, such as classification logits or images.
content: The output of a transformer, as we have so far defined it, is a set of tokens $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. Often we want an output of a different format, such as a single vector of logits for image classification, or in the format of an image for image-to-image tasks. To handle these cases, we typically define a task-specific output layer that takes $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$ as input and produces the desired format as output. For example, to produce a vector of logit predictions we could first sum all the token code vectors in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$ and then, using a single linear layer, project the resulting $d$-dimensional vector into a $K$-dimensional vector (for $K$-way classification).
motivation_md: While transformers process sequences of tokens, real-world tasks often require a single prediction or a specific spatial output, necessitating a final transformation step.
recap_md:
- Transformers output a set of tokens that must be converted for specific tasks.
- Classification often involves pooling (e.g., summing) tokens followed by a linear projection.
- Output layers are customized based on whether the task is classification, regression, or image generation.

title: Permutation Equivariance
one_liner: Transformers are permutation equivariant, meaning permuting the input tokens results in an identically permuted output.
content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are permutation equivariant: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ is a permutation of the order of tokens in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ (i.e., permutes the rows of the matrix). This means that if you scramble (i.e. permute) the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is just a composition of these two types of layers (plus, potentially, residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have: 

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

This property is visualized in @fig-transformers-permutation_equivariance.

(see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.)
motivation_md: Permutation equivariance reflects the fact that standard attention treats tokens as a set rather than a sequence; the model's processing of a token depends on its content and relationship to others, not its absolute index.
recap_md:
- A function is permutation equivariant if permuting the input leads to the same permutation in the output.
- Both attention and tokenwise MLP layers possess this property.
- Consequently, the entire transformer architecture is permutation equivariant unless explicit positional information is added.

title: Tokenization as Convolution
one_liner: Tokenization can be implemented as a convolutional layer where the kernel size and stride both equal the patch size.
content:
The first step in working with transformers is to tokenize the input. The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. This operation can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{T}[n(N/K)+m,c_{\texttt{2}}] = \nonumber\\
&b[c_{\texttt{2}}] +  \sum_{c_{\texttt{1}}=1}^{C_{\texttt{in}}} \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[c_{\texttt{1}},c_{\texttt{2}},k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},K n-k_1,K m-k_2] \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{(tokenization)}
\end{aligned}$$
where, for RGB images, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$, $C_{\texttt{in}}=3$, and $C_{\texttt{out}}=d$ (the token dimensionality). This assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$; otherwise the input can be resized or padded. This is equivalent to a `conv` operator with the following parameters:

```python
T = conv(x_in, channels_in=3, channels_out=d, kernel=K, stride=K) # tokenize
```
motivation_md: Viewing tokenization as a convolution allows us to use optimized deep learning libraries to efficiently transform raw images into the token sequences required by Transformers.
recap_md:
- Image tokenization involves projecting non-overlapping $K \times K$ patches into vectors.
- This is mathematically equivalent to a convolution with kernel size $K$ and stride $K$.
- This operation maps an image with $C_{in}$ channels to a sequence of tokens with dimensionality $d$.

title: Query-Key-Value Projections as Convolutions
one_liner: Query, key, and value projections in transformers are equivalent to multichannel convolutions with a kernel size of 1.
content:
The query, key, and value projections in attention layers apply the same linear transformation (e.g., $\mathbf{W}_q$) to each token vector (each row of $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$). Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized below (@fig-transformers-conv_matmul_equivalence):

(see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.)

Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
motivation_md: Recognizing projections as $1 \times 1$ convolutions highlights the relationship between Transformers and CNNs, showing that Transformers use standard neural operations in a specific sequence-oriented way.
recap_md:
- Q, K, and V projections apply a shared linear weight matrix to every token.
- This shared operation is identical to a $1 \times 1$ convolution across the token sequence.
- This equivalence allows attention projections to be implemented using standard convolutional layers.

title: Vector Embedding
one_liner: A vector embedding is a mapping $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ where an input $\mathbf{x}$ is transformed into a high-dimensional vector $\mathbf{z}$.
content: $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$. Typically both $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ are high-dimensional vectors, and $\mathbf{z}$ is called a **vector embedding** of $\mathbf{x}$. The mapping $f$ is trained so that the resulting representation is useful for downstream tasks.
motivation_md: Vector embeddings allow raw data to be mapped into a structured mathematical space where relationships between data points can be more easily analyzed or processed by machine learning models.
recap_md:
- A vector embedding is the result of a mapping function $f$ from an input space to a representation space.
- Both input and embedding are typically high-dimensional vectors.

title: Disentangled Representation
one_liner: A disentangled representation is one where the dimensions of the embedding $\mathbf{z}$ correspond to independent factors of variation.
content: A representation is considered **disentangled** when the dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ are independent factors of variation. In this way, the representation space $\mathcal{Z}$ captures distinct, non-overlapping features of the data.
motivation_md: Disentangling factors of variation makes representations more interpretable and robust, as individual dimensions can correspond to specific physical or semantic properties like pose, lighting, or color.
recap_md:
- Dimensions in a disentangled representation act as independent factors of variation.
- This property helps isolate specific characteristics of the data within the embedding space.

title: Compression

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

one_liner: A good representation is parsimonious, capturing only the essential characteristics of data necessary for human-interest tasks.
content:
A good representation is one that is parsimonious and captures just the essential characteristics of the data necessary for tasks of human interest. There are at least three senses in which compressed representations are desirable:

1. Compressed representations require less memory to store.

2. Compression is a way to achieve invariance to nuisance factors. Depending on the task, nuisances might include camera noise, lighting conditions, and viewing angle. Factoring out and discarding these nuisances makes the representation more useful for tasks like object recognition where semantics remain constant despite environmental changes.

3. Compression embodies Occam's razor: among competing hypotheses that explain the data equally well, the simplest is most likely to be true. Many representation learning algorithms, such as autoencoders, seek simple representations from which raw data can be regenerated, assigning high likelihood to the data. In representation learning, this means preferring the more compressed of two equally well-fitting representations.

Many algorithms capture these goals by penalizing or constraining the complexity of the learned representation. This penalty must be paired with another objective to avoid degenerate solutions where the representation contains nothing. Usually, the goal is to compress the signal while preserving specific information. Autoencoders and contrastive learning are two primary examples of this approach.
motivation_md: Compression is necessary to reduce storage costs, remove irrelevant 'nuisance' noise, and adhere to the principle of simplicity (Occam's razor) to improve generalization.
recap_md:
- Compression reduces memory requirements and filters out nuisance factors like lighting or noise.
- It follows Occam's razor by seeking the simplest representation that explains the data.
- Complexity penalties are used to force compression while preserving essential information.

title: Minimum Description Length Principle

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

one_liner: The minimum description length principle is a version of Occam's razor applied to data representation.
content: This version of Occam's razor is also known as the **minimum description length principle**. It suggests that the best representation of data is the one that leads to the shortest overall description of the data.
motivation_md: The MDL principle provides a formal framework for balancing the complexity of a model with its ability to describe data, preventing overfitting.
recap_md:
- MDL is a formalization of Occam's razor.
- It prioritizes representations that minimize the length of the data description.

title: Prediction

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

one_liner: A defining property of a good representation is its ability to facilitate the prediction of important world properties.
content:
The purpose of a visual system is to enable actions that achieve desirable future outcomes. Predicting the future is therefore essential, and representations should act as a good substrate for prediction. 

This idea generalizes beyond the future; we may want to predict the past (inferring what happened yesterday from today's observations) or perform abstract predictions like "theory of mind" (inferring another agent's thoughts). In general, prediction refers to the inference of any arbitrary property of the world given observed data. Facilitating the prediction of important world properties—the future, the past, mental states, cause and effect—is perhaps the defining property of a good representation.

Most vision-based representation learning algorithms focus on compressed encodings that are predictive of the future to support decision making. Other overlapping goals include making representations disentangled, interpretable, and actionable (useful for control). These goals often complement each other; for instance, more compressed representations may be simpler and easier for humans to interpret.
motivation_md: Representations exist to support action; since effective action requires understanding what will happen next (or what is currently hidden), a representation's utility is measured by its predictive power.
recap_md:
- Good representations serve as a substrate for predicting future, past, or abstract world properties.
- Prediction is closely linked to decision making and taking effective actions.
- Predictive goals often overlap with compression and interpretability.

title: Imputation

position.section_title: What Makes for a Good Representation?

one_liner: Imputation is the problem of predicting gaps or missing values in measurements.
content: Imputation is the problem of predicting gaps in measurements. Examples include filling in missing pixels in a corrupted image or superresolving a movie to play at a higher framerate.
motivation_md: Real-world data is often noisy, incomplete, or low-resolution; imputation allows us to reconstruct the intended signal from partial observations.
recap_md:
- Imputation involves filling in missing data points or gaps in measurements.
- Common examples include image inpainting and video super-resolution.

title: Autoencoder
one_liner: An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself via a low-dimensional representational bottleneck.
content:
**Autoencoders** are one of the oldest and most common kinds of representation learners. An autoencoder is a function that maps data back to itself (hence the "auto"), but via a low-dimensional representational **bottleneck**, as shown in @fig-representation_learning-autoencoder_diagram:

(see figure: {\small (left) An autoencoder maps from points in data space, to points in representation space, and back. (right) An example of running an autoencoder on an input image of a bird.)

On the right of this figure is an example of an autoencoder applied to an image. While the output is intended to be the same as the input, the key trick is to impose constraints on the intermediate representation $\mathbf{z}$ so that it becomes useful. The most common constraint is compression: $\mathbf{z}$ is a low-dimensional, compressed representation of $\mathbf{x}$.
motivation_md: By forcing data through a narrow bottleneck and requiring the model to reconstruct the original input, autoencoders pressure the system to learn the most essential features of the data.
recap_md:
- Autoencoders map input data to a representation space and then back to the original data space.
- They utilize a low-dimensional bottleneck to force the learning of compressed representations.
- The goal is to reconstruct the input while capturing its essential features in the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$.

title: Bottleneck
one_liner: A bottleneck is a low-dimensional intermediate layer in a neural network that forces data compression.
content: A **bottleneck** is a low-dimensional representational constraint within a model, such as an autoencoder, as shown in (see figure: {\small (left) An autoencoder maps from points in data space, to points in representation space, and back. (right) An example of running an autoencoder on an input image of a bird.). It forces the network to find a compressed representation of the input data.
motivation_md: Bottlenecks are used to prevent models from simply memorizing input data, forcing them to extract meaningful patterns and features instead.
recap_md:
- A bottleneck is a reduced-dimension layer in a representation learning architecture.
- It serves as a constraint that necessitates data compression.

title: Margin
one_liner: A margin is a distance threshold used in contrastive and triplet losses to determine when points are sufficiently separated.
content: Hadsell et al.'s contrastive loss and the triplet loss add the concept of a **margin** to the vanilla formulation. Under this approach, the loss only pushes or pulls points when the distance between them is less than a specified amount $m$, called the margin. Otherwise, points are considered far enough apart or close enough.
motivation_md: In contrastive learning, a margin prevents the model from wasting effort on pairs that are already well-separated, focusing optimization on more difficult or ambiguous examples.
recap_md: - The margin $m$ defines a distance threshold for applying contrastive loss.

title: Alignment and Uniformity Properties
one_liner: Contrastive loss encourages embeddings to satisfy two key properties: alignment of positive pairs and uniformity across the hypersphere.
content: Wang and Isola showed that the contrastive loss (specifically the InfoNCE form) encourages two simple properties of the embeddings: alignment and uniformity. Alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair will map to the same point in the embedding space; that is, the mapping is invariant to the difference between the views. Uniformity comes from the negative term, which encourages embeddings to spread out and tend toward an evenly spread, uniform distribution. For this to work out mathematically, the embeddings must be normalized (each embedding vector must be a unit vector). Otherwise, the negative term can push embeddings toward being infinitely far apart. It is standard practice in contrastive learning to apply $L_2$ normalization to the embeddings, resulting in a uniform distribution over the surface of the $M$-dimensional hypersphere, where $M$ is the dimensionality of the embeddings.
motivation_md: These properties ensure that related inputs are mapped close together (alignment) while preventing the model from collapsing all inputs to a single point (uniformity).
recap_md: - Alignment ensures positive pairs map to similar points in the embedding space.

title: Alignment
one_liner: Alignment is the property where two views in a positive pair map to the same point in the embedding space.
content: Alignment is the property that two views in a positive pair will map to the same point in the embedding space. This means the mapping is invariant to the difference between the views.
motivation_md: Alignment ensures that different versions of the same underlying concept or object are recognized as being the same by the model.
recap_md: - Alignment makes the embedding mapping invariant to differences between views of a positive pair.

title: Uniformity
one_liner: Uniformity is the property that embeddings spread out to form an evenly distributed, uniform distribution.
content: Uniformity comes from the negative term in contrastive loss, which encourages embeddings to spread out and tend toward an evenly spread, uniform distribution.
motivation_md: Uniformity prevents feature collapse, ensuring the model uses the full capacity of the embedding space to distinguish between different data points.
recap_md: - Uniformity is driven by the negative term in the loss function.

title: Embedding Normalization
one_liner: Applying $L_2$ normalization to embeddings ensures they form a uniform distribution on a hypersphere rather than drifting infinitely apart.
content: For uniformity to work out mathematically, the embeddings must be normalized, meaning each embedding vector must be a unit vector. Without normalization, the negative term in the loss can push embeddings toward being infinitely far apart from each other. In contrastive learning and other forms of representation learning, it is standard practice to apply $L_2$ normalization. This results in embeddings tending toward a uniform distribution over the surface of the $M$-dimensional hypersphere, where $M$ is the dimensionality of the embeddings.
motivation_md: Normalization constrains the embedding space to a fixed geometry (the hypersphere), which makes the distance-based loss functions stable and well-defined.
recap_md: - Embeddings must be unit vectors to prevent the negative term from pushing them infinitely far apart.

title: Alignment and Uniformity Losses
one_liner: Contrastive learning can be decomposed into explicit loss terms for alignment and uniformity.
content:
Contrastive learning may be explicitly decomposed into one loss for alignment and another for uniformity, with the following forms:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^+) \sim p_{\texttt{pos}}} [\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^+)\right\rVert_2^{\alpha}]\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}(f;t) &= \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}, \, \mathbf{x}^- \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [e^{-t\left\lVert f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}^-)\right\rVert_2^2}]\\
    \mathcal{L}(f;\alpha,t,\lambda) &= \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{align}}(f;\alpha) + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{unif}}
\end{aligned}$$

where $p_{\texttt{pos}}$ is the distribution of positive pairs and $\alpha$, $t$, and $\lambda$ are hyperparameters of the losses.
motivation_md: Decomposing the loss allows for finer control over the trade-off between how closely positive pairs are aligned and how uniformly the embeddings are distributed.
recap_md: - The alignment loss measures the distance between positive pairs raised to the power of $\alpha$.

title: Perceptual Group
one_liner: A perceptual group is a visual representation consisting of groups of primitive elements that form meaningful structures like contours or objects.
content:
In the tradition of computer vision and human vision science, the **perceptual group** is a central object of interest. While a camera sees raw RGB pixel values, the human mind sees structures such as contours, surfaces, objects, and events. Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as *groups of primitive elements*: for example, a contour is a group of points that form a line, and an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive whole. Identifying these meaningful perceptual groups is a longstanding area of interest in both human and computer vision.

(see figure: A few kinds of perceptual organization in the human visual system.)
motivation_md: Perceptual grouping allows vision systems to move from raw pixel data to higher-level, meaningful structures that are easier to reason about.
recap_md: - Perceptual groups are structures formed by grouping primitive elements like points or parts.

title: Why Group?
one_liner: Grouping is a form of representation learning that discovers language-like structures from unsupervised principles to facilitate downstream processing.
content: Grouping is a special case of representation learning, and the reasons to group are the same: groups serve as a good substrate for downstream analysis and processing. Perceptual organization involves structures like objects, spatial relationships, shapes, and events, which are similar to the elements used to describe an image in text. While modern trends involve mapping images to text to use natural language processing tools, perceptual organization aims to achieve similarly powerful, symbolic, and semantic representations through bottom-up grouping rules. It is about *discovering* language-like structures from unsupervised principles rather than relying on human-language supervision.
motivation_md: By discovering discrete, symbolic structures like 'objects' from raw data, grouping provides a more effective way for machines to reason about the world without needing explicit human labels.
recap_md: - Grouping provides a discrete, semantic substrate for downstream vision tasks.

title: Code Vector
one_liner: A code vector is a representation of the data within a cluster, often summarizing the main modes of behavior in a dataset.
content: Many clustering algorithms not only partition the data but also compute a representation of the data within each cluster; this representation is sometimes called a code vector. The most common code vector is the cluster center, $\mu$, which is the mean value of all datapoints assigned to the cluster. Clusters can also be represented by other statistics of the data assigned to them, such as the variance of this data or some arbitrary embedding vector, though this is less common. The set of cluster centers, $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1}^k$, serves as a representation of a whole dataset, summarizing its main modes of behavior.
motivation_md: Clustering algorithms need a way to summarize and represent the groups they identify. Code vectors provide a compact mathematical description of each cluster, enabling data compression and interpretation of the dataset's primary characteristics.
recap_md: - A code vector represents the data points within a specific cluster.

title: Cluster Center
one_liner: The cluster center is the mean value of all datapoints assigned to a cluster and serves as its most common code vector.
content: The most common code vector is the cluster center, $\mu$, which is defined as the mean value of all datapoints assigned to the cluster. While clusters can be represented by other statistics, such as variance or arbitrary embedding vectors, the cluster center is the standard representation. The set of all cluster centers, $\{\mu_i\}_{i=1}^k$, represents the entire dataset by summarizing its main modes of behavior.
motivation_md: The cluster center provides a simple, mathematically optimal summary of a group of points by minimizing the average distance to all members of that group.
recap_md: - The cluster center $\mu$ is the mean of all points in a cluster.

title: $K$-Means
one_liner: K-means is a clustering algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by minimizing the distance between datapoints and their assigned cluster code vectors.
content:
K-means is a popular clustering algorithm that partitions data into $k$ clusters. Each datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ is assigned to a cluster indexed by an integer $a_i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, and each cluster is associated with a code vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$. The $k$-means objective is to minimize the distance between each datapoint and the code vector of its assigned cluster:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{kmeans}} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_{a_i} - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^2_2
\end{aligned}
$$

This objective ensures that the code vector is a good approximation of the datapoints it represents, providing a faithful but compressed representation of the dataset. The algorithm optimizes two sets of parameters: the cluster assignments (represented by an encoder function $f$) and the code vectors (represented by a decoder function $g$).

[FIGURE:83e2c20af43a1fa5 | A learning diagram for k-means ($L_2$) clustering. It shows an input 'Data' represented as {x^(i)} entering a central box via an arrow. Inside the box, the 'Objective' is...]

The process can be viewed as a learning algorithm similar to an autoencoder, where the bottleneck consists of discrete integers rather than continuous vectors. Because the cluster assignments are discrete, gradient descent is not applicable, and a specific optimization strategy is required.
motivation_md: K-means solves the problem of finding a compressed, discrete representation of a dataset. It is used to discover underlying groups and simplify complex data into a fixed number of representative prototypes.
recap_md: - Partitions data into $k$ clusters by minimizing the sum of squared distances to cluster centers.

title: Optimizing $k$-means
one_liner: K-means is optimized using block coordinate descent, alternating between updating cluster assignments and recomputing cluster means.
content:
K-means uses an optimization algorithm called block coordinate descent, which alternates between fully minimizing the objective with respect to two parameter blocks: the cluster assignments $\{a_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and the code vectors $\{\mathbf{z}_j\}_{j=1}^k$. 

The update rules are:
1. Assign each datapoint to the nearest cluster:
$$\begin{aligned}
    a_i &\leftarrow \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,k\}} \left\lVert\mathbf{z}_j - \mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2
\end{aligned}$$
2. Set each code vector to be the mean of the datapoints assigned to it:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{z}_j &\leftarrow \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(a_i = j)\mathbf{x}^{(i)}
\end{aligned}$$

These steps repeat until a fixed point is reached. The second update is optimal because the mean of a dataset minimizes the sum of squared distances to its points. This iterative process of computing means and reassigning data is why the algorithm is named $k$-means.

(see figure: A scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing several clusters of colored data points. Five distinct clusters are visible: yellow, blue, red, orange, and maroon. Large 'X' markers in corresponding...)
(see figure: A 2D scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing five distinct clusters of data points, each colored differently: yellow, blue, red, orange, and maroon. Each cluster has a large 'X' mark of the same...)
(see figure: A 2D scatter plot on x_1 and x_2 axes showing five distinct clusters of data points, each colored differently: yellow, blue, red, brown, and orange. Each cluster contains a large 'X' marker of...)
(see figure: A scatter plot on a 2D plane with axes x_1 and x_2 showing five distinct clusters of data points. Each cluster is colored differently (blue, yellow, red, maroon, and orange) and has a large 'X'...)
motivation_md: Since the cluster assignment parameters in k-means are discrete, standard gradient descent cannot be used. Block coordinate descent provides an efficient, iterative way to reach a local optimum by solving simpler sub-problems.
recap_md: - Alternates between assigning points to the nearest center and updating centers to the mean of assigned points.

title: $K$-Means from Multiple Perspectives
one_liner: K-means can be viewed as a representation learning algorithm, a generative model, or an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck.
content: K-means can be understood through multiple complementary perspectives. It is a representation learning algorithm, similar to an autoencoder but with a discrete bottleneck. It can also be viewed as a simple generative model, specifically a 'vanilla' form of a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). These relationships form a tapestry where models like VAEs and GMMs extend the concepts of autoencoders and $k$-means into formal probabilistic frameworks. Recognizing the small 'deltas' or differences between these models helps in understanding the broader landscape of machine learning.
motivation_md: Understanding k-means from different angles allows researchers to connect simple clustering to more complex probabilistic models like GMMs and VAEs, providing a unified view of representation learning.
recap_md: - K-means is equivalent to an autoencoder with a discrete bottleneck.

title: Clustering in Vision
one_liner: In computer vision, clustering is related to perceptual grouping, where visual elements are organized into structures like contours and objects.
content: In the field of vision, clustering is closely related to perceptual grouping. Humans perceive the world as organized into levels of structure, such as contours, surfaces, objects, and events. These structures are essentially clusters of related visual elements; for example, a contour is a group of points forming a line, and an object is a group of parts forming a cohesive whole. Algorithms like $k$-means can discover these structures when applied in a suitable feature space.
motivation_md: Perceptual grouping explains how high-level objects emerge from low-level sensory data. Clustering algorithms provide a mathematical way to simulate this human ability to organize visual information.
recap_md: - Relates clustering algorithms to the human ability to organize visual elements into cohesive structures.

title: Contrastive Learning
one_liner: Contrastive learning is a compression strategy that supervises representations to be invariant to different viewing transformations.
content: Contrastive learning is a compression strategy where a representation is supervised to be invariant to certain viewing transformations. This results in a compressed representation that captures only the properties common between different data views, such as different camera angles or imaging modalities. It is closely related to clustering; while contrastive learning maps similar points to similar embeddings, clustering is an extreme version where similar points are mapped to the exact same embedding.
motivation_md: Instead of just limiting the number of bits (like an information bottleneck), contrastive learning allows us to explicitly supervise which information to keep by focusing on features that remain constant across different views of the same object.
recap_md: - Learns representations by enforcing invariance across different views of the same data.

title: Data Views
one_liner: Data views are different ways of observing the same scene or object, such as through different cameras or imaging modalities.
content: In the context of contrastive learning, data views refer to different observations of the same underlying data. For example, two different data views could correspond to two different cameras looking at the same scene, or two different imaging modalities, such as color and depth. Contrastive learning aims to capture properties that are common across these different views while throwing away view-specific noise.
motivation_md: By using multiple views of the same data, learning algorithms can distinguish between essential features (which appear in all views) and incidental features (which appear in only one), leading to more robust representations.
recap_md: - Represents different perspectives or modalities of the same data point.

title: Causal Attention
one_liner: Causal attention is a masking strategy where each token in a sequence can only attend to previous tokens.
content:
(see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.)

This kind of matrix is called causal because each output index $i$ only depends on input indices $j$ such that $j < i$. If $\mathbf{A}$ is an attention matrix, then this strategy is called causal attention. This is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence. This approach can dramatically speed up training because all the sub-sequence prediction problems (predict $\mathbf{t}_{n-1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-2}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-1}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n+1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$) are supervised at the same time.
motivation_md: Causal attention is essential for autoregressive modeling, where the goal is to predict the next token in a sequence based only on preceding information. By masking future tokens, it prevents the model from "cheating" during training and allows the simultaneous calculation of predictions for every position in the sequence, significantly improving training efficiency.
recap_md: - Causal attention ensures that output at index $i$ only depends on inputs at indices $j < i$.

title: Multilayer Masked Attention
one_liner: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction in deep networks by maintaining the property that outputs only depend on previous input tokens across all layers.
content:
This strategy also works for transformers with more than one layer, where the masking strategy looks like shown in @fig-transformers-multilayer_masked_attention.

(see figure: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction with a deep net.)

Notice that the output tokens on every layer $l$ have the property that $\mathbf{t}^l_n$ only depends on $\mathbf{T}^0_{1:n-1}$, where $\mathbf{T}^0$ are the initial set of tokens input into the transformer. Also notice that, after the first layer, all subsequent layers can use causal attention that is not shifted in time, and the previous property is still maintained. Finally, notice that the subnetwork that predicts each subsequent output token overlaps substantially with the subnetworks that predict each previous token. That is, there is sharing of computation between all the prediction problems.
motivation_md: In deep transformer architectures, it is necessary to maintain the causal constraint through every layer to ensure that the final prediction for a token does not inadvertently incorporate information from future tokens in the input sequence.
recap_md: - In multilayer transformers, output $\mathbf{t}^l_n$ depends only on initial tokens $\mathbf{T}^0_{1:n-1}$.

title: Positional Encodings
one_liner: Positional encoding concatenates a code representing a token's position within a signal onto each token to overcome the permutation equivariance of transformer operations.
content: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes; the only change is that the outputs get permuted. A consequence is that tokens do not encode their position within the representation of the signal. Sometimes, however, we may wish to retain positional knowledge. For example, knowing that a token is a representation of the top region of an image can help identify that the token is likely to represent sky. Positional encoding concatenates a code representing position within the signal onto each token. If the signal is an image, then the positional code should represent the x- and y-coordinates. However, it need not represent these coordinates as scalars; more commonly we use a periodic representation of position, where the coordinates are encoded as the vector of values a set of sinusoidal waves take on at each position.
motivation_md: Because transformer operations are permutation equivariant, they treat inputs as an unordered set. Positional encodings are necessary to inject information about the order or spatial arrangement of tokens, which is often critical for understanding context in text or images.
recap_md: - Transformers are permutation equivariant, meaning they do not inherently recognize token order.

title: Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
one_liner: Sinusoidal positional encoding represents coordinates using a vector of values from a set of sinusoidal waves at different frequencies.
content:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{p}_x &= [\sin(x), \sin(x/B), \sin(x/B^2), \ldots, \sin(x/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p}_y &= [\sin(y), \sin(y/B), \sin(y/B^2), \ldots, \sin(y/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p} &= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}_x\\ \mathbf{p}_y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ where $x$ and $y$ are the coordinates of the token. This representation is visualized in @fig-transformers-positional_codes:

(see figure: Positional codes.)
motivation_md: Using sinusoidal waves of varying frequencies allows the model to represent relative positions and generalize to sequence lengths or image resolutions not seen during training, as the periodic nature provides a continuous and structured coordinate system.
recap_md: - Position is encoded as a vector of sine wave values at different scales $B^P$.

title: Learned Positional Codes
one_liner: Learned positional codes are spatial representations that the model optimizes during training rather than using fixed mathematical functions.
content: Another strategy is to simply let the positional codes be learned by the model, which could potentially result in a better representation of space than sinusoidal codes.
motivation_md: While fixed sinusoidal encodings are robust, allowing the model to learn its own positional embeddings can result in representations that are more specifically tailored to the nuances of the dataset and the specific task at hand.
recap_md: - Positional codes can be learned parameters rather than fixed sinusoidal functions.

title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

position.section_title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

one_liner: Fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers are all affine transformations that differ in how their weight matrices are structured and determined.
content:
(see figure: A comparison of three neural network layer types: fully connected (fc), convolutional (conv), and self-attention (attn). For each, it shows a wiring graph of connections between input and output...)

Many layers in deep nets are special kinds of affine transformations. Three we have seen so far are fully-connected layers (`fc`), convolutional layers (`conv`), and self-attention layers (`attn`). All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$. In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as some function of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `conv` layers this function is very simple: just make a Toeplitz matrix that repeats the convolutional kernel(s) to match the dimensionality of $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `attn` layers the function that determines $\mathbf{W}$ is a bit more involved, and typically we don't use biases $\mathbf{b}$.

Each of these layers can be represented as a matrix, and examining the structure in these matrices can be a useful way to understand their similarities and differences. The matrix for an `fc` layer is full rank, whereas the matrices for `conv` and `attn` layers have low-rank structure, but different kinds of low-rank structure.
motivation_md: Understanding the structural differences between these layers helps in choosing the right architecture for a task. While fully connected layers are general, convolutional and attention layers use specific matrix structures to achieve efficiency and capture inductive biases like translation invariance or global dependencies.
recap_md: - All three layer types can be expressed as the affine transformation $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$.

title: Graph Neural Networks
one_liner: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a general class of architectures for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set.
content: Transformers can be considered as a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs). GNNs are a very general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer is doing exactly that: it takes an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applies a network of transformations over that set until after enough layers a final representation or prediction is read out.
motivation_md: GNNs provide a flexible framework for data that doesn't fit into a standard grid, like social networks or molecules. Viewing transformers as GNNs helps unify different architectural concepts under the umbrella of set-based processing.
recap_md: - GNNs process sets by defining a graph of operations over the elements.

title: Natural Image
one_liner: A natural image is a sample from the extremely small subset of all possible pixel combinations that represents real-world visual scenes.
content:
First, we need to understand what we mean by a natural image. An image is a very high dimensional array of pixels $\ell\left[n,m\right]$ and therefore, the space of all possible images is very large. Even if you consider very small thumbnails of just $32\times32$ pixels and three color channels, with 8 bits per channel, there are more than $10^{7,398}$ possible images. Of course, most of them will just be random noise. @fig-spaces_real_images shows one image, with size $32\times32$ color pixels, sampled from the set of natural images, and one typical example from the set of all images. A typical sample from the set of all images is $32\times32$ pixels independently sampled from a uniform distribution.

(see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32\times32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...)
motivation_md: The concept of a 'natural image' is vital because computer vision models are designed to exploit the specific statistical properties and structures found in real-world scenes, which occupy only a tiny fraction of the total mathematical space of possible pixel grids.
recap_md: - Natural images occupy a tiny fraction of the total space of possible pixel combinations.

title: Markov Random Field (MRF) Models

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

one_liner: Markov random field models assume that a pixel's probability distribution is independent of the rest of the image if enough surrounding pixels are specified.
content: Markov random field (MRF) models are a powerful class of image models with a precise mathematical form. The core intuition for these models is that if the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. Fitting and sampling from the MRF structure requires the mathematical tools of graphical models.
motivation_md: MRF models provide a structured way to capture local dependencies in images, allowing for statistical modeling of image data without needing to model every global pixel interaction simultaneously.
recap_md:
- A pixel's state is independent of distant pixels given its local neighborhood.
 - They provide a precise mathematical framework for probabilistic graphical models in imaging.
 - They are used to fit and sample from complex image structures.

title: Efros and Leung Texture Generation Model

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

one_liner: The Efros and Leung model synthesizes textures by conditioning a central pixel's value on a large enough region of nearby pixels.
content: The Efros and Leung texture generation model introduces an algorithm for texture synthesis that exploits intuitions about the Markov structure of images to synthesize visually compelling textures. The intuition of the model is that if you condition on a large enough region of nearby pixels around a center pixel, that effectively determines the value of the central pixel.
motivation_md: This model was developed to synthesize realistic textures by leveraging the local statistical regularities found in natural images.
recap_md:
- Exploits the Markov structure of images for texture synthesis.
 - Conditions the value of a central pixel on its surrounding neighborhood.
 - Capable of generating visually compelling textures from local information.

title: Nonlocal Means Denoising Algorithm

position.section_title: Nonparametric Markov Random Field Image Models

one_liner: The nonlocal means algorithm denoises an image by calculating a weighted sum of pixels based on the similarity of their local neighborhoods.
content:
The nonlocal means denoising algorithm defines a denoised image as a weighted sum of all other pixels in the image, weighted by the similarity of the local neighborhoods of each pair of pixels. More formally, the denoised value is given by:
$$\ell_{\mbox{NLM}}[n,m] = \sum_{k,l} w_{n,m}[k,l] \ell[k,l]$$
where the weights are defined as:
$$w_{n,m}[k,l] = \frac{1}{Z_{n,m}} \exp{\frac{- \left| \ell[N_{k,l}] - \ell[N_{n,m}] \right| ^2}{h^2}},$$
In this expression, $N_{i, j}$ denotes an $h \times h$ region of pixels centered at $i, j$, and $Z_{n,m}$ is a normalization factor so that $\sum_{kl} w_{n,m}[k,l] = 1$. The parameter $h$ is typically set to $10 \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the estimated image noise standard deviation.

[FIGURE:c5b8102b308188df | Four square panels demonstrating the Non-Local Means weighting function. The first pair shows a brick wall texture with a white dot at the center; its corresponding weight map shows a grid of white...]

Regions of support for the nonlocal means denoising algorithm. Note the sampling at image regions with similar local structure as the image position to be denoised.

(see figure: Nonlocal means denoising algorithm results. (left) Original image without noise. (middle) Noisy image. (right) Denoised image.*Source*:Figure from @Baudes2011)

The algorithm effectively removes additive Gaussian noise by averaging pixels with similar local neighborhoods.
motivation_md: Traditional denoising often blurs edges; nonlocal means preserves structure by averaging pixels that share similar local patterns, regardless of their spatial distance.
recap_md:
- Denoises by computing a weighted average of pixels across the entire image.
 - Weights are determined by the similarity of $h \times h$ local neighborhoods.
 - Effectively removes Gaussian noise while preserving repetitive structural patterns.

title: Low-level Image Regularities
one_liner: Low-level image regularities are statistical patterns used to build image models for synthesis and denoising without understanding image content.
content: Low-level regularities of images are utilized to build statistical models that do not try to understand the actual content of the pictures. Modeling these statistical regularities enables many tasks, including both image synthesis and image denoising.
motivation_md: By focusing on low-level statistics rather than high-level semantics, researchers can develop efficient algorithms for fundamental tasks like noise reduction and texture generation.
recap_md:
- Focuses on statistical patterns rather than semantic content.
 - Enables tasks like image synthesis and denoising.
 - Forms the basis for many low-level statistical image models.

title: Space of Natural Images
one_liner: The space of natural images is a very small subset of the space of all possible images.
content:
The space of natural images is just a very small part of the space of all possible images. For example, in the case of color images with $32 \times 32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like noise. Simple models try to constrain this space, but while they are useful in several applications, they often fail to provide a strong enough model to sample new, realistic images.

(see figure: The space of natural images is just very small part of the space of all possible images. In the case of color images with $32 \times 32$ pixels, most of the space is filled with images that look like...)
motivation_md: Understanding that natural images occupy a tiny manifold within the space of all possible pixel combinations is crucial for developing effective compression, denoising, and generative models.
recap_md:
- Natural images represent a tiny fraction of all possible pixel combinations.
 - Most random pixel combinations result in noise rather than recognizable images.
 - Simple models only slightly reduce the space of possible images.

title: Texture
one_liner: A texture is an image composed of similar-looking elements where the representation focuses on statistics rather than individual elements.
content: A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually. This concept is intimately related to human perception.
motivation_md: Defining texture statistically allows for the analysis and synthesis of complex patterns without needing to explicitly model every individual component.
recap_md:
- Composed of a set of similar-looking elements.
 - Represented by the statistics of elements rather than individual details.
 - Closely linked to how humans perceive visual patterns.

title: Infinite Texture Generation Algorithm
one_liner: The infinite texture generation algorithm creates new images by cropping pieces from a very large source image of a texture.
content:
Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm: if we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images. While successful in practice, this algorithm provides little understanding of how human perception works, how to modify textures, or what representations are useful for measuring texture similarity.

(see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.)
motivation_md: This 'trivial' approach serves as a baseline for texture synthesis, highlighting the difference between simple data reuse and actual statistical modeling.
recap_md:
- Generates textures by cropping pieces from a large source image.
 - Effective in practice but lacks theoretical depth regarding perception.
 - Does not help in understanding texture similarity or modification.

title: Subitizing

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

one_liner: Subitizing is the ability to determine the number of objects in a display without counting them, typically limited to fewer than five elements.
content: Subitizing is the ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them. This phenomenon only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.
motivation_md: Subitizing is a fundamental cognitive process that distinguishes rapid, automatic number perception from the slower, sequential process of counting.
recap_md:
- Refers to instant recognition of quantity without counting.
 - Generally limited to displays of fewer than five items.
 - Represents a specific threshold in human visual perception.

title: Steerable Pyramid

position.section_title: Image Pyramids and Multiscale Image Analysis

one_liner: The steerable pyramid provides a clean separation of the image into different scales and orientations.
content: The steerable pyramid decomposes an image into isotropic spatial frequency bands. This process provides a clean separation of the image into different scales and orientations.
motivation_md: It is used to analyze images by separating features based on both their size (scale) and their direction (orientation), which is useful for texture analysis and computer vision.
recap_md: - It decomposes images into isotropic spatial frequency bands.

title: Multiscale Image Pyramid

position.section_title: Image Pyramids and Multiscale Image Analysis

one_liner: A multiscale image pyramid is a set of images at different resolutions used to achieve scale invariance in tasks like object detection.
content: To introduce scale invariance in image processing, one possible solution is to change the size of a template to cover a wide range of possible sizes. However, this is computationally expensive because detecting large objects requires convolutions with big kernels. An alternative is to change the image size, resulting in a multiscale image pyramid. (see figure: Multiscale image pyramid. Each image is 25 percent smaller than the previous one. The red box indicates the size of a template used for detecting birds. As the size of the template is fixed; it will...) In this pyramid, each image is obtained by scaling down the image from the previous level (for example, by reducing the number of pixels by 25 percent). This allows the detection of objects at different sizes using a single, small template, keeping the convolutions computationally efficient.
motivation_md: Detecting objects of varying sizes with a fixed-size template is difficult; pyramids allow efficient scale-invariant detection by resizing the image instead of the template.
recap_md: - It enables scale invariance by representing an image at multiple resolutions.

title: Linear Image Transforms
one_liner: A linear image transform represents an image as a vector of coefficients obtained by projecting the input image onto a set of projection vectors.
content: For an input image $\boldsymbol\ell$ with $N$ pixels, a linear transform is defined as $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\ell$, where $\mathbf{r}$ is a vector of dimensionality $M$ and $\mathbf{P}$ is a matrix of size $N \times M$. The columns of $\mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, ..., \mathbf{P}_{M-1}]$ are the projection vectors. The vector $\mathbf{r}$ contains the transform coefficients $\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{P}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\ell$, which correspond to a different representation of the image than the original pixel space.
motivation_md: Linear transforms provide alternative representations of image data, often making certain features easier to analyze or compress than in the original pixel space.
recap_md: - It maps an image $\boldsymbol\ell$ to a coefficient vector $\mathbf{r}$ using a projection matrix $\mathbf{P}$.

title: Invertible Transforms
one_liner: Invertible transforms allow the recovery of the original input image from its projection coefficients using a set of basis vectors.
