motivation_md: Standard training focuses on average performance, which leaves systems vulnerable to specific, targeted failures. Robustness techniques aim to protect against these worst-case scenarios.
recap_md: - Adversarial robustness focuses on minimizing worst-case error instead of average error.

title: Data Augmentation
one_liner: Data augmentation expands a dataset by adding random transformations of existing datapoints to simulate the effect of having more real data.
content:
Data augmentation augments a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For example, common data augmentations can be applied to an image to create variations.

(see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.)

When you do this for every image in a dataset, you are essentially mapping from a smaller dataset to a larger dataset. Since more data is usually better, this simulates the effect of adding more real data. It is one of the most important tools in machine learning, effectively converting "small data" into "big data."

[FIGURE:d88031ceb8315562 | A flowchart showing the process of data augmentation. It starts with a 'Small dataset' represented by the set {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N, which passes through a 'Data augmentation' block...]

For each $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}$ pair in the original dataset, you add $M$ new synthetic pairs $\{T(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^M$, where $T$ is a data transformation function with stochastic parameters $\theta \sim p_{\theta}$. For example, if $T$ is a `crop` function, $\theta$ would be the coordinates specifying where to apply the crop, randomly selected for each of the $M$ generated versions.
motivation_md: Machine learning is data-driven, and performance often scales with data volume. Augmentation provides a low-cost way to increase dataset size and improve model generalization.
recap_md: - Data augmentation creates synthetic training examples using stochastic transformations.

title: Invariance in Data Augmentation
one_liner: Invariance in data augmentation assumes that the target output remains unchanged even when the input is transformed.
content:
In many data augmentation scenarios, we do not apply any transformation to the $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$ values. The assumption is that the target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are invariant to the augmentations of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$. If $y(\mathbf{x})$ is the true $\mathbf{y}$ for an input $\mathbf{x}$, we assume:
$$\begin{aligned}    y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta)) \quad \forall \theta \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{$y$ invariant to $T$}
\end{aligned}$$
For scene classification, mirror augmentation is appropriate because mirroring a scene does not change its class label. However, for optical character recognition, mirror augmentation is not suitable because the mirror image of a 'b' looks like a 'd'. Character recognition is not mirror invariant. Similarly, molecular data with chiral structures may behave differently than their mirror images.
motivation_md: Applying transformations that preserve the label helps the model learn to ignore irrelevant variations in the input data, focusing only on features essential for classification.
recap_md: - Invariance means the label $y$ remains the same after the input $x$ is transformed.

title: Equivariance in Data Augmentation
one_liner: Equivariance in data augmentation requires transforming the target output in a way that corresponds to the transformation applied to the input.
motivation_md: For tasks like segmentation or object detection, the labels are spatially linked to the input. Equivariant augmentation ensures the labels remain correct after the input is moved or cropped.
recap_md: - Equivariance ensures that transformations applied to the input are matched by corresponding transformations to the label.

title: Paired Translation
one_liner: Paired translation is a setting where training data consists of explicit pairs of corresponding items from two different domains.
content:
In the paired translation setting, training data consists of explicit correspondences between items in different domains, such as an original image and its colorized version. This is distinguished from unpaired translation, where such direct mappings are not provided in the training set.

(see figure: (left) An example of paired image-to-image translation (colorization) versus (right) unpaired translation (photo to Cezanne). Figure adapted from @CycleGAN2017)
motivation_md: Distinguishing between paired and unpaired data is crucial for selecting the appropriate generative architecture, as paired data allows for direct supervised learning while unpaired data requires more complex distribution-matching techniques.
recap_md: - Paired translation uses training examples where each input has a specific, known target output.

title: Emergent Pairing in GANs
one_liner: GANs can learn mappings between distributions without instance-level supervision because the pairing between input and output emerges to satisfy the global objective.
content:
GANs possess a useful property for solving translation tasks: they train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$ without knowing the specific pairing between $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ values. Instead, this pairing is emergent, self-organizing so that all $\mathbf{z}$-vectors map to realistic images and collectively cover the data distribution.

When training a GAN to map from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$ values, the objective is:

$$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(g_{	heta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{y})) \big] \end{aligned}$$

In this formulation, $\mathbf{y}$ plays the role of the data and $\mathbf{x}$ plays the role of the noise. Such a GAN self-organizes so that outputs are realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values and different inputs map to different outputs without requiring paired supervision. While this GAN may learn the correct mapping, the problem contains many symmetries; for example, a permutation of the mapping achieves the same loss because the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution, not instance-level matching. The discriminator checks if an output belongs to the set of realistic values rather than matching a specific target instance.
motivation_md: Standard supervised learning requires expensive paired datasets. GANs solve this by allowing models to learn mappings between sets of data based only on the overall distribution, enabling tasks like style transfer where exact pairs don't exist.
recap_md: - GANs learn mappings between distributions through emergent self-organization rather than predefined pairs.

title: Unpaired vs Unsupervised Learning
one_liner: Unpaired learning is distinct from unsupervised learning because supervision is still provided via set-level labels.
content: We call this unpaired learning rather than unsupervised because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which set each datapoint belongs to. That is, we know whether each image is an $\mathbf{x}$ or a $\mathbf{y}$.
motivation_md: This distinction clarifies that while we lack instance-to-instance links, we still possess critical categorical information that guides the learning process.
recap_md: - Unpaired learning uses set-level labels rather than instance-level correspondences.

title: Cycle-Consistency
one_liner: Cycle-consistency is the principle that translating an object from one domain to another and back should return it to its original state.
content:
A regular GAN objective applied to mapping from $X$ to $Y$ solves the unpaired translation problem but cannot distinguish between the correct mapping and many other symmetric solutions. To break this symmetry, we use cycle-consistency. The idea is that if we translate from $X$ to $Y$ and then translate back from $Y$ to $X$, we should arrive where we started. For example, in language, translating "apple" to the French "pomme" and then back to English should return "apple."

This trick allows for checking the quality of a translation system even for unfamiliar languages. Because we expect many translations to be roughly one-to-one, cycle-consistency losses act as regularizers that encourage the learned mapping to maintain this one-to-one property.
motivation_md: Unpaired GANs suffer from mode collapse or incorrect mappings because many permutations satisfy the distribution-matching goal. Cycle-consistency provides a structural constraint to ensure the mapping is meaningful and reversible.
recap_md: - Cycle-consistency requires that $f(g(x)) \approx x$ and $g(f(y)) \approx y$.

title: Backtranslation
one_liner: In natural language processing, the concept of cycle-consistency is referred to as backtranslation.
content: In natural language processing, the idea of cycle-consistency is known as backtranslation.
motivation_md: Using backtranslation allows NLP models to leverage large amounts of monolingual data to improve translation quality by ensuring consistency across languages.
recap_md: - Backtranslation is the NLP equivalent of cycle-consistency.

title: CycleGAN
one_liner: CycleGAN is a technique for unpaired image-to-image translation that uses dual GAN objectives combined with cycle-consistency losses.
content:
The CycleGAN model translates between domain $X$ and domain $Y$ using a complete objective that combines standard GAN losses with cycle-consistency losses:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\ \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \end{aligned}$$

The full objective is:
$$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\ \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big] \end{aligned}$$

This model ensures that outputs in domain $Y$ look realistic to a $Y$-discriminator (and vice versa) and that the mappings are cycle-consistent. 

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)

While these losses encourage one-to-one functions and reduce valid solutions, symmetries may still exist. If the $X$-to-$Y$ mapping and its inverse are both permuted, CycleGAN may still be satisfied despite the mapping being incorrect.
motivation_md: CycleGAN enables high-quality image-to-image translation (like turning horses into zebras) without requiring any direct pairs of images, which are often impossible to obtain.
recap_md: - CycleGAN combines two GANs with an $L_1$ cycle-consistency loss.

title: Trend Toward General-Purpose Generative Models
one_liner: The current trend in AI is to replace specialized, bespoke systems with general-purpose conditional generative models.
content: Many problems in computer vision can be framed as structured prediction, for which conditional generative models provide a unified solution. There is a significant trend in the field to replace bespoke systems designed for specific tasks—such as object detectors or image captioning systems—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This shift toward general-purpose modeling tools reduces the need for special-purpose systems for specific vision problems.
motivation_md: General-purpose models simplify the AI pipeline by using a single architecture to solve many different tasks, leading to more robust and versatile systems.
recap_md: - AI is moving away from task-specific architectures toward unified generative models.

title: Data Bias and Shift
one_liner: Data bias and shift occur when the distribution of data encountered during deployment differs from the distribution used during training.
content: The goal of learning is to acquire rules from past data that perform well on future data. While machine learning theory often assumes that the future is identically distributed as the past, in reality, this is rarely true. Discrepancies between training and deployment distributions—known as data bias and shift—are responsible for many failures of machine learning in industry and society.
motivation_md: Understanding data shift is essential for building reliable systems that don't fail when they encounter real-world conditions that differ from their training environment.
recap_md: - Data shift occurs when training and testing distributions are not identical.

title: Distribution Shift
one_liner: Distribution shift occurs when the data distribution of future results changes, confounding probabilistic guarantees.
content: In many cases, we are confounded by a shifting data distribution. Shifting data is the rule, not the exception, and it impacts the probabilistic guarantees over future results.
motivation_md: In machine learning, we often assume that training and testing data come from the same distribution. However, in real-world applications, data distributions are rarely static. Understanding distribution shift is critical because it explains why models that perform well in the lab may fail when deployed in a changing environment.
recap_md: - Distribution shift refers to the phenomenon where the underlying data distribution changes over time.

title: Name That Dataset!
one_liner: The Name That Dataset! game demonstrates that computer vision datasets often have distinct, recognizable styles due to bias.
content: In the paper @Torralba2011, the authors propose a game called Name That Dataset! (see figure: Let's play the *Name That Dataset!* game. Modified from @Torralba2011. The game consists in associating each set of three images with the name of the dataset, from the list on the right, they belong...) The figure shows three random images from 12 famous computer vision datasets, and the goal is to match the images with each dataset name. The point of the game is to show that it is easy to recognize the style of images and to identify the dataset they belong to. If the datasets were unbiased samples of the same visual world, it would be impossible to win the game; yet researchers with experience on these datasets can get around 75 percent of the matches right.
motivation_md: This game serves as a pedagogical tool to prove that datasets are not neutral representations of reality. By showing that humans can identify a dataset just by looking at the 'style' of a few images, it highlights the presence of significant collection and selection biases in standard computer vision benchmarks.
recap_md: - The game involves matching random images to the specific computer vision dataset they originated from.

title: The Value of Training Examples
one_liner: The value of a training example measures its effectiveness when used to test on a different distribution.
content: The value of training examples can be quantified by testing a model trained on one dataset against another. In @tbl-market_bias, each number represents the value of one training example from one dataset when used to test on another. For instance, a value of 0.25 means that you need 4 times more training examples than when using a sample derived from the same testing distribution. While these specific results are from 2011 and computer vision datasets have evolved, they illustrate the 'market value' for samples across different datasets.
motivation_md: Not all data is created equal. When there is a mismatch between training and testing distributions, the 'effective' size of your dataset drops. This concept helps practitioners understand the cost of dataset bias in terms of the extra data required to achieve equivalent performance.
recap_md: - The value of an example is relative to the testing distribution.

title: Photographer Bias
one_liner: Photographer bias refers to the systematic preferences in viewpoint and composition that skew the statistics of image databases.
content: Photographer bias is one of the most common biases in image databases and is surprisingly difficult to eliminate. The views that are recognized faster also match the viewpoints that are preferred when taking a picture of those objects. Such preferred viewpoints introduce biases on how objects are captured, making the statistics of object pose in photographs different from the statistics of how objects are actually seen. This bias exists for both objects and scenes. When taking pictures, photographers consider factors like camera orientation (e.g., the horizon's position), object locations (such as the rule of thirds), arrangements, shadows, occlusions, and environmental conditions like weather or time of day. All these factors are taken into consideration, consciously or not, when deciding which pictures to take.
motivation_md: Computer vision models often struggle in the real world because they are trained on 'good' photos. Understanding photographer bias helps researchers realize that their models might be learning the habits of photographers rather than the actual geometry or appearance of objects in the wild.
recap_md: - Photographer bias skews image statistics toward preferred viewpoints and compositions.

title: Canonical Orientation
one_liner: A canonical orientation is a preferred viewpoint that correlates with easier and faster object recognition.
content: Steve Palmer et al. showed that participants have consistent preferences for particular viewpoints of objects, known as canonical orientations. In a study where participants were shown photographs of objects in 12 different orientations, these preferences correlated with how easy it was to recognize each object. Speed and accuracy of classification were used as measures of recognition ease. The study demonstrated that people recognized objects better when presented in a canonical orientation. (see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)
motivation_md: Identifying canonical orientations explains why certain images are more 'iconic' than others. In computer vision, this helps explain why models might perform better on standard, well-posed images than on candid or unusual viewpoints.
recap_md: - Canonical orientations are the viewpoints humans prefer and recognize most quickly.

title: Collection Bias
one_liner: Collection bias arises from the specific sources and techniques used to gather data, leading to non-diverse and unrepresentative datasets.
content: There are many potential data sources, such as egocentric videos, internet images, and vacation photographs, all with different biases. It is often straightforward to identify the capture technique merely by examining the images in a dataset. For example, a Google image search for "mug" returns images that are far from a diverse collection. (see figure: Pictures of mugs returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.) These pictures look very different from the settings in which one usually encounters mugs, such as inside a dishwasher or sink. Instead, they are typically taken against flat backgrounds under canonical points of view. Other subtle biases include most handles appearing on the right side and a lack of natural occlusions.
motivation_md: Collection bias is a major hurdle in creating robust AI. If a model only sees 'clean' images from the web, it will likely fail when encountering the messy, occluded, and poorly lit environments of the real world.
recap_md: - Collection bias stems from the specific methods and sources used to acquire data.

title: Annotation Bias
one_liner: Annotation bias occurs when annotators' choices of images, labels, and language introduce systematic errors or social biases into a dataset.
content: When annotating images, annotators choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This often correlates with viewpoint preferences and photographer biases, as certain images might be easier to annotate or segment, risking a compounding effect. Furthermore, annotations require language choices that serve as an important source of bias, especially social bias.
motivation_md: Even if the images themselves were perfect, the human process of labeling them adds another layer of subjectivity. Annotation bias highlights that the 'ground truth' in a dataset is actually a product of human judgment and linguistic shortcuts.
recap_md: - Annotation bias results from the subjective choices annotators make regarding labels and image selection.

title: Social Bias
one_liner: Social bias refers to the reflection of stereotypes or societal inequalities in data collection protocols and labeling.
content: Social bias can affect both images and their associated labels, referring to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. These biases can originate from the data collection protocol or existing societal biases. For example, images might be captured only in certain world regions or contain stereotypes. Labels can also reflect social assumptions, such as a dataset that associates doctors with males and nurses with females. These biases can have a negative social impact once models are deployed, making it important to be aware of them and use mitigation techniques.
motivation_md: Social bias in AI is a critical ethical concern. If models learn and amplify societal prejudices, they can cause real-world harm. Identifying these biases is the first step toward building fair and equitable technology.
recap_md: - Social bias involves the representation of stereotypes or regional imbalances in data and labels.

title: Constant Brightness Assumption
one_liner: The constant brightness assumption posits that the brightness of pixels remains unchanged as they move through a scene over time.
content:
One special sequence is when the image has a global motion with constant velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. In such a case, we can write:
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = \ell _0 (x-v_xt,y-v_yt)
$$
where $\ell _0(x,y)= \ell (x,y,0)$ is the image being translated, and $v_x$ and $v_y$ are constants. At time $t$ the image $\ell _0(x,y)$ is translated by the vector $(v_x t, v_y t)$. The pixel value at location $(x=0, y=0)$ at time $t=0$ will appear at time $T$ in location $(x=v_x T, y=v_y T)$.

Continuous values for $x$, $y$, and $t$, and continuous images $\ell _0(x,y)$ are used to allow for any velocity values. This model assumes that the brightness of the pixels does not change while the scene is moving, a principle known as the constant brightness assumption. This assumption serves as the initial hypothesis for most motion estimation algorithms.
motivation_md: This assumption simplifies the complex problem of motion estimation by providing a mathematical constraint: the intensity of a moving point remains constant. This allows algorithms to track features across frames by searching for matching brightness levels.
recap_md:
- Assumes pixel intensity remains constant as a scene moves over time.
- Models global motion as a translation of the initial image $\ell_0$ by a velocity vector.
- Serves as the fundamental starting point for most motion estimation algorithms.

title: Modeling Sequences in the Fourier Domain

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

one_liner: The Fourier Transform of a globally moving image is the product of the static image's 2D transform and a delta wall representing the velocity.
content:
The Fourier Transform (FT) of a globally moving image, using the shift property, is:
$$
\mathscr{L} (w_x,w_y,w_t) = \mathscr{L}_0 (w_x, w_y) \delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)
$$
The continuous FT of the sequence is equal to the product of the 2D FT of the static image $\ell _0(x,y)$ and a delta wall. 

(see figure: Fig (a) A sequence with one spatial dimension showing a static rectangular pulse. b) The rectangular pulse moves to the left at a speed $v=-0.5$ and c) moving towards the left, $v=-1$. As we work...)

For a sequence with one spatial dimension $\ell (x,t)$ containing a moving blurry rectangular pulse, the FT across the spatial frequency $w_x$ is approximately a sinc function. Across the temporal frequency $w_t$, if the signal is constant, its FT is a delta function. Therefore, the FT is a sinc function contained inside a delta wall in the line $w_t=0$. When the pulse moves, the sinc function is skewed along the frequency line $w_t + v_x w_x = 0$. This is a skewing rather than a rotation, as the locations of the zeros remain at the same $w_x$ locations. Faster speeds result in larger skewing of the FT.
motivation_md: Analyzing motion in the frequency domain reveals how velocity skews the signal's energy. This perspective is useful for designing spatio-temporal filters that can isolate or remove specific motions.
recap_md:
- The FT of a moving sequence skews the static image's transform along a plane defined by velocity.
- The energy of a moving image lies on a "delta wall" in the frequency domain.
- Spatial frequency zeros remain fixed while the temporal frequency shifts based on speed.

title: Sinc Function

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

one_liner: The sinc function is the Fourier Transform of a box kernel, defined as $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}$.
content:
The sinc function is the Fourier Transform (FT) of a box kernel. In the continuous domain, the sinc function has the form:
$$
\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}
$$
This function has its maximum at $x=0$ and then has decreasing oscillations.

[FIGURE:cddd5de71ef162b7 | A graph of the normalized sinc function, $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}$. The curve has a global maximum of 1 at $x=0$ and crosses the x-axis at integer values including $x = -1, 1, 2...]
motivation_md: The sinc function is fundamental in signal processing as the ideal low-pass filter in the frequency domain and the result of transforming a rectangular window.
recap_md:
- Defined as $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}$.
- Represents the Fourier Transform of a rectangular (box) kernel.
- Features a central peak at zero and periodic zero-crossings at integer values.

title: Causal Filters
one_liner: Causal filters are filters whose output variations only depend on the past values of the input.
content: Causal filters are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This puts the following constraint: $h [n,m,t]=0$ for all $t<0$. This means that if the input is an impulse at $t=0$, the output will only have non-zero values for $t>0$. If this condition is satisfied, then the filter output will only depend on the input's past for all possible inputs.
motivation_md: Causality is a physical requirement for any real-time system, as the system cannot react to an input before it has actually occurred.
recap_md:
- Output depends only on current and past input values.
- The impulse response $h[n,m,t]$ must be zero for all $t < 0$.
- Essential for real-time signal processing applications.

title: Non-causal Filters
one_liner: Non-causal filters are filters where the output has a dependency on future inputs.
content: Non-causal filters are filters where the output has a dependency on future inputs.
motivation_md: While not physically realizable in real-time, non-causal filters are used in post-processing where the entire signal or sequence is already recorded and available.
recap_md:
- Output depends on future input values.
- Cannot be implemented in real-time systems.
- Useful for offline data processing and image restoration.

title: Anti-causal Filters
one_liner: Anti-causal filters are filters where the output only depends on future input values.
content: Anti-causal filters are filters where the output only depends on the future: $h [n,m,t]=0$ for all $t>0$.
motivation_md: Anti-causal filters represent the theoretical opposite of causal filters, often used in mathematical decompositions of zero-phase filters.
recap_md:
- Output depends exclusively on future inputs.
- The impulse response $h[n,m,t]$ is zero for all $t > 0$.
- Primarily a theoretical construct used in signal analysis.

title: Heaviside Step Function
one_liner: The Heaviside step function $u[t]$ is a function that is zero for negative values and one otherwise.
content:
The Heaviside step function, $u [t]$, is defined as:
$$
u [t] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}
$$
The Heaviside step function is an infinite length function.

[FIGURE:3bdfa12be361a5d6 | A discrete-time stem plot of the unit step function $u[t)$. For integer values $t < 0$, the signal is zero, and for $t \ge 0$, the signal is constant at 1. The plot shows blue dots at $t = -5, -4...]
motivation_md: The Heaviside step function is used to model signals that switch on at a specific time and stay on, and to mathematically enforce causality in filter definitions.
recap_md:
- Value is 0 for $t < 0$ and 1 for $t \ge 0$.
- Used to represent the activation of a system or signal.
- Often used to define causal impulse responses.

title: IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) Filters
one_liner: IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters are filters whose impulse response has infinite support, often described by difference equations.
content: Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support; these are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are those that, given a bounded input $| \ell _{in} [n,m,t] |<A$, produce a bounded output $| \ell _{out} [n,m,t] | <B$. For stability to occur, the impulse response must be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. For example, a filter may be stable if and only if the absolute value of a specific parameter, such as $| \alpha |$, is less than 1.
motivation_md: IIR filters can achieve complex frequency responses with much lower computational costs (fewer coefficients) than FIR filters, though they require careful design to ensure stability.
recap_md:
- Characterized by an impulse response that never returns to exactly zero.
- Typically implemented using feedback (recursive difference equations).
- Stability requires that bounded inputs produce bounded outputs.

title: Multitask Training
one_liner: Multitask training involves sharing data between tasks by defining a broader task for which individual tasks are special cases.
content: Because we have finite data for any given task, it can help to share data between tasks. Suppose we have two tasks, $A$ and $B$. To borrow data from task $B$ to increase the data available for task $A$, one approach is to broaden the task itself. The idea is to define a new task, $AB$, for which tasks $A$ and $B$ are special cases. Then we can train $AB$ on both the data for task $A$ and for task $B$.
motivation_md: Deep learning models are often limited by the amount of task-specific data available. Multitask training solves this by allowing models to leverage data from related tasks, improving generalization by learning from a broader objective.
recap_md: - Share data between tasks to overcome the limitations of finite datasets.

title: Data Imputation
one_liner: Data imputation is a metatask where a model predicts missing information, such as color channels or masked pixels, to learn general representations.
content: Data imputation is an example of a metatask like $AB$. One example of data imputation is to predict missing color channels; this is the colorization problem, or task $A$. Another data imputation problem is predicting a chunk of pixels masked out of the image; this is the inpainting problem, which we can call task $B$. We can train a joint colorization-inpainting model if we simply set up both as data imputation and train a general data imputation model. This model can be trained on both colorization training data and inpainting training data.
motivation_md: Data imputation serves as a powerful framework for multitask training. By treating different problems (like inpainting and colorization) as missing data problems, a single model can learn from diverse datasets and develop more robust features.
recap_md: - Treat specific tasks like colorization and inpainting as instances of a general missing data problem.

title: One-Shot Learning
one_liner: One-shot learning is the ability to learn to recognize a new concept after seeing it just once.
content: A common criticism of deep learning systems is that they are data hungry. To learn a new concept (e.g., "is this a dog?") may require showing a deep net thousands of labeled examples of that concept. Conversely, humans can learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once, an ability known as one-shot learning.
motivation_md: Standard deep learning requires massive datasets, which is inefficient compared to human intelligence. One-shot learning aims to bridge this gap by enabling models to generalize from a single instance, reducing the need for large labeled datasets.
recap_md: - The ability to learn a new concept from only one labeled example.

title: Few-Shot Learning
one_liner: Few-shot learning refers to the process of training a model to perform a task using only a small number of examples.
content: Few-shot learning refers to learning from just a few examples. It is part of a spectrum of learning efficiency that includes one-shot learning (one example) and zero-shot learning (no adaptation).
motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. Few-shot learning allows models to adapt to new tasks without requiring large-scale data collection, making AI more practical for niche applications.
recap_md: - Learning from a very limited number of training examples.

title: Zero-Shot Learning
one_liner: Zero-shot learning occurs when a model works out of the box on a new problem with zero adaptation whatsoever.
content: The zero-shot setting refers to when a model works out of the box on a new problem, with zero adaptation whatsoever. This is often contrasted with few-shot learning, which requires a small number of examples.
motivation_md: Zero-shot learning is the ultimate goal for generalizable AI, allowing models to handle tasks they were never explicitly trained on by leveraging broad prior knowledge and semantic understanding.
recap_md: - Model performs a new task with zero additional training or adaptation.

title: Transfer Learning
one_liner: Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly.
content: Transfer learning deals with how to use prior knowledge to solve new learning problems quickly. It provides the means to use existing priors to accelerate the learning process for novel tasks.
motivation_md: Training models from scratch for every new task is computationally expensive and data-intensive. Transfer learning allows models to reuse features or knowledge learned from previous tasks to improve performance on new ones.
recap_md: - Uses prior knowledge to accelerate learning on new problems.

title: Problem Setting for Transfer Learning
one_liner: The transfer learning problem setting involves pretraining a model on one task and adapting it to solve a new, related task.
content: Suppose you have a classifier $f_{	heta}$ trained to recognize wheat versus corn. If you later need to recognize wheat versus soybeans, instead of training a new classifier from scratch, you can use $f_{	heta}$ to accelerate the learning of the new classifier. Transfer learning algorithms involve two parts: pretraining, which is how to acquire prior knowledge in the first place, and adaptation, which is how to use that prior knowledge to solve a new task. In this example, pretraining involves the wheat versus corn classifier, and adaptation involves updating it for wheat versus soybeans. (see figure: Transfer learning consists of two phases: first we pretrain a model on one task and then we adapt that model to perform a new task.)
motivation_md: When tasks change, retraining from scratch is wasteful. This setting formalizes how to reuse existing models to adapt to new requirements efficiently, saving time and computational resources.
recap_md: - Pretraining: Acquiring prior knowledge from an initial task.

title: Pretraining
one_liner: Pretraining is the phase of transfer learning focused on acquiring prior knowledge from an initial task.
content: Pretraining is the process of how to acquire prior knowledge in the first place within a transfer learning framework. It involves training a model on a source task to establish a foundation for later adaptation.
motivation_md: Pretraining allows a model to learn general features that are useful across many different specific tasks, providing a strong starting point that makes learning the final task much faster and more effective.
recap_md: - The first phase of transfer learning.

title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

one_liner: Conditional diffusion models incorporate conditioning variables into the denoising function to guide the generative process toward specific outputs.
content:
Diffusion models can be made conditional by concatenating the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function: $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$ Both diffusion models and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. To make them conditional, we augment the original training pairs $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ with additional paired observations $\mathbf{c}$ to become $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. If $f_{\theta}$ is given a description of an image as an additional input, it can better solve its prediction task, becoming sensitive to text commands and denoising toward an image that matches that text.

(see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.)
motivation_md: Standard diffusion models generate samples from a distribution but lack control over the specific content. By conditioning the denoising process on external data like text or labels, we can guide the model to generate specific, desired outputs.
recap_md: - Conditional diffusion models add auxiliary information to the denoising function input.

title: Structured Prediction in Vision
one_liner: Structured prediction is a framework for predicting high-dimensional, organized outputs like label maps, depth maps, or meshes from image inputs.
content: Whenever you want to make a prediction of an image, conditional generative models are a suitable modeling choice. While some problems like image colorization are graphics-oriented, most vision problems involve predicting labels or geometry. In object detection and semantic segmentation, the target output is a high-dimensional and structured label map. Similarly, geometry estimation produces depth maps, voxel grids, or meshes. Structured prediction is the tool needed for solving these problems, making conditional generative models a good choice for high-dimensional structured objects.
motivation_md: Many computer vision tasks require outputs that are more complex than a single category, such as pixel-wise labels or 3D geometry. Structured prediction allows models to handle these high-dimensional, spatially organized outputs.
recap_md: - Vision tasks like segmentation and depth estimation require high-dimensional, structured outputs.

title: Image-to-Image Translation
one_liner: Image-to-image translation is the process of mapping an input image to an output image, effectively translating between different representations of data.
content: Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, defined here as any array of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by number of channels). These problems are common in computer vision and include colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation. One way to think about these problems is as translating from one view of the data to another. For example, semantic segmentation translates from a color-based view of the world to a semantic-based view. This perspective defines the problem of **image-to-image translation**, analogous to translating between languages.
motivation_md: Many vision tasks can be unified under a single framework where the goal is to transform one image representation (like a sketch or a label map) into another (like a photo).
recap_md: - Image-to-image translation maps an input array to an output array of similar structure.

title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
one_liner: Conditional GANs for image-to-image translation use a generator to map input images to output images and a discriminator to evaluate realism.
content:
One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, such as the "pix2pix" method. In this setting, the generator maps an input image (like a facade layout map) to an output image (like a photo). The generator is typically implemented with an image-to-image architecture like a U-Net or a transformer, while the discriminator uses a regular CNN to map the output image to a real-versus-synthetic score. 

(see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)

In some implementations, noise inputs are omitted because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ provides enough entropy to create variety, though this results in a single deterministic prediction $\mathbf{y}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$.
motivation_md: Standard GANs generate images from random noise. By conditioning the GAN on an input image, we can perform specific transformations like turning a semantic map into a realistic photograph.
recap_md: - The generator uses a U-Net or similar architecture to transform input images.

title: cGAN as a Learned Loss Function
one_liner: A conditional GAN can be viewed as a regression problem where the discriminator acts as a learned loss function that adapts to the data structure.
content:
A conditional GAN setup can be viewed as a regression problem with a learned loss function $d_{\phi}$. 

(see figure: The discriminator of a GAN as a learned loss function.)

This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize the specific errors the generator is making. To stabilize optimization, a conventional regression loss, such as $L_1$, is often added to the objective: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_G\max_D \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert_1 \big] \end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: Hand-designed loss functions like MSE often fail to capture complex human perceptions of realism. A learned discriminator can automatically discover which features are important for making an image look 'real'.
recap_md: - The discriminator serves as a loss function that adapts to the generator's current errors.

title: PatchGAN
one_liner: PatchGAN is a discriminator architecture that penalizes images based on the realism of local patches rather than the entire image.
content: A PatchGAN discriminator scores each patch in an output image as real or fake and averages these scores for the total loss: $$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k]) \end{aligned}$$ where $k \times k$ is the patch size. This is equivalent to the sliding window action of a CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can be implemented as a CNN that outputs a feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions depending on the architecture.
motivation_md: Scoring an entire image as real or fake can be difficult and requires many parameters. PatchGAN focuses on local texture and style, which is often sufficient for image-to-image tasks and provides more training samples per image.
recap_md: - PatchGAN evaluates the realism of $k \times k$ image patches independently.

title: PatchGAN Receptive Field
one_liner: The receptive field of a PatchGAN discriminator determines the scale of the structures and errors it can penalize.
content:
The PatchGAN strategy has two main advantages: it is easier to model patch-level realism with fewer parameters, and there are more patches available in the training data than full images. However, a PatchGAN can only penalize errors observable within a single patch. 

(see figure: Varying the receptive field (patch size) of the convolutional discriminator affects what kinds of structure the discriminator enforces. These results are from @pix2pix2017)

A $1\times1$ discriminator cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics like edge structure, leading to blurry results. Larger receptive fields enforce higher-order realism but cannot model structures larger than the patch size, potentially causing tiling artifacts. Very large discriminators (e.g., $286\times286$) may perform poorly due to having fewer training examples for large regions.
motivation_md: Choosing the right patch size is a trade-off between capturing global structure and maintaining the statistical advantages of local evaluation.
recap_md: - Small patches focus on color/texture but may result in blurriness.

title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation learns to map between domains without requiring direct correspondences between specific training examples.
content:
Unpaired translation is used when paired training data $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ is hard to obtain, such as translating a photo into a Cezanne painting. 

(see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.)

In this setting, we cannot rely on direct supervision because we lack examples of the exact same scene in both domains. Instead, the model must learn the general style of a domain (e.g., Cezanne's brushstrokes and pastel tones) from a set of images and apply those stylistic changes to a photo from a different set. This distinguishes the **unpaired translation** setting from the paired setting.
motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, it is impossible to get 'before and after' pairs (e.g., a photo of a summer scene and the exact same scene in winter). Unpaired translation allows models to learn from two independent collections of images.
recap_md: - Unpaired translation maps between domains without one-to-one image correspondences.

title: Technical Setting for Generative and Representation Learning
one_liner: Generative and representation learning relate data and latent variables through deterministic generators and encoders, where the generator acts as the inverse of the encoder.
content: Consider random variables $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ related as follows, with $g$ being a deterministic generator (i.e., decoder) and $f$ being a deterministic encoder: $$\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}} &\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}} \\ &\hat{\mathbf{z}} = f(\mathbf{x}) &\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g(\mathbf{z}) \end{aligned}$$ The functions $f$ and $g$ are trained so that $g \approx f^{-1}$, which means that $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \approx \mathbf{x}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{z}} \approx \mathbf{z}$. Representation learning maps from a data domain to a simple embedding space, while generative modeling performs the opposite mapping. (see figure: Generative modeling performs the opposite mapping from representation learning.) A critical distinction in most generative models is that we assume we know the distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, typically in a simple form such as a unit Gaussian, which allows us to sample from it and generate images via $g$.
motivation_md: This technical setting provides a formal framework to unify representation learning and generative modeling as inverse processes, enabling the use of latent spaces for both data compression and synthesis.
recap_md: - Representation learning maps data to an embedding space, while generative modeling maps from embeddings back to data. - The generator and encoder are trained to be approximate inverses of each other. - Generative models assume a known latent distribution, typically a unit Gaussian, to facilitate sampling.

title: Data Log Likelihood
one_liner: The data log likelihood measures the log probability of the observed data under a specific model parameterization.
content: One of the most important quantities we will measure is the data log likelihood function $L(\{\mathbf{x}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta)$, which measures the log likelihood of the data under the model $p_{\theta}$: $$\begin{aligned} L(\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N, \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ Many methods use a max likelihood objective, optimizing $L$ with respect to $\theta$. To compute the likelihood function, we need to compute $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$.
motivation_md: Log likelihood is a standard objective function in statistical modeling because it transforms products of probabilities into sums, making optimization computationally tractable and numerically stable.
recap_md: - It is defined as the sum of the log probabilities of individual data points under the model. - Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) seeks to find parameters that maximize this value.

title: Marginal Likelihood
one_liner: The marginal likelihood expresses the probability of data by integrating over all possible unobserved latent variables.
content: One way to express the probability function is as the marginal likelihood of $\mathbf{x}$, marginalizing over all unobserved latent variables $\mathbf{z}$: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$ The advantage of expressing $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ in this way is that, assuming we know $p_{\mathbf{z}}$, the rest of the modeling problem is reduced to learning the conditional distribution $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z})$, which can be modeled using $g$. For example, we could model $p_{\theta}(X \bigm | \mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu = g(\mathbf{z}), \sigma = \mathbf{1})$, placing a unit Gaussian distribution over $X$ centered on $g(\mathbf{z})$.
motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to model complex data distributions by combining a simple latent distribution with a conditional generator, effectively handling unobserved factors.
recap_md: - It calculates the total probability of data by summing (integrating) over all possible latent states. - This approach simplifies modeling by focusing on the conditional distribution of data given a latent code.

title: Variational Autoencoders
one_liner: A variational autoencoder (VAE) is a model that transforms a standard autoencoder into a generative model capable of synthesizing new data.
content: The variational autoencoder (VAE) is a model that turns an autoencoder into a generative model that can synthesize data.
motivation_md: Standard autoencoders are good for compression but lack a structured latent space for sampling; VAEs solve this by imposing a probabilistic structure.
recap_md: - VAEs extend the autoencoder framework to support data synthesis. - They bridge the gap between representation learning and generative modeling.

title: The Decoder of an Autoencoder is a Data Generator
one_liner: The decoder of an autoencoder acts as a generator by mapping latent representations back to the original data domain.
content: The decoder of an autoencoder is a mapping from a representation of the data, $\mathbf{z}$, back to the data itself, $\mathbf{x}$. Given a $\mathbf{z}$, we can synthesize an image by passing it through the decoder of the autoencoder. (see figure: The relationship between an autoencoder and a generative model.) However, generative modeling requires a distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ from which we can sample different $\mathbf{z}$ from scratch. An autoencoder doesn't directly provide this. If you sample a random $\mathbf{z}$ (e.g., from a unit Gaussian) and feed it through the decoder, the sample might be very different from what the decoder was trained on, potentially resulting in arbitrary, out-of-distribution behavior.
motivation_md: Understanding the decoder as a generator is the first step toward creating generative models, but it highlights the need for a well-defined latent distribution to ensure valid synthesis.
recap_md: - Decoders map latent codes to data reconstructions or new samples. - Without a defined latent distribution, random sampling often produces poor results.

title: Complexity of Autoencoder Latent Space
one_liner: The latent space of a standard autoencoder can be as complex and difficult to model as the original data space.
content: In general, the embedding space of an autoencoder might be just as complicated to model as the data space we started with. (see figure: The latent space of an autoencoder can be just as complex as the data space.)
motivation_md: This complexity explains why simple sampling from a standard autoencoder's latent space fails, necessitating regularization techniques like those used in VAEs.
recap_md: - Unconstrained latent spaces often lack the simple structure needed for easy sampling. - The complexity of the embedding space can mirror the complexity of the input data.

title: Turning an Autoencoder into a Generative Model
one_liner: Variational autoencoders convert autoencoders into generative models by regularizing the latent distribution and adding noise to the encoder's output.
content: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a way to turn an autoencoder into a proper generative model, which can be sampled from and which maximizes data likelihood under a formal probabilistic model. The process involves two main steps: (1) regularize the latent distribution to squish it into a Gaussian (or some other base distribution), and (2) add noise to the output of the encoder.
motivation_md: These two simple modifications ensure the latent space is continuous and structured, allowing the model to generate realistic new data points through sampling.
recap_md: - Latent regularization forces the embedding space to follow a known distribution like a Gaussian. - Adding noise during encoding helps the model become robust and ensures the latent space is well-populated.

title: The VAE Hypothesis Space
one_liner: VAEs are maximum likelihood models that represent complex data distributions as infinite mixtures of simple distributions.
content: VAEs are max likelihood generative models which distinguish themselves through their particular hypothesis space and optimization algorithm. While models like autoregressive models use products of simple conditional distributions, VAEs model complicated distributions as sums of simple distributions. You can think about this as transforming a base distribution $p_{\mathbf{z}}$ to a modeled distribution $p_{\theta}$ by applying a deterministic mapping $g_{\theta}$ and then putting a blip of Gaussian probability around each point in the range of this mapping. (see figure: From a finite mixture of Gaussians to an infinite mixture.) VAEs can be constructed using various base distributions for $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{z})$ and $p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})$, effectively acting as metamodels whose components can be other density models.
motivation_md: The mixture-based hypothesis space allows VAEs to approximate highly complex, non-Gaussian data distributions by combining many simple, tractable components.
recap_md: - VAEs treat the generative process as an infinite mixture of simple distributions. - They use a deterministic mapping followed by stochastic noise to define the data distribution. - The framework is flexible enough to incorporate various base distributions as components.

title: Image Rectification Algorithms
one_liner: Image rectification algorithms transform stereo pairs to minimize distortions and facilitate matching, often requiring known camera calibrations or fundamental matrices.
content: Image rectification algorithms are optimized to minimize image distortions and may provide better performance for stereo algorithms. While many implementations assume camera calibrations are known, other rectification algorithms can operate under weaker conditions, such as knowing the fundamental matrix. Many software packages provide standard code for performing these rectifications.
motivation_md: Rectification simplifies the stereo matching problem by aligning corresponding points along horizontal scanlines, reducing a 2D search to a 1D search.
recap_md: [FIGURE:fig-stereoblock | Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017]

title: Learning-Based Methods for Stereo
one_liner: Neural network approaches now dominate stereo vision by implementing matching and filtering either as separate stages or within a single end-to-end optimization.
content: As is the case for most other vision tasks, neural network approaches now dominate stereo methods. The two primary stages of a stereo algorithm—matching and filtering—can be implemented separately by neural networks or integrated together into a single, end-to-end optimization framework.
motivation_md: Traditional hand-crafted stereo algorithms struggle with complex textures and occlusions; deep learning allows the system to learn robust features and regularization directly from data.
recap_md:
- Neural networks are the current dominant approach for stereo vision tasks.
- Matching and filtering can be handled by separate networks or a single end-to-end model.

title: Output Representation for Stereo
one_liner: Stereo output can be represented as disparity or depth, with disparity often being easier to estimate and model for noise.
content: An important question in stereo vision is how to represent the output, as the ultimate goal is estimating the 3D structure of the scene. We can estimate either the disparity or the depth. Disparity might be easier to estimate because it is independent of the camera parameters. It is also easier to model noise in disparity space, as we can assume that noise is independent of the disparity value. Conversely, when using depth directly, estimation errors tend to be larger for distant points.
motivation_md: Choosing the right representation affects the accuracy of the 3D reconstruction and the complexity of the noise model used during estimation.
recap_md:
- Output can be represented as disparity or depth.
- Disparity is independent of camera parameters and simplifies noise modeling.
- Depth estimation error increases for points further from the camera.

title: Disparity Planarity Property
one_liner: For flat surfaces, the second-order derivative of disparity along any spatial direction is zero.
content: An interesting property of disparity is that for flat surfaces, the second-order derivative along any spatial direction, $\mathbf{x}$, is zero: $$\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2} = 0.$$ This equality does not hold for depth. This property allows for the introduction of a simple regularization term that favors planarity in the reconstructed scene.
motivation_md: This mathematical property provides a simple way to enforce a 'smoothness' or 'flatness' constraint in stereo algorithms, which helps resolve ambiguities in textureless regions.
recap_md:
- The second-order derivative of disparity is zero for flat surfaces: $\frac{\partial^2 d}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2} = 0$.
- This property is unique to disparity and does not apply to depth.
- It is used to create regularization terms that favor planar surfaces.

title: Disparity to Depth Conversion
one_liner: Depth values are recovered by inverting the returned disparity for a given pixel.
content: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d[n,m]$ into depth values $z[n,m]$, we need to invert the disparity, that is: $$z [n,m] = \frac{1}{ d [n,m] }$$
motivation_md: While algorithms often compute disparity for computational convenience, applications like robotics and 3D mapping require actual depth in physical units.
recap_md:
- Depth $z$ is the inverse of disparity $d$.
- The relationship is defined by $z[n,m] = 1 / d[n,m]$.

title: Recovering World Coordinates from Depth
one_liner: 3D coordinates in the camera frame are recovered using depth, image coordinates, and the inverse of the intrinsic camera matrix.
content: To recover the world coordinates for every pixel, we assume a pinhole camera model. Using the depth $z[n,m]$ and the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$, we obtain the 3D coordinates for a pixel with image coordinates $[n,m]$ in the camera reference frame as: $$\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = z[n,m] \times \mathbf{K}^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Note that $\mathbf{K}$ represents the intrinsic camera parameters for the reference image.
motivation_md: Converting 2D pixel locations into 3D space is essential for understanding the physical geometry of a scene and for tasks like obstacle avoidance or 3D modeling.
recap_md:
- 3D coordinates are calculated using depth $z$ and the inverse intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$.
- The formula maps 2D image coordinates $[n, m]$ to 3D camera frame coordinates $[X, Y, Z]$.

title: Two-Stage Networks for Stereo
one_liner: Two-stage stereo networks use separate neural components to extract features and then compute matching costs to estimate disparities.
content: Given two images, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$, the disparity at each location can be computed by a function: $$\hat{\mathbf{d}} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$$ The objective is for the estimated disparities, $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$, to be close to ground truth disparities, $\mathbf{d}$. Training sets like the KITTI or scene flow datasets provide ground truth disparities from calibrated stereo cameras. A typical loss function used for optimization via gradient descent is: $$J(\theta) = \sum_t \left| \mathbf{d} - f_{\theta} (\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) \right|^2$$ When matching and filtering are implemented separately, one common formulation uses one neural network to extract features from both images, $g(\mathbf{i}_1)$ and $g(\mathbf{i}_2)$, and a second network to compute the matching cost and estimate disparities: $$f(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2) = c \left( g(\mathbf{v}_1), g(\mathbf{v}_2) \right)$$
motivation_md: Decoupling feature extraction from matching allows for more modular design and the use of shared weights, which ensures that features are compared in a consistent latent space.
recap_md:
- Disparity is estimated as a function of two input images optimized against ground truth.
- Feature extraction $g(\mathbf{i})$ and matching cost $c(\cdot)$ can be handled by distinct network components.
- Models are typically trained using gradient descent on a squared error loss.

title: CNN Stereo Processing Pipeline
one_liner: The CNN stereo pipeline involves rectification, feature extraction with shared weights, cost volume formation, and 3D convolutional aggregation.
content:
A common approach for stereo processing using CNNs follows these steps:

- Rectify the stereo pair so that scanlines in each image depict the same points in the world.
- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights.
- Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position and stereo disparity. This volume can be referenced to the horizontal and vertical positions of one input image.
- Train and apply a 3D convolutional neural net (CNN) to aggregate costs over the 3D cost volume to estimate the best disparity for each pixel. This 3D CNN performs a role similar to the regularization step in non-neural approaches like Semi-Global Matching (SGM), but with superior performance.

(see figure: Block diagram of CNN stereo processing, abstracted from the block diagrams of @Chang2018, @Zhang2019GANet, @Kendall2017)
motivation_md: This pipeline standardizes the transition from raw stereo images to a dense disparity map, leveraging 3D convolutions to learn complex spatial dependencies that traditional regularization methods cannot capture.
recap_md:
- The pipeline includes rectification, shared-weight feature extraction, and cost volume formation.
- A 3D CNN aggregates costs to estimate the best disparity per pixel.
- This approach replaces and outperforms traditional regularization methods like SGM.

title: Stereo Anaglyph
one_liner: A stereo anaglyph is a 3D image created by superimposing two laterally displaced views in different colors, such as red and cyan, which appear three-dimensional when viewed through corresponding color filters.
content:
A stereo anaglyph is an image created using two cameras, one displaced laterally from the other. In a typical example, the right camera's image appears in red and the left camera image appears in cyan. If you view this image with a red filter covering the left eye and a cyan filter covering the right eye, then the right eye will see only the right camera's image and the left eye will see only the left camera's image. This allows the subject to pop out into a three-dimensional (3D) stereo image. The relative displacement between each camera's image of objects changes as a function of their depth, which allows us to form a 3D interpretation of the scene when viewing the image with the glasses.

(see figure: (a) Stereo anaglyph of the Titanic @McManus2022. The red image shows the right eye's view, and cyan the left eye's view. (b) When viewed through red/cyan stereo glasses the cyan variations appear in...)
motivation_md: Stereo anaglyphs provide a simple way to encode 3D depth information into a single 2D image that can be viewed with inexpensive color-filtered glasses, mimicking how our eyes perceive depth through lateral displacement.
recap_md: - Uses two laterally displaced camera views superimposed in different colors (usually red and cyan).

title: Image Rectification
one_liner: Image rectification is a manipulation used to align the locus of potential matching features along a single pixel row.
content: Image rectification is a manipulation often used to place the locus of potential matches along a pixel row.
motivation_md: In stereo vision, finding matching points between two images is computationally expensive; rectification simplifies this search to a 1D horizontal line, significantly increasing efficiency.
recap_md: - Aligns potential feature matches along horizontal pixel rows.

title: Distance Estimation from a Single Observation Point
one_liner: The distance to an object can be estimated from a single elevated observation point using the height of the observer and the angle to the object relative to the horizon.
content:
(see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

This method measures the location of an object, such as a boat, relative to the horizon line. An observer stands on top of an elevated point (a mountain, tower, or building) at a known height, $h$. The observer measures the angle $\alpha$ between the horizontal (obtained by pointing toward the horizon) and the position of the boat. We can then derive the boat distance to the base of the point of observation, $d$, by the simple trigonometric relation: $$d = \frac{h}{\tan (\alpha)}$$ This method is not very accurate and might require high observation points, which might not be available, but it allows us to estimate the boat position with a single observation point if the observer's height above the water is known. It also requires incorporating the earth curvature when the boat is far away.
motivation_md: This technique allows for distance estimation when only one observation point is accessible, provided the observer's elevation is known.
recap_md: - Estimates distance $d$ using height $h$ and angle $\alpha$ via $d = h / \tan(\alpha)$.

title: Triangulation
one_liner: Triangulation is a method of determining the distance to an object by measuring angles from two distinct observation points separated by a known baseline distance.
content:
(see figure: Two methods to estimate the distance of a boat from the coast. (left) The first method uses a single observation point, with knowledge of the observer's height above the water. (right) The second...)

Triangulation requires two different observation points along the coast separated by a distance $t$. At each point, we measure the angles, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, between the direction of the boat and the line connecting the two observation points. Then we can apply the following relation: $$d = t \frac{\sin (\alpha) \sin (\beta)}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}$$ For this method to work, we need a large distance $t$ so that the angles are significantly different from $90$ degrees.
motivation_md: Triangulation provides a more accurate way to measure distance than single-point observation by using a baseline and two angles, forming the geometric basis for stereo vision.
recap_md: - Calculates distance using a baseline $t$ and two angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

title: Parallax Effect
one_liner: The parallax effect is the relative displacement of features across two images, which is directly related to the distance between the observer and the scene.
content: The relative displacement of features across two images is known as the parallax effect. This displacement is related to the distance between the observer and the observed scene. Just as in the example of estimating the distance to boats in the sea, our brain uses disparities across the two eye views to measure distances to objects.
motivation_md: Parallax is the fundamental physical phenomenon that allows biological and computer vision systems to perceive depth from multiple viewpoints.
recap_md: - Refers to the relative displacement of features between two different views.

title: Free Fusion
one_liner: Free fusion is the technique of converging or diverging the eyes to fuse a stereogram into a 3D image without using a stereoscope.
content: Free fusion consists in making the eyes converge or diverge in order to fuse a stereogram without needing a stereoscope. Making it work requires practice.
motivation_md: Free fusion allows individuals to experience 3D depth from stereograms using only their eyes, demonstrating the brain's ability to process disparity without specialized hardware.
recap_md: - Involves voluntary eye convergence or divergence to merge two images.

title: Random Dot Stereograms
one_liner: Random dot stereograms are pairs of random-pattern images that reveal 3D structure through feature displacement, proving depth can be perceived without other visual cues.
content:
Random dot stereograms, introduced by Bela Julesz, are a demonstration that humans can perceive depth using the relative displacement of features across two views even in the absence of any other depth cues. The random images contain no recognizable features and are quite different from the statistics of the natural world. However, this does not affect our ability to compute the displacements between the two images and perceive 3D structure.

(see figure: Random dot stereogram. Both images are almost identical. The difference is that there is a square in the middle that is displaced by a few pixels left-right between the two images. When each image it...)
motivation_md: These stereograms prove that the brain can perform stereo matching based purely on correlation and disparity, independent of object recognition or other monocular depth cues.
recap_md: - Demonstrates depth perception using only image disparity without recognizable objects.

title: Stereo Pinhole Camera
one_liner: A stereo pinhole camera is a variation of a pinhole camera that uses two holes to produce 3D-capable images, such as anaglyphs, in a single shot.
content: Stereo cameras generally are built by having two cameras mounted on a rigid rig so that the camera parameters do not change over time. We can also build a stereo pinhole camera. A pinhole camera is formed by a dark chamber with a single hole in one extreme that lets light in, which gets projected into the opposite wall to form an image. By playing with the shape and number of pinholes, we can create different types of cameras. In particular, we can build a camera that produces anaglyph images in a single shot by making two pinholes instead of just one.
motivation_md: This concept illustrates how the principles of stereo vision can be integrated into simple optical hardware to capture depth information directly.
recap_md: - Uses two pinholes instead of one to capture stereo information.

title: GAN Generator and Discriminator
one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks consist of a generator that synthesizes data from noise and a discriminator that classifies data as real or synthesized.
content: GANs consist of two neural networks: the **generator**, $g_{	heta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, which synthesizes data from noise, and a **discriminator**, $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$, which tries to classify between synthesized data and real data.
motivation_md: To learn complex data distributions without a hand-defined loss function, GANs use a competition between two networks to automatically discover the features that distinguish real data from synthetic data.
recap_md: - The generator $g_{\theta}$ maps latent noise $\mathcal{Z}$ to the data space $\mathcal{X}$.

title: GAN Minimax Game
one_liner: The generator and discriminator play an adversarial minimax game where the generator attempts to fool the discriminator while the discriminator learns to detect synthetic data.
content: The $g_{\theta}$ and $d_{\phi}$ play an adversarial game in which $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better and better at generating synthetic images while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better and better at detecting any errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem can be written as a minimax game: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: This minimax formulation provides a mathematical framework for training generative models through competition, ensuring that the generator improves only by producing increasingly realistic samples.
recap_md: - The objective is a minimax optimization where the discriminator maximizes classification accuracy and the generator minimizes it.

title: GAN Optimization via Alternating Gradient Steps
one_liner: GAN optimization alternates between updating the discriminator to maximize classification accuracy and updating the generator to fool the current discriminator.
content:
This objective may be easier to understand if we think of the objectives for $g_{\theta}$ and $d_{\phi}$ separately. Given a particular generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images (synthetic images are anything output by $g_{\theta}$). The objective of $d_{\phi}$ is logistic regression between a set of real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$.

Let the optimal discriminator be labeled $d_{\phi}^*$. Then we have:
$$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Now we turn to $g_{\theta}$'s perspective. Given $d_{\phi}^*$, $g_{\theta}$ tries to solve the following problem:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Because the optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current behavior of $g_{\theta}$, as soon as we change $g_{\theta}$ to better fool $d_{\phi}^*$, then $d_{\phi}^*$ is no longer optimal. To optimize a GAN, we simply alternate between taking one gradient step on the generator objective and $K$ gradient steps on the discriminator objective. In practice, setting $K=1$ is often sufficient.
motivation_md: Since the optimal discriminator changes whenever the generator is updated, the two networks must be optimized iteratively to maintain the adversarial balance required for convergence.
recap_md: - The discriminator's task is equivalent to performing logistic regression between real and synthetic samples.

title: GANs as Statistical Image Models
one_liner: GANs are statistical image models that learn to match data statistics through a learned discriminator rather than hand-defined functions.
content: GANs are related to statistical image and texture models. For example, in the Heeger-Bergen model, images are synthesized by optimizing pixels until certain statistics match those of a source texture, such as subband histograms. In the language of GANs, the loss that checks for such a match is a kind of discriminator; it outputs a score related to the difference between a generated image's statistics and the real image's statistics. However, unlike a GAN, this discriminator is hand-defined in terms of certain statistics of interest rather than learned. Additionally, GANs amortize the optimization via learning. That is, GANs learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples rather than arriving at samples via an optimization process that starts from scratch each time we want to make a new sample.
motivation_md: Traditional texture models require expensive per-image optimization and hand-crafted features; GANs improve on this by learning the relevant features and providing a fast, direct mapping from noise to data.
recap_md: - GAN discriminators serve as learned versions of hand-defined statistical matching functions.

title: Utility of Generative Models
one_liner: Generative models synthesize data for content creation and help us understand the visual world by modeling the process of creation.
content: Generative models are models that synthesize data. They can be useful for content creation—artistic images, video game assets, and so on—but also are useful for much more. Generative models also learn good image representations, and conditional generative models can be viewed as a general framework for answering questions and making predictions. As Richard Feynman famously wrote, "What I cannot create, I do not understand." By modeling creation, generative models also help us understand the visual world around us.
motivation_md: Beyond just making pretty pictures, generative modeling is a path toward understanding the underlying structure of data and learning useful representations for other tasks.
