recap_md: - Generative models are used for content creation and learning robust image representations.

title: Relationship between Generative Modeling and Representation Learning
one_liner: Generative modeling and representation learning are essentially inverse problems, mapping between simple base distributions and complex data.
content:
Generative models and representation learning are models that learn mappings both to and from data. The intuition is that generative models map a simple base distribution (i.e., noise) to data, whereas representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations (**embeddings**). These two problems are, essentially, inverses of each other. Many algorithms explicitly treat them as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one direction can inform the solution in the other direction.

In neural networks, we can describe the sequence of mappings from raw data to abstracted representations as representation learning. Alternatively, in backward order, deep nets are mappings from abstracted representations to ever more concrete representations of the data. This backward ordering is the direction in which deep generative networks work. Both modeling directions are valid, and the full picture looks like this:

(see figure: The relationship between representation learning and generative modeling. Here we label one side as "Data" and the other as "Embedding"; but what's the precise difference between these two things?...)

Moving backward through a net is also what backpropagation does, but it computes a different function: backpropagation computes the gradient $\nabla f$ whereas here we focus on the inverse $f^{-1}$.
motivation_md: Understanding the symmetry between generation and representation allows us to build models that can both understand existing data and create new, plausible examples.
recap_md: - Generative modeling maps noise to data, while representation learning maps data to embeddings.

title: Embeddings
one_liner: Embeddings are simple underlying representations of data produced by representation learning.
content: The intuition is that generative models map a simple base distribution (i.e., noise) to data, whereas representation learning maps data to simple underlying representations (**embeddings**). These two problems are, essentially, inverses of each other. Many algorithms explicitly treat them as inverse problems, where solving the problem in one direction can inform the solution in the other direction.
motivation_md: Embeddings provide a compact, manageable way to represent complex data, making it easier for machines to process and find patterns.
recap_md: - Embeddings are the output of representation learning that map complex data to a simpler space.

title: Latent Variables as Representations
one_liner: Latent variables in generative models act as complete representations of the data, capturing all unobserved factors that affect the output.
content: In generative models with latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, the role of the latent variable is to specify all unobserved factors that might affect the output of a model. For example, if a model predicts the color of a black and white photo, it is a mapping $g: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is the black and white input, $\mathbf{y}$ is the color output, and $\mathbf{z}$ is any other information needed to make the mapping deterministic (such as the color of a t-shirt). In the extreme case of unconditional generative models, all properties of the generated images are controlled by the latent variables. Crucially, latent variables are representations of the data. In unconditional models, they are a *complete* representation, meaning all information in the data is represented within them.
motivation_md: By treating latent variables as representations, we can use generative models to extract meaningful features from data without explicit labels.
recap_md: - Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ capture unobserved factors of variation in the data.

title: Harris Corner Detector Derivation
one_liner: The Harris corner detector is derived by approximating the squared intensity difference of a small image translation using a Taylor series expansion and a second-moment matrix.
content:
To derive the equation of the Harris corner detector, we treat an image as a continuous function $\ell(x,y)$. We define the squared intensity difference, $E(\Delta x, \Delta y)$, induced by a small translation $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ summed over a small image patch $P$ as:

$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) = \sum_{(x, y) \in P} \left( \ell(x,y) - \ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \right)^2$$

By expanding $\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y)$ about $\ell(x, y)$ using a Taylor series, we get:

$$\ell(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y) \approx \ell(x, y) + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \Delta x + \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \Delta y$$

Substituting this approximation back into the intensity difference equation and expressing it in matrix form yields:

$$E(\Delta x, \Delta y) \approx \left[ \Delta x ~~ \Delta y \right] \mathbf{M} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{array} \right]$$

where the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is defined as:

$$\mathbf{M} = \sum_{(n, m) \in P} \begin{bmatrix} (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x})^2 & \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} & (\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y})^2 \end{bmatrix}$$
motivation_md: To detect corners reliably, we need a mathematical way to measure how much an image patch changes when shifted in any direction. This derivation provides a local quadratic approximation of the intensity change, allowing us to identify regions with high gradients in multiple directions.
recap_md: - The detector measures the squared intensity difference $E$ resulting from a small shift $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$.

title: Local Image Descriptors
one_liner: Local image descriptors provide a representation of image regions that allows for matching features across different images despite changes in lighting or location.
content: Matching corresponding image features requires a local description of the image region to allow matching like regions across two images. SIFT uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create an image descriptor that is sensitive to local image structure, but that is insensitive to minor changes in lighting or location which may occur across the two images of a stereo pair.
motivation_md: Simple pixel-by-pixel comparison fails when lighting or camera positions change. Local descriptors provide a robust way to identify the same physical point in different images by summarizing the structure of its neighborhood.
recap_md: - Local descriptors enable matching of corresponding features across different images.

title: SIFT
one_liner: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) uses histograms of local orientations to create image descriptors robust to lighting changes and small translations.
content:
SIFT uses histograms of oriented filter responses to create an image descriptor that is sensitive to local image structure, but insensitive to minor changes in lighting or location across a stereo pair. 

[FIGURE:faa7107c0d4f9db0 | A four-panel figure demonstrating SIFT descriptors. Panels (1) and (2) are grayscale photos of a hand under different lighting. Panels (3) and (4) show corresponding vector fields where small line...]

[FIGURE:d0b75366352a79a7 | A diagram illustrating the creation of a SIFT keypoint descriptor. On the left, an $8 \times 8$ grid of local image gradients is shown with small arrows of varying orientations and magnitudes...]

As shown in the figures, images under different lighting conditions may look different in pixel intensity but appear similar in local orientation. SIFT descriptors exploit this by taking histograms of local orientation over spatial regions, which allows the descriptors to be robust to small image translations.
motivation_md: SIFT was developed to solve the problem of matching features when images undergo transformations like scaling, rotation, or illumination changes, which typically break simple correlation-based matching.
recap_md: - SIFT descriptors use histograms of oriented gradients to capture local structure.

title: Interpolation between feature matches
one_liner: Depth interpolation between matched points can be achieved using probabilistic methods like belief propagation or dynamic programming.
content: Methods to interpolate depth between the depths of matched points include probabilistic methods such as belief propagation. Under assumptions about the local spatial relationships between depth values, optimal shapes can be inferred provided the spatial structure over which inference is performed is a chain or a tree. A related inference algorithm, dynamic programming, uses similar constraints on spatial structure for exact inference.
motivation_md: Feature matching only provides depth at specific points. To create a dense depth map, we need to fill in the gaps between these points using spatial consistency assumptions.
recap_md: - Belief propagation and dynamic programming can infer optimal shapes from sparse matches.

title: Semiglobal Matching (SGM)
one_liner: Semiglobal matching (SGM) approximates a global stereo solution by applying one-dimensional processing across multiple orientations.
content: Hirschmuller's algorithm, called semiglobal matching (SGM), applies the one-dimensional processing over many different orientations to approximate a global solution to the stereo shape inference problem.
motivation_md: Global optimization for stereo matching is computationally expensive. SGM provides a more efficient approximation by combining multiple 1D path optimizations to simulate 2D consistency.
recap_md: - SGM uses multiple 1D optimizations to approximate a global 2D solution.

title: Constraints for Arbitrary Cameras
one_liner: Matching points between cameras with arbitrary orientations requires geometric constraints beyond simple horizontal disparity.
content:
While parallel cameras allow for simple disparity calculations, general stereo pairs involve cameras with arbitrary orientations. In such cases, disparity may not follow standard parallel-camera equations. For two calibrated cameras related by a generic translation $\mathbf{T}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}$ where the optical axes are not parallel, we must identify corresponding points using geometric constraints.

(see figure: How can we identify the specific point $\mathbf{p)

To identify candidate matches, we use the fact that an observed point in camera 1, $\mathbf{p}_1$, corresponds to a 3D point lying on the ray connecting the camera 1 origin and $\mathbf{p}_1$.

(see figure: The point $\mathbf{p)
motivation_md: In real-world scenarios, cameras are rarely perfectly aligned. Understanding constraints for arbitrary orientations is necessary for general 3D reconstruction and stereo vision.
recap_md: - Arbitrary camera setups involve both translation and rotation between viewpoints.

title: Epipolar Plane
one_liner: The epipolar plane is the plane containing the origins of two cameras and a specific 3D point in the world.
content:
Given a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world, the epipolar plane is defined as the plane that contains the two camera origins and that 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$.

(see figure: Geometry of a stereo pair and terminology. The figure shows the epipolar plane, epipolar lines, and epipoles ($e_1$ and $e_2$), for a given point $\mathbf{P}$. As we move the point $\mathbf{P}$, only...)
motivation_md: The epipolar plane reduces a 3D search problem to a 2D geometric constraint, forming the basis for efficient stereo matching.
recap_md: - The epipolar plane is defined by the two camera centers and a point in space.

title: Epipolar Lines
one_liner: Epipolar lines are the intersections of the epipolar plane with the camera planes, restricting the search for matching points to a single line.
content:
The epipolar lines are the intersection between the epipolar plane and the camera planes. When the point $\mathbf{P}$ moves in space, the epipolar plane and epipolar lines change.

(see figure: Geometry of a stereo pair and terminology. The figure shows the epipolar plane, epipolar lines, and epipoles ($e_1$ and $e_2$), for a given point $\mathbf{P}$. As we move the point $\mathbf{P}$, only...)

The epipolar line in camera 2 corresponds to the projection of the line $O_1 P$ into the camera plane. Therefore, given an image point $\mathbf{p}_1$ in camera 1, we know that its corresponding match in camera 2 must lie somewhere along the uniquely defined epipolar line. This constraint significantly simplifies the search for matches between images.
motivation_md: Without epipolar lines, finding a matching point would require searching the entire second image. This constraint restricts the search to a 1D line, making stereo matching computationally feasible.
recap_md: - Epipolar lines are formed by the intersection of the epipolar plane and the image planes.

title: Homography from Camera Rotation
one_liner: When images are taken from the same point by rotating a camera without translation, corresponding points across images are related by a homography regardless of their distance.
content:
Consider the three images shown in @fig-example_three_images.

[FIGURE:1db46673e5bbe185 | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, taken at a tilted angle. The image shows complex architectural forms with orange brick and metallic surfaces, illustrating how a homography transformation can...]

[FIGURE:8267e250a2c64ddf | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, featuring complex, non-rectilinear architecture with tilted walls and metallic surfaces. In the foreground, a brick amphitheater with curved seating and...]

[FIGURE:83ad2f9f3b5c333e | A photograph of a modern brick and metal building with complex, non-orthogonal geometry. The image shows a tall orange brick structure with numerous windows and a silver, metallic section with...]

These three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera. There is no translation between the three camera positions as the photographer kept the camera origin static when moving the camera. Under this condition, the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.
motivation_md: In general computer vision, point correspondences depend on depth. However, when a camera only rotates, the depth component cancels out, allowing us to map points between views using a simple linear transformation (homography). This is the fundamental principle behind creating panoramic photos.
recap_md:
- Images taken from a fixed origin with pure rotation are related by a homography.
 - This relationship is independent of the scene's depth or 3D structure.

title: Proof of Homography for Camera Rotation
one_liner: The mapping between two cameras differing only in orientation is a $3\times3$ matrix transformation of their 2D positions in homogeneous coordinates.
content:
The mapping between feature point locations in two cameras differing only in their 3D orientation, as shown in @fig-rotation_homography, is a $3\times3$ matrix transformation of their 2D positions written in homogeneous coordinates, that is, a homography.

(see figure: Camera rotation generates two images related by a homography.)

We start by setting the world coordinate system aligned with the coordinate system of camera 1. The projection of a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$, into the camera 1 plane (with translation vector zero) is:

$$\lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

Projecting the same 3D point into camera 2 with rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and zero translation:

$$\lambda_2 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

Inverting these equations to relate the common 3D point $\mathbf{P}$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_2 \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This establishes the relationship between corresponding image points in homogeneous coordinates:

$$\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

We can write this as $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ where $\mathbf{H}$ is a $3\times3$ matrix. Thus, camera rotation modifies image point locations by a homography. This holds even if the cameras have different intrinsic parameters.
motivation_md: This proof provides the mathematical foundation for why pure rotation allows for image stitching. By deriving the $3\times3$ homography matrix $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$, we show that the transformation is a linear mapping in homogeneous coordinates.
recap_md:
- The homography matrix for pure rotation is defined as $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$.
 - The relationship $\lambda \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{x}$ maps points between views without needing 3D depth information.

title: Homography from Planar Surfaces
one_liner: When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points on that plane are related by a homography.
content:
A second case for homography is when two cameras observe a 2D plane. In that case, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two camera views, for points inside the plane, are related by a homography (@fig-example_two_images_facade).

[FIGURE:8d12e88a6496cd81 | A photograph of a stone building facade featuring a large dark wooden door with a pointed archway. The scene contains multiple planar surfaces, such as the flat stone wall and the rectangular window...]

[FIGURE:d33152acf9add1c2 | A photograph of a stone building facade with several windows and a large arched wooden door. The flat, planar surface of the stone wall provides a real-world example of a scene where point...]

In the example of a building facade taken from different positions, the coordinates of corresponding points on the planar facade are related by a homography.
motivation_md: While general 3D scenes require complex epipolar geometry, planar surfaces (like walls or floors) simplify the relationship between views. Recognizing this allows for tasks like perspective correction or texture mapping onto flat surfaces.
recap_md:
- Points on a physical 3D plane are related across different camera views by a homography.
 - This applies even if the camera undergoes translation, provided the points lie on the same plane.

title: Proof of Homography for Planar Surfaces
one_liner: Coordinates inside a plane relate to coordinates in the image plane by a homography, regardless of the camera's relative position.
content:
To prove this, we show that the coordinates inside a plane relate to the coordinates in the image plane by a homography independently of the relative position between the plane and the camera. Consequently, the relationship between points across two images of the same plane will also be a homography.

We place the world-coordinate system on the plane so that the plane is defined by $Z=0$ as shown in @fig-homography_plane_geometry.

(see figure: Geometry of a the projection of a planar scene. The origin of the world-coordinates system is placed inside the plane and the $Z$-axis is perpendicular to it.)

Starting with the projection equation:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Using the notation $\mathbf{t}= -\mathbf{R} \mathbf{T}$, and setting $Z=0$ for points on the plane, we have:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Where $\mathbf{c}_i$ is column $i$ of the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$. Since the expression contains the product of two $3 \times 3$ matrices, we can write:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This result shows that the coordinates of points on the plane are related to the corresponding points in the image plane by a homography.
motivation_md: By setting the world coordinate system such that $Z=0$, we reduce the 3D projection to a 2D-to-2D mapping. This mathematical simplification proves that any planar surface in the world can be mapped to an image via a $3\times3$ homography matrix.
recap_md:
- Setting $Z=0$ for a planar surface reduces the projection matrix to a $3\times3$ homography matrix.
 - This proves that the mapping between a physical plane and its image is a linear transformation in homogeneous coordinates.

title: Homography vs Epipolar Constraint
one_liner: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint, but it only applies under specific conditions.
content: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions—such as pure camera rotation or observing a planar surface—while the epipolar constraint always holds for any two views of a 3D scene.
motivation_md: Understanding the trade-off between these constraints is vital for choosing the right model. While epipolar geometry is always available, homographies provide a more restrictive and useful mapping when the scene or camera motion allows for it.
recap_md:
- Homography is a more restrictive (stronger) constraint than epipolar geometry.
 - Epipolar constraints are universal, whereas homographies require specific geometric conditions.

title: Creating Image Panoramas
one_liner: Stitching images to create large panoramas is a popular application of homography.
content: A popular application of the homography is stitching images to create large panoramas. To create a large panorama from multiple pictures, the images need to be taken by a rotating camera without translation.
motivation_md: Panoramas allow us to capture a field of view wider than a single lens can provide. By ensuring the camera only rotates, we can use homographies to perfectly align overlapping images into a single seamless view.
recap_md:
- Panoramas are created by stitching multiple images using homography transformations.
 - Successful stitching requires the camera to rotate around its center without translation.

title: Image Stitching Procedure
one_liner: To stitch images, one must estimate the homography relating them, typically using initial point correspondences.
content:
To stitch together images, one needs to estimate the homography relating the images to be stitched together. While one could estimate the rotation and intrinsic camera matrices to compute the homography, it is usually simpler to follow a correspondence-based procedure.

We start by assuming we have some initial correspondences between each pair of images as shown in @fig-fig_matching_two_images. The correspondences in this example are computed using speeded up robust features (SURF).

(see figure: Two overlapping images and some found correspondences using SURF descriptors. A random set of four correspondences are highlighted.)
motivation_md: Directly measuring camera rotation and internal parameters is difficult. Estimating the homography from image features (like SURF) provides a robust, data-driven way to align images without specialized hardware.
recap_md:
- Image stitching relies on estimating a homography matrix from point correspondences.
 - Feature detection methods like SURF are used to find these initial correspondences.

title: Speeded Up Robust Features (SURF)
one_liner: Speeded Up Robust Features (SURF) is an algorithm used to find correspondences between images.
content: Speeded Up Robust Features (SURF) is a method used to compute correspondences between images for tasks such as homography estimation.
motivation_md: To relate two images, we need to identify the same physical points in both. SURF provides a fast and reliable way to detect and describe these points so they can be matched automatically.
recap_md:
- SURF is a feature descriptor used for finding point correspondences.
 - It is designed to be a robust and efficient alternative to other feature detection methods.

title: Non-semantic Perceptual Groups
one_liner: Perceptual groups can represent coherent structures in our minds even when they go beyond the limits of language and are hard to name.
content: Although the analogy to text makes clear why perceptual organization is important, perceptual groups can also go beyond the limits of language. Some structures we see are hard to name but still clearly represent a coherent group in our heads. Consider, for example, the image in (see figure: How many objects do you see?) below. There are clearly two separate objects, but we don't have names for them. The next sections will cover a few different kinds of perceptual groups that are important in vision.
motivation_md: This concept explains that human vision organizes the world into coherent units even when those units don't correspond to known categories or words, highlighting that perceptual organization is a fundamental visual process independent of high-level semantics.
recap_md: - Perceptual organization can occur without the need for linguistic labels or semantic meaning.

title: K-Means Segmentation
one_liner: $K$-means segmentation groups pixels into clusters based on color similarity to find regions of roughly constant color.
content:
$K$-means is one of the simplest and most useful clustering algorithms for segmentation. It operates on a data matrix of $N$ datapoints by $M$ features per datapoint. To convert the segmentation problem to this format, each pixel is treated as a datapoint and the pixel's color is its feature vector. For ease of visualization, we can use the $ab$ color value as the two-dimensional (2D) feature per pixel. An image represented this way can be plotted as a scatter plot and thought of as samples from a distribution over $ab$ colors, as shown in (see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...).

$K$-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot. If you prefer a probabilistic interpretation, it can be thought of as fitting a mixture of Gaussians to the datapoints to approximate the distribution from which these pixels were sampled. We can segment via $k$-means by simply assigning each pixel to the cluster assignment of its color value. Below we color each pixel in each cluster by the mean color of all pixels assigned to that cluster ((see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.)).

Naturally, $k$-means on $ab$-values finds segments that correspond to regions of roughly a constant color. This simple approach can be surprisingly effective. For instance, it segments a zebra from the background in (see figure: (top row): $k$-means segmentation succeeds on a seemingly hard image. *Photo source*: Fredo Durand. (bottom row): $k$-means fails on an image that, to our eye, looks no more complex.) because the black and white stripes have roughly the same $ab$-values. However, it fails to group more complex patterns that are not defined by color similarity, such as the beach photo in the same figure.
motivation_md: K-means provides a straightforward way to perform image segmentation by treating pixels as data points in a color space, allowing for the discovery of coherent regions based on color similarity.
recap_md: - $K$-means segments images by clustering pixels based on their color features (e.g., $ab$ values).

title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation groups pixels using a distance metric that models the similarity or likelihood of two items belonging to the same object.
content:
Other clustering methods are based on the idea of affinity, where we try to model a distance metric that tells us whether two items should be grouped. The distance metric usually measures how similar two patterns are, or how likely they are to be part of the same object. For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between the color values of the two pixels. Methods that use this idea include those based on graph cuts, spectral clustering, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering.

Contrastive learning is a perfect fit for affinity-based segmentation because contrastive methods learn from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs). Contrastive methods learn an embedding in which datapoints with high affinity are nearby and datapoints with low affinity are far apart. Once we have such an embedding, clustering is easy in the embedding space using an algorithm like $k$-means. One way to do affinity-based clustering is to first use affinities to supervise an embedding in which the data is nearly clustered, then read off the clusters using a simple quantization method like $k$-means.

Affinity-based clustering becomes particularly interesting when we have nontrivial affinities to model, such as those given by human judgments or self-supervised measures. Popular contrastive learning methods like SimCLR, MoCo, and DINO train a mapping from image patches to embedding vectors such that patches from the same image embed near each other. We can run these methods densely across a single image to create a feature map where each pixel's value is an embedding vector. This creates a new image where pixels are similar to others that the model thinks would likely appear in the same scene. If we apply $k$-means to the pixels in this feature map, we can obtain an effective segmentation, as shown in (see figure: Image segmentation using $k$-means over DINO @caron2021emerging features).
motivation_md: Standard color-based clustering fails on complex textures. Affinity-based methods allow the use of learned similarities—often from self-supervised models like DINO—to group pixels based on more sophisticated patterns and context.
recap_md: - Affinity models the distance between items to determine if they belong to the same group.

title: Edge Detection
one_liner: Edge detection identifies boundaries between perceptual structures to create a compact, stable representation of an image's content.
content: A complementary problem to segmentation is boundary detection, because a partitioning of an image can be represented either by partition assignments (segments) or by the boundaries between partitions. Many vision algorithms organize images into different kinds of boundaries between perceptual structures. Early vision algorithms focused on edge detection, where the idea was that the edges in an image should form a good, compact representation of the image's content, because edges are relatively sparse, and they are stable with respect to nuisances like noise and lighting. Subsequent work identified connections between different kinds of edge structure and scene geometry; for example, an edge that represents an occluding contour indicates that there is a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
motivation_md: Edges provide a sparse and robust representation of an image, capturing essential geometric information like depth discontinuities while remaining stable under varying lighting conditions.
recap_md: - Edge detection represents image content through the boundaries between different perceptual structures.

title: Line Drawings
one_liner: Line drawings represent the edge structure of an image in a way that is highly intuitive to humans, though their utility for machines remains an active research area.
content: Line drawings are another way of representing the edge structure in an image, and they seem to be of high interest to humans. This suggests that there may be something useful about representing images in terms of their edge structure. Although there is an active line of research in computer graphics on modeling line drawings, this work has not yet paid off in vision, and it remains unclear whether or not line drawings will one day prove as compelling to visually intelligent machines as they do to us humans.
motivation_md: Humans can easily interpret line drawings, suggesting that edge-based representations capture critical information about the visual world that might be useful for artificial intelligence.
recap_md: - Line drawings represent images through their edge structure.

title: Layers
one_liner: Layers are a pseudo-3D representation that captures depth and ordinal structure by organizing a scene into a stack of planes.
content:
If you have ever seen an early Disney cartoon (e.g., Snow White), you may have noticed a compelling illusion of depth created by parallax between different layers of the animated scene. Animators for these cartoons used a device called a multiplane camera, which worked as follows. A camera looked at a stack of glass planes. On each plane, the animators would draw a different layer of the scene. For example, on the back plane would be the sky, then there would be mountains on the next plane, then trees, and then the foreground characters. [FIGURE:2af0dbf22adfc9da | A technical patent drawing of a multiplane camera system labeled 'FIG. 1'. It shows a tall vertical frame with multiple horizontal layers (labeled A through E) stacked vertically, which are used to...]

During filming the planes could be shifted back and forth to create parallax where the foreground planes move by more quickly than the planes further back. This device works because it is a rough approximation to the actual 3D structure of the world. In computer vision, layer-based representations like this have been popular as a way of capturing some aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world; sometimes layers and other related pseudo-3D representations are called 2.5D representations. Layers are not just an approximation to true depth, but also capture geometric structure that is not well-represented by depth. Layers capture ordinal structure and often this is the structure we care about; for example, if we want to pick up a piece of paper in our pile, the main thing that matters is if it is on top.
motivation_md: Modeling the full 3D world is computationally expensive. Layers provide a '2.5D' alternative that captures essential depth ordering and parallax effects seen in the real world.
recap_md: - Layers organize a scene into a stack of planes to approximate 3D structure and depth.

title: 2.5D Representations
one_liner: 2.5D representations are pseudo-3D models, such as layers, that capture aspects of depth without the complexity of a full 3D world model.
content: In computer vision, layer-based representations have been popular as a way of capturing some aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world; sometimes layers and other related pseudo-3D representations are called 2.5D representations.
motivation_md: This concept provides a middle ground between 2D images and full 3D models, allowing vision systems to reason about depth and occlusion more efficiently.
recap_md: - 2.5D representations use layers to capture depth information.

title: Ordinal Structure
one_liner: Ordinal structure refers to the relative depth ordering of objects, which is often more important for interaction than precise metric distance.
content: Layers are not just an approximation to true depth, but also capture geometric structure that is not well-represented by depth. Consider a pile of papers on your desk. The depth difference between one page and the next might only be a millimeter—too small to show up on standard depth sensing cameras. But the layer structure is obvious. Look back at (see figure: How many objects do you see?): the depth order is obvious even though you might have no idea how far apart these objects are in metric space. Layers capture ordinal structure and often this is the structure we care about; for example, if we want to pick up a piece of paper in our pile, the main thing that matters is if it is on top.
motivation_md: In many tasks, knowing which object is in front of another (the order) is more critical and easier to perceive than knowing the exact distance in millimeters.
recap_md: - Ordinal structure captures the relative depth order of objects rather than their exact metric distance.

title: Texture Gradients

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Texture gradients provide 3D information by measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions.
content:
Another source of 3D information are texture gradients. Since distant things appear smaller than closer things, measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions allows for a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure.

[FIGURE:74c32638e485d003 | A close-up photograph of a textured metal surface with a repeating grid of small, square-based pyramidal bumps. The perspective view shows the bumps receding into the distance, illustrating how...]

This image contains multiple 3D cues: shading effects (bump shapes), texture gradients (relative size between bumps), and linear perspective due to the regular arrangement of the bumps. Many methods using texture gradient cues have been proposed over time.
motivation_md: Texture gradients allow a vision system to infer depth from a single image by exploiting the geometric regularity of surfaces. By observing how the scale and density of a texture change across an image, we can estimate the orientation and distance of surfaces without needing multiple viewpoints.

title: Shadows and Interreflections

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Shadows and interreflections serve as important cues for understanding the 3D structure and spatial location of objects in a scene.
content: Another source of information about the 3D scene structure are shadows and interreflections. Interreflections can inform us about the location of an object, such as a ball, relative to its support surface. The use of shadows and interreflections by the human visual system has been the focus of many studies, and there are also computational approaches that use these cues to recover 3D geometry.
motivation_md: Shadows and interreflections provide critical information about the contact points and relative positions of objects. They help resolve ambiguities in depth that other cues might miss, particularly regarding whether an object is touching a surface or floating above it.

title: Aerial Perspective

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Aerial perspective is a depth cue where distant objects appear with lower contrast due to atmospheric dispersion.
content:
When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere. This effect gets accentuated when there is fog. Therefore, contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called aerial perspective or atmospheric perspective.

[FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee | A photograph of a deep mountain valley illustrating aerial perspective. The foreground mountains are dark green and high contrast, while the distant mountain peaks appear lighter, bluer, and lower in...]

Objects far in the background have lower contrast than objects closer to the camera. One example of using haze to infer depth is found in computational research.
motivation_md: In large-scale outdoor scenes, geometric cues may be sparse. Aerial perspective provides a continuous signal for depth based on atmospheric effects, allowing for the estimation of distance over kilometers where other cues like binocular stereo fail.

title: Familiar Objects

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Depth can be estimated by detecting familiar objects with known sizes to provide absolute depth measurements.
content: Depth can also be estimated by detecting familiar objects with known sizes. One example is people detection. Objects with known sizes can be used to estimate absolute depth, while many other cues can only give relative depth measurements. Using object sizes to reason about 3D geometry is a recognized approach in computer vision.
motivation_md: Most monocular depth cues (like texture or shading) only provide relative depth (which object is closer). By identifying objects of a known physical size, such as humans or cars, a system can calculate the actual metric distance (absolute depth) to those objects.

title: Linear Perspective

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Linear perspective provides strong cues for 3D reconstruction based on the geometric convergence of lines.
content: Linear perspective provides strong cues for 3D reconstruction. It is a fundamental geometric principle used to understand how 3D space is projected onto a 2D image plane.
motivation_md: Linear perspective is one of the most powerful cues for reconstructing 3D scenes from 2D images, as it relies on the predictable way parallel lines converge at vanishing points to define the layout of the environment.

title: Translating Depth Map to Point Cloud

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: A depth map can be translated into a 3D point cloud using a calibrated camera's intrinsic parameters.
content:
A depth map translates into a point cloud where each pixel is mapped to a 3D point. This requires a calibrated camera (i.e., knowing the intrinsic camera parameters). Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud for each pixel is:
$$\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ are the pixel coordinates of a point, $z(\mathbf{p})$ is the depth measured at that location, and $\mathbf{P}$ are the final 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, making the pixel locations explicit, the equation can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    X[n,m] &= \left( n-c_x \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \nonumber \\
    Y[n,m] &= \left( m-c_y \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \nonumber \\
    Z[n,m] &= z[n,m] 
\end{aligned}$$
where $a$, $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the intrinsic camera parameters in pixel units. This shows that the 3D point coordinates are represented by three images $X[n,m]$, $Y[n,m]$, and $Z[n,m]$ with the same size as the input image.
motivation_md: While a depth map is a 2D grid of distances, many 3D applications require the actual spatial coordinates of surfaces. This translation allows us to move from an image-centric view to a world-centric 3D representation, enabling tasks like 3D modeling and navigation.

title: Turbo Colormap

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: The turbo colormap is a modified version of the jet colormap used to visualize depth maps and distinguish them from grayscale images.
content:
Depth maps are usually visualized using the turbo colormap, which is a modification of the jet colormap from Matlab. This convention is used as it differentiates a depth map from a natural gray-scale image.

[FIGURE:5e64d445bf392d94 | Two vertical color bars labeled 'Jet' and 'Turbo' showing rainbow color maps used for depth visualization. Both bars transition from dark blue at the bottom, labeled 'Near', through cyan, green...]

The jet colormap can be problematic as it has a nonmonotonic intensity profile, which the turbo colormap aims to address.
motivation_md: Standard grayscale images represent intensity, while depth maps represent distance. Using a specific colormap like 'turbo' helps researchers visually distinguish depth data from intensity data and provides a more perceptually uniform way to see depth variations.

title: Mesh

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: A mesh connects 3D points with triangles to represent surfaces, requiring perceptual organization beyond simple point clouds.
content: In a point cloud, there is no notion of grouping of 3D points; the points are isolated and not connected to each other. Translating a depth map or a point cloud into a mesh requires solving the perceptual organization problem first. A mesh connects points with triangles, but it only makes sense to connect points that belong to the same surface or that are in contact.
motivation_md: Point clouds are just collections of coordinates. To perform realistic rendering, physics simulations, or surface analysis, we need to know how those points form continuous surfaces. Meshes provide this topological structure.

title: Ground Plane as a Depth Cue
one_liner: The ground plane provides a critical depth cue because the distance between an object's contact point and the horizon line relates directly to its distance from the camera.
content: The ground plane is a special plane because it supports most objects. This is different than a wall; while both are planes, the ground has an ecological importance that a wall does not have. The point of contact between objects and the ground plane informs about its distance. Specifically, the distance between the contact point and the horizon line is related to the distance between the object and the camera. Objects further away have a contact point projecting onto a higher point in the image plane.
motivation_md: In 2D images, determining the 3D distance of objects is challenging. The ground plane serves as a reliable reference because most objects rest upon it, allowing the visual system to use the vertical position of contact points relative to the horizon as a proxy for depth.
recap_md:
- The ground plane is ecologically significant because it supports most objects in a scene.
 - The image position of an object's contact point with the ground indicates its distance from the camera.
 - Objects further away project to higher points on the image plane relative to the ground.

title: Computing the Horizon Line
one_liner: The horizon line can be computed as the cross-product of two vanishing points, each derived from the intersection of parallel lines in homogeneous coordinates.
content:
Using homogeneous coordinates, we can detect the horizon line by finding vanishing points. If lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ correspond to the 2D projection of 3D parallel lines, we obtain their vanishing point as their intersection via the cross-product $\boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$. If we have another set of parallel lines in the same plane, $\boldsymbol{l}_3$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_4$, we can compute a second vanishing point. Finally, the horizon line is the line passing through both vanishing points, computed as their cross-product in homogeneous coordinates.

(see figure: Using parallel lines, in homogeneous coordinates, to compute vanishing points and the horizon line.)
motivation_md: The horizon line is essential for understanding the orientation of a camera relative to a scene. This technique allows us to mathematically recover the horizon from simple geometric features like parallel lines found on floors or ceilings.
recap_md:
- Vanishing points are found by the cross-product of parallel lines in homogeneous coordinates.
 - Two vanishing points from the same plane define the horizon line.
 - The horizon line itself is the cross-product of two distinct vanishing points.

title: Detecting Vanishing Points
one_liner: Vanishing points can be estimated manually by intersecting parallel edges or automatically using edge detection and RANSAC voting.
content:
Vanishing points can be estimated by selecting pairs of long edges in an image corresponding to parallel 3D lines in the scene and finding their intersection. In scenes with dominant orthogonal orientations, three vanishing points are typically found.

(see figure: Most object boundaries in this photograph are oriented parallel to one of the world-coordinates reference frame (the world-coordinates frame is chosen in this way on purpose). All the parallel 3D...)

Vanishing points can be extracted automatically by first detecting image edges and their orientations and then using RANSAC to group the edges: every pair of edges votes for a vanishing point, and the point with the largest support is selected. There are also learning-based approaches for vanishing point detection using graphical models or deep learning based approaches such as DeepVP and NeurVPS.
motivation_md: Vanishing points provide information about the 3D structure of a scene and camera calibration. Automating their detection allows computer vision systems to understand perspective and orientation in complex environments like city streets or offices.
recap_md:
- Vanishing points are the intersections of image lines that are parallel in 3D space.
 - RANSAC can be used to automatically detect vanishing points by finding the intersection with the most edge support.
 - Modern methods utilize deep learning models like DeepVP or NeurVPS for robust detection.

title: Cross-Ratio
one_liner: The cross-ratio is a geometric quantity of four collinear points that remains preserved under perspective projection.
content:
Perspective projection transforms many aspects of the 3D world when projecting into the 2D image: angles and relative lengths are not preserved, and parallel 3D lines do not project into 2D parallel lines unless they are parallel to the camera plane. However, some geometric properties are preserved, such as straight lines remaining straight. The cross-ratio is another such preserved quantity.

The cross-ratio of four collinear points is defined by the expression:
$$CR \left( \mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4 \right) 
= 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right|}
{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right|}$$
where $\left| \mathbf{P}_i -\mathbf{P}_j \right|$ is the euclidean distance between points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and $\mathbf{P}_j$, using heterogeneous coordinates.

[FIGURE:c3a83d33f5a7a7b5 | A diagram showing four collinear points labeled $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, and $P_4$ arranged along a single pink line. The points are spaced out from bottom-left to top-right to illustrate the geometric...]
motivation_md: Since perspective projection distorts lengths and angles, we need a mathematical invariant to relate 2D image measurements back to 3D world properties. The cross-ratio provides this link.
recap_md:
- The cross-ratio is a projective invariant involving four collinear points.
 - It is calculated using the Euclidean distances between the points in heterogeneous coordinates.
 - It remains constant even when the points are viewed from different camera perspectives.

title: Cross-Ratio Invariance
one_liner: The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant, remaining identical for sets of points related by a projective transformation.
content:
The cross-ratio is considered the most important projective invariant. Two sets of points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ related by a projective transformation have the same cross-ratio, regardless of the choice of origin $\mathbf{O}$ or scale factor. That is:
$$CR(\mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4) = CR(\mathbf{Q}_1,\mathbf{Q}_2,\mathbf{Q}_3,\mathbf{Q}_4)$$

(see figure: The set of points $\mathbf{P}$ are related to the points $\mathbf{Q}$ (and $\mathbf{R}$) by the cross-ratio. The point $\mathbf{R}_1$ is in infinity because the line connecting the points...)
motivation_md: Invariance is a powerful tool in computer vision. Because the cross-ratio does not change under projection, it allows for object recognition and 3D reconstruction that is independent of the camera's viewpoint.
recap_md:
- The cross-ratio is invariant under any projective transformation.
 - It is independent of the choice of origin or the scale factor used.
 - This property allows for comparing geometric structures across different perspectives.

title: Cross-Ratio with Point at Infinity
one_liner: When one point in a cross-ratio is at infinity, the expression simplifies as the terms containing that point cancel out.
content:
When one of the points is at infinity, all the terms that contain that point are cancelled out; this can also be seen by taking a limit. In the case of the points $\mathbf{R}$ from the projective transformation example, the cross-ratio simplifies to:
$$CR(\mathbf{R}_1,\mathbf{R}_2,\mathbf{R}_3,\mathbf{R}_4) = 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{R}_4 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right| }
{ \left| \mathbf{R}_3 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right|}$$
This value is equal to the cross-ratio of the original points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.
motivation_md: In projective geometry, vanishing points are effectively points at infinity. Being able to calculate the cross-ratio with points at infinity allows us to use vanishing points to measure real-world distances from a single image.
recap_md:
- Points at infinity simplify the cross-ratio formula by cancelling out associated terms.
 - The simplified ratio of distances remains equal to the cross-ratio of the corresponding finite points.
 - This is useful for calculations involving vanishing points in perspective images.

title: Measuring Height using a Reference Object
one_liner: Height can be measured by projecting an object's height onto a reference using vanishing points and the horizon line in homogeneous coordinates.
content:
To measure height using a reference object, we use image coordinates in homogeneous coordinates. For example, to project a desk height onto a bookshelf:

- Estimate the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ passing through the ground points of the desk $\mathbf{g}_d$ and bookshelf $\mathbf{g}_b$ using the cross-product: $\boldsymbol{l}_1 = \mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b$.
- Compute the intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ to find the vanishing point $\mathbf{a} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \mathbf{h}$.
- Compute the line $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ passing through $\mathbf{a}$ and the top of the desk $\mathbf{t}_d$: $\boldsymbol{l}_2 = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{t}_d$. Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel in 3D and vertically aligned.
- Find where $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ intersects the bookshelf by first defining the bookshelf's vertical line $\boldsymbol{l}_3 = \mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b$, then finding the intersection $\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{l}_2 \times \boldsymbol{l}_3$.

These steps can be combined into a single equation:
$$\mathbf{b} = (((\mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_d) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
motivation_md: Measuring the physical size of objects from a single 2D image is difficult. By using a reference object of known height and the geometric properties of the horizon and vanishing points, we can accurately transfer height measurements across a scene.
recap_md:
- Use the ground points of two objects to find a shared vanishing point on the horizon.
 - Project the top of the reference object toward that vanishing point to find the corresponding height on the target object.
 - The entire process can be solved using a sequence of cross-products in homogeneous coordinates.

title: Projective Invariants
one_liner: Projective invariants are measures that remain unchanged after a perspective projection.
content: **Projective invariants** are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
motivation_md: Invariants are the 'ground truth' of geometry; they allow us to identify properties of the 3D world that are not lost or distorted when a camera captures a scene.
recap_md:
- Projective invariants are properties preserved under perspective transformation.
 - The cross-ratio is a primary example of such an invariant.

title: Learning Invariant Representations
one_liner: Learning invariant representations is a classic goal of computer vision where models are incentivized to ignore certain transformations through the objective function.
content: Learning invariant representations is a classic goal of computer vision. While convolutional image filters provide equivariance with camera translation and invariance through pooling, CNNs bake this into the hypothesis space. Alternatively, invariances can be incentivized through the objective function rather than the architecture alone.
motivation_md: In computer vision, we often want models to recognize objects regardless of transformations like camera translation. While architecture can provide some invariance, using the objective function allows for more flexible and learned invariances.
recap_md: [ "Invariant representations are a fundamental goal in computer vision.", "Invariance can be achieved through architectural choices like convolution and pooling.", "Alternatively, invariances can be incentivized directly through the model's objective function." ]

title: Alignment Loss
one_liner: Alignment loss penalizes deviations from a desired invariance by minimizing the distance between representations of a data point and its transformed version.
content: The idea is to simply penalize deviations from the invariance we want. Suppose $T$ is a transformation we wish our representation to be invariant to. Then we may use a loss of the form $\left\lVert f(T(\mathbf{x}))-f(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_2^2$ to learn an encoder $f$ that is invariant to $T$. We call such a loss an alignment loss.
motivation_md: To ensure a model's representation is invariant to a specific transformation, we need a mathematical way to penalize the model when the representation changes after that transformation is applied.
recap_md: [ "Alignment loss penalizes differences between representations of original and transformed data.", "It is typically formulated as the squared Euclidean distance $\left\lVert f(T(\mathbf{x}))-f(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_2^2$.", "This loss encourages the encoder $f$ to be invariant to the transformation $T$." ]

title: Representational Collapse
one_liner: Representational collapse occurs when a model achieves trivial alignment by mapping all data points to the same constant vector.
content: A flaw in using only alignment loss is the possibility of representational collapse. Trivial alignment can be achieved if the encoder $f$ learns to output the zero vector all the time, such that all datapoints get mapped to the same arbitrary vector.
motivation_md: If we only reward a model for making representations similar, the easiest solution is for the model to output the same constant value for everything, which makes the representation useless.
recap_md: [ "Representational collapse is a failure mode where the model outputs a constant vector for all inputs.", "It results in a trivial solution for alignment losses.", "This phenomenon makes the learned representations non-informative." ]

title: Positive and Negative Pairs
one_liner: Contrastive learning uses positive pairs to pull similar representations together and negative pairs to push dissimilar representations apart, preventing representational collapse.
content: Contrastive learning fixes representational collapse by coupling an alignment loss with a second loss that pushes apart embeddings of datapoints for which we do not want an invariant representation. The supervision comes in the form of positive pairs and negative pairs. Positive pairs are two datapoints we wish to align in $z$-space; if we wish for invariance to $T$ then a positive pair should be constructed as $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{+}\}$, where $\mathbf{x}^{+} = T(\mathbf{x})$. Negative pairs, $\{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^-\}$, are two datapoints that should be represented differently. Commonly, negative pairs are randomly constructed by sampling two datapoints independently from the data distribution: $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})$ and $\mathbf{x}^{-} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})$. The objective is to pull together the positive pairs and push apart the negative pairs. (see figure: Contrastive learning.) [FIGURE:699660d27bc5fbbc | A block diagram illustrating contrastive learning with transformations. It shows input data {x^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N, T entering a box labeled 'Contrastive learning (transformations)'. Inside the box...]
motivation_md: To prevent the model from collapsing all representations to a single point, we must explicitly tell it which points should be different. Contrastive learning provides this by using negative samples to create a repulsive force in the embedding space.
recap_md: [ "Positive pairs are samples that should have similar representations, often created via transformations.", "Negative pairs are samples that should have different representations, typically sampled independently.", "Contrastive learning balances pulling positive pairs together and pushing negative pairs apart." ]

title: Contrastive Learning from Co-occurrence
one_liner: Contrastive learning from co-occurrence aligns representations of different sensory signals or views that represent the same underlying scene or data.
content: Contrastive learning can be based on co-occurrence, where the goal is to learn a common representation of all co-occurring signals, such as audiovisual representations or aligning grayscale and color channels. In these cases, the co-occurring signals are referred to as different views of the total data tensor $\mathbf{X}$, denoted as $\mathbf{x} = V_1(\mathbf{X})$ and $\mathbf{y} = V_2(\mathbf{X})$. These views can result from sensory co-occurrences or transformations like channel dropping. Any two signals can be considered transformations of a combined total signal, and any signal and its transformation can be considered two co-occurring ways of measuring the underlying world. (see figure: Contrastive learning from multiple views of the data. Figure inspired by \cite{tian2020contrastive) [FIGURE:8ce923f69bb6f5a1 | A flowchart for contrastive learning showing data input, a processing box, and output functions. The input is data pairs {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N. The central box defines the objective as a sum...]
motivation_md: Different sensors or data channels often provide different views of the same underlying reality. Learning to align these views helps the model capture the shared semantic information across different modalities.
recap_md: [ "Co-occurrence learning aligns different views of the same data, such as audio and video.", "Views can be sensory signals or different transformations of a single data tensor.", "This approach treats multi-modal alignment and transformation-based invariance as essentially the same problem." ]

title: Hadsell et al. Contrastive Loss
one_liner: Hadsell et al. contrastive loss uses a margin to only penalize distances between positive or negative pairs when they fall outside a specified threshold.
content: Hadsell et al.'s "contrastive loss" is an older definition of the term that introduces the concept of a margin to the vanilla formulation. It only pushes or pulls when the distance is less than a specified amount $m$ (the margin); otherwise, points are considered far enough apart or close enough together. The loss is defined as: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) = \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)-m_{\texttt{pos}},0) - \max(m_{\texttt{neg}} - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-),0)$$ where $D$ is a distance function.
motivation_md: Standard distance-based losses might try to push negative samples infinitely far apart. Using a margin allows the model to stop optimizing once samples are different enough, focusing its capacity on more difficult pairs.
recap_md: [ "Hadsell et al.'s loss uses margins to control the push and pull forces between embeddings.", "It only penalizes distances if they fall outside the specified margin $m$.", "This was one of the earliest formulations of what we now call contrastive learning." ]

title: Triplet Loss
one_liner: Triplet loss optimizes the relative distance between an anchor, a positive sample, and a negative sample using a margin.
content: The triplet loss is a popular variation of the contrastive objective that adds a margin $m$ to the formulation. It operates on a triplet consisting of an anchor $\mathbf{x}$, a positive sample $\mathbf{x}^+$, and a negative sample $\mathbf{x}^-$. The loss is defined as: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}^-) = \max(D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^+)) - D(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}^-)) + m, 0)$$ where $D$ is a distance function.
motivation_md: Instead of just making positives close and negatives far, triplet loss focuses on the relative distance: the positive should be closer to the anchor than the negative is, by at least a certain margin.
recap_md: [ "Triplet loss uses an anchor, a positive, and a negative sample simultaneously.", "It enforces that the negative sample is further from the anchor than the positive sample by a margin $m$.", "It is widely used in tasks like face recognition and image retrieval." ]

title: InfoNCE Loss
one_liner: InfoNCE loss treats contrastive learning as a classification problem, using a log-softmax to distinguish a positive sample from multiple negative samples.
content: The InfoNCE loss treats establishing a contrast as a classification problem, moving points apart until the positive sample can be classified separately from all negatives for a given anchor. The formulation is: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^+, \{\mathbf{x}_i^-\}_{i=1}^N) = -\log \frac{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau}}{e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}^+)/\tau} + \sum_i e^{f(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f(\mathbf{x}_i^-)/\tau}}$$ This loss is a log softmax over a vector of scores $f_1(\mathbf{x})^\mathsf{T}f_2(c)/\tau$ with $c \in \{\mathbf{x}^+, \mathbf{x}_1^-, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N^-\}$. You can think of this loss as corresponding to a classification problem where the ground truth class is $\mathbf{x}^+$ and the other possible classes are the negative samples.
motivation_md: By framing contrastive learning as a multi-class classification problem, InfoNCE can leverage the efficiency and properties of the softmax function to compare one positive against many negatives simultaneously.
recap_md: [ "InfoNCE frames contrastive learning as a classification task using a softmax-based loss.", "It compares one positive sample against a set of $N$ negative samples.", "The temperature parameter $\tau$ scales the similarity scores before the softmax." ]

title: Colinearity and Concurrency in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

one_liner: Three 2D points are colinear if the determinant of their concatenated homogeneous coordinate vectors is zero.
content: If three 2D points are colinear, then the determinant of the matrix formed by concatenating the three vectors, in homogeneous coordinates, as columns is equal to zero: $\det( [\mathbf{p}_1~\mathbf{p}_2~\mathbf{p}_3 ])=0$. If three lines intersect in the same point we have a similar relationship: $\det( [\boldsymbol{l}_1~\boldsymbol{l}_2~\boldsymbol{l}_3 ])=0$.
motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify geometric checks for colinearity and concurrency into a single determinant calculation, providing a unified algebraic framework for 2D geometry.
recap_md: - Colinearity of three points $\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3$ is equivalent to $\det([\mathbf{p}_1~\mathbf{p}_2~\mathbf{p}_3]) = 0$.

title: Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

one_liner: A 3D plane can be represented in homogeneous coordinates by the dot product of a parameter vector and a point vector.
content: We can represent planes in 3D using homogeneous coordinates. The equation of a 3D plane is $aX+bY+cZ+d=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$$ where $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$ are the plane parameters and $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z,1]^\mathsf{T}$ are the 3D point homogeneous coordinates.
motivation_md: Using homogeneous coordinates for planes allows 3D planar equations to be expressed as a simple linear product, consistent with how points and lines are handled in 2D projective geometry.
recap_md: - The homogeneous equation of a plane is $\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$.

title: Forward Mapping
one_liner: Forward mapping transforms every pixel from the source image to the target image coordinates, often resulting in artifacts like missing values.
content:
Forward mapping is an algorithm for transforming an image where every pixel in the original image, represented as $[\ell_i,x_i,y_i]$, is transformed by a matrix $\mathbf{M}$. The resulting pixel color is recorded into the calculated coordinates in the target image. As coordinates might result in non-integer values, the result can be rounded to the closest pixel coordinate using nearest neighbor interpolation. While intuitive, forward mapping often produces artifacts such as missing values and aliasing.

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.)

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
motivation_md: Forward mapping is the most intuitive approach to image warping, but it is technically flawed because it doesn't guarantee that every pixel in the destination image will be assigned a value.
recap_md: - Maps source pixels to destination coordinates using a transformation matrix $\mathbf{M}$.

title: Backward Mapping
one_liner: Backward mapping iterates over target image pixels and applies an inverse transform to sample colors from the source image.
content:
(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.)

The best approach for image warping is backward mapping, which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. Interpolation is then used to get the correct color value from the source image. This process guarantees that there will be no missing values (unless the coordinates go outside the frame of the input image) and there will be no aliasing if the interpolation is done correctly. To avoid aliasing, blurring of the input image might be necessary if the density of pixels in the target image is lower than in the input image.

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
motivation_md: Backward mapping ensures every pixel in the output image is filled and allows for high-quality interpolation, avoiding the holes and artifacts common in forward mapping.
recap_md: - Iterates through target pixels and uses the inverse transform $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to find source locations.

title: MIP-mapping
one_liner: MIP-mapping uses a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute high-quality interpolation at various scales.
content: MIP-mapping is a popular technique for high quality and efficient interpolation. It relies on a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute the best neighborhood structure needed to perform the interpolation at each location. This is particularly useful when warping an image onto a curved surface.
motivation_md: MIP-mapping solves the problem of aliasing and computational inefficiency when an image is viewed at different scales or orientations, such as in 3D texture mapping.
recap_md: - Utilizes a multiscale image pyramid for efficient neighborhood selection.

title: Implicit Image Representation
one_liner: An implicit image representation uses a continuous function to reproduce image pixels at any real-valued coordinate.
content: An image is typically an array of values, $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, where each value is indexed as $\ell[n,m]$ for discrete values. Interpolation transforms this discrete image into a continuous signal: $\ell(x,y)$. An implicit image representation via a function $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce the image pixels is a function such that: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ where $x,y$ can take on any real value.
motivation_md: Representing images as continuous functions rather than discrete grids allows for infinite resolution and more flexible manipulation in neural rendering and computer vision.
recap_md: - Models an image as a continuous function $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$.

title: Neural Network Interpolation
one_liner: Neural network interpolation uses a trained network to map continuous coordinates to image intensity values.
content: In nearest neighbors or bilinear interpolation, the parameters of the interpolation function $\theta$ is the input image itself. For example, nearest neighbors interpolation can be written as: $$\ell(x,y) = \ell\left[ \text{round}(x), \text{round}(y) \right]$$ We can extend the space of possible functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ to include other functional forms, such as a neural network. This network takes two image coordinate values $x$ and $y$ as input and outputs the intensity value at that location. The training set for the neural network is the image itself, consisting of input-output pairs $[(x_i, y_i); \ell(x_i,y_i)]$. During training, the neural network memorizes the image; at test time, it can generalize to non-integer coordinate values to interpolate between samples.
motivation_md: Neural networks can learn complex, continuous representations of images that may outperform traditional interpolation methods by capturing higher-order patterns.
recap_md: - Uses a neural network $f_{\theta}$ to map coordinates $(x, y)$ to colors or intensities.

title: Image Alignment
one_liner: Image alignment is the process of identifying the transformation that relates two images.
content: Image alignment is the problem of identifying the transformation $\mathbf{M}$ when given two images, where one image is a transformed version of the other.
motivation_md: Image alignment is fundamental for tasks like image stitching (panoramas), medical imaging registration, and motion tracking in video.
recap_md: - The goal is to find the transformation matrix $\mathbf{M}$ between two related images.

title: Anaglyph Pinhole Camera
one_liner: An anaglyph pinhole camera uses two holes with different color filters to produce a superposition of two images from slightly different viewpoints.
content:
An anaglyph pinhole camera is created by making two holes in a pinhole camera and placing different color filters on each hole. This setup produces an image that is the superposition of two images taken from slightly different viewpoints, where each image has a different color. To perceive the 3D image, the resulting picture is viewed through glasses with matching color filters, such as blue and red filters.

(see figure: One way of playing with pinhole cameras is to build an anaglyph pinhole camera. The anaglyph pinhole camera captures stereo images by projecting an anaglyph image on the projection plane.)
motivation_md: This concept explains how to adapt a simple pinhole camera to capture depth information, allowing for the creation and visualization of 3D stereo images using basic color filtering techniques.
recap_md: - Uses two pinholes with distinct color filters to capture stereo viewpoints simultaneously.

title: Multiview Stereo
one_liner: Multiview stereo refers to the task of perceiving 3D information when more than two cameras are used.
content: If more than two cameras are used, the task is referred to as multiview stereo.
motivation_md: While basic stereo vision uses two viewpoints, many computer vision applications use multiple cameras to improve depth accuracy and coverage.
recap_md: - Involves the use of three or more cameras for 3D reconstruction.

title: Simple Stereo Geometry
one_liner: Simple stereo geometry assumes two identical, horizontally aligned cameras with parallel optical axes to estimate depth from point projections.
content: In a simple stereo setting, two identical cameras with the same intrinsic parameters are used. One camera is translated horizontally relative to the other so that their optical axes are parallel. Assuming calibrated cameras, this geometry allows for depth estimation of a point $\mathbf{P}$ in 3D space by knowing its projection locations: $[x_L,y_L]^\mathsf{T}$ for the left camera and $[x_R,y_R]^\mathsf{T}$ for the right camera. Because the cameras are aligned horizontally, the $y$-coordinates for the projections are equal ($y_L=y_R$), allowing depth estimation to be considered within a single image row from a top-down view.
motivation_md: By simplifying the camera arrangement, we can derive the fundamental geometric relationship between 2D image coordinates and 3D depth.
recap_md: - Assumes identical cameras with parallel optical axes and horizontal translation.

title: Depth from Disparity Derivation
one_liner: Depth can be calculated using the ratio of focal length and baseline distance to the horizontal disparity between corresponding image points.
content:
A simple way to triangulate the depth, $Z$, of a point visible in both images is through similar triangles. In a standard stereo setup with focal length $f$ and camera separation (baseline) $T$, the ratios of height to base for the triangles formed by the point and the cameras must be equal:

$$\frac{T+x_R-x_L}{Z-f} = \frac{T}{Z}$$

Solving for $Z$ yields the depth equation:

$$Z = \frac{fT}{x_L-x_R}$$

The denominator $x_L-x_R$ represents the horizontal disparity between the two projections.
motivation_md: This derivation provides the mathematical formula needed to convert measurable 2D pixel differences (disparity) into physical 3D distance (depth).
recap_md: - Uses similar triangles to relate depth $Z$ to focal length $f$ and baseline $T$.

title: Stereo Matching Problem
one_liner: The stereo matching problem involves identifying which points in two different images correspond to the same 3D point.
content: The stereo matching problem is the challenge of determining which points in one camera image correspond to the same 3D point in another camera image. While geometric depth estimation assumes these correspondences are known, real-world images are complex, making it difficult to automatically identify corresponding projections of a point $\mathbf{P}$.
motivation_md: Before depth can be calculated via triangulation, the system must first solve the correspondence problem to know which pixels to compare.
