motivation_md: Understanding specific camera rotations helps isolate how different degrees of freedom affect the image plane. Rotation around the optical axis is the simplest case of rotational motion, where the resulting flow is independent of scene depth and focal length.
recap_md: - The motion field for optical axis rotation is defined by $\dot{x} = y W_Z$ and $\dot{y} = -x W_Z$.

title: Rotation Around the Y-Axis
one_liner: Rotation around the Y-axis produces a motion field heavily influenced by focal length, appearing as lateral translation for large focal lengths.
motivation_md: This concept explains why zoomed-in rotational movements can be mistaken for translations and how the camera's internal geometry (focal length) dictates the distortion of the motion field.
recap_md: - For large focal lengths, Y-axis rotation approximates constant lateral translation.

title: Camera Rotation as Homography
one_liner: For large angles or time intervals, the relationship between images under camera rotation is described by a homography.
content: In the case of camera rotation, for a large angle (or a large $\Delta t$), the relationship between the image at time $t$ and the image at time $t+\Delta t$ is a homography.
motivation_md: When camera motion is purely rotational, the mapping between frames is independent of scene depth, allowing us to use homographies to align images for tasks like panorama stitching.
recap_md: - Pure camera rotation over time results in a homographic transformation between frames.

title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
one_liner: Changing the focal length over time produces a scaling of the image plane that mimics zoom without creating parallax.
motivation_md: It is important to distinguish between motion caused by the camera moving through space (which provides depth cues via parallax) and motion caused by internal lens adjustments (zoom), which provides no depth information.
recap_md: - Varying focal length creates a radial motion field $\dot{x} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f}x$ and $\dot{y} = \frac{\dot{f}}{f}y$.

title: Optical Flow
one_liner: Optical flow is an approximation of the 2D motion field calculated by measuring the displacement of image brightness between frames.
content:
Optical flow is an approximation to the 2D motion field computed by measuring displacement of image brightness (@fig-visualization_optical_flow). The ideal optical flow is defined as follows: given two images $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, the optical flow $\left[ \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 2}$ indicates the relative position of each pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and the corresponding pixel in $\boldsymbol\ell_2$. 

Optical flow changes if time is reversed. This definition assumes a one-to-one mapping between frames, which fails if objects appear, disappear, or are occluded. It also assumes that a single motion explains all brightness changes, an assumption violated by transparent objects or moving illumination sources. @fig-visualization_optical_flow shows two frames and their optical flow visualized using a standard color code.

(see figure: Two frames of a sequence, ground-truth optical flow (color coded), and the color code to read the vector at each pixel.)
motivation_md: While the 2D motion field is a geometric ideal, optical flow is what we can actually estimate from pixel data. It serves as the primary tool for tracking objects and understanding scene dynamics from video.
recap_md: - Optical flow maps pixels from one frame to their corresponding locations in the next frame.

title: When Optical Flow and Motion Flow Are Not the Same
one_liner: Optical flow and the true 2D motion field can differ when image brightness changes do not correspond to physical 3D motion.
content:
There are several scenarios where motion in image brightness does not correspond to the motion of 3D points in the scene:

- A rotating Lambertian sphere with static illumination produces no image changes (zero optical flow despite physical motion).
- A static sphere with a moving light source produces image changes (optical flow despite no physical motion).
- Moving in front of a textureless wall produces no image changes.
- Waves in water appear to move horizontally while the physical water motion is primarily vertical.
- Specular surfaces, like mirrors or moving cameras in front of specular planes, produce motion fields that do not follow standard geometric models like homographies.

Motion estimation should ideally assign the physical cause to each variation, though basic models often only measure pixel motion.
motivation_md: Recognizing the discrepancy between perceived brightness changes and actual physical motion is crucial for understanding the limitations of motion estimation algorithms, especially in environments with complex lighting or lack of texture.
recap_md: - Optical flow can be zero when physical motion exists (e.g., rotating textureless spheres).

title: Dense Optical Flow Representation
one_liner: Dense optical flow models motion as a continuous velocity field across all image pixels over time.
content:
Motion over time can be modeled as a sequence of dense optical flow images: $\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$. Here, $u(x,y,t)$ and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at coordinates $(x,y)$ at time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. A limitation of this formulation is the lack of an explicit representation of the trajectory of specific scene points, as a fixed $(x,y)$ location may correspond to different scene elements over time.

Alternatively, motion can be modeled as a sparse set of moving points (tracks): $\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$. This requires establishing correspondences (tracking), which is challenging due to perspective and illumination changes. 

Gradient-based methods, such as the Lucas-Kanade method, estimate dense flow using the brightness constancy assumption: $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1) = \ell(x,y,t)$. Using a first-order Taylor expansion, we derive the gradient constraint equation: $u \ell_x + v \ell_y + \ell_t = 0$. To solve for $(u,v)$, we assume motion is locally constant and minimize a weighted loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2$$

This leads to a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations at each location:

$$\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\
\sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
u \\
v
\end{bmatrix}
= 
- 
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\
\sum g \ell_y \ell_t
\end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Gradient-based optical flow estimation using two input frames.)
(see figure: Toy sequence with two moving squares. The red arrows indicate the direction of motion of each square.)
(see figure: Spatial and temporal derivatives for the sequence from @fig-square_grandient_based_1)
(see figure: Computation of all the products between derivatives from @fig-square_grandient_based_2)
motivation_md: Dense representation is necessary for tasks like video compression or per-pixel scene understanding, where knowing the motion of every part of the image is more important than tracking individual landmarks.
recap_md: - Dense optical flow assigns a velocity vector $(u,v)$ to every pixel in the image.

title: Brightness Constancy Assumption
one_liner: The brightness constancy assumption posits that the intensity of a scene element remains unchanged as it moves across image frames.
content:
The brightness constancy assumption says that as a scene element moves in the world, the brightness captured by the camera from that element does not change over time. Mathematically, for a sequence $\ell(x,y,t)$, this is expressed as:

$$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  = \ell(x,y,t)$$

where $u$ and $v$ are the element displacements over one unit of time. This is equivalent to $\ell(x, y, t + 1) = \ell(x-u,y-v,t)$. 

(see figure: Translation to the right of a simple 6x6 size image.)

This assumption only approximately holds. For it to be exact, the scene must contain Lambertian objects illuminated from infinity, with no occlusions, shadows, or interreflections. In reality, pixels may be occluded or new pixels may appear at boundaries, violating the assumption that all pixels in one frame are visible in the next.
motivation_md: This assumption provides the fundamental constraint needed to solve for motion from image intensities, turning an under-determined problem into a solvable mathematical relationship.
recap_md: - It assumes $I(x,y,t) = I(x+dx, y+dy, t+dt)$ for a moving point.

title: Camera Translation
one_liner: The 2D motion field for a translating camera relates image velocity to the camera's linear velocity and the depth of scene points.
motivation_md: Understanding how camera translation generates image motion is fundamental for computer vision tasks like structure from motion and navigation. It allows us to relate 2D pixel changes to 3D camera movement and scene depth.
recap_md: - The motion field for translation depends inversely on the depth $Z$ of the scene points.

title: Lateral Camera Motion
one_liner: Lateral camera motion occurs when a camera translates parallel to the image plane, causing image motion that depends on object depth.
motivation_md: Lateral motion isolates the parallax effect, where the speed of image motion is inversely proportional to depth. This is a primary cue for depth perception in both biological and computer vision.
recap_md: - In lateral motion ($V_Z=0$), image velocity is directly proportional to focal length and inversely proportional to depth.

title: Camera Forward Motion
one_liner: Forward camera motion occurs when the camera translates along its optical axis, resulting in an expanding motion field.
motivation_md: Forward motion is the most common movement for navigating robots and vehicles. It creates a characteristic 'expansion' pattern that helps determine the direction of travel and time to collision.
recap_md: - Forward motion ($V_X=V_Y=0$) results in image velocities that scale with the distance from the image center.

title: Time to Contact
one_liner: Time to contact is the ratio of depth to forward velocity, representing how long until the camera reaches an object.
content: The observed motion in forward camera translation depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact is the time it will take the camera to reach an object located at a distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$. Notably, the rate of expansion in the image does not depend on the focal length $f$.
motivation_md: Time to contact is a critical safety metric for autonomous systems, allowing them to estimate collision times directly from image expansion without needing absolute depth or velocity.
recap_md: - Time to contact is defined by the ratio $Z/V_Z$.

title: Focus of Expansion
one_liner: The focus of expansion is the point in the image plane where the observed motion is zero during camera translation.
motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the camera's heading (direction of translation). By locating this point, a system can determine where it is going regardless of the scene's 3D structure.
recap_md: - The focus of expansion is the stationary point from which all motion vectors appear to radiate.

title: General Camera Motion Field
one_liner: The general camera motion field combines translational and rotational velocities to describe the 2D velocity of image points.
motivation_md: Real-world camera motion is rarely purely translational or rotational. This general model is necessary to decouple the effects of rotation (which doesn't depend on depth) from translation (which does).
recap_md: - The motion field is the sum of a translational component (dependent on depth $Z$) and a rotational component (independent of depth).

title: Euler Angles
one_liner: Euler angles decompose a 3D rotation into three consecutive rotations around the camera-coordinate axes: yaw, pitch, and roll.
motivation_md: Euler angles provide an intuitive way to describe 3D orientation and rotation, which is necessary for calculating how a camera's change in attitude affects the image.
recap_md: - Euler angles consist of rotations around the X (pitch), Y (yaw), and Z (roll) axes.

title: Pure Camera Rotation Motion Field
one_liner: The motion field for pure camera rotation depends only on rotational velocity and camera parameters, independent of scene depth.
motivation_md: Distinguishing rotation from translation is vital because rotation creates image motion that can be confused with translation but provides no depth information. This is why 'shaking' a camera doesn't help with depth perception.
recap_md: - Pure rotation motion fields are independent of the distance to objects in the scene.

title: Visibility Term

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: A binary variable $v_i^{(j)}$ used in the reprojection error sum to account for 3D points that are only visible in a subset of views.
content:
To calculate the final reprojection error, a visibility term $v_i^{(j)}$ is added to account for 3D points that are only visible in a subset of the views. The binary variable $v_i^{(j)}$ indicates if point $i$ is seen from camera $j$. For all points not visible in a specific view, $v_i^{(j)}$ is set to 0, meaning their reprojection error is ignored. This is expressed in the final reprojection error formula:

$$\sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{i=1}^N v_i^{(j)} \left\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i - \pi \left( \mathbf{K}^{(j)} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}^{(j)} ~ \mid ~ -\mathbf{R}^{(j)}\mathbf{T}^{(j)} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{P}^{(j)}_i \right) \right\rVert ^2$$
motivation_md: In multi-view geometry, not every 3D point is visible from every camera. The visibility term ensures the optimization process only considers valid reprojections, preventing hidden or occluded points from skewing the error calculation.
recap_md: - The visibility term $v_i^{(j)}$ is a binary indicator of whether point $i$ appears in camera $j$.

title: Bundle Adjustment

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: The process of optimizing the bundle of rays connecting camera centers and 3D point coordinates to minimize reprojection error.
content:
Bundle adjustment refers to the process of optimizing the "bundle of rays" connecting the camera centers and the coordinates of the 3D points. This optimization of the reprojection error is used to find the final set of 3D points by refining camera poses and the 3D locations of keypoints (and camera intrinsics, if needed). The reprojection error loss is usually rewritten using a robust cost function, typically the Huber kernel.

[FIGURE:0c70d937603b3e14 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of a scene, likely a small object, showing a dense ring of reddish-brown points and a surrounding cloud of grey points. Red wireframe camera frustums are positioned in...]

[FIGURE:426302de0255562e | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of a small object, likely a sugar bowl, composed of numerous colored dots. Above the point cloud, several red wireframe pyramids represent the calculated camera poses...]

[FIGURE:a6d594addba7ef87 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of a scene, showing clusters of colored points representing surfaces and several red wireframe pyramid shapes representing recovered camera positions and orientations...]

[FIGURE:ed6393711d44a414 | A 3D point cloud reconstruction of a building facade and surrounding structures, composed of numerous small colored dots. Several red wireframe pyramids represent the recovered camera positions and...]
motivation_md: Initial estimates of camera positions and 3D points often contain errors. Bundle adjustment jointly refines these parameters to ensure the 3D model is as consistent as possible with the observed 2D images.
recap_md: - Optimizes both camera poses and 3D point locations simultaneously.

title: Interest Points

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Image locations likely to be stable under different geometric transformations and illumination changes.
content: The goal of finding image features is to locate image locations that are likely to be stable under different sets of geometric transformations—such as translation, scaling, rotation, skew, and projective—and illumination changes. These stable regions are called interest points.
motivation_md: To match objects across different images, we need to identify specific, reliable landmarks that don't change their appearance significantly when the camera moves or lighting shifts.
recap_md: - Interest points are regions designed to be invariant to geometric and photometric changes.

title: Moving Element

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: An early term for interest points, referring to image points like corners or lines that could be tracked over time.
content: Initially, interest points were called moving elements. A moving element was defined as any image point that could be identified and followed over time, such as a corner, a line termination point, or a texture element.
motivation_md: This terminology reflects the early focus of computer vision on motion tracking and identifying discrete features that persist through a video sequence.
recap_md: - An early historical synonym for interest points.

title: Interest Point Detectors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Algorithms designed to identify distinct and stable image regions, such as corners or local extrema.
content: Interest point detectors are procedures used to identify distinct image regions. The Harris corner detector is a simple example, as corners are likely to be distinct from their surroundings and stable under geometric transformations. Other important detectors include local extrema of the Laplacian pyramid across space and scale, Harris-Laplace, and maximally stable regions.
motivation_md: Manual identification of features is impossible for large datasets. These algorithms automate the discovery of landmarks that are mathematically likely to be found again in other views.
recap_md: - Detectors like Harris and Laplacian-based methods find stable landmarks.

title: Learning-based Keypoint Detection

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: A formulation of keypoint detection as a learning problem where a classifier is trained to label image patches as keypoints.
content:
Detecting points of interest can be formulated as a learning problem. Given a set of manually annotated examples, a classifier can be trained to automatically label image patches as being centered on a keypoint or not. Examples include Quad-Networks and SuperPoint. Training often involves using synthetic images where keypoints are unambiguously defined or augmenting images with random geometric transformations to create ground truth for a robust classifier.

(see figure: Keypoint detector formulated as a patch classification problem. The classifier labels the patch as containing a keypoint in the center or not.)

(see figure: All the detected keypoints in three views from the sugar bowl. But the images look rather textureless; what is the keypoint detector finding interesting in these images?)

[FIGURE:20cc53bc83ed338f | A grid of 32 small, zoomed-in image patches showing surface irregularities on a sugar bowl. Each patch features a central green dot marking a detected keypoint, highlighting subtle textures and...]

[FIGURE:549e4ecf64ea35ae | A grid of 32 small, zoomed-in image patches showing architectural details like window corners, wall edges, and decorative elements. Each patch features a single bright green dot marking a specific...]

Detectors like SuperPoint can find image regions with strong spatial changes, such as window corners or subtle surface irregularities, which are likely to be found on images of the same object under different viewpoints.
motivation_md: Hand-engineered detectors may fail on complex or subtle textures. Learning-based approaches can discover more robust features by training on diverse data and geometric augmentations.
recap_md: - Uses classifiers to identify keypoints based on learned image patches.

title: Local Image Descriptors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Vectors extracted at keypoint locations that allow for matching the same point across different images.
content:
Once a keypoint detector finds stable regions, a descriptor is extracted at each location to allow finding the same keypoint across different images. Classical descriptors include SIFT, SURF, and ORB. These descriptors often represent the image patch as a vector (e.g., a vector of length 256). Effective descriptors find matches even under different viewpoints and illumination conditions.

(see figure: Examples of descriptors for three keypoints. For each keypoint, the figure shows the corresponding image patch and the computed descriptor. Each descriptor has a length of 256 values.)

[FIGURE:867b7d3bf524344c | A sequence of six photographs showing a small reddish-brown clay pot from slightly different angles. A red dot with a black outline marks a specific interest point on the side of the pot in each...]

[FIGURE:79782851e8d2b5ec | A series of seven photographs of a historic stone building taken from different viewpoints and distances. In the top row, a red dot marks a specific keypoint on a window frame in each wide-angle...]
motivation_md: Knowing where a point is (detection) isn't enough; we need a way to describe what it looks like (description) so we can recognize it in other images.
recap_md: - Descriptors turn image patches into numerical vectors for comparison.

title: Brute-force Matching

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: A matching strategy where features from one image are compared with features from every other image.
content: Brute-force matching involves matching features from one image with features from every other image in a dataset. This approach is feasible when there is a relatively small number of images. Modern implementations may use graph network-based matchers like SuperGlue to perform the actual matching of features.
motivation_md: When the relationship between images is unknown, comparing every image to every other image ensures that all possible connections and overlaps are discovered.
recap_md: - Exhaustively compares features across all image pairs.

title: Recognition-by-Components Theory

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Recognition-by-components theory proposes that humans represent and recognize objects by decomposing them into a small set of geometric parts identified by regions of sharp concavity.
content:
Recognition-by-components theory, proposed by Irving Biederman in 1987, suggests that humans represent and recognize objects from images by decomposing them into parts. This theory is motivated by the observation that even novel, made-up objects can be separated into parts by breaking the object in "regions of sharp concavity." These parts often resemble components of known objects, allowing observers to make sense of unfamiliar forms.

(see figure: What is this? This drawing from Biederman @Biederman1987, shows a novel object. After looking at this drawing we can conclude the following: (1) we have never seen this object before, (2) it can be...)
motivation_md: This theory explains how humans can recognize an infinite variety of objects, including those they have never seen before, by using a finite set of building blocks. It addresses the problem of how the brain represents complex 3D structures from 2D retinal images.
recap_md: - Objects are recognized by decomposing them into simpler geometric parts.

title: Geons

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Geons are a set of 36 basic geometric components, such as cylinders and cones, used as the building blocks for object representation.
content: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on) that he called Geons. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons are defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists of a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
motivation_md: Geons provide a universal "alphabet" for visual objects, allowing the brain to store complex shapes as simple arrangements of robust, easily identifiable geometric primitives.
recap_md: - Geons are 36 basic geometric shapes defined by non-accidental visual properties.

title: Compositionality in Vision

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Compositionality in vision is the idea that objects are formed by combining simpler, shared elements across different object classes.
content:
An important aspect of recognition-by-components theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. Compositionality in the visual world is not as strong as the one found in language, where a fixed set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances (e.g., legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical). Geons are effective for representing artificial objects like tables or phones, but they fail when applied to "stuff" like grass, clouds, and water, or highly textured objects like trees.

Decomposing an object into parts has been an important ingredient of many computer vision object recognition systems.
motivation_md: Compositionality allows for efficient representation; instead of learning every object as a unique whole, the system learns a set of parts and the rules for combining them.
recap_md: - Visual objects are composed of simpler elements shared across different categories.

title: Invariances in Human Vision

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Human object recognition is robust to changes in viewpoint, illumination, and occlusion, though it is not perfectly invariant to all transformations.
content: Object recognition in humans seems to be quite robust to changes in viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, deformations, and styles. However, perception is not completely invariant to those variables. One well-studied property of the human visual system is its invariance to image and 3D rotations. Studies have shown that objects are recognized faster when they appear in canonical poses. When observers learn to recognize a novel object from a single viewpoint, they can generalize to new viewpoints, but recognition time increases with the angle of rotation. When trained with multiple viewpoints, participants recognize all familiar orientations equally quickly. Cognitive science has formulated several hypotheses about these mechanisms, including geometry-based models and view-based templates.
motivation_md: Understanding how humans maintain a stable perception of an object despite changes in its appearance is crucial for developing robust computer vision systems.
recap_md: - Human vision is robust but not perfectly invariant to viewpoint and illumination changes.

title: Mental Rotation

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Mental rotation is the hypothesized process of cognitively rotating a 3D mental representation to compare it with another view.
content:
In a landmark study, Roger N. Shepard and Jaqueline Metzler showed participants pairs of drawings of three-dimensional objects. The pair could show the same object with a 3D rotation or a mirror image. Participants had to decide if the objects were identical. The results showed that reaction time was proportional to the rotation angle between the two views. This supported the idea that participants were performing a mental rotation in order to compare both views, though whether humans actually perform such rotations remains controversial.

(see figure: Two figures related by a 3D rotation. Modified from @Shepard1971aa)
motivation_md: The concept of mental rotation explains why it takes longer to recognize objects from unusual angles and suggests that our internal representations are 3D in nature.
recap_md: - Reaction time for object comparison is proportional to the angle of rotation.

title: Levels of Categorization

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Categorization occurs at three levels of abstraction: superordinate (general), basic (common), and subordinate (specific).
content: Rosch and her collaborators proposed that categorization occurs at three different levels of abstraction: superordinate level, basic-level, and subordinate level. Superordinate categories (e.g., Furniture, Tree) are very general and provide a high degree of abstraction. Basic level categories (e.g., Chair, Oak) correspond to the most common level of abstraction. The subordinate level (e.g., Kitchen chair, White oak) is the most specific. Two objects in the same superordinate category share fewer attributes than two objects in the same subordinate category. This discrete approach to categorization has been dominant in computer vision, as seen in datasets like ImageNet which use taxonomies like WordNet.
motivation_md: Organizing objects into levels of abstraction helps explain how humans balance the need for general categories with the need for specific distinctions.
recap_md: - Categorization is divided into superordinate, basic, and subordinate levels.

title: Prototypes

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category, used by humans to recognize categories by measuring similarity to these central examples.
content: As argued by E. Rosch, natural categories tend to be fuzzy at their boundaries and inconsistent in the status of their constituent members. Rosch suggested that categories can be represented by prototypes, which are the clearest members of a category. She hypothesized that humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity to these prototypes. By using prototypes, it is easier to work with continuous categories, as they are defined by "clear cases rather than its boundaries."
motivation_md: Prototype theory solves the problem of "fuzzy" boundaries in natural categories where objects don't always fit into strict, binary definitions.
recap_md: - Categories are defined by their clearest members (prototypes) rather than strict boundaries.

title: Affordances and Context

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

one_liner: Object recognition involves understanding an object's affordances, which can change based on the specific context or 'occasion meaning.'
content:
Object recognition is not as straightforward as simple categorization because objects can have different affordances depending on the context. In language, an expression has a "standing meaning" (conventional) and an "occasion meaning" (context-specific). The same applies to visual objects. For example, a cardboard box might be categorized as a container in one context, but act as a table in another context.

[FIGURE:cb0694462fa842df | A photograph of a plain cardboard box sitting on a blue carpeted floor in front of a whiteboard covered in complex mathematical equations and diagrams. The image illustrates the challenge of object...]

[FIGURE:e401ae49cd70f460 | A photograph of two yellow chairs facing each other in front of a whiteboard covered in complex mathematical and machine learning diagrams. Between the chairs is a cardboard box acting as a table...]
motivation_md: Pure categorization fails to capture how we actually use objects; understanding context-dependent affordances is necessary for functional vision.
recap_md: - Objects have different affordances and meanings depending on the context.

title: Prompting
one_liner: Prompting edits the input data to solve a new problem by prepending or mixing a prompt signal with the input string or data.
content:
Prompting edits the input data to solve a new problem. This technique is very popular in natural language processing (NLP), where text-to-text systems can have natural language prompts prepended to the string that is input to the model. For example, a general-purpose language model can be prompted with [`Make sure to answer in French`, `X`], for some arbitrary input `X`. Then the output will be a French translation of whatever the model would have responded to when queried with `X`.

Prompting is visualized in (see figure: Prompting: a prompt $\mathbf{p}$ is combined with the input $x$ to change the output $y$.), where $\oplus$ represents concatenation, addition, or potentially other ways of mixing prompts and input signals.
motivation_md: Prompting allows a single, fixed model to perform new tasks without modifying its internal weights. By simply changing the input context, users can guide the model's behavior toward specific outputs, making it a highly efficient method for task adaptation.
recap_md: - Prompting modifies the input data rather than the model parameters to achieve a new task.

title: Visual Prompting
one_liner: Visual prompting adapts vision systems by prepending or combining visual data, such as pixels or tokens, with the input image.
content: Visual prompting applies the concept of prompting to vision systems. First, prompting methods from NLP can be directly used for prompting the text inputs to vision-language models. Second, prompting can also be applied to visual inputs. Just like we can prepend a textual input with text, we can prepend a visual input with visual data, yielding a method called visual prompting. This can be done by concatenating pixels, tokens, or other visual formats to a vision model's inputs. This requires a model that takes variable-sized inputs; luckily this includes most neural net architectures, such as convolutional neural nets (CNNs), recurrent neural nets (RNNs), and transformers. Alternatively, we can combine the visual prompt with the input query in other ways, such as by addition.
motivation_md: Visual prompting extends the flexibility of text-based prompting to the visual domain, allowing vision models to adapt to new tasks by modifying the input image or feature space rather than retraining the network.
recap_md: - Visual prompting involves adding or concatenating visual data to an input to change a model's behavior.

title: Pixel Prompting
one_liner: Pixel prompting involves directly editing input pixels by adding an optimized image signal that changes the model's behavior for a specific task.
content:
One simple way of prompting a vision system is to directly edit the input pixels. As shown in (see figure: A prompt can be made out of pixels: a prompt image (which looks like a border of noise here) is added to the input image in order to change the model's behavior. Three different prompts are shown...), the prompt is an image $\mathbf{p}$ that is added to the input image $\mathbf{x}$. The prompt looks like noise, but it is actually an optimized signal that changes the model's behavior. For example, a prompt can be optimized to make a model predict a dog's species versus its expression.

Mathematically, this kind of prompting is very similar to adversarial noise. Because of this similarity, early papers sometimes referred to it as adversarial reprogramming. However, here we are not adding noise that hurts performance but instead adding noise that improves performance on a new task of interest. Given a set of $M$ training examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^M$, we learn a prompt via the following optimization problem: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{p}} \sum_{i=1}^M \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + \mathbf{p}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathcal{L}$ is the loss function for our problem.
motivation_md: Pixel prompting provides a way to repurpose a frozen vision model for new classification tasks by finding a specific 'noise' pattern that, when added to inputs, triggers the desired output behavior.
recap_md: - Pixel prompting adds an optimized image signal $\mathbf{p}$ to the input $\mathbf{x}$ to adapt a model to a new task.

title: Token Prompting
one_liner: Token prompting adds a learnable $d$-dimensional code vector to the input tokens of a vision transformer to modulate its behavior via the attention mechanism.
content:
Rather than adding a prompt in pixel space, it is also possible to add a prompt to an intermediate feature space. One way to do this is to use a token as the prompt for a vision transformer architecture. This new token is concatenated to the input of the transformer, which is a set of tokens representing image patches, as seen in (see figure: Prompting a transformer with a learnable input token. The prompt token is mixed into the network via attention; therefore \textit{no} parameters of the original network have to be updated (see...).

The token is a $d$-dimensional code vector optimized to change the behavior of the transformer to achieve a desired result, such as increased performance on a new dataset. The attention mechanism works as usual, except now all input tokens also attend to the prompt. The prompt thereby modulates the transformation applied to the input tokens on the first layer, which is how it affects the transformer's behavior.
motivation_md: Token prompting allows for efficient adaptation of Vision Transformers by inserting a small number of learnable parameters (the tokens) into the input sequence, avoiding the need to fine-tune the entire network.
recap_md: - A learnable prompt token is concatenated with image patch tokens in a transformer.

title: Promptable Models
one_liner: Promptable models are trained to adapt their behavior at test time based on user-provided instructions, such as text or visual strokes.
content: It is also possible to train a model to be promptable, so that at test time it adapts better to user prompts. An advantage of this approach is that we can train a model to understand human-interpretable prompts. For example, we could train the model so that its behavior can be adapted based on text instructions or based on user-drawn strokes. In fact, any system that interactively adapts to user inputs can be considered a promptable system. Many promptable systems use the tools of conditional generative modeling to train systems that are conditioned on user text instructions.
motivation_md: Training models to be explicitly promptable makes them more versatile and user-friendly, allowing non-experts to control complex model behavior through natural language or simple interactions.
recap_md: - Promptable models are designed to adapt to human-interpretable inputs like text or strokes.

title: Domain Adaptation
one_liner: Domain adaptation refers to methods for aligning training and test data distributions when they originate from different domains.
content: Often, the data we train on comes from a different distribution, or domain, than the data we will encounter at test time. For example, a recognition system trained on internet photos may be deployed on a self-driving car where the imagery looks very different. Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa. One option is to adapt the test data $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ to look more like the training data, so the model $f$ works well on both. Alternatively, we can adapt the training data to look like the test data before training $f$. In either case, the goal is to make the distribution of test and train data identical, so that a method working on one will work just as well on the other.
motivation_md: Machine learning models often fail when the environment they are deployed in (test domain) differs from their training environment (source domain). Domain adaptation solves this by bridging the gap between these distributions.
recap_md: - Domain adaptation aligns the distributions of training and test data to ensure model performance.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
one_liner: Unsupervised domain adaptation aligns training and test distributions using unlabeled test inputs when labels are only available for the training domain.
content: Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs $\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_i\}_{i=1}^N$ at testing time. This setting is referred to as unsupervised domain adaptation. In this case, we cannot use test labels but can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa). One way to do so is to use a generative adversarial network (GAN) that translates the data in one domain to look identically distributed as the data in the other domain. A simple version of this approach is illustrated in (see figure: Unpaired domain adaptation via adversarial translation.).
motivation_md: In many real-world scenarios, obtaining labels for a new target domain is expensive or impossible. Unsupervised domain adaptation allows us to leverage unlabeled data to bridge the domain gap.
recap_md: - Unsupervised domain adaptation uses unlabeled test data to align distributions with the training domain.

title: Generative Data
one_liner: Generative data consists of synthetic samples from a generative model that can be used to augment or improve training for transfer learning.
content:
Generative models produce synthetic data that looks like real data. Generative data (i.e., synthetic data sampled from a generative model) is not just a cheap copy of real data; it can be more data and better data. It can be more data because we can draw an unbounded number of samples that interpolate and remix the training data in novel ways. Generative models can also produce better data because the data comes coupled with a procedure that has structure that can be exploited to manipulate the data distribution.

Using large, pretrained generative models as data sources is a popular research area. In this usage, you are transferring knowledge about data to accelerate learning for a new problem. The function being learned can be trained from scratch, but it leverages the generative model's knowledge about what images look like and how the world works.
motivation_md: Generative data overcomes the limitations of finite datasets by providing an infinite source of diverse, structured samples, allowing models to learn from the underlying logic of a generative process.
recap_md: - Generative data provides an unbounded source of synthetic samples for training.

title: Smooth Prior
one_liner: A smooth prior penalizes variations in the optical flow to encourage spatial consistency.
content:
Another penalizes variations on the optical flow (**smooth prior**):
$$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = 
\sum_{x,y} \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}  \right)^2 +
\left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}  \right)^2 + \left( \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \right)^2$$
motivation_md: In optical flow estimation, the brightness constancy constraint alone is often insufficient to solve for motion at every pixel. A smooth prior provides a regularization term that assumes neighboring pixels likely move together, helping to resolve ambiguities in featureless regions.
recap_md: - Penalizes large spatial derivatives of the horizontal and vertical flow components.

title: Layer-Based Motion Estimation
one_liner: Layer-based motion estimation represents a scene as a collection of superimposed layers, each containing a rigid object with its own motion parameters.
content:
Until now we have not made use of any of the properties of the motion field derived from the 3D projection of the scene. One way of incorporating some of that knowledge is by making some strong assumptions about the moving scene. If the scene is composed of rigid objects, then we can assume that the motion field within each object will have a specific parametric form. In this case, instead of a moving camera we have rigid moving objects. The 2D motion field can then be represented as a collection of superimposed layers, each layer containing one object and occluding the layers below. Each layer will be described by a different set of motion parameters. 

The parametric motion field can be incorporated into the gradient-based approach. The motion parameters can then be estimated iteratively using an expectation-maximization (EM) style algorithm. At each step we estimate, for each pixel, which layer it is likely to belong to, and then estimate the motion parameters of each layer. The idea of using layers to represent motion was first introduced by Wang and Adelson in 1994.
motivation_md: Standard motion estimation often treats every pixel independently or assumes global smoothness. Layer-based estimation incorporates the physical reality that scenes are often composed of discrete rigid objects, allowing for more accurate modeling of complex motions and occlusions.
recap_md: - Models the scene as a stack of layers where each layer represents a rigid moving object.

title: Motivation for Learning-Based Motion Estimation
one_liner: Learning-based methods address modeling errors and exploit semantic cues that traditional first-principles motion models cannot easily capture.
content:
Model-based methods for motion estimation describe equations of motion from first principles, but learning-based methods are necessary because these models make assumptions that are not always true. Furthermore, other sources of information can reveal properties about motion that cannot be modeled but can be learned. 

Causes of modeling errors include failure of the brightness constancy assumption, the presence of occlusions, shadows, changes in illumination, and new structures appearing due to resolution changes or deformable surfaces. Many motion computations also involve approximations, such as using finite size discrete convolutions for derivatives. Additionally, other motion-relevant cues may be present, such as monocular depth cues or semantic knowledge of familiar objects (e.g., buildings are stationary, trees have many occlusions). These semantic properties can be implicitly exploited by a learning-based model.
motivation_md: Traditional models often fail in real-world conditions like lighting changes or occlusions. Learning-based approaches allow the system to adapt to these complexities and utilize high-level scene understanding that is difficult to encode manually.
recap_md: - Addresses failures in brightness constancy and modeling approximations.

title: Supervised Models for Optical Flow Estimation
one_liner: Supervised optical flow estimation uses datasets with ground truth motion to train models to predict flow directly from input frames.
content: The simplest formulation for learning to estimate optical flow is when we have available a dataset of image sequences with associated ground truth optical flow. Researchers have used synthetic data, lidar, or human annotations to build datasets with ground truth motion. While previous approaches used ground truth data primarily for evaluation, supervised models use it to train a model to predict motion directly from the input frames.
motivation_md: By using ground truth data, models can learn the complex mapping from pixel intensity changes to actual motion vectors, bypassing the need for hand-crafted heuristics or manual parameter tuning.
recap_md: - Utilizes datasets with ground truth motion from synthetic sources, lidar, or human labels.

title: Direct Approach for Optical Flow
one_liner: The direct approach uses neural networks to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames without explicit architectural priors.
content:
As in the case of stereo, we can train a function to estimate optical flow from two frames: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$ One of the first approaches to use this formulation with neural networks was FlowNet. The architecture is simple.

(see figure: In FlowNet the direct approach estimates optical flow directly from a pair of frames.)

The direct approach learns to estimate optical flow directly from a pair of frames. This architecture makes no assumptions about which architectural priors are needed to compute optical flow from images. The architecture is trained end-to-end using ground truth optical flow.
motivation_md: A direct end-to-end approach allows a neural network to discover the most relevant features and transformations for motion estimation automatically, rather than relying on human-designed stages like cost volumes or pyramids.
recap_md: - Estimates flow vectors directly from two input frames using an end-to-end trained function.

title: Modular Architecture for Optical Flow
one_liner: Modular architectures for optical flow follow traditional steps like feature extraction and cost volume aggregation within a trainable end-to-end framework.
content:
Another common approach is to define an architecture that follows the same steps as traditional approaches:

- Extract features from each image using a pair of networks with shared weights, often via a feature pyramid.
- Form a 3D cost volume indicating the local visual evidence of a match between the two images for each possible pixel position, generally referenced to the first frame.
- Train and apply a CNN to aggregate the costs over the cost volume to estimate a single best optical flow for each pixel position.
- Use a coarse-to-fine estimation procedure where optical flow estimated at a coarse scale is used to warp features at a finer scale to compute a refined cost volume.

(see figure: Motion estimation. (1) Extract features from each image; (2) compute a 3D cost volume; and (3) aggregate the cost volume in order to estimate the best optical flow for each pixel.)

Other variations incorporate concepts such as coarse-to-fine refinement, matching, and smoothing. The main difference from traditional matching or gradient-based methods is that instead of using predefined functions, these modular architectures are trained end-to-end to minimize optical flow error relative to ground truth data.
motivation_md: By mimicking traditional computer vision pipelines, modular architectures can leverage proven geometric principles (like cost volumes and pyramids) while still benefiting from the optimization power of deep learning.
recap_md: - Combines traditional vision steps like feature pyramids and cost volumes with end-to-end training.

title: Endpoint Error
one_liner: The endpoint error is the average distance between the estimated optical flow vector and the ground-truth vector across all pixels.
content:
In supervised optical flow estimation, the most common loss is the **endpoint error**, which is the average, over the whole image, of the distance between the estimated optical flow vector, $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and the ground-truth vector, $(u,v)$:
$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \right) =
\sum_{n,m} (\hat{u}[n,m] - u[n,m])^2 + (\hat{v}[n,m] - v[n,m])^2$$
The sum is over all the pixels in the image. Each pixel has an estimated optical flow $(\hat{u}[n,m],\hat{v}[n,m])$.

[FIGURE:94e55f574651d9ae | A vector diagram illustrating the endpoint error in optical flow estimation. Two vectors originate from the same point: a longer vector labeled $(u,v)$ representing the ground truth, and a shorter...]
motivation_md: To train supervised models, a clear metric is needed to quantify the difference between predicted motion and actual motion. Endpoint error provides a direct Euclidean measure of this discrepancy.
recap_md: - Measures the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth flow vectors.

title: Handling Occlusions in Optical Flow
one_liner: Handling occlusions involves detecting pixels that are hidden or revealed during motion alongside estimating the optical flow.
content: One of the challenges for estimating optical flow is that, as objects move, they will occlude some pixels from the background and reveal new ones. Therefore, together with the estimated flow it is also convenient to detect occluded pixels. If we have ground truth data, we can train a function to estimate optical flow and the occlusion map from two frames: $$\left[ \hat{\mathbf{u}}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \hat{\mathbf{o}} \right] = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell_1, \boldsymbol\ell_2 \right)$$
motivation_md: Standard optical flow assumes every pixel in the first frame has a corresponding pixel in the second. Detecting occlusions is necessary to prevent the model from trying to find matches for pixels that are no longer visible.
recap_md: - Estimates an occlusion map $\hat{\mathbf{o}}$ in addition to the flow vectors.

title: Adapting Generative Data via Latent Variables
one_liner: Adapt generative training data by editing the latent variables of a pretrained model to produce specific desired image features.
content: Latent variables provide a structure for adapting generative data. Suppose a generative model produces outdoor images, but the training set lacks specific combinations, such as cows on a beach. If the model is pretrained to produce a wide variety of images, it may have the capacity to generate these specific scenes with minor adjustments. By editing the latent variables of the model, you can force it to produce the required images, effectively adapting the training data for a specific downstream task like object classification.
motivation_md: Standard generative datasets may lack specific edge cases or local variations needed for a particular task. Instead of collecting new data, we can leverage the internal representations of a pretrained generative model to synthesize the missing data.
recap_md: [FIGURE:16-hex-asset-id | ...]

title: Learned Loss

position.section_title: Other Kinds of Knowledge that Can Be Transferred

one_liner: A learned loss is a loss function whose parameters are pretrained rather than manually defined.
content: A **learned loss** refers to a loss function where the line defining the loss is itself pretrained. Instead of using a fixed mathematical objective, the parameters governing the loss calculation are learned from data.
motivation_md: Manually designing loss functions that capture complex human preferences or structural nuances is difficult; learning the loss function allows the model to optimize for more sophisticated objectives.
recap_md: - A learned loss is a pretrained component of the optimization system.

title: Learned Optimizer

position.section_title: A Combinatorial Catalog of Transfer Learning Methods

one_liner: A learned optimizer is an optimization algorithm that is itself pretrained to improve the training of other models.
content: A **learned optimizer** is a pretrained component that replaces standard optimization algorithms like SGD. In this framework, the logic for updating model parameters is learned rather than hard-coded.
motivation_md: Standard optimizers like SGD or Adam are general-purpose; a learned optimizer can discover update rules that are more efficient for specific architectures or data distributions.
recap_md: - The optimizer itself is a pretrained model that guides adaptation.

title: Transfer Learning as Empirical Risk Minimization

position.section_title: A Combinatorial Catalog of Transfer Learning Methods

one_liner: Transfer learning methods can be categorized as empirical risk minimization (ERM) with different components optimized during pretraining or adaptation.
content:
Many transfer learning methods follow a format of pretraining one component and then adapting it or other components. These methods can be framed as empirical risk minimization (ERM) as shown in the following table:

| Method | Learning | Inference |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Generative data | $\arg\min_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\theta}(x)$ |
| Distillation | $\arg\min_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), t(x))]$ | $f_{\theta}(x)$ |
| Prompting | $\arg\min_{\epsilon} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x \oplus \epsilon), y)]$ | $f_{\theta}(x \oplus \epsilon)$ |
| Finetuning | $\arg\min_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\theta}(x)$ |
| Probes / heads | $\arg\min_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(h_{\phi}(f_{\theta}(x)), y)]$ | $h_{\phi}(f_{\theta}(x))$ |
| Learned loss | $\arg\min_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\theta}(x)$ |
| Learned optimizer | $\arg\min_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\theta}(x)$ |

Note: The $\oplus$ symbol indicates concatenation or addition. Domain adaptation is omitted as it does not map neatly to ERM.
motivation_md: Providing a unified mathematical framework (ERM) allows for a systematic comparison of seemingly disparate transfer learning techniques based on which parts of the objective are fixed or learned.
recap_md: - Transfer learning involves pretraining and then adapting specific system components.

title: In-Context Learning

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

one_liner: In-context learning is a form of adaptation where a sequence model updates its behavior based on previously seen items in a sequence.
content: In-context learning is a type of adaptation emergent in sequence modeling. Models like RNNs, CNNs, and transformers update their behavior based on items already processed in a sequence. In an RNN, the hidden state changes as it processes data, which in turn changes the mapping from input to output. If an RNN is fed a sequence of training examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{y}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}\}$, its hidden state effectively learns a function $f$. When a new query $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}$ is provided, the RNN produces an output $\mathbf{y}^{(n+1)}$ based on this learned state. In this way, the sequence model acts as a learning algorithm where the "learning" happens within the context of the input sequence.
motivation_md: Traditional learning requires gradient updates to weights; in-context learning allows a model to adapt to new tasks or data distributions instantly during a single forward pass.
recap_md: - Sequence models adapt their behavior through internal state updates as they process data.

title: Introduction to Image Representations
one_liner: Images are typically represented as ordered arrays of pixel values, but alternative representations can make geometric information more explicit.
content: Images have traditionally been represented as ordered arrays of pixel values, where each pixel is described by a grayscale value or three color arrays. This chapter explores alternative ways to represent images and geometry beyond this standard approach.
motivation_md: While ordered arrays are convenient for signal processing and convolutions, they may not be the most efficient way to handle geometric transformations or sparse data.
recap_md: - Standard image representation uses ordered arrays of pixel intensities.

title: Ordered Array Image Representation
one_liner: The ordered array representation treats an image as a regular spatial grid of sampled pixel intensities.
content:
The **ordered array** representation defines an image as:
$$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[
\begin{matrix}
\ell[1,1] & \dots & \\
\vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\
 & \dots  & \ell[N,M] \\
\end{matrix}
\right]$$
Each value in the array is a sample on a regular spatial grid, where $s$ represents the pixel intensity at a specific location. This is the standard representation used in signal processing, making it straightforward to describe operations like convolution.
motivation_md: This representation is the natural output of digital sensors and aligns perfectly with the mathematical definition of discrete convolution.
recap_md: - Images are stored as matrices where each entry corresponds to a grid location.

title: Set of Pixels Image Representation
one_liner: The set of pixels representation encodes an image as a collection of points, explicitly listing the color and location of each pixel.
content:
An image can be represented as a **set of pixels**:
$$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$
where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity or color recorded at the specific spatial location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry of the image explicit. It simplifies certain operations, such as geometric transformations; for example, translating an image to the right by one pixel is achieved by creating a new set $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$. This approach is very common in geometry-based computer vision.
motivation_md: Representing images as sets allows for easier manipulation of spatial coordinates, which is useful for tasks like rotation, translation, and 3D reconstruction.
recap_md: - Images are collections of points with explicit $(x, y)$ coordinates.

title: Evolution of CNN Stereo Methods
one_liner: CNN-based stereo methods have evolved from surpassing handcrafted features to addressing generalization issues and optimizing 3D cost volume processing through iterative algorithms.
content: The performance of methods following the standard stereo block diagram surpassed that of methods with handcrafted features. More recent work has addressed the problem of poor generalization to out-of-training-domain test examples. Because training and computing the 3D neural network to process the cost volume can be expensive in time and memory, recent work has obtained both speed and performance improvement through developing an iterative algorithm to avoid 3D filtering.
motivation_md: Early CNN stereo methods struggled with generalization and high computational costs; this evolution tracks the shift toward more robust and efficient architectures like iterative algorithms.
recap_md:
- CNN-based stereo methods outperformed traditional handcrafted feature approaches.
 - Modern research focuses on improving generalization to unseen domains.
 - Iterative algorithms are used to reduce the high memory and time costs of 3D cost volume filtering.

title: Middlebury Stereo Evaluation
one_liner: The Middlebury stereo web page provides a comprehensive comparison of stereo algorithms on a common dataset to track the field's advancement.
content: The Middlebury stereo web page provides a comprehensive comparison of many stereo algorithms, compared on a common dataset, with pointers to algorithm descriptions and code. One can use the web page to evaluate the improvement of stereo reconstruction algorithms over time. The advancement of the field over time is very impressive.
motivation_md: Standardized benchmarks are necessary to objectively measure and compare the performance of different stereo reconstruction algorithms over time.
recap_md:
- Middlebury provides a common dataset and leaderboard for stereo algorithm comparison.
 - It serves as a historical record of the rapid advancement in stereo reconstruction accuracy.

title: Current Status of Stereo Vision
one_liner: Accurate depth estimation from stereo pairs remains an unsolved problem, often requiring multiview geometry for reliable results.
content: Accurate depth estimation from stereo pairs remains an unsolved problem. The results are still not reliable. In order to get accurate depth estimates, most methods require many images and the use of multiview geometry methods to reconstruct the 3D scene. Stereo matching is often also formulated as a problem of estimating the image motion between two views captured at different locations. For an in-depth study of the geometry of stereo pairs, specialized literature such as Hartley and Zisserman (2004) or Faugeras (1993) should be consulted.
motivation_md: Understanding the current limitations of stereo vision explains why researchers often turn to multiview geometry or motion estimation for more robust 3D reconstruction.
recap_md:
- Two-view stereo depth estimation is often unreliable on its own.
 - High accuracy typically requires multiple images and multiview geometry techniques.
 - Stereo matching can be framed as a specific case of motion estimation.

title: Introduction to Homographies
one_liner: A homography is a general geometric transformation that maps pixels between images when the scene is planar or the cameras are related by pure rotation.
content:
In general, there is not a simple geometric transformation that maps pixels from one image into the pixels of another image across different viewpoints; finding that mapping usually requires knowing the 3D location of each point and the relative camera motion. However, there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple transformation that allows warping one image into another without knowing the 3D scene structure. This occurs when the scene is planar or when the two cameras are related just by a rotation. In those two cases, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by a homography.

[FIGURE:d89ebe83f072de38 | A photograph of a row of academic books on a shelf, focusing on titles related to computer vision and perception. The books are arranged vertically, showing their spines with titles such as 'The...]

[FIGURE:4c2d17b07db71aed | A photograph of a bookshelf containing several academic books related to computer vision and perception. Visible titles include 'Perception as Bayesian Inference', 'The Retina', 'Foundations of...]

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography.
motivation_md: Homographies allow for image warping and alignment without needing complex 3D reconstruction, provided specific geometric conditions (planarity or pure rotation) are met.
recap_md:
- Homographies map pixels between views without requiring 3D scene structure knowledge.
 - They apply specifically to planar scenes or cameras related by pure rotation.
 - This transformation generalizes simpler 2D transforms like translation and rotation.

title: Applications of Homographies
one_liner: Homographies are used for perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, and creating bird's-eye views.
content: Homographies can be used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, creating bird's-eye views, correcting keystone distortions for projected images, and many others.
motivation_md: Homographies provide the mathematical basis for common image processing tasks like creating panoramas or fixing the perspective of a photographed document.
recap_md:
- Key applications include image stitching (panoramas) and perspective correction.
 - They are essential for augmented reality and correcting keystone distortions in projections.

title: Definition of Homography
one_liner: A homography is a projective transformation that preserves straight lines and can be represented by a $3 \times 3$ matrix multiplication in homogeneous coordinates.
content:
A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. The homography is a function $h$ that maps points into points, $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$, with the property that if points $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are colinear, then the transformed points $h(\mathbf{p}_1)$, $h(\mathbf{p}_2)$, and $h(\mathbf{p}_3)$ are also colinear. Such a function, $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$, can be written in homogeneous coordinates as a product with a matrix:

$$\begin{bmatrix}    x' \\    y' \\    w'     \end{bmatrix}    =    \begin{bmatrix}    a & b & c \\    d & e & f \\    g & h & i    \end{bmatrix}    \begin{bmatrix}    x \\    y \\    1     \end{bmatrix}$$

This can be written in the short form:
$$\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{p}'$ correspond to 2D points in homogeneous coordinates, and $\mathbf{H}$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
motivation_md: Defining homographies as matrix operations in homogeneous coordinates allows for efficient computation of complex projective transformations using linear algebra.
recap_md:
- A homography is a projective transformation that maps points while preserving collinearity.
 - It is represented by a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$ acting on homogeneous coordinates.
 - The fundamental relationship is expressed as $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$.

title: Proof of Collinearity Preservation
one_liner: Collinearity is preserved under homography because the transformation of a line equation in homogeneous coordinates results in another valid line equation.
content: To prove that colinear points remain colinear after the homography we can use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. From the homography equation $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, we have that $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$. Replacing this into the equation of the line gives $(\mathbf{H} ^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$, which corresponds to the equation of the line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$.
motivation_md: Proving collinearity preservation confirms that homographies belong to the class of projective transformations, ensuring that straight edges in the world remain straight in the warped image.
recap_md:
- The proof uses the homogeneous line equation $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$.
 - Substituting $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$ shows the new points satisfy a new line equation $(\mathbf{H}^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$.

title: Properties of Homographies
one_liner: In a general homography, collinearity is preserved, but angles and lengths are not.
content: In a general homography, angles and lengths are not preserved. Therefore, parallel lines might not remain parallel, and lines of identical length might have different lengths after a homography. (see figure: Homography. Colinear points remain colinear after transformation. Angles between lines are not preserved.) shows how a planar grid gets transformed after applying a homography.
motivation_md: Understanding what a homography does and does not preserve is crucial for predicting how shapes will distort during image warping or perspective correction.
recap_md:
- Homographies preserve collinearity (straight lines stay straight).
 - Angles, lengths, and parallelism are generally not preserved.
 - A planar grid transformed by a homography will typically appear distorted in perspective.

title: Biological Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Biological motion describes the typical motion patterns of biological organisms.
content: Swedish psychologist Gunnar Johansson, while working on Gestalt laws of motion perception, introduced the term biological motion to describe the typical motion of biological organisms.
motivation_md: The concept was introduced to categorize and study the specific patterns of movement unique to living beings, distinguishing them from the motion of inanimate objects within the study of visual perception.
recap_md:
- Biological motion refers to the specific movement patterns characteristic of living organisms.
- The term was coined by Swedish psychologist Gunnar Johansson.

title: Rigidity Assumption

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: The rigidity assumption posits that 2D transformations with a unique rigid body interpretation should be interpreted as a rigid body moving in space.
content: The rigidity assumption was introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979 as a solution to the problem of structure from motion (SFM). Ullman stated: "Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion."
motivation_md: This assumption provides a necessary constraint for solving the structure from motion problem, allowing the recovery of 3D geometry from 2D sequences by assuming the observed object does not deform.
recap_md:
- Proposed by Shimon Ullman in 1979 to solve the structure from motion problem.
- Assumes that 2D point transformations represent the motion of a rigid 3D body if such an interpretation is unique.

title: Sparse SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Sparse SFM involves recovering structure from the temporal trajectories of a sparse set of points.
content: Sparse SFM (Structure from Motion) is defined by the use of temporal trajectories of a sparse set of points to reconstruct 3D scenes.
motivation_md: Sparse SFM is computationally more efficient than dense methods because it only tracks a limited number of distinct keypoints, making it suitable for real-time applications and large-scale reconstructions.
recap_md:
- Focuses on a sparse set of points rather than every pixel.
- Uses temporal trajectories of these points to determine structure.

title: Tomasi and Kanade SFM Algorithm

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: The Tomasi and Kanade algorithm is an early SFM technique for rigid bodies that uses orthographic projection and keypoint tracking.
content: One of the first algorithms for structure from motion for rigid bodies was introduced by Tomasi and Kanade. For simplicity, their approach assumed parallel projection (orthographic camera) instead of perspective projection. The algorithm took as input a video sequence captured by a moving camera looking at a static scene. The video was first processed by extracting keypoints and tracking them over time. The input to the reconstruction algorithm was the keypoint trajectories and the output was the 3D locations of those points with respect to a reference world-coordinate system, usually defined by the first frame in the video. This model was later extended by Sturm and Triggs to handle perspective projection.
motivation_md: This algorithm established a foundational framework for reconstructing 3D geometry from 2D video by simplifying the camera model to orthographic projection, making the initial mathematical problem more tractable.
recap_md:
- Uses orthographic (parallel) projection for simplicity.
- Reconstructs 3D locations from keypoint trajectories tracked over a video sequence.
- Output is typically relative to the coordinate system of the first video frame.

title: Sparse SFM Problem

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: The sparse SFM problem aims to recover 3D scene structure and camera locations from a set of images with overlapping content.
content:
Given a set of $M$ images with overlapping content, the goal of sparse SFM is to recover the 3D structure of the scene and the location of the camera for each image. This technique can be applied to diverse scenarios, such as an object captured from multiple angles by a moving camera or images taken within a large environment like a plaza.

motivation_md: The sparse SFM problem addresses the need to reconstruct 3D environments and camera trajectories from 2D image collections, which is essential for applications in mapping, robotics, and augmented reality.
recap_md:
- Goal: Recover 3D scene structure and camera locations from multiple images.
- Input: A set of $M$ images with overlapping content.
- Applicability: Works for both small objects and large-scale environments.

title: SFM Problem Formulation

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: The SFM problem involves recovering 3D points and camera parameters from corresponding 2D image points across multiple views.
content: In the sparse SFM problem, we consider $N$ distinct points $\mathbf{P}_i$ in a scene that are matched across $M$ different views. The projection of point $\mathbf{P}_i$ as seen by camera $j$ is denoted by $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$. Each view is associated with camera parameters: intrinsic parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ and extrinsic parameters (rotation ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$ and translation ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$). If all images are captured by the same camera, the intrinsic matrices ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ remain constant, though this assumption is not strictly necessary. The goal is to use the set of corresponding 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$ to recover the 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and the camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$, and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ for each camera $j$.
motivation_md: Formalizing SFM as a mathematical problem allows for the development of algorithms that can systematically solve for unknown 3D geometry and camera poses using observable 2D data.
recap_md:
- $N$ 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ are projected as 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$ across $M$ views.
- Goal: Recover 3D coordinates, intrinsic parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, and extrinsic parameters ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}, {\mathbf T}^{(j)}$.
- Capital letters denote 3D world coordinates; lowercase letters denote image coordinates.

title: SFM Minimal Number of Observations

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: A solution to the SFM problem exists when the number of observations $2NM$ is greater than or equal to the total unknowns $3N + 6(M-1)-1$.
content: To determine the minimal number of observations required for SFM, we count the unknowns for calibrated cameras where intrinsic parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ are known. There are $3N$ unknowns for the $N$ 3D points. Assuming the first camera is at the origin, we solve for $M-1$ cameras. Rotations contribute $3(M-1)$ unknowns, and translations (up to a scale factor) contribute $3(M-1)-1$ unknowns, totaling $3N + 6(M-1)-1$ unknowns. With $2NM$ observations from image coordinates, a solution is possible when: $$2NM \geq 3N + 6(M-1)-1$$ If $M=1$, the problem cannot be solved. Uncalibrated cameras add approximately $3M$ additional unknowns.
motivation_md: Understanding the minimal requirements for observations ensures that a given set of images contains enough information to mathematically permit a unique reconstruction of the 3D scene.
recap_md:
- Total unknowns for calibrated cameras: $3N + 6(M-1)-1$.
- Total observations: $2NM$ (assuming all points visible in all images).
- SFM is unsolvable with only a single camera view ($M=1$).

title: Scale Drift

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Scale drift is the accumulation of slight numerical errors in scale factors when triangulating new frames in a sequence.
content: Scale drift occurs when points are not visible in every view, requiring new images to be triangulated with respect to their closest neighbor rather than a common reference.
