[FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736 | A diagram illustrating the CLIP training process. It shows input data as a set of pairs {\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\ell}^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N entering a box labeled 'CLIP'. Inside the box, the...]

In this formulation, $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, and $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$ (the surface of a hypersphere). The system uses an image encoder $f_{\ell}$ and a text encoder $f_t$. Image inputs are $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, while text inputs are $d_t$ dimensional tokens. The objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss. Both $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ output unit vectors via $L_2$-normalization, ensuring the denominator of the loss cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
motivation_md: CLIP was designed to learn visual concepts from natural language supervision at scale, enabling zero-shot transfer to various downstream tasks without requiring task-specific labeled data.
recap_md:
- Uses a symmetric InfoNCE loss to align image and text embeddings.
- Employs separate encoders for images ($f_\ell$) and text ($f_t$).
- Normalizes outputs to unit vectors on a hypersphere to stabilize contrastive learning.

title: CLIP Training Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

one_liner: CLIP training involves maximizing the dot product between embeddings of matching image-text pairs while minimizing it for mismatched pairs in a batch.
content:
The CLIP training procedure begins by sampling a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. These are processed using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$ to produce text embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t\}_{i=1}^N$ and image embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\}_{i=1}^N$. 

To compute the loss, the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ is calculated for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Terms where $i = j$ are positive pairs, and the objective seeks to maximize these dot products. Terms where $i \neq j$ are negative pairs, and the objective seeks to minimize these dot products.

(see figure: CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative...)
motivation_md: By training on a large batch of pairs simultaneously, the model learns to distinguish the correct description of an image from many incorrect alternatives, forcing the encoders to capture meaningful semantic features.
recap_md:
- Samples a batch of $N$ image-caption pairs for simultaneous processing.
- Maximizes the dot product for positive pairs ($i=j$) and minimizes it for negative pairs ($i \neq j$).
- Uses dual encoders to map different modalities into a comparable embedding format.

title: CLIP Embedding Space

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

one_liner: The CLIP embedding space is a shared vector space where the angle between text and image embeddings is small if the text accurately describes the image.
content: After training, the text encoder $f_t$ and image encoder $f_\ell$ map their respective inputs to the same embedding space. In this space, the angle between a text embedding and an image embedding will be small if the text matches the image. Because the encoders output unit vectors, the dot product between them is proportional to the angle between the vectors.
motivation_md: A shared embedding space allows for direct comparison between different modalities, enabling tasks like cross-modal retrieval and zero-shot classification.
recap_md:
- Maps images and text into a single, unified vector space.
- Proximity in the space (small angle/high dot product) indicates a semantic match.
- Uses unit vectors so that dot products reflect angular similarity.

title: CLIP Mapping Visualization

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

one_liner: Visualizing CLIP mappings via t-SNE reveals how image and text encoders group features like color and shape at different layers.
content:
CLIP mappings can be visualized by reducing the dimensionality of encoder outputs using t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE). For the image encoder, early layers tend to group images by color, while later layers group them by shape. Conversely, for the text encoder, color and shape words are equally accessible, as they are both superficial features in text-space compared to the processing required to extract shape from pixels.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the...)
motivation_md: Visualization helps researchers understand the internal representations of the model, revealing what features (like color or shape) the model prioritizes at different stages of processing.
recap_md:
- Uses t-SNE to project high-dimensional embeddings into a 2D space for analysis.
- Shows that image encoders process low-level features (color) before high-level features (shape).
- Highlights differences in how text and image modalities represent the same concepts.

title: CLIP Shared Embedding Visualization

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

one_liner: Shared embedding visualization shows normalized image and text embeddings aligned on a hypersphere, with matching pairs located near each other.
content:
The final stage of the CLIP process involves normalizing encoder outputs and computing the alignment between image and text embeddings. After normalization, all embeddings lie on the surface of a hypersphere. Visualization of this joint space (often using kernel PCA with a cosine kernel) shows that text descriptions are embedded near the image embeddings that match them.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning joint embedding)

Note that 2D visualizations are limited when projecting 768-dimensional embeddings. In these visualizations, the first principal component is sometimes removed as it may code for a global offset between the two modalities.
motivation_md: Visualizing the joint embedding space confirms that the contrastive training successfully aligned the two different modalities into a single semantic map.
recap_md:
- Embeddings are normalized to lie on the surface of a hypersphere.
- Matching text and image pairs cluster together in the shared space.
- Kernel PCA is used to project high-dimensional alignments into interpretable 2D plots.

title: Instance Segmentation
one_liner: Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output localized objects represented as pixel-level masks for each individual instance.
content:
Instance segmentation combines the ideas of object detection and semantic segmentation. The goal is to output a set of localized objects, but rather than representing them as bounding boxes, they are represented as pixel-level masks.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)

The difference from semantic segmentation is that if there are $K$ objects of the same type, instance segmentation outputs $K$ masks. Conversely, semantic segmentation cannot tell how many objects of the same type there are, nor can it delineate between two overlapping objects of the same type; it only provides an aggregate region of pixels for that object type.

One approach to instance segmentation follows the object localization pipeline: after bounding boxes are proposed and labeled, the cropped image within each box is fed to a binary semantic segmentation function. This function predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$, whether it belongs to the object or not, resulting in an instance mask for each box. The architecture is illustrated in @fig-instance_segmentation_architecture.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)

In this architecture, $f_0$ is a low-cost detector that proposes regions likely to contain instances. The function $f_1$ performs classification and segmentation of the instance:
$$\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i,   \hat{\mathbf{s}}_i \right]= f_j(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)$$
where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ is the binary label confidence, and $\hat{s}_i \left[ n,m \right]$ is the instance segmentation mask.
motivation_md: Standard semantic segmentation identifies which pixels belong to a class (e.g., "car") but cannot distinguish between different individuals of that class. Instance segmentation solves this by uniquely identifying and masking every separate object instance, which is critical for tasks like autonomous driving or counting individual items in a scene.
recap_md: - Combines object detection (localization) with semantic segmentation (pixel-level masking).

title: Instance Segmentation Loss
one_liner: The instance segmentation loss is a weighted sum of classification, localization, and segmentation losses.
content:
The loss for instance segmentation can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses:
$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$

The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not. If the object is present (indicated by the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$), the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$ inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation $\mathbf{s}_i$. The parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ control the weight each loss has on the final total loss.
motivation_md: To train a model that simultaneously identifies, locates, and masks objects, a multi-task loss function is required. This formulation ensures the network optimizes for all three objectives—class accuracy, box precision, and mask fidelity—simultaneously.
recap_md: - Combines classification, bounding box localization, and pixel-wise segmentation losses.

title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
one_liner: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual information with natural language processing techniques, typically using transformers to process both modalities.
content: Vision-language models (VLMs) require an understanding of language models and natural language processing (NLP). One common way to model language in these systems follows the same format as modern computer vision systems: tokenize the text, then process it with a transformer. This approach applies the transformer architecture, which is also used for images, to text data to enable joint understanding of visual and linguistic information.
motivation_md: Many real-world tasks require understanding both images and text simultaneously, such as captioning images, answering questions about a photo, or searching for images using natural language descriptions.
recap_md: - Integrate computer vision and natural language processing (NLP).

title: Language Models
one_liner: Language models process text by tokenizing it and applying architectures like transformers to model linguistic patterns.
content: Language models are a central part of natural language processing (NLP). One modern approach to modeling language follows the same format as computer vision systems: the text is tokenized and then processed with a transformer. This allows the system to apply the same transformer-based mechanisms used for images to the domain of text.
motivation_md: Language models provide the mathematical framework for machines to represent, understand, and generate human language, serving as the foundation for tasks like translation, summarization, and multimodal vision-language tasks.
recap_md: - Involves tokenizing text and processing it through a transformer architecture.

title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
one_liner: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of study dedicated to modeling and understanding human language.
content: Natural language processing (NLP) is a field that studies how to model language.
motivation_md: NLP exists to bridge the gap between human communication and computer understanding, enabling machines to process, interpret, and generate text or speech in a way that is useful for humans.
recap_md: - The field of study focused on modeling and processing human language.

title: Word-level Encoding
one_liner: Word-level encoding maps each word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code.
content: Word-level encoding is a scheme for representing text as numbers by mapping each word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. For a vocabulary of $K$ different words, this method requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes.
motivation_md: Computers cannot process raw text; they require numerical input. Word-level encoding provides a straightforward way to convert discrete words into vectors that a neural network can process.
recap_md: - Maps each unique word to a specific one-hot vector.

title: Character-level Encoding
one_liner: Character-level encoding assigns a one-hot code to each individual character in a vocabulary rather than to whole words.
content: Character-level encoding is a strategy where a one-hot code is assigned to each character in a vocabulary (such as alphanumeric characters and punctuation) rather than to each unique word. While this requires only a few dozen codes, the disadvantage is that representing a single word requires a sequence of one-hots, which the model must then learn to process.
motivation_md: Word-level encodings struggle with large vocabularies and out-of-vocabulary words. Character-level encoding solves this by using a very small, fixed set of tokens that can construct any possible word, though it increases the sequence length the model must handle.
recap_md: - Assigns one-hot codes to individual characters and punctuation marks.

title: Byte-pair Encoding
one_liner: Byte-pair encoding is a subword tokenization method that assigns codes to common small chunks of text or substrings.
content: Byte-pair encoding achieves a middle ground between word-level and character-level encoding by assigning a one-hot code to small chunks of text. These chunks are common substrings found in text, such as "th" or "ing." This strategy is popular in modern language models like the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) series and the Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) model.
motivation_md: This method balances vocabulary size and sequence length. It handles rare words by breaking them into common subword components, making it more efficient than character-level encoding and more flexible than word-level encoding.
recap_md: - Encodes common substrings or text chunks rather than full words or single characters.

title: Self-contained Captions
one_liner: Figure captions should be self-contained so that readers can understand the main takeaway without reading the full paper.
content: Because you can assume that many of the readers of your figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, to help both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader. (see figure: Figure and caption from \cite{FreemanShapetime}. The caption should be understandable by itself, and should point to what the reader should take away from the figure.)
motivation_md: Readers often skim figures and captions before or instead of reading the entire text; self-contained captions ensure the core message is communicated even to these skimmers.
recap_md: [ "- Captions should be understandable on their own without requiring the reader to consult the main text.", "- Effective captions explicitly state what the reader is supposed to notice or take away from the figure." ]

title: Writing with Equations
one_liner: Sentences containing equations should flow smoothly even if the formulas are replaced by simple placeholder sounds.
content: Equations interposed with text can pose a challenge to the reader. Knuth suggests that because many readers will skim over formulas on their first reading, your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by 'blah' or some other grunting noise. Mermin adds that when referring to an equation, you should identify it by a phrase as well as a number. For example, instead of saying 'inserting (2.47) and (3.51) into (5.13)', it is better to say 'inserting the form (2.47) of the electric field $E$ and the Lindhard form (3.51) of the dielectric function $\epsilon$ into the constitutive equation (5.13)'.
motivation_md: Readers often skim formulas; writing sentences that remain grammatically and logically coherent without the math helps maintain the narrative flow and accessibility of the paper.
recap_md: [ "- Ensure sentences remain readable and grammatically sound even if complex formulas are ignored.", "- Identify equations using both a reference number and a descriptive phrase to help the reader track the logic." ]

title: Tone
one_liner: A generous and honest tone in writing promotes reliability and builds positive relationships within the research community.
content: The tone of your writing is important. You should avoid the pressure to oversell, hide drawbacks, or disparage others' work. If your work has a shortcoming, it is much better that you point it out than to have someone else do so later. Papers written from the point of view that "we're all good researchers, doing our best" are much more pleasant to read than papers written from the standpoint that everyone else is an idiot. A generous tone wins over the reader and promotes long-lasting friendships with people who study the same problems you do. You should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable, always conveying an accurate impression of the performance of an algorithm and letting readers know if something doesn't work in important cases.
motivation_md: Maintaining a professional and humble tone prevents future embarrassment when flaws are discovered and fosters a collaborative rather than adversarial relationship with the research community.
recap_md: [ "- Avoid overselling results and be transparent about the limitations or shortcomings of your work.", "- Adopt a generous attitude toward other researchers' work to build a reputation for reliability and professionalism." ]

title: Author List
one_liner: Prioritize paper quality over author list position, and err on the side of inclusion when a collaborator requests coauthorship.
content: The quality of the papers you write matters so much more than your positions within the author lists of the papers. If adding more authors will make a paper better, then you should add more authors. If a collaborator feels they should be an author, but you yourself are not sure, it is generally a good idea to trust the collaborator and to add them as a coauthor. It's much better to be one of many authors on a great paper than to be one of just a few authors on a mediocre paper.
motivation_md: Collaborative research often produces higher quality results; being generous with authorship prevents interpersonal conflict and prioritizes the long-term impact of the work.
recap_md: [ "- Focus on the overall quality of the research rather than your specific rank in the author list.", "- Trust collaborators who request authorship, as it is better to share credit on a high-quality paper." ]

title: Avoiding Rejection
one_liner: To avoid rejection, authors must ensure they deliver on promises, cite relevant work, provide believable results, and maintain high writing quality.
content: With the task of rejecting at least three-quarters of the submissions, conference area chairs are grasping for reasons to reject a paper. Common reasons include: authors not delivering what they promise; missing important references, which suggests the authors are not up on the state of the art; results that are too incremental or similar to previous work; results that are not believable or lack sufficient tests to support claims; poor writing quality; and mistakes or incorrect statements.
motivation_md: Understanding the criteria that reviewers and area chairs use to filter papers allows authors to proactively address common pitfalls before submission.
recap_md: [ "- Ensure the paper delivers on all claims and includes a comprehensive review of the state of the art.", "- Provide strong evidence for results and maintain high standards for writing and technical accuracy." ]

title: Borderline Papers
one_liner: Borderline papers, which require the most decision-making effort from area chairs, can be categorized as "cockroaches" or "puppies with six toes."
content:
As an area chair, the very good and the very bad papers are easy to deal with, and most of the decision-making effort goes to the borderline papers. These borderline papers often fall into two categories: cockroaches and puppies with six toes.

| (a) Cockroach | (b) Puppy with six toes |
|---------------|-------------------------|
| [FIGURE:3637d778a0cfa4e4 | Cockroach] | [FIGURE:f26a67a9fa46ad5c | Puppy with six toes] |

**Table Caption**: Borderline papers from an area chair's perspective. (a) The cockroach represents a mundane, hard-to-reject paper with no glaring issues [@cockroach]. (b) The six-toed puppy represents a delightful paper with some minor, easily spotted flaw, leading to potential rejection [@puppy].
motivation_md: Categorizing borderline papers helps authors understand why certain papers struggle in the review process despite not being "bad" in an obvious way.
recap_md: [ "- Borderline papers consume the majority of an area chair's decision-making time.", "- These papers typically fall into categories of being either mundanely solid ('cockroaches') or innovatively flawed ('puppies with six toes')." ]

title: Cockroaches
one_liner: "Cockroach" papers lack exciting contributions but are hard to reject because they show incremental improvements and have no glaring flaws.
content:
"Cockroaches" have no exciting contributions, but the reviews are ok and the results show incremental improvement to the state of the art. They're hard to kill (hence the nickname), and maybe two-thirds are accepted as posters, and one-third are rejected. As an author, it's best to work harder for the fresh results, to bring papers like this out of the cockroach category.

| (a) Cockroach | (b) Puppy with six toes |
|---------------|-------------------------|
| [FIGURE:3637d778a0cfa4e4 | Cockroach] | [FIGURE:f26a67a9fa46ad5c | Puppy with six toes] |

**Table Caption**: Borderline papers from an area chair's perspective. (a) The cockroach represents a mundane, hard-to-reject paper with no glaring issues [@cockroach]. (b) The six-toed puppy represents a delightful paper with some minor, easily spotted flaw, leading to potential rejection [@puppy].
motivation_md: Identifying the 'cockroach' pattern encourages authors to aim for more significant, exciting contributions rather than just safe, incremental progress.
recap_md: [ "- Cockroach papers are characterized by incremental improvements and a lack of exciting new ideas.", "- While difficult to reject, these papers rarely achieve high-impact status like oral presentations." ]

title: Puppies with Six Toes
one_liner: "Puppies with six toes" are delightful, fresh papers that are easy to reject because of a minor, obvious flaw.
content:
At the other end of the spectrum of borderline papers are "puppies with six toes." These are delightful papers, but with an easy-to-see flaw. The flaw may not matter (like six toes on a puppy) but makes the paper easy to reject, even though the paper may be fresh and wonderful. Maybe two-thirds of those papers get rejected, and one-third maybe accepted as posters. As an author, it may be better to wait for another submission cycle with a paper like this, to remove the easy to spot flaw. Then the paper might receive an oral presentation at a subsequent conference submission cycle.

| (a) Cockroach | (b) Puppy with six toes |
|---------------|-------------------------|
| [FIGURE:3637d778a0cfa4e4 | Cockroach] | [FIGURE:f26a67a9fa46ad5c | Puppy with six toes] |

**Table Caption**: Borderline papers from an area chair's perspective. (a) The cockroach represents a mundane, hard-to-reject paper with no glaring issues [@cockroach]. (b) The six-toed puppy represents a delightful paper with some minor, easily spotted flaw, leading to potential rejection [@puppy].
motivation_md: Recognizing this category warns authors that even great ideas can be derailed by minor, avoidable mistakes that give reviewers an easy excuse to reject.
recap_md: [ "- These papers are innovative and high-quality but contain a visible flaw that invites rejection.", "- Removing the 'sixth toe' (the minor flaw) can elevate a paper from rejection to a top-tier presentation." ]

title: Only the good papers count
one_liner: Only the really good papers matter for your career, so it makes sense to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research work.
content: While the number of papers a student has can be a rough measure of research productivity, mentors, faculty search committees, and industrial research managers find that only the good papers count. Even if some institutions simply count papers, you should still strive to make all your papers good. This emphasis is illustrated in @fig-impact, which shows the relationship between paper quality and its impact on one's career. Because only high-quality papers truly matter for professional advancement, it is essential to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research work. (see figure: Plot of conjectured data showing the impact of a paper on one's career, as a function of paper quality.)
motivation_md: Graduate students often feel pressured to maximize their paper count, but professional impact is driven by quality. Understanding this helps researchers focus on excellence over volume.
recap_md: - Research productivity is often measured by paper count, but career impact is driven by paper quality.

title: Organization
one_liner: A good research paper should state the problem, explain why existing solutions are unsatisfactory, present a better solution, and discuss related work.
content: Effective paper organization follows a logical progression of ideas. Start by stating which problem you are addressing while keeping the audience in mind; you must ensure they care about the problem, sometimes by explaining why it is important. Next, briefly state other existing solutions and explain why they are unsatisfactory, as your work would be unnecessary if they were. Then, explain your own solution, compare it with others, and demonstrate why it is better. Finally, discuss related work where similar techniques have been applied to different problems. This structure typically maps to standard section headings: 1. Introduction, 2. Related work, 3. Main idea, 4. Algorithm (including specific approaches and implementations), 5. Experiments, and 6. Discussion.
motivation_md: Standardized organization helps readers navigate technical content and understand the specific contribution of a paper relative to existing work.
recap_md: - Define the problem and motivate why it matters to the audience.

title: The Paper's Introduction
one_liner: You must write a dynamite introduction that makes it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, and why it is interesting.
content: A paper's introduction must be easy to read and immediately clarify the paper's purpose. It should define what problem the paper solves, why that problem is interesting, what specific contributions are new, and why the approach is effective. As Kajiya notes, you must provide this information up front to ensure the reader understands the value of the work immediately.
motivation_md: The introduction is the first thing a reader sees; if it fails to communicate the paper's value and novelty quickly, the reader may lose interest.
recap_md: - The introduction must clearly state the problem, the solution, and the novelty of the work.

title: Main Idea
one_liner: Using a simple example to capture the main idea of a paper can effectively communicate complex concepts and highlight specific drawbacks in existing methods.
content: When appropriate, it is very helpful to show a simple example that captures the main idea of the paper. For instance, @fig-wavelet conveys a main idea simply by showing how wavelets lack translation invariance. The figure illustrates that as a signal translates, the representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form. This simple visualization points out the drawback of aliased subbands that was the focus of the research. (see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...)
motivation_md: Complex technical arguments are often easier to grasp when distilled into a single, clear illustrative example or figure.
recap_md: - Use a simple example to convey the core intuition or main idea of the paper.

title: Experimental Results
one_liner: Modern research standards require that assertions be backed up with experimental evidence, typically through quantitative comparisons with the state-of-the-art.
content: Modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers expect a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there are no previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different purpose. (see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
motivation_md: Empirical validation is necessary to prove that a proposed method actually works and provides an improvement over existing techniques.
recap_md: - Back up all claims with quantitative experimental data.

title: How to End the Paper
one_liner: Instead of ending with a list of unfinished 'Future Work,' a paper should conclude by reviewing its contributions and explaining how the research landscape has changed.
content: Authors should resist the temptation to end a paper with a "Future Work" section that enumerates unfinished tasks or shortcomings. Ending a paper by summarizing where it falls short is a weak conclusion. Instead, the paper should finish by reviewing the material presented and emphasizing the contributions. It should address how the world has changed now that the reader has finished the paper, what new research directions have been opened, and what can be achieved now that was not possible before.
motivation_md: The conclusion is the final impression a reader has; focusing on contributions rather than failures ensures the work's impact is clearly understood.
recap_md: - Avoid ending with a "Future Work" section that highlights what was left unfinished.

title: General Writing Tips
one_liner: The most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind, anticipating their needs and expectations at every step.
content: The most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind, constantly asking what the reader knows so far and what they expect next. A good writer acts like a great host who anticipates every need of their house guest, such as taking their coat or offering a drink. By knowing what the reader might be wanting at every moment, the author helps them navigate the information effectively.
motivation_md: Writing is a form of communication; focusing on the reader's experience ensures that the information is transmitted clearly and logically.
recap_md: - Always consider the reader's current knowledge and future expectations.

title: Use Fewer Words
one_liner: Vigorous writing is concise, containing no unnecessary words or sentences to ensure clarity and respect page limits.
content: Vigorous writing is concise; a sentence should contain no unnecessary words and a paragraph no unnecessary sentences. In scientific writing, being concise helps authors stay within page limits and makes the text clearer and easier to understand. For example, a technical paragraph can often be rewritten to significantly reduce word count (e.g., from 149 words to 88 words) without changing its meaning. Tighter text allows authors to include more information or additional figures while improving overall clarity.
motivation_md: Conciseness is vital in academic publishing due to strict page limits and the need for clear communication of complex ideas.
recap_md: - Omit unnecessary words and sentences to make writing more vigorous and clear.

title: Classification Loss
one_liner: To learn model parameters, we must define a loss function that captures the classification task and is tractable to optimize.
content:
In order to learn the model parameters, we need to define a loss function that will capture the task that we want to solve. One natural measure of classification error is the misclassification error, which counts the number of misplaced labels over the dataset:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) =
    \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^{K}
    \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \neq y^{(t)}_c ).
\end{aligned}$$

where $T$ is the number of images in the dataset. However, it is hard to learn the function parameters using gradient descent with this loss as it is not differentiable. Finding the optimal parameters of function $f_\theta$ requires defining a loss function that is tractable to optimize during the training stage.
motivation_md: While misclassification error is the most intuitive metric for accuracy, its non-differentiable nature makes it unsuitable for gradient-based optimization. We need differentiable loss functions to effectively train neural networks.
recap_md: - Misclassification error counts the total number of incorrect class predictions across a dataset.

title: Misclassification Error
one_liner: Misclassification error measures the number of incorrect predictions made by a classifier over a dataset.
content:
The misclassification error is a measure of classification error defined by the number of misplaced ones over the dataset. For a function $f$, this can be written as:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) =
    \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^{K}
    \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \neq y^{(t)}_c ).
\end{aligned}$$

where $T$ is the number of images in the dataset and $K$ is the number of classes.
motivation_md: This metric provides a direct count of how many times a model's prediction failed to match the ground truth, serving as a simple baseline for evaluating performance.
recap_md: - It is calculated as the sum of indicator functions where the predicted label does not match the true label.

title: Cross-Entropy Loss for Exclusive Classes
one_liner: Cross-entropy loss is a differentiable function used for exclusive classes by maximizing the likelihood of the ground truth labels.
content:
If we interpret the function $f$ as estimating the probability $p(Y_c=1 \mid {\bf x}) = \hat{y}_c$, with $\sum_c \hat{y}_c =1$, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:
$$
\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c}
$$
where $y^{(t)}_c$ is the ground truth value of $Y_c$ for image $t$. Maximizing this likelihood corresponds to minimizing the cross-entropy loss, which is obtained by taking the negative log of the likelihood equation, resulting in a total classification loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})
     = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)
$$

The cross-entropy loss is differentiable and is commonly used in image classification tasks.
motivation_md: When classes are mutually exclusive, we treat the model output as a probability distribution. Cross-entropy provides a smooth, differentiable surface for optimization that penalizes confident incorrect predictions more heavily than the discrete misclassification error.
recap_md: - It assumes classes are exclusive and the sum of predicted probabilities equals one.

title: Multiclass Binary Cross-Entropy Loss
one_liner: Multiclass binary cross-entropy loss is used for multilabel classification where classes are not mutually exclusive.
content:
If classes are not exclusive, the likelihood of the ground truth data is:
$$\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{c=1}^K \left( \hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{y^{(t)}_c} \left( 1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \right) ^{1-y^{(t)}_c}$$
where the outputs $\hat{y}_c$ are computed using a sigmoid layer. Taking the negative log of the likelihood gives the multiclass binary cross-entropy loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c) + (1-y^{(t)}_c) \log(1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$
motivation_md: In multilabel scenarios, an image can belong to multiple classes simultaneously. This loss treats each class as an independent binary classification problem, allowing the model to predict multiple labels for a single input.
recap_md: - Used for multilabel classification where outputs are typically passed through a sigmoid function.

title: Top-1 Performance
one_liner: Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times the true class matches the highest scored prediction.
content:
The top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set:

$$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)})$$

where $y^{(t)}$ is the ground truth class of image $t$. This evaluation metric only works for the exclusive class case since it assumes a single ground truth class per image. For the multilabel case, one may instead check if each label is predicted correctly.
motivation_md: Top-1 accuracy is the standard metric for evaluating how often a classifier's most confident guess is correct.
recap_md: - Measures the frequency of the highest-probability prediction matching the ground truth label.

title: Top-5 Performance
one_liner: Top-5 performance measures the percentage of times the true label is within the five highest scoring predictions.
content: In some benchmarks (such as ImageNet), researchers also measure the top-5 performance, which is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions. Top-5 is useful in settings where the labels might be ambiguous, or where multiple labels for one image might be possible. The top-5 measure is less precise and it is used when the test set only contains one label despite that multiple labels might be correct.
motivation_md: In large-scale datasets with many similar classes, a model might be penalized for choosing a 'cat' instead of a 'tabby cat'. Top-5 accuracy accounts for this ambiguity by checking if the correct answer is among the model's top candidates.
recap_md: - Useful for datasets with high label ambiguity or many fine-grained classes.

title: Confusion Matrix
one_liner: A confusion matrix summarizes classifier performance by showing the percentage of times classes are correctly identified versus confused with others.
motivation_md: Simple accuracy metrics don't tell you *which* classes your model is struggling with. A confusion matrix reveals specific patterns of error, such as a model consistently mistaking cats for dogs.
recap_md: - Diagonal entries represent correct predictions (per-class accuracy).

title: Shortcomings of Image Classification
one_liner: Image classification faces limitations due to ambiguous class boundaries, linguistic nuances, and the potential for models to rely on contextual shortcuts.
content:
The task of image classification has several limitations when used to produce meaningful descriptions of real-world scenes. One important shortcoming is the assumption that we can unambiguously answer whether an image contains a specific object. Class definitions can be ambiguous or boundaries can be soft, as shown in the following figures:

[FIGURE:360abab54729bcf5 | A photograph of an older, white Renault 4 hatchback with a blue hood parked on a gravel surface. The car is shown from a front-three-quarter angle, with buildings and other modern cars in the...]

[FIGURE:a64dd9969f9fe987 | A photograph of two cars, a blue sedan in the foreground and a green SUV behind it, both heavily covered in a thick layer of snow. The snow forms a large, rounded mound on top of each vehicle...]

[FIGURE:2e461a626376ea7e | A photograph taken from the driver's seat of a car looking through the windshield into a dark rock tunnel. The car's dashboard and rearview mirror are visible in the foreground, framing the view of...]

[FIGURE:2f43ff582bf7c58e | A photograph of a car body shell in an assembly plant, held by a red robotic arm and a red 'SMART Cart' base. The car is incomplete, lacking windows, wheels, and interior components, illustrating the...]

[FIGURE:479c0a519751a2ba | A small yellow toy car with a strawberry decal on its roof and hood is parked in front of a cardboard castle. The image illustrates the ambiguity of object classification, questioning whether a toy...]

[FIGURE:aee6e4196eafb081 | A photograph of a white plate containing a slice of watermelon. A piece of the red fruit has been carved out into the silhouette of a car and placed separately on the plate, illustrating the...]

Questions such as whether a car under construction, a toy car, or a car-shaped piece of watermelon should be classified as a "car" do not have simple answers. Language also plays a role; for example, a pepper is botanically a fruit but culinarilly a vegetable.

(see figure: A pepper is a fruit according to botanics, and it is a vegetable according to the culinary classification.)

Furthermore, image classification does not require localizing objects. A function $f$ might achieve high performance by using "shortcuts" or contextual biases in the dataset—such as identifying grass to predict a horse or detecting blurry backgrounds for insects—rather than learning a true representation of the object. This can mislead us into believing a classifier works better than it actually does.
motivation_md: Understanding the pitfalls of image classification—such as label ambiguity and dataset bias—is crucial for developing robust systems that generalize to the real world rather than just exploiting statistical correlations.
recap_md: - Class boundaries are often ambiguous (e.g., toy cars vs. real cars).

title: Lucas-Kanade Method
one_liner: A gradient-based method for optical flow estimation that solves a system of linear equations derived from the brightness constancy assumption and a local spatial smoothness constraint.
content: The Lucas-Kanade method, introduced in 1981, is a popular gradient-based technique for optical flow estimation. The algorithm approximates the change between consecutive frames using a first-order Taylor expansion. Combined with the constant brightness assumption, this results in a linear constraint for the optical flow at each pixel. If the motion $(u,v)$ is small compared to spatial image changes, the expansion of $\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)$ around $(x,y,t)$ is: $$\ell(x +u, y+v, t + 1)  \simeq \ell(x,y,t) + u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t + \mbox{h. o. t.}$$ Ignoring higher-order terms leads to the gradient constraint equation: $u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$. This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ at location $(x,y)$ to be along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell= \left( \ell_x, \ell_y \right)$, a relationship that describes the aperture problem. To estimate motion uniquely, the method assumes the motion field is constant over a local neighborhood, implemented by minimizing a weighted sum over a neighborhood $g(x,y)$: $$\mathcal{L}(u, v) = \sum g \left| u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t \right| ^2$$ The solution is found by setting the derivatives with respect to $u$ and $v$ to zero, resulting in the matrix form: $$\begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x ^ 2  & \sum g \ell_x \ell_y \\ \sum g \ell_x \ell_y & \sum g \ell_y ^ 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} \sum g \ell_x \ell_t \\ \sum g \ell_y \ell_t \end{bmatrix}$$ The solution at each location can be computed analytically as $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \textbf{b}$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is the $2 \times 2$ matrix. The motion at location $(x,y)$ is uniquely defined if $\mathbf{A}$ is invertible. If the rank of $\mathbf{A}$ is 1, the flow is constrained to a 1D line. (see figure: Gradient-based optical flow estimation using two input frames.)
motivation_md: It provides a practical way to estimate motion by turning the under-determined brightness constancy equation into a solvable system of linear equations through the assumption of local motion consistency.
recap_md: - It uses a first-order Taylor expansion and the brightness constancy assumption to derive a gradient constraint.

title: Gradient Constraint Equation
one_liner: The linear equation $u \ell_x + v \ell_y + \ell_t = 0$ that relates spatial and temporal image gradients to the velocity components of optical flow.
content: By combining the brightness constancy assumption with a first-order Taylor expansion and ignoring higher-order terms, we arrive at the gradient constraint equation: $$u \ell_x  + v \ell_y + \ell_t  = 0$$ This equation constrains the motion $(u,v)$ at location $(x,y)$ to lie along a line perpendicular to the image gradient $\nabla \ell = (\ell_x, \ell_y)$. This relationship describes the aperture problem, where the motion component parallel to an image edge cannot be determined from local information alone.
motivation_md: It establishes the fundamental relationship between image intensity changes and motion, serving as the starting point for most gradient-based optical flow algorithms.
recap_md: - It is derived from the brightness constancy assumption and a first-order Taylor expansion.

title: Harris Corner Detector for Optical Flow Reliability
one_liner: A method to identify image regions where optical flow estimation is reliable by analyzing the conditioning of the local structure matrix.
content: To identify regions where optical flow estimation is reliable, one can analyze the conditioning of the matrix $\mathbf{A}$. As in the Harris corner detector, the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue indicates the direction of minimal image change under translation. Regions with small minimum eigenvalues suffer from the aperture problem. To avoid expensive eigenvalue computations, Harris proposed using the quantity: $$R = \det (\mathbf{A}) - \lambda \mathrm{Tr}\hspace{1pt} (\mathbf{A})^2$$ where $\lambda \approx 0.05$. The figure below shows $R$ and the estimated optical flow in the regions with $R > 2$. Reliable motion is typically estimated in these regions, which correspond to 'good features to track'. While increasing the aperture size (using a larger Gaussian filter $g$) can expand these reliable regions, it also results in smoother flows that may not respect object boundaries. (see figure: Estimated optical flow in the regions with $R > 2$ (around *good features to track* @shi1994goodfeatures)
motivation_md: Optical flow is often ambiguous in regions with 1D structure; this method identifies 'good features to track' where the image structure is 2D, ensuring more stable and unique motion solutions.
recap_md: - Reliability is measured using $R = \det (\mathbf{A}) - \lambda \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{A})^2$ to avoid expensive eigenvalue calculations.

title: Gaussian Pyramid for Large Displacements
one_liner: A multi-scale approach that uses low-resolution image scales to make large motions small enough for gradient-based optical flow methods to work.
content: One solution to the problem of large displacements in optical flow estimation is to compute a Gaussian pyramid for the input sequence. By processing the images at multiple scales, the low-resolution levels effectively make the motion smaller. This allows gradient-based approaches, which typically rely on small-motion assumptions, to work more effectively before the results are refined at higher resolutions.
motivation_md: Gradient-based methods rely on Taylor expansions that are only valid for very small movements; pyramids allow these methods to work on large displacements by shrinking them at coarser scales.
recap_md: - Large displacements are handled by computing a Gaussian pyramid for the input sequence.

title: Iterative Refinement for Optical Flow
one_liner: An iterative process that minimizes photometric reconstruction error to improve the accuracy of optical flow estimates.
content: While the gradient-based approach is efficient, it only approximates the motion field by ignoring higher-order Taylor terms. A more accurate approach involves directly minimizing the photometric reconstruction error: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$ By applying gradient descent to this loss, we can iteratively improve the flow estimate. In each iteration $n$, the current flow $(u_n, v_n)$ is used to warp the frame, and updates $\Delta u_n$ and $\Delta v_n$ are computed. This process is often performed on a Gaussian pyramid, starting at the lowest resolution to handle larger motions and upsampling the result to initialize the next level. This process is shown in the figure below. (see figure: Multiscale iterative refinement for optical flow. Optical flow estimation is done on a Gaussian pyramid. (left) First, we run a few iterations on the lowest resolution scale of the pyramid (where the...)
motivation_md: Standard gradient-based methods are linear approximations that fail for complex motion; iterative refinement allows for non-linear optimization, leading to significantly more accurate and robust flow fields.
recap_md: - It directly minimizes the photometric reconstruction error using gradient descent.

title: Photometric Reconstruction Error
one_liner: A loss function measuring the squared difference between a reference frame and a second frame warped by the estimated optical flow.
content: The photometric reconstruction error is a loss function used to estimate optical flow by directly comparing image intensities. It is defined as: $$L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})= \sum_{x,y} \left| \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t)) \right| ^2$$ Unlike basic gradient-based methods that rely on Taylor approximations, minimizing this error directly accounts for the full intensity difference between the reference frame and the warped target frame.
motivation_md: It provides a direct physical measure of how well a calculated motion field explains the change between two images, serving as the objective function for optimization-based flow estimation.
recap_md: - It is defined as $L = \sum | \ell_1 (x+u,y+v,t+1) - \ell_2 (x,y,t) |^2$.

title: Horn-Schunck Formulation
one_liner: A global optical flow estimation method that combines photometric reconstruction error with a regularization term to penalize fast variations in the estimated flow field.
content: The Horn-Schunck formulation, introduced in 1981, estimates optical flow by minimizing a global objective function. This function incorporates a regularization term that penalizes fast variations in the estimated flow field: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = L(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2,\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) + \lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$$ Here, $L$ represents the photometric reconstruction error, and $R$ is a regularization term that encourages smoothness across the motion field.
motivation_md: Local methods like Lucas-Kanade can fail in homogeneous regions; this formulation uses global regularization to propagate motion information from edges into featureless areas, creating a dense, smooth flow field.
recap_md: - It adds a regularization term $\lambda R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$ to the photometric reconstruction error.

title: Slow Prior
one_liner: A regularization term that penalizes large velocities in an optical flow field by summing the squared magnitudes of the velocity components.
content: The slow prior is a regularization term used in optical flow estimation to penalize large velocities. It is defined as: $$R(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum_{x,y} \left( u(x,y) \right)^2 + \left( v(x,y) \right)^2$$ By adding this term to the optimization objective, the resulting motion field is biased toward smaller displacements, which can help stabilize estimation in ambiguous image regions.
motivation_md: In the absence of strong image evidence, it is often safer to assume that objects are moving slowly; this prior regularizes the solution by penalizing unnecessarily large velocity vectors.
recap_md: - It is defined as the sum of squared velocity components $u^2 + v^2$ over all pixels.

title: Height Propagation to Supported Objects
one_liner: Project an object's height onto a reference line by finding vertically aligned parallel 3D lines connecting the object to a known structure.
content: As before, we will project the bottle height on the reference line on the corner of the bookshelf. To do this we need to find two vertically aligned parallel 3D lines that connect the bottle's top and bottom points with the bookshelf. The first line, $\boldsymbol{l}_1$, is the line connecting the bottom of the bottle, $\mathbf{g}_e$, and the point $\mathbf{b}$. These two points are at the same height from the ground plane as $\mathbf{b}$ corresponds to the top of the desk and $\mathbf{g}_e$ is the point of the bottle that is in contact with the top of the desk. The intersection of the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ give us point $\mathbf{a}$. Connecting point $\mathbf{a}$ with the top of the bottle, point $\mathbf{t}_e$, gives us the second line, $\boldsymbol{l}_2$. The intersection of this line with the reference bookshelf line is the point $\mathbf{c}$. The distance between the point $\mathbf{c}$ and the ground in 3D is the sum $h_{\text{bookshelf}}+h_{\text{desk}}$. Writing everything into a compact equation results in: $$\mathbf{c} = (((\mathbf{g}_e \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_e) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
motivation_md: To measure the height of objects that are not resting directly on the ground by transferring their height to a calibrated reference structure through a hierarchy of supported surfaces.
recap_md: - Use the contact point and a reference point at the same height to find a vanishing point on the horizon. - Connect the vanishing point to the top of the object to intersect the reference line. - The resulting 3D height is the sum of the heights in the support hierarchy.

title: Supported-by Hierarchy
one_liner: The supported-by hierarchy describes the structural relationship between objects in a scene used to correctly parse and propagate geometric measurements.
content: This procedure highlights the importance of the correct parsing of the supported-by hierarchy between objects in the scene.
motivation_md: To correctly calculate the absolute height of an object by accounting for the heights of all surfaces supporting it in a vertical stack.
recap_md: - Represents the vertical stacking or support relationships between objects in a scene. - Crucial for correctly summing heights when propagating measurements from the ground plane.

title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
aliases: calibration of the projected world axis
one_liner: We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane.
content: Assume we know the location of some arbitrary 3D distance to the origin on each axis, denoted by $\alpha_X$, $\alpha_Y$ and $\alpha_Z$. To place the ticks for $k\alpha_X$, $k\alpha_Y$ and $k\alpha_Z$ for all $k$, we use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane. This requires the location of the horizon line of a reference plane (the ground plane), the position of the orthogonal vanishing point, and the real measure of one object in the scene. (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) As shown in the procedure, we can use the cross-ratio to estimate the location of the points $Y= k \alpha_X$ where $\alpha_X$ is an arbitrary constant. Due to perspective projection, the image projection of the point $Y= k \alpha_X$ will not be evenly spaced. To calibrate the axis, we need the dimensions of an object in the scene along the three axes. For example, using a bookshelf height (197 cm) and a table base radius (50 cm), we can solve for the image locations of the ticks $\alpha_X=\alpha_Y=\alpha_Z=1$ m.
motivation_md: To establish a metric coordinate system within a 2D image, enabling the measurement of real-world distances along the X, Y, and Z axes.
recap_md: - Uses the cross-ratio invariant to place coordinate ticks along projected axes. - Requires the horizon line, orthogonal vanishing points, and at least one known real-world measurement. - Ticks for world coordinates are not evenly spaced in the image due to perspective projection.

title: Locating a 3D Point from a Single View
one_liner: The trick consists in using context to estimate 3D from a single image.
content: The procedure for locating a 3D point from a single view involves using context—such as the object the point belongs to, the horizon line, and vanishing points—to estimate 3D geometry. If a point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object in contact with the ground, the object's geometry provides the information to localize the projection of $\mathbf{P}$ on the ground plane, denoted $\mathbf{G}$. (see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...) Once the image location $\mathbf{G}$ is known, we project it to the world-coordinate axis. To estimate the $Y$-coordinate, we find the line $\boldsymbol{l}_3$ passing through $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, then find its intersection with the horizon line at point $\mathbf{v}$. The line $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ passing through $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ intersects the $Y_w$-axis at coordinate $P_y$. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates are obtained by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ with the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.
motivation_md: To resolve the depth ambiguity inherent in a single 2D image by using the ground plane and object contact points as geometric references.
recap_md: - Identify the point's projection on the ground plane based on the object's contact with the floor. - Project the ground point to the world-coordinate axes using lines intersecting the horizon and vanishing points.

title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
one_liner: This method uses only the vanishing points to extract the camera parameters.
content: Camera calibration can be performed using only vanishing points under certain conditions. The first step is finding three orthogonal vanishing points in the image, which in many scenes are aligned with the world coordinate axes. Assuming three orthogonal vanishing directions $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$, we can derive constraints on the projection matrix. By inverting the vanishing projection equation, we get $\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$. Since the vectors are orthogonal ($\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$), and $\mathbf{R}$ is orthonormal, we obtain a relationship depending only on the intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K}$: $\mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0$. We define the conic matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$. If the skew parameter is zero, $\mathbf{W}$ has a specific structure with four values ($a, b, c, d$), allowing us to solve a system of linear equations $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$ using singular value decomposition (SVD). Finally, $\mathbf{K}$ is recovered via Cholesky factorization of $\mathbf{W}$ and normalized.
motivation_md: To calibrate a camera's internal parameters using only the geometric regularities, such as parallel lines, found in a typical scene without requiring a physical calibration pattern.
recap_md: - Orthogonal vanishing directions provide linear constraints on the conic matrix $\mathbf{W}$. - The intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is recovered from $\mathbf{W}$ using Cholesky factorization. - This method assumes the camera skew is zero and requires three orthogonal vanishing points.

title: Conic Matrix
one_liner: The conic matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ relates vanishing points to intrinsic camera parameters.
content: $$\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$$ This is also known as the **conic matrix** and it has lots of different properties.
motivation_md: To provide a mathematical representation of camera intrinsics that can be solved linearly using geometric constraints from observed vanishing points.
recap_md: - Defined as the product of the inverse transpose of the intrinsic matrix and the inverse intrinsic matrix. - Provides a linear system to solve for camera calibration when orthogonal vanishing points are known.

title: Shading

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation.
content: Shading refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation.
motivation_md: To provide a powerful visual cue for perceiving the 3D shape and curvature of objects based on how their surfaces interact with light.
recap_md: - Intensity changes depend on surface normal, light direction, and albedo. - Serves as a primary cue for depth and shape perception in computer vision.

title: Shape from Shading

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

one_liner: Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.
content: Shape from shading studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations. It utilizes the relationship between surface orientation, light sources, and observed image intensity to infer 3D geometry.
motivation_md: To reconstruct the detailed 3D surface of an object from a single grayscale image by analyzing light intensity variations.
recap_md: - Inverts the physical process of light reflection to estimate surface normals. - Relies on the mathematical relationship between image intensity and surface geometry.

title: Cascade of Classifiers
one_liner: A sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy used to efficiently localize objects in images.
content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. A cascade of classifiers pushes the idea of multi-step search to the limit by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

The algorithm for the cascade of classifiers is:

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)

Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location, where each test checks for a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were inspired by the game "Twenty Questions."

In a cascade, computational power is allocated to image regions more likely to contain the target object, while flat or featureless regions are rejected quickly. The following figure shows how a cascaded classifier allocates computing power when trained to detect faces; the heat map intensity is proportional to the number of cascade levels applied to each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

The scanning window approach (1 level) and selective search (2 levels) are special cases of this algorithm. While a cascade usually starts with a full list of bounding boxes and lacks a refinement stage, one could be added for transformations like rotations.
motivation_md: Object localization is computationally expensive because most image regions are background. Cascades solve this by using fast, cheap filters to discard obvious background early, reserving expensive, accurate computation only for promising candidate regions.
recap_md: - Uses a sequence of classifiers where each stage is more complex and accurate than the last.

title: YOLO
one_liner: An object detection model that makes predictions by looking at the image globally.
content: YOLO (You Only Look Once) is an example of an object detection model that makes predictions by looking at the image globally. While it may not be as accurate as some scanning methods, it can be computationally more efficient.
motivation_md: YOLO was developed to provide a faster alternative to traditional scanning window or region-based methods by treating detection as a single regression problem from image pixels to bounding box coordinates and class probabilities.
recap_md: - Processes the entire image globally in a single pass.

title: Object Localization Loss
one_liner: A combined loss function that accounts for both classification accuracy and the spatial precision of detected bounding boxes.
content:
The object localization loss takes into account two complementary tasks: classification and localization. Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) checks if the predicted label matches the ground truth, while localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth.

The detector outputs a set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. We associate each detection with a ground truth label to form the set $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. Predicted boxes overlapping with ground truth are optimized for location and label; those that do not overlap are assigned to the background class ($\mathbf{y}_i=0$) to reduce their class score.

(see figure: (left) Detector output (using a low threshold to generate many detections). (middle) Ground truth bounding boxes (one color per instance). (right) Detector outputs that overlap with ground truth...)

Classification loss is typically measured using cross-entropy:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

Localization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$ can be measured using Intersection over Union (IoU):
[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})$$
Alternatively, L2 regression loss can be used, though it is not scale invariant:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The overall loss is the sum of both components:
$$\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$$
where $\lambda$ balances the two losses and the indicator function ensures localization loss is only calculated for non-background boxes.
motivation_md: Training an object detector requires a single objective function that penalizes both wrong labels and poorly aligned boxes, allowing the model to learn both tasks simultaneously via backpropagation.
recap_md: - Combines classification (cross-entropy) and localization (IoU or L2) into a single objective.

title: Classification Loss
one_liner: A measure of how well the predicted label for a bounding box matches the ground truth label.
content:
Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) determines if the predicted label matches the ground truth at a specific location. Since each bounding box can only have one class, we use the cross-entropy loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the total number of classes.
motivation_md: In object detection, the model must not only find objects but also correctly identify what they are. Classification loss provides the gradient needed to improve the model's categorical accuracy.
recap_md: - Measures label accuracy using cross-entropy loss.

title: Localization Loss
one_liner: A measure of the spatial distance or overlap between a predicted bounding box and the ground truth object location.
content:
Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures how close the detected location is to the ground truth object location. A typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the **Intersection over Union** (IoU).

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1. As it is a similarity measure, the loss is defined as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

IoU is translation and scale invariant. A simpler but non-scale-invariant alternative is the L2 regression loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

L2 loss is larger for big bounding boxes. The following graph compares IoU loss and L2 regression loss for two square bounding boxes as a function of relative $x$-displacement:

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)
motivation_md: To accurately locate objects, the model needs a differentiable metric that penalizes coordinates that deviate from the ground truth, guiding the bounding box to wrap tightly around the object.
recap_md: - Quantifies the error in bounding box coordinates.

title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
one_liner: A measure of similarity between two bounding boxes calculated as the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union.
content:
Intersection over Union (IoU) is a typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes. 

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, where 0 means no overlap and 1 means the bounding boxes are identical. Because IoU is a similarity measure, it can be converted into a localization loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$
IoU is frequently used to evaluate object detectors because it is translation and scale invariant.
motivation_md: Standard distance metrics like L2 are sensitive to the size of the object. IoU provides a normalized metric that works equally well for small and large objects by focusing on the percentage of overlap.
recap_md: - Ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect match).

title: L2 Regression Loss
one_liner: A loss function that measures the squared difference between the coordinates of the predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.
content:
L2 regression loss is a simple loss used to optimize object detectors by calculating the squared difference between predicted and ground truth coordinates:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$
While it is translation invariant, it is not scale invariant; the loss is naturally larger for larger bounding boxes. The following graph compares the IoU loss and the L2 regression loss for two square bounding boxes as a function of relative $x$-displacement:

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)
motivation_md: L2 loss is easy to compute and differentiate, making it a straightforward choice for regression tasks like predicting bounding box coordinates, despite its lack of scale invariance.
recap_md: - Calculates the sum of squared errors for bounding box coordinates.

title: Average Precision-Recall Evaluation
one_liner: A common evaluation method for object localization that summarizes the precision-recall curve into a single average precision score.
content:
The most common approach for evaluating object localization is measuring the average precision-recall. This requires assigning detection outputs to ground truth labels.

**Assign detections to ground truth labels**: Detections are sorted by their confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$. For each box in decreasing order, compute the IoU with all ground truth boxes. If the highest IoU exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5), the detection is marked correct and the ground truth box is removed to avoid double counting. Otherwise, it is marked incorrect. Remaining ground truth boxes are marked as missed.

**Precision-recall curve**: This measures performance as a function of the decision threshold $\beta$. **Precision** is the percentage of correct detections among all detections above the threshold:
$$Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}$$
**Recall** measures the proportion of ground truth instances detected:
$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)

The average precision (AP) summarizes the non-monotonic precision-recall curve as a single number between 0 and 1, representing the area under the curve.
motivation_md: Detectors often produce many candidate boxes with varying confidence. Precision and recall together provide a complete picture of how many objects were found versus how many false alarms occurred, and AP summarizes this trade-off.
recap_md: - Precision measures the accuracy of detections, while recall measures the coverage of ground truth objects.

title: Comparison of Image Representations
one_liner: While ordered arrays are standard for computer input, set representations facilitate handling irregular geometries and three-dimensional image formation.
content: Although both previous representations might seem equivalent, the set representation makes it easy to deal with other image geometries where the points are not on a regular array. That representation can also be extended by representing geometry in different ways such as using homogeneous coordinates, or positional encoding. These three representations induce different ways of thinking about architectures to process the visual input. These representations are not opposed and can be used simultaneously. The ordered array of pixels is the format that computers take as input when visualizing images. However, a set of pixels is the most common format when thinking about three-dimensional (3D) geometry and image formation. Therefore, it is always important to be familiar with how to transform any representation into an ordered array.
motivation_md: Different image representations are suited for different tasks; arrays are optimized for computer processing, while sets are better for irregular geometries and 3D modeling.
recap_md: - Ordered arrays are the standard format for computer input. - Set representations are better for irregular geometries and 3D modeling. - Different representations can be used simultaneously.

title: Continuous Function Image Representation
one_liner: An image can be represented as a continuous function $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$ mapping a location to an intensity or color.
content: Another option is to represent an image as a continuous function whose input is a location $(x, y)$ and whose output is an intensity, or a color, $\ell$: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ This image representation is commonly used when we want to make image priors more explicit. The function $f_{\theta}$ is parameterized by the coefficients $\theta$. This function becomes especially interesting when the parameters $\theta$ are different than the original pixel values. They will have to be estimated from the original image. But once learned, the function $f$ should be able to take as input continuous spatial variables.
motivation_md: Representing images as continuous functions allows for explicit image priors and the ability to query the image at any continuous spatial coordinate.
recap_md: - Images can be modeled as functions mapping coordinates to intensity. - Parameters $\theta$ are estimated from the original image. - This representation allows for continuous spatial variable input.

title: Heterogeneous Coordinates
one_liner: Heterogeneous coordinates are conventional Cartesian descriptions of points in 2D or 3D, typically denoted with rounded brackets.
content: Conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$, are referred to as heterogeneous coordinates and written with rounded brackets. Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$.
