The transformation rule from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates is simply to add an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ It is the same if the vector has three dimensions: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
motivation_md: Heterogeneous coordinates are the standard Cartesian way to describe positions, but they are often converted to homogeneous coordinates to simplify geometric transformations.
recap_md: - Conventional Cartesian coordinates like $(x,y)$ or $(x,y,z)$. - Typically written using rounded brackets. - Converted to homogeneous form by adding a 1 as the last coordinate.

title: Homogeneous Coordinates
one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$, often used to simplify geometric transformations.
content: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. The transformation rule from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates is simply to add an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ It is the same if the vector has three dimensions: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ We refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions as heterogeneous coordinates (written with rounded brackets), while their corresponding homogeneous coordinate representations are denoted by square bracketed vectors.
motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates are used in computer vision to represent points in a way that makes transformations like translation and perspective projection linear.
recap_md: - Represents an $N$-dimensional vector using $N+1$ dimensions. - Typically written using square brackets. - Facilitates linearizing geometric transformations.

title: Scale Invariance of Homogeneous Coordinates
one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates are scale-invariant, meaning all non-zero scalings of a coordinate vector represent the same point.
content: The homogeneous coordinates have the additional rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent. For example, to represent a 2D point, we have (transforming from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates): $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. (see figure: Transformation rule between heterogeneous and homogeneous coordinates in 2D. All the points along the dotted line correspond to the same point in heterogeneous coordinates. Note that the points...) A point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant (any point within the line that passes through the origin translates into the same point in heterogeneous coordinates). We can already see that this is closely related to the operation performed by perspective projection. It is important to mention that while you can add two points in heterogeneous coordinates, you can not do the same in homogeneous coordinates!
motivation_md: Scale invariance in homogeneous coordinates naturally models how objects at different distances can project to the same point on an image plane.
recap_md: - Non-zero scalings of a homogeneous vector represent the same point. - Geometrically, this corresponds to points along a line through the origin. - Point addition is not valid in homogeneous coordinates.

title: Conversion between Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Coordinates
one_liner: To convert from homogeneous to heterogeneous coordinates, divide all entries of the vector by the value of the last dimension.
content: To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation of the point, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$
motivation_md: After performing transformations in homogeneous space, we must convert back to standard Cartesian coordinates to interpret the results as physical locations.
recap_md: - Divide all entries by the last dimension $w$ to return to heterogeneous space. - Maps a projective line back to a single Cartesian point. - Reverses the coordinate augmentation process.

title: Small Angle Rotation Approximation
one_liner: For very small angles, the rotation matrix can be approximated using Taylor development where $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$.
content: If the angle of rotation is very small, then we can approximate the rotation matrix by its Taylor development: $$\mathbf{R} \simeq \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta & 0 \\ -\theta & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ For small $x$, $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$. For small angles a rotation becomes a shear. In general, for all angles, a rotation can be written as two shears and a scaling.
motivation_md: Approximating rotations for small angles simplifies calculations in physics and engineering, turning non-linear trigonometric problems into linear ones.
recap_md: - Uses Taylor development: $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ and $\cos(\theta) \approx 1$. - Small angle rotations approximate a shear transformation. - Full rotations can be decomposed into two shears and a scaling.

title: Euclidean Transformation
one_liner: A Euclidean transformation is a combination of rotations and translations that preserves lengths and angles between lines.
content: When chaining rotations and translations only we will have a euclidean transformation (lengths and angles between lines are preserved).
motivation_md: Euclidean transformations describe 'rigid body' motions where the shape and size of an object do not change, which is essential for modeling physical movement.
recap_md: - Formed by chaining only rotations and translations. - Preserves both lengths and angles between lines. - Also known as a rigid transformation.

title: Relative Importance of Phase and Amplitude

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

one_liner: The appearance of many natural images is dominated by the phase of their Fourier transform rather than the magnitude.
content: One might ask which is more important in determining the appearance of an image: the magnitude of the Fourier transform or its phase. @fig-phaseoramp shows the result of a classical experiment that consists of computing the Fourier transform for two images and building two new images by swapping their phases. (see figure: Swapping the amplitude and the phase of the Fourier Transform of two images. Each color channel is processed in the same way.) The appearance of the resulting images is mostly dominated by the phase of the image they come from. For example, an image built with the phase of a stop sign looks like the stop sign even if the amplitude comes from a different image. The phase signal determines where the edges and colors are located, while the final colors are altered as the amplitudes have changed.
motivation_md: Understanding whether the magnitude or phase of the Fourier transform carries more structural information helps in prioritizing components for image reconstruction and processing tasks.
recap_md: - The phase of the Fourier transform typically dominates the visual appearance and structural layout of natural images.\n- Swapping phases between images shows that edges and object locations are primarily encoded in the phase component.\n- Amplitude changes tend to alter global color and intensity distributions rather than the underlying geometry.

title: DFT Magnitude of Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

one_liner: A remarkable property of natural images: the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency.
content: A remarkable property of natural images is that the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency. The magnitude of the DFT of natural images is quite similar across different real images and can be approximated by $A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$ with $a$ and $b$ being two constants. We will talk more about this property when discussing statistical models of natural images in @sec-stat_image_models. This typical structure of the DFT magnitude of natural images has been used as a prior for many tasks such as image denoising.
motivation_md: Identifying universal statistical properties of natural images, like the $1/f$ decay of spectral magnitude, allows for the creation of effective priors in tasks like denoising and compression.
recap_md: - Natural images exhibit a DFT magnitude that is highest at low frequencies and decays as frequency increases.\n- The magnitude can be modeled mathematically as $A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$.\n- This predictable spectral structure serves as a useful prior for image restoration and statistical modeling.

title: Image-Dependent Component Importance

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

one_liner: The relative importance of phase and amplitude in image reconstruction varies depending on the specific content and texture of the image.
content: The relative importance of phase and amplitude depends on the image. While phase often carries most of the information, the amplitude contains very useful information as shown in @fig-phasevsamp. In experiments where the phase is randomized or the amplitude is replaced by a generic $1/f$ form, the contribution of each component becomes clear. For many images, the phase is the most important component, but for others, such as pseudo-periodic thread textures, the amplitude is the most important component for defining the image content.
motivation_md: Recognizing that the importance of phase versus amplitude is not universal but depends on image content (like texture) is crucial for selecting appropriate features for image analysis.
recap_md: - The dominance of phase over amplitude is not universal and depends on the specific image content.\n- For textured or periodic images, the amplitude can be more critical for defining the image's appearance than the phase.\n- Experiments using generic $1/f$ amplitudes help isolate the structural information contributed by the phase.

title: Amplitude for Periodic Patterns

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

one_liner: The amplitude of the Fourier transform is particularly effective at capturing and describing images that contain strong periodic patterns.
content: The amplitude is great for capturing images that contain strong periodic patterns. In such cases, the amplitude can be better than the phase. This observation has been the basis for many image descriptors. The amplitude is somewhat invariant to location, although it is not invariant to the relative location between different elements in the scene. However, the phase is a complex signal that does not seem to make explicit any information about the image.
motivation_md: Amplitude provides a location-invariant way to identify repeating textures and patterns, which is useful for building robust image descriptors and classification systems.
recap_md: - Amplitude is superior to phase for representing and identifying strong periodic patterns in images.\n- Many image descriptors leverage the location-invariance properties of the Fourier amplitude.\n- Unlike phase, amplitude explicitly highlights the presence of repeating structures regardless of their absolute position.

title: Visualizing Patterns in the Fourier Domain

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

one_liner: Certain image features, such as strong contrasts and periodic patterns, manifest as distinct, easily identifiable structures in the Fourier domain.
content: Some image patterns are easily visible in the Fourier domain. For instance, strong image contrasts produce oriented lines in the Fourier domain. Periodic patterns are also clearly visible; a periodic pattern in the image domain produces periodic impulses in the Fourier domain. The location of the impulses will be related to the period and orientation of the repetitions as shown in @fig-quiz.
motivation_md: Visualizing images in the Fourier domain allows for the easy detection of global features like orientation and periodicity that might be harder to quantify in the spatial domain.
recap_md: - Strong contrasts in an image appear as oriented lines in its Fourier transform.\n- Periodic spatial patterns result in discrete impulses (spikes) in the Fourier domain.\n- The position and orientation of Fourier impulses correspond to the frequency and direction of the image's repetitions.

title: Transfer Function
one_liner: The transfer function of a filter is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel.
content: We can write a linear filter as a product in the Fourier domain: [FIGURE:eb36ec0cfa3e5a10 | Transfer function of a linear filter.] The function $H \left[u, v \right]$ is called the **transfer function** of the filter. The transfer function of a filter is the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel.
motivation_md: Defining filters in the frequency domain simplifies the operation of convolution into a simple multiplication, making it easier to design and analyze system behavior.
recap_md: - The transfer function $H \left[u, v \right]$ is the Fourier transform of a filter's spatial convolution kernel.\n- In the Fourier domain, filtering is performed by multiplying the input signal's transform by the transfer function.\n- This representation allows for intuitive analysis of how a filter affects different frequency components.

title: Spectral Content Modification by Linear Filters
one_liner: Linear filters modify an image by reweighting existing spectral components rather than creating new ones.
content: The transfer function allows us to interpret filters by how they modify the spectral content of the input signal. Because the Fourier transform of the output is the product of the input's transform and the transfer function, a linear filter simply reweights the spectral content of the signal. It does not create new content; it can only enhance or decrease the spectral components already present in the input. A convolution between two signals does not create new spectral content. To create new spectral components not present in the input, nonlinearities must be applied.
motivation_md: Understanding that linear systems only scale existing frequencies helps in predicting filter behavior and recognizing when a process must be nonlinear to achieve certain effects.
recap_md: - Linear filters act by reweighting (enhancing or attenuating) the existing frequency components of a signal.\n- Convolution between two signals never introduces new spectral content that was not in the input.\n- Generating new frequencies requires the application of nonlinear operations.

title: Amplitude Gain
one_liner: The amplitude gain is the magnitude of the filter's transfer function in polar form.
content: If we use the polar form: $$H \left[u,v \right] = \left|H \left[u, v \right] \right| \exp \left( {j \, \angle H \left[u, v \right]} \right) $$ the magnitude $\left| H \left[u, v \right] \right|$ is the **amplitude gain**.
motivation_md: Separating the transfer function into magnitude and phase allows engineers to independently analyze how much a filter amplifies or attenuates specific frequencies.
recap_md: - Amplitude gain is the absolute value (magnitude) of the complex transfer function $H \left[u, v \right]$.\n- It describes how the amplitude of each frequency component is scaled by the filter.\n- It is often analyzed alongside the phase response to fully characterize a linear system.

title: A World of Simple Objects

position.section_title: A Simple World: The Blocks World

one_liner: For the purposes of this chapter, let's think of a world composed of a very simple (yet varied) set of objects.
content: For the purposes of this study, we consider a world composed of a simple yet varied set of objects. These objects are made of flat surfaces that can be horizontal or vertical, resting on a white horizontal ground plane. These objects can be constructed by cutting, folding, and gluing colored paper as shown in @fig-simpleObjects. We do not assume the exact geometry of these objects is known in advance. ![A world of simple objects. Print, cut, and build your own blocks world!](figures/simplesystem/simpleObjects.png){#fig-simpleObjects width="100%"}
motivation_md: Using a simplified "blocks world" allows for the study of computer vision and projection principles without the complexity of arbitrary 3D geometries.
recap_md: - Objects consist of flat horizontal and vertical surfaces.\n- All objects rest on a common horizontal ground plane.

title: Parallel Projection
one_liner: In this image formation model, the light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane.
content: One of the simplest forms of projection is parallel (or orthographic) projection. In this image formation model, the light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane. This type of projection produces images in which objects do not change size as they move closer or farther from the camera, and parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image. This is different from perspective projection, where the image is formed by the convergence of the light rays into a single point (focal point). ![(a) Close up picture without zoom. Note that near edges are larger than far edges, and parallel lines in 3D are not parallel. (b) Picture taken from far away using zoom resulting in an image that can be described by parallel projection.](figures/simplesystem/parallelProjection.png){#fig-parallelProjection width="100%"}
motivation_md: Parallel projection simplifies geometric analysis because it preserves parallelism and object scale, making it useful for technical drawings and specific computer vision tasks.
recap_md: - Objects do not change size as they move closer or farther from the camera.\n- Parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image.

title: Perspective Projection
one_liner: The image is formed by the convergence of the light rays into a single point (focal point).
content: In perspective projection, the image is formed by the convergence of light rays into a single point, known as the focal point. This differs from parallel projection, where parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image. If special care is not taken, most pictures taken with a camera will be better described by perspective projection, as shown in @fig-parallelProjection (a). ![(a) Close up picture without zoom. Note that near edges are larger than far edges, and parallel lines in 3D are not parallel. (b) Picture taken from far away using zoom resulting in an image that can be described by parallel projection.](figures/simplesystem/parallelProjection.png){#fig-parallelProjection width="100%"}
motivation_md: Perspective projection accurately models how human eyes and standard cameras perceive the 3D world, capturing depth through size variation and vanishing points.
recap_md: - Light rays converge into a single focal point.\n- Parallel lines in 3D do not necessarily remain parallel in the 2D image.

title: Parallel Projection via Zoom
one_liner: One way of generating images that can be described by parallel projection is to use the camera zoom.
content: ![(a) Close up picture without zoom. Note that near edges are larger than far edges, and parallel lines in 3D are not parallel. (b) Picture taken from far away using zoom resulting in an image that can be described by parallel projection.](figures/simplesystem/parallelProjection.png){#fig-parallelProjection width="100%"} One way of generating images that can be described by parallel projection is to use the camera zoom. If we increase the distance between the camera and the object while zooming, we can keep the same approximate image size of the objects, but with reduced perspective effects, as shown in @fig-parallelProjection (b). In such images, 3D parallel lines in the world are almost parallel in the image, although some weak perspective effects remain.
motivation_md: This technique allows photographers and researchers to achieve the geometric properties of parallel projection using standard perspective-based camera equipment.
recap_md: - Increase camera distance while zooming to maintain object size.\n- Reduces perspective effects so 3D parallel lines appear nearly parallel.

title: Hitchcock Zoom Effect
one_liner: Changing the zoom to compensate a moving camera can be used to create movie effects.
content: Changing the zoom to compensate for a moving camera can be used to create specific movie effects. This method was introduced by Alfred Hitchcock to create a sequence, centered on a subject, where the background appears to move away from or closer to the subject while the subject's size remains stable.
motivation_md: This effect creates a sense of unease or realization by distorting the background's perspective relative to a fixed foreground subject.
recap_md: - Changing the zoom to compensate for a moving camera creates cinematic effects.\n- It allows the background to move relative to a fixed subject.

title: Simple Projection Model
one_liner: The first step is to characterize how a point in world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ projects into the image plane.
content: The first step is to characterize how a point in world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ projects into the image plane. @fig-projection (a) shows the parameterization of the world and the camera coordinate systems. The camera center is inside the 3D plane $X=0$, and the horizontal axis of the camera ($x$) is parallel to the ground plane ($Y=0$). The camera is tilted so that the line connecting the origin of the world coordinates system and the image center is perpendicular to the image plane. The angle $\theta$ is the angle between this line and the $Z$-axis. The image is parameterized by coordinates $(x,y)$. ![A simple projection model. (a) World axis and camera plane. (b) Visualization of the world axis projected into the camera plane with parallel projection. The $Z$-axis is identical to the $Y$-axis up to a sign change and a scaling.](figures/simplesystem/projection2.png){#fig-projection width="100%"} In this simple projection model, the origin of the world coordinates projects on the origin of the image coordinates. Therefore, the world point $(0,0,0)$ projects into $(0,0)$. Assuming that pixels are square and the constant factor $\alpha=1$, the transformation between world coordinates and image coordinates can be written as follows: $$\begin{aligned} x &=& X \\ y &=& \cos(\theta) Y - \sin(\theta) Z \end{aligned}$$ With this particular parametrization, the world coordinates $Y$ and $Z$ are mixed after projection. From the camera, a point moving parallel to the $Z$-axis will be indistinguishable from a point moving parallel to the $Y$-axis.
motivation_md: Establishing a formal coordinate transformation allows for the precise calculation of where 3D objects will appear in a 2D image.
recap_md: - Maps world coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ to image coordinates $(x,y)$.\n- Uses the equations $x = X$ and $y = \cos(\theta) Y - \sin(\theta) Z$.

title: Image as a Surface

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: The image is an array of intensity values (color values) indexed by location.
content: The observed image is a function, $$\ell(x,y)$$ that takes as input location, $(x,y)$, and it outputs the intensity at that location. In this representation, the image is an array of intensity values (color values) indexed by location. ![Image as a surface. The vertical axis corresponds to image intensity. For clarity here, we have reversed the vertical axis. Dark values are shown higher than lighter values.](figures/simplesystem/imageAsSurface.jpg){#fig-imageAsSurface width="100%"}
motivation_md: Treating an image as a mathematical surface or function allows for the application of calculus and signal processing techniques to analyze visual data.
recap_md: - Represents an image as a function $\ell(x,y)$ of intensity values.\n- Intensity values are indexed by their spatial location.

title: Edges

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

one_liner: Edges denote image regions where there are strong changes of the image with respect to location.
content: Edges denote image regions where there are strong changes of the image with respect to location. Those variations can be due to a multitude of scene factors (e.g., occlusion boundaries, changes in surface orientation, changes in surface albedo, shadows). ![Edges denote image regions where there are sharp changes of the image intensities. Those variations can be due to a multitude of scene factors (e.g., occlusion boundaries, changes in surface orientation, changes in surface albedo, and shadows).](figures/simplesystem/edgeLabeling.png){#fig-edgeLabeling width="90%"}
motivation_md: Identifying edges is a fundamental step in computer vision for segmenting objects and understanding the geometry of a scene.
recap_md: - Regions with strong intensity changes relative to location.\n- Caused by factors like occlusion, orientation changes, or shadows.

title: Encoder and Decoder
one_liner: An autoencoder consists of an encoder $f$ that maps high-dimensional data to an embedding and a decoder $g$ that performs the inverse mapping.
content: An autoencoder $F$ consists of two parts, an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$, with $F = g \circ f$. The encoder, $f: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^M$, maps high-dimensional data $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ to a vector embedding $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^M$. Typically, the key property is that $M < N$, meaning the model performs dimensionality reduction, although autoencoders can also be constructed without this property by placing other explicit or implicit constraints on $\mathbf{z}$. The decoder, $g: \mathbb{R}^M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$, performs the inverse mapping to $f$, and ideally $g$ is exactly the inverse function $f^{-1}$.
motivation_md: Autoencoders are used to learn efficient, compressed representations of data. By forcing the model to reconstruct the input through a bottleneck, it learns to capture the most essential features of the data distribution.
recap_md: - The encoder $f$ maps high-dimensional input $\mathbf{x}$ to a lower-dimensional embedding $\mathbf{z}$.

title: Dimensionality Reduction
one_liner: Dimensionality reduction is the process of mapping data from a high-dimensional space to a lower-dimensional embedding space.
content: Dimensionality reduction is performed when $M < N$, where $N$ is the input dimension and $M$ is the embedding dimension. Although autoencoders are a primary tool for this, they can also be constructed without this property, in which case they do not perform dimensionality reduction but instead may place other explicit or implicit constraints on the embedding $\mathbf{z}$.
motivation_md: High-dimensional data is often redundant or noisy. Reducing its dimensionality helps identify the most important features, saves storage, and simplifies downstream computational tasks.
recap_md: - It occurs when the embedding dimension $M$ is strictly less than the input dimension $N$.

title: Reconstruction Loss
one_liner: Reconstruction loss measures the error between the original input and its reconstructed version, typically using squared error.
content: A typical choice for training autoencoders is the squared error reconstruction loss, defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\texttt{recon}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{x}) = \left\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2$.
motivation_md: To optimize an autoencoder, we need a mathematical objective that quantifies how well the model is preserving information. This loss provides the gradient necessary to update the encoder and decoder parameters.
recap_md: - It quantifies the difference between the original input $\mathbf{x}$ and the reconstructed output $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

title: Autoencoder Learning Problem
one_liner: The autoencoder learning problem seeks to find an encoder and decoder that minimize the expected reconstruction error of the data.
content: The learning problem is to find optimal functions $f^*$ and $g^*$ such that: $$f^*,g^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{f,g} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}} \left\lVert g(f(\mathbf{x})) - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2 $$ The idea is to find a lower dimensional representation of the data from which we are able to reconstruct the data. An autoencoder is fine with throwing away redundant features but aims to avoid losing information. The particular loss function determines what kind of information is preferred when a hard choice must be made. The $L_2$ loss decomposes as $\left\lVert g(f(\mathbf{x})) - \mathbf{x}\right\rVert_2^2 = \sqrt{\sum_i (g(f(\mathbf{x}))_i - x_i)^2}$, which cares about matching individual pixel intensities. Other loss functions can be used to penalize higher-order statistics, allowing for the reconstruction of edges, textures, and other perceptual structures. (see figure: A block diagram representing an $L_2$ autoencoder. On the left, input data {\mathbf{x}^{(i)}}_{i=1}^n$ enters a box labeled '$L_2$ autoencoder'. Inside the box, the objective function is defined...)
motivation_md: This formulation allows for unsupervised learning of features. By minimizing reconstruction error, the model is forced to discover the underlying structure of the data without requiring manual labels.
recap_md: - The objective is to minimize the expected squared distance between input $\mathbf{x}$ and reconstruction $g(f(\mathbf{x}))$.

title: Predictive Encodings
one_liner: Predictive representation learning uses a prediction task as a pretext to train an encoder that produces useful data embeddings.
content: In predictive representation learning, the goal is to use prediction as a way to train a useful representation. The data is first encoded into an embedding $\mathbf{z}$, which is then mapped to a target prediction. This composition of functions can be trained with a prediction task to yield a good data encoder. The prediction task serves as a pretext task for learning good representations. Examples include predicting future frames in a video, the next pixel in an image, or an image's semantic class. While the latter is identical to training a classifier, the goal is to obtain a good image encoding rather than the classifier itself. (see figure: Examples of different pretext tasks.)
motivation_md: Predictive tasks allow models to learn from the inherent structure of data (like temporal or spatial context) without needing explicit human-provided labels for every feature we want the model to learn.
recap_md: - It trains an encoder by solving a prediction task where the embedding $\mathbf{z}$ is an intermediate step.

title: Pretext Task
one_liner: A pretext task is a prediction problem designed to induce good data representations rather than to be useful in its own right.
content: A pretext task is a prediction task used to train a data encoder to produce useful embeddings $\mathbf{z}$. This setup resembles supervised learning, but it is distinct because we do not have exemplar output representations for the target task. Instead, the supervision is provided by the pretext task itself, which we hope induces representations that are useful for other downstream applications.
motivation_md: Pretext tasks solve the problem of learning from unlabeled data by creating 'synthetic' supervised problems based on the data's own internal structure.
recap_md: - It is a proxy task used to learn an encoder $f$ that produces meaningful embeddings $\mathbf{z}$.

title: Predictive Coding
one_liner: Predictive coding is the theory that the brain transmits only the difference between its internal predictions and actual sensory signals.
content: Predictive coding is a theory in neuroscience stating that the sensory cortex only transmits the difference between its predictions and the actual observed signal. While predictive representation learning focuses on learning the representation that makes good predictions, predictive coding focuses on using such a representation to compress signals by only transmitting the 'surprises' or prediction errors.
motivation_md: This concept explains how biological systems can be highly efficient by ignoring expected information and focusing neural resources on novel or unexpected stimuli.
recap_md: - It posits that the brain transmits the error (surprise) between predictions and observations.

title: Predictive Representation Learning Problem
one_liner: The predictive learning problem formally defines training an encoder and predictor to minimize the distance between a target and its prediction from an embedding.
content: Formally, let $\mathbf{y}$ be the prediction target and $D$ be a distance function, such as $L_2$. Predictive representation learning involves training an encoder $f$ and a predictor $g$ to minimize the distance between the target and the prediction. [FIGURE:4b90715c8d8cd84b | A flow diagram illustrating predictive representation learning. On the left, input data is represented as a set {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^n. An arrow points into a central box labeled 'Predictive...] Unlike autoencoders, there is no standard setting for the relative dimensionalities of the input ($N$), embedding ($M$), and target ($K$); these depend on the specific task, such as image classification where $N$ is large and $K$ is the number of classes.
motivation_md: Formalizing the problem allows for the application of standard optimization techniques to learn embeddings that are specifically tuned to be predictive of certain targets.
recap_md: - The objective is to minimize the distance $D$ between the target $\mathbf{y}$ and the prediction $g(f(\mathbf{x}))$.

title: Incremental-mode SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Incremental-mode SFM minimizes reprojection error by starting with a pair of images and sequentially adding new images to estimate scene structure and camera parameters.
content: Incremental-mode SFM is a standard approach to minimize reprojection error by starting with only a pair of images. Matches between those two images are used to compute the fundamental and essential matrices, while accounting for outliers using RANSAC. An initial 3D reconstruction of the matched points is then computed using triangulation. Subsequently, another image is added and the process is repeated until all images have been incorporated, resulting in approximated camera poses and 3D locations for a subset of detected keypoints. Online or incremental-mode SFM approaches attempt to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as and when a new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is run periodically whenever a sufficient number of points have been newly added. This approach is often used in applications where all images are not available a priori or where real-time performance is desired.
motivation_md: This approach is designed for scenarios where all images are not available at the start or where real-time performance is desired, allowing for the estimation of scene structure and camera parameters as new data arrives.
recap_md: - It starts with a pair of images to compute initial matrices and 3D points via triangulation.

title: Robust Cost Function

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: A robust cost function, such as the Huber kernel, is used to rewrite the reprojection error loss to handle outliers and refine camera intrinsics.
content: In Structure from Motion, the reprojection error loss is usually rewritten using a robust cost function, with the Huber kernel being a typical choice. This formulation is also used to refine camera intrinsics if needed.
motivation_md: Standard least-squares loss is sensitive to outliers; robust cost functions like the Huber kernel reduce the influence of outliers, such as bad matches, on the final reconstruction.
recap_md: - It is used to rewrite the reprojection error loss to make it more resilient to outliers.

title: Batch-mode SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Batch-mode SFM computes scene structure after processing all input images simultaneously, running bundle adjustment once across all cameras and 3D points.
content: Batch-mode SFM, also known as offline SFM, computes the scene structure after processing all input images. In this mode, bundle adjustment only needs to be run once, albeit across a potentially large number of cameras and 3D points. This mode leverages images from all available viewpoints right from the outset. However, if new images are added, the entire SFM pipeline needs to be rerun.
motivation_md: Batch-mode SFM is used when all images are available upfront, allowing the system to leverage global information from all viewpoints simultaneously for a potentially more consistent reconstruction.
recap_md: - It processes all images at once and typically runs bundle adjustment only a single time.

title: Dense SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Dense SFM computes 3D reconstructions for nearly every image pixel by optimizing photometric error, resulting in rich models useful for navigation and mixed reality.
content: In dense SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) of the image pixels. The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, making them useful in applications like robot navigation or mixed reality. Dense SFM approaches usually optimize photometric error—the difference in grayscale or RGB intensities of corresponding pixels across images—rather than the 3D reprojection error used in point feature-based methods. However, these dense techniques tend to be much slower than sparse SFM methods and often require more assumptions, such as the scene being Lambertian or the images having a substantially smaller baseline motion.
motivation_md: While sparse SFM provides a skeleton of a scene, dense SFM provides a complete surface reconstruction necessary for applications like robot navigation and mixed reality where knowing the location of every point is critical.
recap_md: - It reconstructs almost every pixel in an image rather than just sparse keypoints.

title: Photometric Error

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

one_liner: Photometric error is the difference in grayscale or RGB intensities between corresponding pixels across different images.
content: Photometric error is the difference in grayscale or red-green-blue (RGB) intensities of corresponding pixels across images. Dense SFM approaches usually optimize this error, in contrast to point feature-based methods that minimize a 3D reprojection error.
motivation_md: Photometric error provides a way to compare images directly based on pixel values, which is essential for dense reconstruction where discrete features may be hard to track.
recap_md: - It measures the difference in color or intensity between corresponding pixels in multiple images.

title: Radiance Field
one_liner: A radiance field is a function that maps scene coordinates and viewing angles to color and volumetric density, modeling the scene as a cloud of particles.
content: A radiance field is a representation of part of the plenoptic function, based on the idea that the optical content of a scene can be modeled as a cloud of colorful particles with different levels of transparency. Such a representation can be rendered into images using volume rendering. A radiance field $L$ is defined as a mapping from the coordinates in a scene to color and density (transparency) values. The coordinates can be 2D ($X,Y$) or 3D ($X,Y,Z$) and may also contain angular dimensions ($\psi$ and $\phi$) representing the viewing angle. Representing color using $r,g,b$ values and density with a scalar $\sigma$, the radiance field is the function: $$\begin{aligned} L: X,Y,Z,\psi,\phi \rightarrow r,g,b,\sigma \quad\quad\triangleleft \quad\text{radiance field} \end{aligned}$$ The angular coordinates allow an object's color to vary depending on the viewing angle, which is necessary for shiny surfaces. The subcomponents $L^c$ and $L^\sigma$ denote the outputs for color and density respectively: $$\begin{aligned} L^c&: X,Y,Z,\psi,\phi \rightarrow r,g,b\\ L^{\sigma}&: X,Y,Z,\psi,\phi \rightarrow\sigma \end{aligned}$$
motivation_md: Radiance fields allow for a continuous, differentiable representation of a scene that can capture complex lighting and geometry, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis through volume rendering.
recap_md: - It maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to RGB color and volumetric density.

title: Seeing in Flatland
one_liner: In a 2D Flatland world, radiance fields map 2D coordinates to color and density, which can be rendered into 1D images.
content: Radiance fields can be studied in a 2D world for simplicity, similar to the one in the book *Flatland* where characters are simple shapes on a 2D plane. (see figure: The scene we are modeling. The circle of black triangles on the left are the cameras. The 1D images they see are shown on the right. These images are denoted as {\ oldsymbol\ell^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N.) In this world, inhabitants see one-dimensional (1D) renderings of the 2D world. The cameras (black triangles) produce the 1D photos seen on the right of the figure, showing the scene from different angles. A radiance field for this scene maps each possible input coordinate $(X,Y)$ to a corresponding output color $L^c$ and density $L^{\sigma}$. (see figure: How a radiance field maps coordinates to colors/densities. (left) Input (X,Y) coordinates, visualized with X-values in the green channel and Y-values in the blue channel. (right) Radiance field...)
motivation_md: Using a 2D Flatland analogy simplifies the visualization and mathematical complexity of radiance fields, making the core concepts of coordinate mapping and rendering easier to understand before moving to 3D.
recap_md: - Flatland serves as a 2D simplification where radiance fields map (X, Y) to color and density.

title: Vector Fields
one_liner: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector of values to each position in a spatial domain.
content: Radiance fields are an example of vector fields, which are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, a vector field might be represented as $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X, Y,$ and $Z$ are coordinates and $v_1, v_2$ are specific values. Field-based representations are an important method for representing scenes broadly.
motivation_md: Vector fields provide a general mathematical framework for representing continuous properties across space, which is essential for modeling physical phenomena and scene representations like radiance fields.
recap_md: - A vector field maps spatial coordinates to a vector of one or more values.
